Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on suppliers to Russia’s defense industry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:02:32 EEST
23:02:32 KST

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) to impose sanctions on Russian entities and individuals. These parties are involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles or supply equipment and components to Russian defense industry enterprises for use in military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, and drones.
Relevant decrees, Nos. 1058/2024 and 1059/2024, are dated October 24 and have been published on the head of state’s official website.
The first sanction list includes 51 individuals and 44 legal entities involved in the manufacture of ballistic missiles—weapons that the Russian Federation uses to attack critical and civilian infrastructure, as well as to shell Ukrainian cities and communities. These entities produce and supply raw materials, equipment, and tools used to create long-range strike systems, including the Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal.
The sanction package specifically targets Russian enterprises that manufacture weaponry, components, and related software, as well as the executives of these companies.
All individuals subject to these sanctions are citizens of the Russian Federation. Of the 44 entities on the first list, 42 are registered in the Russian Federation, while two are registered in the People's Republic of China.
Additionally, sanctions have been imposed on 32 Russian citizens and 35 Russian companies that are part of the production and supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, tools, components, electronics, and raw materials intended for entities that serve Russia’s defense-industrial complex.
Sanctions have also been imposed on enterprises belonging to the Russian industrial group Rusal—entities that are significant to the aggressor state and involved in the production of military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, drones, and other military hardware.
"We are systematically identifying enterprises involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles and other weaponry, and applying sanctions against them. We are also working to extend these sanctions to other jurisdictions. Taken together, these measures should significantly weaken the capacity of the Russian military-industrial complex to manufacture weapons," noted Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Advisor and Presidential Commissioner for Sanction Policy.

China’s J-20 stealth jet designers plan to put powerful radar into aircraft wing
Military aircraft designers propose a wing-mounted early-warning radar to expand coverage during air combat
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Chao Kongin Beijing
Fighter jets typically house their main radars behind a radome in the nose, while conventional airborne early-warning aircraft often carry large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage.
Although aircraft wings offer a large surface area, their relatively thin cross-sections leave limited internal space for radar equipment.
Top Chinese military aircraft designers have now proposed a revolutionary method to integrate large antenna arrays into aircraft wings, using flight manoeuvres and coordinated formations of unmanned aircraft to expand radar coverage.
The design was outlined in a study published online on October 10 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Measurement & Control Technology, which presented wing-mounted radar as a new approach to building multifunctional, high-performance airborne early-warning systems.

France arrests 135 amid protests, extends curfews in various cities as police use tear gas in Lyon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:59:15 UTC
22:59:15 KST

Melike Pala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
French authorities reported 135 arrests nationwide Saturday as police fired tear gas in Lyon and extended nighttime curfews for unaccompanied minors in several northern cities, broadcaster BFMTV reported.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said authorities had made 135 arrests across the country as of 1 pm local time (1100GMT).
The nighttime curfew, initially introduced in Lille, Denain, Douai and Wattignies, was extended until Monday morning and expanded to Marly and Valenciennes, according to a prefectural decree.
The restrictions apply to designated areas, including large parts of central Lille, and prohibit unaccompanied minors from being outdoors between 8 pm local time (1800GMT) and 6 am.
In Lyon, police fired tear gas to disperse a gathering of around 150 people near Lyon 3 University, BFMTV reported.
The gathering, composed mainly of young people, lasted around 20 minutes before police dispersed participants in what authorities described as an unauthorized march.
Authorities also banned demonstrations in several parts of Lyon, citing concerns about further unrest.
In Grenoble, individuals attempting to block the A480 motorway caused a collision between two vehicles, leaving two people with minor injuries, according to the broadcaster.
Meanwhile, police in Paris carried out 635 security checks aimed at preventing potential disturbances.
Authorities said officers seized several items, including a knife, an angle grinder and protective equipment such as filtered masks and diving goggles.
Authorities in Montpellier, Nancy, Caen and Annecy also rejected requests to hold demonstrations.
In Nice, nearly 10 people had been arrested by midday for allegedly carrying knuckle-dusters and protective equipment, according to BFMTV.

Israel has forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said.

The Palestinian Authority criticised the Israeli actions as a "collective punishment", calling for international pressure on Israel to protect Palestinians.
"The growing threats to expand the scope of forced displacement and destruction require urgent international action that goes beyond condemnation to adopt tangible and deterrent measures," the PA’s foreign ministry said in a statement following the events.

‘An attempt to win votes from illegal settlers’

"Netanyahu and the radical ministers in his government are trying to win as many votes as possible from the settlers," he said.
Amnesty International warned that upcoming elections must not deflect attention from Israel’s international crimes, urging continued scrutiny and accountability.
Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries.
Across the occupied West Bank, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement.

Starlink Is Back at 400+ Km/h as Ukraine Breaks Through Speed Restrictions After High-Level Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:56:00 UTC
22:56:00 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Starlink Is Back at 400+ Km/h as Ukraine Breaks Through Speed Restrictions After High-Level Talks
After days of restrictions that disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, Starlink and Starshield are back at high speeds following direct talks at the highest political level, Ukraine’s defense minister says.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has confirmed that Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems are once again operating at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour, restoring connectivity critical to Ukrainian military operations, including drones, logistics, and battlefield communications.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Responding to journalists’ questions on October 24, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said the ministry’s monitoring systems had recorded the restoration of high-speed connectivity.
“The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording the restoration of Starlink and Starshield connectivity at high speeds. We are registering speeds exceeding 400 km/h, with stable connections,” Khmara said.
The minister attributed the development to direct negotiations and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s efforts at the highest political level.
“This is another example of how direct dialogue and the President of Ukraine’s persistent position at the highest level deliver results. Above all, this result is important for our front line, our military personnel, drone operations, logistics, and communications,” Khmara said.
He added that the Ministry of Defense would continue monitoring and documenting the performance of Starlink and Starshield systems.The announcement marks a significant change from the situation reported just a day earlier.
On October 23, Zelenskyy said Starlink and Starshield speed restrictions remained in place, despite earlier claims that connectivity had been restored.
The restrictions were first reported overnight on October 14, when SpaceX introduced a speed limit of approximately 160 km/h for Starshield terminals operating in motion, without advance warning to Ukrainian forces.
In some cases, Ukrainian units reported losing connectivity at even lower speeds. The disruptions affected interceptor drones, medium-range strike missions, reconnaissance, and frontline logistics.
On October 16, Zelenskyy said the restrictions had prevented Ukrainian forces from intercepting some Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which can travel at speeds exceeding 400 km/h.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,980 Troops, 413 Vehicles, and 64 Artillery Systems in One Day

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,980 Troops, 413 Vehicles, and 64 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,980 troops and hundreds of pieces of military equipment over the past 24 hours, bringing its total personnel losses since the start of the full-scale invasion to approximately 1,576,600, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 24.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost five tanks and three armored combat vehicles, bringing cumulative losses in those categories to 12,444 and 25,600, respectively.
Another 64 artillery systems were added to the tally, raising the total to 51,565, while two multiple-launch rocket systems and two air defense systems brought those figures to 2,232 and 1,722, respectively.
Ukraine also reported eight ground robotic systems lost, bringing the cumulative total to 3,011. Another 1,855 operational-tactical UAVs were recorded, pushing estimated losses in that category to 579,064.
Russia’s aviation losses remained unchanged at 449 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while cruise missile losses stayed at 5,138. Naval losses remained at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 413 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the past day, bringing cumulative losses to 166,501. One additional piece of special equipment raised that total to 4,852.
Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 181 times across the front during the latest reporting period, with particularly intense fighting in the Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk sectors, where Ukrainian forces recorded 23 and 19 Russian attacks, respectively.
Earlier, on October 23, a missile strike reportedly hit Russia’s Proton defense electronics plant in Orel, which manufactures components used in Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.

Civic activist and UAnimals founder Todorchuk appointed to head AFU Main Directorate for Communications
Ukraine

16:54:58 EEST
22:54:58 KST

Oleksandr Todorchuk, Ukrainian entrepreneur, civic activist, founder of the animal welfare organization UAnimals, co-founder of the communications agency Gres Todorchuk, and current service member, has announced his appointment as head of the Main Directorate for Communications of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
"I have joined the General Staff team, taking charge of the Main Directorate for Communications of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. It is a great responsibility and a significant challenge... I will put forth my best efforts to strengthen this area, as I genuinely believe in the importance of communications during wartime," Todorchuk wrote on Facebook on Saturday, thanking the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapaty, for the trust placed in him.
He noted that he is currently getting to know the team and familiarizing himself with the scope of work, while also seeking individuals to join the directorate’s team. "It will be challenging, fast-paced, and certainly interesting. Let us combine our knowledge and experience where they are truly needed today and can be of service to the country," Todorchuk wrote.
Born in 1988, Todorchuk is a law graduate of Kyiv International University. In 2010, he co-founded the communications agency Gres Todorchuk, which specializes in communications, cultural, social, and educational projects, together with Yaroslava Gres. In 2016, he established UAnimals, an organization that began its work by campaigning against the exploitation of animals in the entertainment industry. He was mobilized into the Armed Forces of Ukraine in March 2022.
Earlier, the Main Directorate of Communications of the Armed Forces of Ukraine was headed by Colonel Bohdan Mykolaiovych Senyk, who had led the Armed Forces’ Public Relations Directorate since 2016.

Ukraine begins process of joining OECD Nuclear Energy Agency – Shmyhal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

Ukraine begins process of joining OECD Nuclear Energy Agency – Shmyhal
According to Ukrinform, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal reported this on Telegram.
He said that "the next step will be an agency assessment mission to analyze Ukraine's nuclear sector, our technical capabilities, as well as our institutional and legal framework. Based on the mission's findings and subsequent decisions by member states, Ukraine may become the next NEA member."
"I had the honor of addressing the meeting's participants and presenting Ukraine's vision for further cooperation with the agency. I am grateful to OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann and NEA Director-General William Magwood for their support for Ukraine and assistance in advancing our path toward membership," Shmyhal said.
He stressed that "joining the NEA is an important step toward full OECD membership, European integration and the implementation of the highest nuclear safety standards. Future membership will enable Ukraine to participate more actively in the work of expert committees and working groups, deepen scientific and technical cooperation, and develop research and professional training."
"At the same time, Ukraine is ready to make its own contribution to the agency's work. We have a strong nuclear energy sector, developed infrastructure, experienced engineers and scientists, and extensive expertise in the operation and modernization of nuclear power plants, nuclear safety, radioactive waste management and the development of advanced technologies. We also have unique experience in operating a nuclear energy system during a full-scale war. This experience could benefit the international community in matters of emergency preparedness and risk management. Ukraine is ready to undergo the necessary assessment process, fulfill its obligations, and become an active and responsible member of the NEA community," Shmyhal said.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukraine is applying for membership in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development's Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA).
The Nuclear Energy Agency is an intergovernmental agency established within the framework of the OECD.
The NEA's mission is to assist its member countries in maintaining and further developing, through international cooperation, the scientific, technological and legal bases required for the safe, environmentally sound and economical use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.

Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:51:08 UTC
22:51:08 KST

Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
Sudan is suffering from a cost-of-living crisis affecting millions across the country.
Azhari Mohamed drives his minibus and eight passengers seven times a day from the Shagar neighbourhood in the Port of Sudan to the city centre and back again.
But despite the long hours – working from 6am to 9pm – fuel shortages in the city have made it difficult for the 60-year-old to make a living.
Azhari’s minibus uses three gallons (11 litres) of petrol a day, costing him about 105,000 Sudanese pounds ($11.30 a day, according to Sudan’s parallel-market exchange rate). With fuel increasingly difficult to obtain, he now spends two days on the road and a third day queuing for fuel.
He can spend more than five hours waiting in line when he needs to fill the tank of his minibus and often finds petrol has run out before his turn comes. When that happens, he goes to the back of the queue at another petrol station hoping to fill up there.
The shortages have led to price rises with a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol now costing 40,000 Sudanese pounds ($4.30) in Gazira State, south of Khartoum, while in Port Sudan it is 35,000 pounds ($3.80) a gallon.
“We can no longer work because of the fuel shortages. The transport fares are no longer enough to cover the cost of running the vehicle and our household expenses,” Azhari told Al Jazeera.
He says the long hours spent queueing for petrol is time he could spend earning money to support his family.
“I spend long hours of the day waiting to refuel, so I have to work extra hours at night to make up for the time I lose during the day,” he said. “My livelihood depends on what I earn each day.”
After subtracting his vehicle’s operating costs, Azhari has just 50,000 Sudanese pounds ($5.40) left a day, barely enough to cover the needs of his family, which includes his wife and daughter who is at university and needs support for her tuition fees and daily expenses.
“We just need fuel to be available so we can work,” he said. “If fuel is available, we will not face this obstacle.”
Due to the crisis, Sudan’s Transport Chambers Union, which regulates public and private transport services, this month raised intercity bus fares by 40% and minibus fares by 30%.
Aziza Ibrahim from the Umm al-Qura neighbourhood of Port Sudan, works as a cleaner to support her four children. Just getting to work by bus has become a huge financial burden for the 38-year-old, who has cut back her work days to three times a week due to the high travel costs.
Before the war, a journey from her home to the main transport station in the city centre cost 700 Sudanese pounds ($0.08) per passenger. Fares have since risen to 2,500 pounds ($0.27) on some routes, while others charge 2,000 pounds ($0.22).
“I go to work three days a week to reduce transport costs. I need 11,000 pounds ($1.18) a day for the round trip between my home and workplace,” she told Al Jazeera.
Transport costs now consume nearly half of Aziza’s monthly salary of 400,000 pounds ($43), while costly treatment for her diabetes is another financial burden.
“Sometimes I have to borrow money just to be able to go to work. I repay it at the beginning of the month when I receive my salary, which is barely enough to cover my family’s needs,” she told Al Jazeera.
According to the United Nations Development Programme, the war has pushed average incomes in Sudan back to levels last seen in the 1990s.
That is partly due to the effects of the civil war on Sudan’s oil sector. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) began on April 15, 2023.
Last year, the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum estimated war-related losses at $20 billion. The World Bank has reported that attacks on the Balila oil field disrupted supplies to the Khartoum refinery, which previously met about 60% of the country’s demand for petrol and liquefied petroleum gas.
War damage has seen a sharp decrease in oil production, leaving Sudan reliant on imports amid the global fuel crisis that has pushed up prices of gas, petrol and diesel, among other commodities.
Economic analyst Sidi Ohaj said that the government requirements for petroleum importers have also contributed to the shortages. They include a stipulation that importers must deposit 200kg of gold in the Central Bank and own fuel storage facilities in order to operate in Sudan. Some importers have been unable to meet those requirements, forcing them out of the market which reduces supply.
“One of the causes of the current crisis is the government’s decision to regulate the operations of petroleum import companies,” Sidi told Al Jazeera. “Some companies did not meet the requirements, which led to their exit from the market. This reduced supply relative to demand.”
The government needs to urgently ease import procedures to increase domestic supplies, he said, with shortages affecting the wider economy.
But as the war between the United States and Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets, there is little hope the situation will improve any time soon.
“The continuation of the war [in Sudan], particularly drone attacks that threaten infrastructure across Sudan, is one of the main challenges facing the oil sector,” Sidi told Al Jazeera.
Prices have also risen due to the energy crisis, impacting the purchasing power of citizens and profits of businesses.
Ahmed al-Haj is a local trader in Omdurman market who sells skincare products, such as petroleum jelly, which he packages himself . He said high energy prices are costing almost all areas of his business.
“The raw materials for the products I sell are imported. Higher diesel and petrol prices have increased the cost of transporting a tonne of goods by 30 to 50 percent,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera.
“That increase is then reflected in the price of the products.”
When electricity cuts force him to use a fuel-powered generator for heating or packaging, the additional fuel costs add to his daily bills.
Deliveries within Omdurman, which previously cost 5,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.70) now cost between 10,000 and 12,000 pounds ($1.07 and $1.29). Reaching customers in other states has become impossible due to the high transport costs.
“Transport and distribution workers have also reduced the number of trips they make, leading to goods piling up at traders’ premises,” he added.

Aamir Latif

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China's border city of Dandong on Saturday, accompanied by Beijing's top political advisor, state media reported.
Kim reportedly reached Dandong via the New Yalu River Bridge connecting North Korea and China.
China's top political advisor Wang Huning accompanied Kim during his visit to Dandong, which is located in northeast China's Liaoning province, Beijing-based Xinhua News reported.
Wang, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, conveyed President Xi Jinping's "cordial greetings and best wishes" to Kim.
No further details about Kim's visit and meetings with Chinese officials were provided.
The visit comes a day before the anniversary of China's entry into the 1950-1953 Korean War.
Kim was expected to return to North Korea after Saturday's visit, Seoul-based Yonhap News reported.
China and North Korea opened the 3-kilometer (2-mile) New Yalu River Bridge this month after a long delay, aiming to revive trade after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions.
Kim's last visited China in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Xi.

The head of Hebron's municipality said an additional 1,300 may also be forced to leave.
The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack killed two Israeli soldiers.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the military would launch a large-scale operation after the soldiers were killed when two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at a military checkpoint near the city. The Israeli military said the gunmen were shot dead.

Israeli-born oligarch behind Russia's $14 billion sanctions-evading cash network linked to Iran, Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:41:54 UTC
22:41:54 KST

As Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu calls for Israel to prepare an economy capable of operating around international sanctions, one Israeli citizen has already become a central figure in Russia's efforts to circumvent Western financial restrictions. Ilan Shor, a Moldovan oligarch born in Israel who holds Israeli citizenship, is behind a vast Russian payment network that has processed billions of dollars since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. American authorities now accuse that network of serving not only Russia but also Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Hamas. 
Four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin has developed an array of mechanisms to keep international trade and financial transactions moving despite Western sanctions. One of the most significant is A7, an international payments company established in 2024 by Shor, 39. He holds a 51% stake in the company, while the remaining 49% belongs to Promsvyazbank, or PSB, a Russian state-owned bank itself subject to extensive international sanctions.
An investigation published this week by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), working with independent Russian media outlet Proekt, revealed the extraordinary scale of A7's operations. Between November 2024 and July 2025, the company processed at least 283 tons of Russian banknotes, worth more than $14 billion. Internal documents showed how the company used cash brokers, financial intermediaries and companies registered outside Russia to help businesses complete payments that conventional banking channels had made increasingly difficult. 
How billions in Russian cash reach foreign suppliers
At the heart of the operation is Moscow's Sadovod Market, a sprawling wholesale and retail complex in the southeastern part of the Russian capital. According to the investigation, brokers operating there receive payment instructions from Russian businesses seeking to purchase goods overseas, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Rather than transferring money directly through Russian banks, clients hand over large quantities of rubles in cash.
The brokers place the banknotes in numbered bags, which are transported to an A7 cash-processing center. There, teams of cashiers count the money and record the amounts, bag numbers and payment instructions. The cash is then delivered to PSB, which deposits the funds into A7 accounts. Companies registered outside Russia subsequently arrange payments to foreign recipients, often through intermediaries in Kyrgyzstan, Hong Kong and other jurisdictions. The result, investigators found, is that the Chinese banks receiving the transfers may have no visibility into the original Russian source of the money.
The scale of the transactions is substantial. A payment register from late 2024 contained approximately 2,300 proposed or documented transfers linked to brokers at Sadovod, most intended for recipients in mainland China or Hong Kong. Many were routed through accounts belonging to a Kyrgyz state-owned trading company. A7 has also promoted the speed of its system, announcing in December 2025 that it had completed a transfer to China in just one hour and 40 minutes. 
The Kremlin has taken a direct interest in the project. During a video conference with President Vladimir Putin in September 2025, Shor presented A7's achievements and plans for expansion. He reported that the platform was processing approximately 1,500 to 2,000 transactions daily and described payment volumes running into trillions of rubles. The company also outlined plans to expand its operations in Asia, where it said more than half of its payments were being directed. These figures were company claims and have not all been independently verified.
US sanctions and alleged connections to Iran and Hamas
On October 1, the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions on the A7 network, designating it a significant transnational criminal organization. The department described A7 as a shadow banking operation that uses money-laundering techniques to disguise illicit payments as legitimate commercial transactions and move enormous sums across borders in violation of sanctions and other laws.
The American allegations extend far beyond Russian trade. According to the Treasury Department, A7 has provided financial support to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Iranian-backed organizations, including Hamas. U.S. authorities also linked the network to Nobitex, Iran's largest digital asset exchange, sanctioned by Washington in June 2026, and to transactions associated with North Korean cryptocurrency exchange hacks and other illicit activity.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the action was intended to dismantle financial infrastructure that enables Iran and other U.S. adversaries to evade sanctions and move illicit funds. A7 has rejected the American allegations of wrongdoing, saying it operates compliance procedures and was established to facilitate payments for Russian businesses facing what it considers illegitimate restrictions. The company's denials include the allegations concerning Iran and terrorist organizations. 
From Israel to the Kremlin's protection
Shor's personal history is as unusual as the financial operation he now oversees. Born in Tel Aviv in 1987 to a family originally from Moldova, he moved with his parents to Chisinau during the 1990s. His father, Miron Shor, established a successful duty-free retail business, which Ilan joined as a young man. After his father's death, he took control of the family enterprise and expanded into other sectors, building a business empire before entering Moldovan politics.
His political career was overshadowed by one of Moldova's largest financial scandals. In 2017, Shor was convicted in connection with the theft of approximately $1 billion from the country's banking system, a case widely known in Moldova as the "theft of the century." Initially sentenced to seven and a half years in prison, he remained free during his appeal and fled to Israel in 2019. In April 2023, a Moldovan appeals court increased his prison sentence to 15 years for fraud and money laundering. His political party was subsequently banned. Shor has maintained that he was the victim of political persecution by Moldova's pro-Western authorities. 
After spending several years in Israel, Shor relocated to Russia, where he emerged as an outspoken supporter of Putin and increasingly appeared in Kremlin-aligned media. Despite remaining wanted by Moldova, he has continued to conduct major business operations from Russia under the protection of the country's political establishment. His role in A7 has made him a prominent figure in Moscow's efforts to maintain international financial connections despite Western restrictions.
The revelations come as Netanyahu warns that Israel could eventually face economic and banking sanctions of its own and has instructed advisers to examine alternative financial arrangements, including blockchain technology and cryptocurrencies. Netanyahu has not proposed adopting A7's methods, and his comments concerned preparations for possible future restrictions, rather than sanctions already imposed on Israel's banking system. Nevertheless, Shor's story illustrates both the scale that sanctions-resistant payment networks can reach and the serious legal and security consequences they can face when their activities attract international scrutiny.

'We urge Indian businesses to continue and expand trade with Tehran': Envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:40:46 UTC
22:40:46 KST

NEW DELHI: With US sanctions squeezing Indian firms trading in Iranian petroleum and petrochemicals, Tehran has a message for Indian businesses: "Both sides are determined to strengthen economic relations and to find practical ways to ensure the continuation of bilateral trade."Iran's ambassador to India, Mohammad Fathali, told TOI that sanctions and payment disruptions had dented trade and "the prices of some goods in Iran have increased for common people," but ruled out "essential shortages,” including Indian basmati rice, a major Indian export to Iran, saying Tehran had prepared for disruptions and had multiple import channels. “We do not expect these challenges to lead to shortages of essential goods, including Indian basmati rice,” Fathalisaid, adding that price rises reflected wider economic pressures rather than supply shortages.Amid US sanctions on Indian firms over Iranian petroleum trade,Iran’s ambassador to India urged Indian businesses to continue and expand trade with Tehran, acknowledging that sanctions and payment disruptions had reduced bilateral trade “to some extent”.Iran’s ambassador also pitched the country’s energy market to Indian firms, saying Tehran was ready to engage companies interested in the sector. “Any company that wishes to operate and trade in Iran’s energy market can benefit from the opportunities available in this market,” Fathali said.
Citing room to expand cooperation in energy, agriculture and essential goods, he said: "We welcome all Indian companies to expand their trade cooperation with Iran."Iran is among the biggest buyers of Indian basmati as well as tea outside India, but he said there is no need to fear “essential shortages”, as Iran had prepared for disruptions and supplies still move through regular channels.After 47 years under sanctions, Iran had learnt to blunt their impact, he said, pointing to advances in nanotechnology, biotechnology and other fields.Asked whether concrete measures were being discussed to protect bilateral trade from US sanctions, Fathali said communication with Indian partners was continuing. “Selecting and implementing such measures requires expert discussions and the necessary coordination between the relevant parties,” he said, adding that both sides were determined to find practical ways to sustain trade.Pointing to Iran’s experience under sanctions, Fathali said its strategic location and 15 neighbouring countries offered opportunities to diversify trade and economic partnerships. He said Tehran would continue seeking practical solutions to protect its economic interests and maintain mutually beneficial trade relations."There are various ways to support bilateral trade in the face of challenges arising from sanctions… Options are reviewed and pursued in line with the existing circumstances and available capacities.”
The govt, he added, was working to protect livelihoods, sustain production and ensure basic supplies: "The people of Iran…weathered many storms and crises throughout its history…deserve a better life, along with economic stability and prosperity."On Chabahar port, whose US sanctions waiver for Indian operations expired on April 26, Fathali reaffirmed Tehran’s commitment to developing the strategic gateway, which gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia. Iran also welcomed investment from beyond India, saying it was open to participation by “any country interested in contributing to the development” of the port.On renewed talks with Washington, he said Tehran had never shied away from dialogue, but trust remained shattered: "On all three occasions when we entered into negotiations with the United States, war followed... Iran seeks negotiations to achieve a genuine result, not to provide another opportunity for pressure to be imposed on the country."

Sikorski: Musk Should Fly to Mars, Avoid Mixing Business and Politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has said he hopes Elon Musk “flies to Mars”, warning the US-based tech entrepreneur against mixing business with politics.
Sikorski, who has a history of public online spats with Musk, made the comments on Friday during a conference in the city of Łódź in central Poland, where he was asked about Europe’s dependence on US technology, including the satellite system owned by Musk.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sikorski said: “Mixing business with politics usually ends badly, especially when we talk about Elon Musk… I wish Musk well, he’s a great inventor and I hope he will fly to Mars one day.”
Starlink is an invaluable tool in Ukraine’s defense against Russian attacks, but has been subject to controversy amid accusations of intentional drops in service coverage over the course of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Sikorski accused Musk of trying to “interfere in the politics of different countries”, after Ukrainian officials earlier this month said services from Starshield – the military version of Starlink – were drastically limited, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warning that “people will die” as a result.
The reduction in Starlink connectivity came amid a deterioration in Kyiv-Washington relations following the White House’s announcement earlier this month that Russia would be allowed to sell diesel to global markets.
US Senators Threaten Nomination Block Over Ukraine Starlink Curbs
Poland pays around $50 million annually for Starlink services used in Ukraine as part of Warsaw’s support for Kyiv in defending against Moscow’s aggression.
Sikorski said that companies in Europe are already developing alternatives to Starlink.
Europe holds the cards
On Thursday, Finland-based tech firms ICEYE and Nokia announced that they have joined forces to help Ukraine develop its own satellite communications system in partnership with Ukraine’s defense ministry.
Amid a renewed diplomatic drive by Washington to broker an end to Russia’s war in Ukraine after months of stalled negotiations, Sikorski highlighted what he said was Europe’s important role in finding a resolution to the conflict.
“Europe holds the cards”, Sikorski said, adding that Europe finances the Ukrainian state, continues to hold Russian assets that were frozen over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine and delivers weapons to Kyiv to aid in its defense.
“[Russia] has realized that this cannot be resolved solely by an agreement with the US, and that Europe is in the game,” Sikorski added.

Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:39:26 UTC
22:39:26 KST

Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?
Authorities are investigating the rare attack on a Christian church; the assailants remain unidentified and at large.
Security forces in Jordan are searching for three gunmen who opened fire at a church in Karak governorate on Friday, killing eight people and injuring dozens more, according to Jordan’s Ministry of Health.
King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties”, as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to terrorist attacks.
Authorities are calling this rare attack on a Christian place of worship an act of terror, with the perpetrators yet to be identified.
Here’s what we know about how the attack unfolded, and what was behind it.
What happened during the church shooting in Karak?
On Friday afternoon, three masked gunmen opened fire during a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud.
Survivors said they heard an explosion just after the start of the service. Two attackers who arrived in a vehicle were joined by a third carrying a semi-automatic rifle. They entered the church and opened fire for several minutes.
One survivor, Nasser al-Burqan, a lawyer, told the Reuters news agency that one of the attackers, standing about two metres (6.5 feet) away, pointed a handgun at him and opened fire.
“When everything finally quietened down, I looked out the window behind me, and I saw two [assailants] – one was masked, the other was not; he was carrying a handgun,” said al-Burqan, a lawyer.
Later, his son, who had also been present, called him to say he had been shot in the leg and was being treated in hospital.
Tarek Ammarin, who was visiting a relative injured in the attack, now in hospital, said: “A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word.”
Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a list of officials condemning what he called a “wicked” attack.
“God willing, this country will remain safe,” he said.
State news channel Al-Mamlaka reported that security forces were deployed to the church and were in pursuit of the two suspects who had arrived in a vehicle.
How many people were killed or injured?
Eight people were killed in the shooting, including seven who died at the scene and one who succumbed to her injuries hours after the attack, Jordan’s Petra news agency reported on Saturday.
Of the 40 people injured, 27 are still in hospital. The Director of Prince Ali Military Hospital in Karak said one person is in critical condition, after undergoing surgery.
Who carried out the attack?
The identity of the three attackers has not been confirmed, with government statements referring to them as “unknown assailants”.
Security camera footage of the attack has been circulating online, however. Video broadcast by Al-Mamlaka shows three people shooting outside the church and running towards its entrance.
Other footage also shows the attackers opening fire on a group of men outside the building trying to flee.
Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin Al-Farrayeh said a group of “extremists” that have “no relationship to humanity” were responsible for the attack, though no specific groups were mentioned.
Why was the church targeted?
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said on Friday that the attack was a by-product of terrorist ideology and “blind extremism”, but did not give specifics about the attackers.
The motive remains unclear since the attackers’ identities have yet to be revealed.
Where is Karak, and what do we know about its Christian community?
Karak governorate is about 120km (75 miles) south of Amman and is home to many from Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s population of 11.5 million people.
Taylor Luck, senior Middle East correspondent at the Christian Science Monitor, told Al Jazeera that Jordan’s Christians “pride themselves on [their] interfaith solidarity and coexistence”.
He said that Christians and Muslims have lived side-by-side in Karak for generations and that if the attack had been carried out in an attempt to divide the community, it is more likely that the “community come[s] back even stronger”.
Jordan is also home to many biblical sites that draw visitors from around the world.
What has the response been to this shooting?
Several countries, including Azerbaijan, Iraq, Poland, Palestine and Qatar, have issued statements condemning the attack and expressing their solidarity with Jordan.
Ahmed al-Tayeb, the grand imam of Al-Azhar in Cairo, a leading Sunni religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of the victims, calling the shooting a “heinous terrorist attack”.
“This crime contradicts the teachings of the Abrahamic religions and reveals that its perpetrators are devoid of all compassion, humanity and morality,” he wrote in a social media post.
The United States embassy in Jordan also released a statement on X offering condolences to victims and survivors of the attack.
“On behalf of the American people, we offer our most heartfelt condolences to the victims and survivors of the terror attack today at a church in Karak, Jordan,” it said.
The Jordanian Prime Minister declared three days of mourning following the attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public buildings.
Has Jordan experienced similar attacks before?
Yes, although they are rare.
In 2016, the ISIL (ISIS) group carried out a series of attacks across Karak, including a deadly siege on a Crusader-era castle in which 10 people were killed, including a Canadian tourist and seven police officers. Dozens of others were injured.
Four attackers were later killed by Jordanian security forces following a long standoff.

More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:38:05 UTC
22:38:05 KST

More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Everyone is due an extra hour’s sleep on Sunday as the clocks will roll back an hour at 3am to 2am.
Daylight saving time in the Netherlands has been in place since 1977, following the oil crisis of the 70s, when saving energy on lighting became a priority.
The clocks go forward in spring, on the last Sunday of March, to give lighter evenings. Staying on summer time into the winter would mean very dark mornings, so in October the clocks return to standard time.
The EU has debated ending daylight saving time altogether and the European Parliament voted to stop it in 1996 but member states have not yet committed to it.
So tomorrow you can lie in a little longer.

Breadcrumb
UAE's Ras Al Khaimah shuts all beaches as neighbours grapple with oil spill
Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after an offshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighbouring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah.
The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given.
The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said.
The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions.
Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict's environmental fallout.
Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts' planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island.
The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE's first commercial gaming licence in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027.
Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East.
Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday.
UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.

How Operation Santa Claus grew from Christmas donations to ‘engine’ of change
Fundraising drive has evolved over its nearly 40 years from simply disbursing funds to building sustained relationships with NGOs
Over nearly four decades, Operation Santa Claus (OSC) has grown from a quirky holiday fundraiser into an “engine” for community change in Hong Kong.
For some beneficiaries, the journey was a full circle. Rachel Chow Chiu-yan learned about the fundraising drive in Young Post when she was a student, later pitched for funds on behalf of a group helping teenage girls and later joined the charity.
“Ten to 20 years ago, Operation Santa Claus disbursed some funding to charities that saw it as seed money. Now, after successful pilot schemes, the initiatives have been replicated,” Chow, former senior manager of the programme, said.
The drive was established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988.

Merve Berker
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Saturday called for reforms to make the UN Security Council more just and inclusive, stressing the need to strengthen the organization's ability to address global crises.
In a message marking UN Day and the 81st anniversary of the organization's founding, shared by Türkiye's Communications Directorate on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal, Erdogan said the UN's founding mission remains increasingly important amid global challenges.
"It has become particularly important to establish a more just and inclusive structure for the UN Security Council that can meet the expectations of the international community," he said.
Erdogan cited ongoing wars, humanitarian disasters, climate change, hunger, poverty, racism, xenophobia and Islamophobia as challenges demonstrating the continued importance of the UN.
He said the organization, established after two world wars to "save succeeding generations from the scourge of war," has assumed significant responsibilities in maintaining international peace and security and promoting development and prosperity.
Referring to Gaza, Erdogan said the deaths of more than 74,000 people in the "genocide," along with conflicts elsewhere, demonstrate the urgency of reform.
He called on countries to uphold the UN Charter more strongly and support reforms aimed at improving the effectiveness of the organization's principal bodies.
Erdogan also reaffirmed Türkiye's support for the UN80 Initiative launched by Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
"We are working in close cooperation with the organization toward our goal of making Istanbul a UN hub," he said.
Congratulating UN personnel worldwide, Erdogan reiterated Türkiye's determination to support efforts toward a more effective and inclusive international system.

Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to ₹10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.
LUCKNOW: Indian Railways has decided to extend its Optional Travel Insurance Scheme (OTIS) to passengers booking reserved tickets through Passenger Reservation System (PRS) counters from October 27, in compliance with Supreme Court directions.In an order issued on Saturday, the Railway Board directed all zonal railways to make necessary arrangements for implementing the scheme at reservation counters.The decision follows the Supreme Court's October 6 order in the Union of India versus Radha Yadav case.Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to Rs 10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.The policy also provides Rs 7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability, up to Rs 2 lakh towards hospitalisation expenses and Rs 10,000 for transportation of mortal remains.According to the Railway Board, insurance will remain optional, and reservation staff must inform passengers about its availability before booking.
Passengers opting for insurance must provide a mobile number and pay the premium through digital payment modes only.
The premium will be collected along with the ticket fare.Insurance policy details will be communicated to passengers through their registered mobile numbers.The Board clarified that the existing terms and conditions applicable to IRCTC e-ticket insurance will also apply to tickets purchased at reservation counters.Divisional railway managers and commercial officers have been directed to monitor implementation, while zonal railways must submit compliance reports confirming operational readiness.

Harmonized regulatory frameworks urged in Africa to advance pharmaceutical self-reliance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
21:32:57 CST
22:32:57 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Industry experts and stakeholders on Friday called for concerted action to establish a robust ecosystem for bioequivalence testing to ensure locally manufactured generic medicines across Eastern and Southern Africa are safe, accessible, and scientifically proven.
The call was made during a regional workshop focused on developing a White Paper on bioequivalence testing and regulatory harmonization in Eastern and Southern Africa, held in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. The five-day event, which ran from Oct. 19 to 23, highlighted the critical need for harmonized regulatory frameworks and expanded domestic testing capacity to eliminate costly reliance on overseas facilities.
Jointly organized by the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the Ethiopian government and the World Bank, the workshop brought together national regulators, pharmaceutical manufacturers, experts and researchers, as well as development partners to establish a comprehensive regional framework for bioequivalence testing.
Experts and policymakers at the gathering emphasized that relying on external testing facilities imposes significant economic burdens and causes regulatory approval delays for locally manufactured generic drugs. They stressed the urgent need to expand domestic testing capacity to support sustainable pharmaceutical growth across the region.
Addressing the workshop, Girum Hailu, a senior policy and partnership specialist at IGAD, highlighted several critical gaps affecting the sector, including limited regional bioequivalence testing facilities, heavy dependence on overseas testing, high study costs, and inconsistent regulatory requirements across borders.
To overcome these challenges, experts advocated for advancing regulatory harmonization aligned with international standards, implementing phased, risk-based compliance pathways for legacy products, and establishing shared regional testing capacity backed by strong oversight mechanisms to support local manufacturers.
Stakeholders also underscored the vital importance of making bioequivalence services more affordable and accessible to local pharmaceutical manufacturers, outlining priority investments and capacity-building measures for accredited centers across the region. ■

"The exhibition features a series of precious historical photographs and detailed textual records, showcasing the firm resolve of the Chinese people as a whole to uphold the one-China principle and safeguard national sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity," Yang said.
Hu Jieguo, secretary-general of the China Council for the Promotion of Peaceful National Reunification in Western Africa, said Taiwan was liberated from Japanese colonial rule and returned to China 81 years ago.
"This victory was not a gift, but was paid for with the blood, sweat, and tears of millions of Chinese sons and daughters who stood united against foreign aggression," Hu said, noting that the commemoration in Nigeria carries special significance as China and Nigeria share historical experiences of resisting foreign invasion and colonialism.
Gui Tao, deputy editor-in-chief of Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau, said the exhibition, held in five African countries including Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Nigeria and Mozambique, looks back at an important chapter of history and affirms peace, justice and historical fact.
"The African people, including the people of Nigeria, endured the suffering brought by colonialism, just as China did, and went through the same historical process of striving for national independence, state sovereignty and national dignity," Gui said.

Sheriff Ibrahim, head of the Centre for Contemporary China-Africa Research in Nigeria, said Nigeria recognizes the one-China principle and that the Nigerian government has continued to reaffirm this position.
"There is a certain similarity between China's efforts to maintain national unity and Nigeria's own experience in maintaining its territorial integrity," Ibrahim said, expressing confidence that China would eventually achieve peaceful reunification with Taiwan.

Justice chancellor: Wild boar cannot be made to suffer when training hunting dogs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Justice chancellor: Wild boar cannot be made to suffer when training hunting dogs
The Ministry of Regional Affairs and the Ministry of Climate should establish clear legal rules for training hunting dogs using live wild boars to ensure animal welfare and legal clarity, the Chancellor of Justice's Office says.
Four years ago in May, the regional affairs minister issued a regulation on measures to prevent and control African swine fever, introducing an exemption under which the ban on keeping pigs outdoors does not apply to wild boars kept for training hunting dogs.
The Estonian Union for the Protection of Animals asked the chancellor of justice to examine whether the regulation complies with the Animal Protection Act. The organization also pointed out that the law provides no legal basis for using wild boars kept in artificial environments to train hunting dogs and that no detailed requirements have been established for such training.
Deputy Chancellor of Justice-Adviser Olari Koppel said the ban on keeping pigs outdoors is a biosecurity measure and that the minister has the authority to introduce exemptions, provided they comply with EU law and do not undermine animal disease prevention. Koppel therefore sees no reason to believe that the exemption for training hunting dogs violates these conditions.
However, he noted that the regulation only provides an exemption from the ban on keeping pigs outdoors. It does not provide a legal basis for using wild boars to train hunting dogs or authorize activities prohibited under the Animal Protection Act.
"The absence of a specific legal provision does not, however, mean that such an activity is prohibited, provided other applicable rules are followed," Koppel said, adding that it must be possible to conduct training without endangering the animal's welfare.
The law does not establish a specific legal basis or detailed requirements for training hunting dogs using live wild boars. The activity is primarily governed by the Nature Conservation Act and the general animal welfare requirements arising from it.
Under the Animal Protection Act, animals must not be subjected to suffering or pain. According to Koppel, if hunting dog training cannot be conducted without causing such harm, the executive branch cannot make the activity permissible through regulations, guidelines or administrative practices.
"In that case, only the Riigikogu can decide through legislation whether the objective of the training and the benefits it provides justify making an exception to the prohibition established by law," Koppel said.
Koppel said the lack of clarity in the regulations is a problem. To address it, the Ministry of Regional Affairs and the Ministry of Climate should establish the conditions for training hunting dogs in legislation rather than merely in guidelines or explanatory memorandums. This would ensure compliance with animal welfare requirements and provide legal clarity.

Molodist Film Festival Marks 55 Years, Bringing International Cinema to Kyiv Oct. 24-Nov. 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The 55th Molodist International Film Festival will take place in Kyiv from Oct. 24 to Nov. 1, 2026.
One of Eastern Europe’s leading film events marks its anniversary with a new visual identity while maintaining its mission of discovering emerging talent and helping debut filmmakers find their place in world cinema.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Founded in 1970 as a student film showcase, Molodist has evolved over more than five decades into an international platform for emerging filmmakers. Its program features feature-length debuts and short films – fiction, documentary and animation – by filmmakers from Ukraine and around the world.
From student films to an international festival
The first festival lasted just two days and featured 33 short films made by students of the Kyiv State Institute of Theatrical Arts named after Ivan Karpenko-Kary. The event was founded by film directors Vadym Chubasov and Viktor Ivchenko.
Since then, Molodist has become a platform for discovering new talent and introducing Ukrainian audiences to international cinema. The festival is accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF), which recognizes its standing on the international film circuit.
The competition program includes student films, short films and feature-length debuts, with a dedicated competition for documentaries. The non-competition program features sections such as Festival of Festivals, Forma, The Century of the Greats and Midnight Screening, among others.
Russia Hits Central Kyiv With Cluster Missile
The festival’s top award is the Scythian Deer statuette, presented to winners of its competition programs.
Oleh Sentsov to head the international jury
The international jury of the 55th Molodist Film Festival will be chaired by Oleh Sentsov, a Ukrainian film director, screenwriter and writer, former Kremlin political prisoner and serviceman in the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
Sentsov directed the feature films “Gamer” (2011) and “Numbers” (2019), as well as the documentary “Real” (2024). His honors include the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought in 2018, Ukraine’s Taras Shevchenko National Prize in 2016 and France’s Legion of Honour.
The international jury also includes Matthijs Wouter Knol of the Netherlands, CEO and executive director of the European Film Academy, Iranian filmmaker and human rights advocate Mahnaz Mohammadi, Ukrainian theater director Yevhen Lavrenchuk, and Latvian film scholar and critic Anita Uzulniece.
The jury will assess student films, shorts and feature-length debuts from around the world and select the recipient of the festival’s Grand Prix.
A separate jury for the National Competition will include Ukrainian director Viacheslav Turyanytsia, Polish film programmer Radek Lipka and French-British film programmer and Film Republic founder Xavier Henry-Rashid.
How to attend the festival
Screenings will take place at the Zhovten Cinema and the House of Cinema in Kyiv. Festival passes are already on sale. Students can purchase passes at a discounted rate, while Ukrainian military personnel are eligible for free passes upon verification of their service status.
Over 55 years, Molodist has grown from a student film showcase into an international cinema forum while retaining its core mission: supporting a new generation of filmmakers and introducing audiences to films that will help shape the future of cinema.

CIA contractor accused of leaking US reports on Israel to journalist girlfriend who published them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:29:57 UTC
22:29:57 KST

A classified U.S. intelligence assessment warning that Israel could descend into civil conflict, claims that Israeli officials pressed the Trump administration to assassinate a senior Iranian leader, and a secret report detailing efforts to secure American military support beyond Donald Trump's presidency are among the revelations at the center of a major intelligence leak scandal in Washington. 
On Friday, the FBI arrested a CIA contractor suspected of passing classified information to his journalist girlfriend, whose reporting included five stories based on sensitive intelligence, three of them directly concerning Israel.
The suspect, Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of Washington, D.C., held a Top Secret security clearance with access to highly sensitive intelligence. Prosecutors allege that for months he exploited his access to U.S. intelligence systems to examine classified reports unrelated to his duties and pass information to his romantic partner, who operated an independent news publication on Substack. Investigators linked his access to sensitive documents with telephone conversations between the couple and the publication dates of articles allegedly containing information from those reports.
American authorities have not publicly identified the journalist, referred to in the FBI affidavit as "Individual 1," or disclosed the subjects of the classified reports. However, documents obtained by ynet indicate that she is American journalist Aída Chávez, founder of the independent investigative publication Capital & Empire. Chávez previously worked for The Hill, contributed to The Washington Post and served as a congressional correspondent for The Intercept and Washington correspondent for The Nation. Five articles published on her website match the dates identified in the FBI affidavit, while a passage from a September fundraising appeal appears almost word for word in the document. Chávez has not been charged with any offense in connection with the investigation.
Israel's alleged assassination request and fears of civil war
One of the most significant articles appeared on May 28, under the headline "EXCLUSIVE: Israel Privately Pressing U.S. to Kill Iran's Lead Negotiator and Launch New Strikes." Chávez reported that Israeli officials had urged the Trump administration to assassinate Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament and a central figure in negotiations between Tehran and Washington. According to the report, Israel sought to persuade the Americans to abandon negotiations and resume attacks on Iran's oil infrastructure, believing further economic damage could trigger widespread protests and potentially bring down the Iranian regime.
Chávez said her reporting drew on a classified intelligence assessment circulated within the U.S. intelligence community and conversations with officials familiar with its contents. The FBI affidavit states that Brinksman accessed a classified report on May 26 and called his girlfriend three times that day. Two days later, she published an article that investigators say contained information from the same report.
Another article, published on July 29, described a U.S. intelligence assessment concerning Israel's efforts to preserve its strategic relationship with Washington as American public support for Israel weakened. According to Chávez, Israeli officials were seeking to embed their country more deeply within the American military, intelligence and defense industries, making it more difficult for future administrations to reduce cooperation. The reported strategy included discussions about a possible permanent U.S. military base in Israel, expanded joint weapons development and stronger ties with influential American technology executives. Investigators said Brinksman accessed a Top Secret document on July 28, spoke with his girlfriend several times that day and that an article containing information from the document appeared the following day.
The third Israel-related article, published on October 5 in cooperation with Drop Site News, concerned a reported CIA assessment titled "Fracture From Within." According to two American sources cited in the article, the assessment was prepared in August by the CIA's Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging conventional intelligence assumptions and examining alternative scenarios. It warned that Israel's political crisis, disputes over military conscription for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, economic pressure, social divisions and the psychological consequences of prolonged warfare could combine to produce severe internal conflict or even institutional breakdown ahead of the October 27 election.
The reported assessment raised concerns about armed military veterans returning from combat with psychological trauma, worsening political polarization and mounting resentment over exemptions from military service. It also examined the possibility of foreign technology companies withdrawing from Israel, deteriorating regional relationships and Hamas or Hezbollah exploiting domestic instability. Crucially, the report did not constitute an official U.S. intelligence prediction that civil war would occur. It was an assessment of potential risks and scenarios, as described by the journalist's sources.
The FBI affidavit details another striking sequence of events. Brinksman allegedly accessed a classified document several times in August and again on October 1. Telephone records show that he spoke with his girlfriend for 47 minutes that day, followed by another conversation lasting 37 minutes. Four days later, the article on Israel's potential internal collapse appeared.
The two remaining articles concerned other Middle Eastern developments. On March 11, Chávez reported that Bahrain had brought in forces from Jordan to help suppress protests over its involvement in the war with Iran. On May 13, she reported on a classified CIA assessment describing divisions among Washington's Gulf allies, with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain favoring continued strikes against Iran while Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait preferred renewed negotiations. Investigators allege that classified information accessed by Brinksman also appeared in these reports.
More than 800 calls and a trail of classified documents
The evidence that led investigators to Brinksman is detailed in a 13-page FBI affidavit. He began working for a U.S. government agency in 2020 before moving to a contractor serving the same agency. In 2022, he took a position involving computer systems integration, including work transferring data between classified and unclassified systems. CIA Director John Ratcliffe confirmed that Brinksman had provided services to the agency.
His position required him to work inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF, a secure area where personal phones and electronic devices are prohibited. Employees must use identification cards to enter and leave, creating records that became central to the investigation. According to the FBI, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified reports, left the secure area and contacted his girlfriend, sometimes within minutes. Investigators believe these intervals allowed him to retrieve his personal phone, possibly from his vehicle, and communicate sensitive information.
In one example, the journalist called Brinksman at 8:41 a.m. on March 11. Less than half an hour later, he accessed a classified intelligence report at 9:09 a.m. and again at 10:01 a.m. He subsequently left the secure facility and received another call from her that evening, lasting about 14 minutes. An article published that day allegedly contained Top Secret information from the document he had examined.
Investigators found records of more than 800 telephone calls or attempted calls between the couple during 2026. They also examined computers at Brinksman's workplace and discovered that he was among no more than six people who had accessed the journalist's Substack publication from that facility during the period under investigation. According to the affidavit, no other individual combined access to all five classified reports with visits to all five articles that authorities believe contained information from those documents.
A notebook discovered on Brinksman's desk on October 10 also attracted investigators' attention because corners had been torn from several pages. An FBI agent noted that individuals who transmit sensitive information sometimes write notes to reproduce accurate or near-verbatim quotations. However, the affidavit did not establish that the notebook contained leaked secrets or provide direct evidence that its missing pages had been used to transmit information.
‘I'm helping her build her publication’
One of the most personal details in the investigation emerged from an email Brinksman sent to a friend in November 2025. He described his new relationship with a journalist who had recently become independent and explained that he was helping her establish a publication focused on foreign policy. He added that the project had proved surprisingly fulfilling. Other emails examined by investigators supported the conclusion that the two were romantically involved.
According to the affidavit, their collaboration extended beyond conversations about published stories. On March 13, Brinksman received permission to edit a Google Docs document concerning a Middle Eastern country. Minutes later, he suggested a wording change, which his girlfriend marked as resolved. The article published that day matches a Chávez report concerning Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer, a prominent supporter of Israel, and congressional votes related to the war with Iran. Investigators did not identify classified information in that particular article. Brinksman had also sought advance publication clearance, as required of security clearance holders, for articles he co-authored with the journalist.
Brinksman's background adds an unusual dimension to the allegations. A graduate of Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service, he co-authored a study published in May 2019 titled "Millennial Considerations on Insider Threat: Are We A Threat Or An Opportunity?" The research examined the risks posed by employees with access to sensitive information and proposed measures to prevent security breaches, including employee training, monitoring potential warning signs and addressing vulnerabilities associated with social media and mobile technology. Seven years later, Brinksman faces allegations involving precisely the kind of insider threat his research sought to help organizations prevent.
Chávez describes Capital & Empire as an independent publication investigating the interests driving American military and economic policy. In a September fundraising appeal, she said she had published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that she believed the public deserved to know about. She also encouraged readers with inside information to provide leaks.
Brinksman has been charged with unlawfully transmitting national defense information, an offense carrying a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg accused him of going far beyond his duties to obtain closely guarded American intelligence and passing it to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish it. Eisenberg described the alleged conduct as a betrayal of the trust placed in someone holding a security clearance. FBI Director Kash Patel pledged to pursue anyone who abuses access to government secrets, while Ratcliffe said the arrest followed a referral from the CIA and warned that unauthorized disclosures could endanger intelligence sources, ongoing operations and agency personnel. Brinksman remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

22:25:46 KST

Cornell University’s Jane Doe told faculty members that she felt  “unsupported and disbelieved” by the Ivy League university’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, NBC reported on Wednesday.
In a letter to Cornell’s faculty senate, Doe provided what she called a secondhand account of a meeting between Kotlikoff and the then-president of her sorority, Tri Delta.
“After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff’s initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’” Doe wrote in the letter. “She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story.”
The meeting was held months after October 19-20, 2024, when Doe was allegedly raped by seven members of the now-defunct Chi Phi fraternity.
She alerted campus police to the incident on November 8, 2024.
Cornell claims comments were taken out of context
The meeting that Jane Doe is claiming to provide a secondhand account of occurred in January 2025.
In the letter, Doe wrote that her sorority president told her that at least one other faculty member “appeared distressed” at Kotlikoff’s line of questioning, and said that the person believed that “the President’s response was inappropriate.”
Cornell said in a statement that while Kotlikoff did make a similar comment at the meeting, the secondhand account was taken out of context.
“The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account,” the statement added. “The question ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024. He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”
Cornell's Jane Doe felt the administration didn't believe her
But Jane Doe said in her letter that the comment left her feeling unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff.
“It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school.”
This comes ahead of a vote of no confidence in Kotlikoff’s administration.
Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told NBC that the letter she wrote to the faculty senate was for “informational purposes only.”
“Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it,” Giuffra said. “Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate.”
