12 Absolutely Banging Proper Watches Under $400
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

The wonderful counter to rising prices at the very top end of the watch world is that, frankly, things have never looked better for those seeking proper mechanical watches on a budget. Entry-level timepieces keep getting better and cheaper—and this isn't just from newly established microbrands hoping to make a name for themselves, but from the major players, too.
Recently, I was asked to pick a couple of wallet-friendly watches for WIRED's Gear newsletter, and it sent me down a glorious rabbit hole where I was genuinely surprised by superb timepieces well below what WIRED has previously set for affordable watches (the sub-$1,000 bracket). Far from dropping three figures on a decent automatic, you can now get almost anything you desire from a watch for far less than $500.
To check my math and make sure I wasn't going slightly crazy, I reached out to WIRED's wider circle of watch experts with a devilishly tricky, unenviable challenge: Pick their favorite mechanical watch for less than $400, the sort of price where quartz watches dominate. It was a hard ask, but they delivered. Here's the list—all are exceptional value, and watches we'd be delighted to sport on our wrists.
Caravelle Sea Hunter
Caravelle has no right to make a mechanical dive watch this attractive and capable for a mere $300, but here it is. The secret to its timeless look is that Bulova's budget brand sensibly fashioned this modern Sea Hunter heavily on the diver's design from the late 1960s, while bumping the size up to a more modern 39 mm. Elegant and stylish, it's practically a GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watch. But with 200 meters of waterproofing, a 120-click unidirectional bezel, and a 42-hour power reserve, the Sea Hunter is a compelling sports watch. Throw on a rubber strap for diving, a nato for casual (our pick is Artem), or stick with the three-link steel bracelet for a more classic look.
Orient Bambino Version 7 38 mm
Unquestionably one of the best-value automatic dress watches you can buy today, the $295 Orient Bambino’s timeless 38-mm design with white dial and leather strap has been carefully shrunken down from the original 40.5-mm casing, making this piece incredibly wearable (both in these smaller watch times and when case sizes inevitably get larger again.) You can view the automatic Japanese movement through the exhibition case back, and there's even 30 meters of water resistance—not that you should be swimming with such a watch. Want something less traditional? Go for the pink dial with a stainless steel bracelet.
Brew Metric Lite Retro
This new smaller take on Brew's original Metric Retro is the choice of Mike Christensen, British GQ's lifestyle director and watch editor. Cashing in on the current trend for very small watches, Mike loves that this 30-mm piece is wearable for both men and women. “This li'l Brew number is so retro they decided to call it exactly that,” he says. At just $375, the stainless steel Metric Lite Retro, complete with a matching bracelet, uses an automatic movement visible through the open caseback. It has 50 meters of water resistance, and even sapphire crystal atop the striking dial. Proper retro charm that's forgiving on the bank balance.
Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound
Chris Hall, a watch expert who writes for WIRED, The New York Times, Financial Times, and others, as well as his excellent The Fourth Wheel Substack, recommends the Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound at $259. “It was the model that marked Timex’s return to mechanical watches about a decade ago, and unlike so many watches at this level, it isn’t a rip-off of something else: It’s a tribute to one of Timex’s own designs,” Hall says. “It’s small, quirky, and very much its own thing. Never mind the mechanics, getting real personality and credibility at this price is what’s really impressive.” At 34 mm on a leather strap, the design feels pure, and the 30-meter water resistance is a bonus.
Sea-Gull 1963 “International Edition”
Looking a little further afield can often pay off in the watch world. A prime example is the Sea-Gull 1963, a hand-wound mechanical chronograph based on a vintage pilot's timepiece originally built for the Chinese Air Force back in 1961. Many call this watch the gateway drug to watch collecting, but there are a few different versions. Here we've gone for the “International Edition,” which seems to be a budget model of the 1963 Sea-Gull, as it sells alternative iterations for more on its own website. The design is faithful (including the ST1901 movement), the 38-mm size is perfect, and you can't argue with the unfathomably low $269 price.
Baltic HMS
Founded in 2016 by Etienne Malec and debuting on Kickstarter in 2017, this French micro-brand was inspired by the watch collection Malec inherited from his late father, whose family hailed from northern Poland near the Baltic Sea. The brand has quickly become a darling of watch reviewers, so it's no surprise that two of WIRED's watch experts have chosen the 1940s-inspired three-hand HMS (cheating ever so slightly as the HMS clocks in at $430).
Robin Swithinbank, who writes on watches for The New York Times, Financial Times, and Business of Fashion, and hosts the Luxury Society Podcast, has been won over by the 38-mm HMS 002 Silver (above right). “At any price, I like my watches simple, legible, and hardwired with the kind of style that never dies. Baltic absolutely nailed it with this,” he says. Powered by an automatic Miyota 8315 movement with a 60-hour power reserve, it also has 50 meters of water resistance.
Tim Vaux, who writes for both Hodinkee and British GQ about watches, prefers the HMS 003 Salmon (above left). It's smaller than the 002 at 36.5 mm, but still uses the Miyota 8315 movement. “In 2026, there’s no need to look at the household names anymore. The HMS 003 has one of the most classically configured dials you’ll find at any price,” Vaux says. “Walk into a room wearing this and nods of approval will come from all angles. With the Salmon dial, you can’t go wrong.”
Bulova A-11 Hack Watch
As Caravelle's big brother, Bulova has appeared in our bargain watch roundups before. Still, this time, Felix Scholz, editor-in-chief of Revolution Australia and cohost of OT: The Podcast, chose the A-11 Hack Watch, on sale for just $357. “Military watches hold a special place in the hearts of watch enthusiasts,” Scholz says. “And while they might not be rare or intrinsically valuable, the hacking watches produced by numerous American makers during the Second World War are among the greatest.”
Legible and functional, Scholz says such pieces are a true slice of history, and that Bulova is one of the historic manufacturers of this type. “The A-11 Hack captures the spirit, but the less martial blue dial feels contemporary, and doesn't make you look like you're LARPing as a reenactor.”
Citizen Tsuyosa
Pickings are admittedly slim for genuine automatic GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watches under $400, but take a look at the $396 Citizen Tsuyosa with its classic black dial and integrated stainless steel bracelet. It features a 40-mm case, 50 meters of water resistance, sapphire crystal, 42-hour power reserve, and a 3 o’clock date window that will see you from beach to boardroom. If black is too serious, Citizen offers several dial hues (gold and green is a nice combo).
WIRED's top pick, however, is the new, more wearable 37-mm range conveniently on sale right now at just under our $400 target. If you venture above $600, park Citizen and go for the Lorier Falcon or Traska Commuter 36 instead.
Vostok Amphibia
WIRED watch expert Laura McCreddie-Doak has seen our Chinese chrono option and upped the ante with this Russian dive watch. Vostok traces back to the Soviet Union's Chistopol Watch Factory, a supplier to the USSR Ministry of Defense during World War II. This Amphibia 420269 (there are many, many other models) has a 2416B automatic movement that offers a 31-hour power reserve. Bafflingly just $151 on a steel bracelet, it's rated for 200 meters of water resistance, thanks to its unique, pressure-tightening case design. “This watch needs no other justification for inclusion on this list other than it was worn by Bill Murray as Jacques Cousteau-alike Steve Zissou in Wes Anderson’s The Life Aquatic,” says McCreddie-Doak.
Seiko 5 Sports
Finally, we come to the almost inevitable inclusion of the Seiko 5 Sports automatic. The familiar and affordable Seiko 5 Sports line began in 1968 as a tougher, sportier evolution of the 1963 Seiko Sportsmatic 5. The lineup is still going strong with dozens of variants plus a back catalog of thousands. That explains why, for the second time on this list, two of our experts chose the 5 Sports.
WIRED watch writer and author Josh Sims says the Seiko 5 Sports “is the MPV of watches: dependable, rugged, adaptable, as happy in the city as out of it. For my money—and this really is a lot of watch for, relatively, not a lot of money—it also has the cool of not being Swiss. Seiko isn’t just a giant of Japanese watchmaking; it’s a giant of watchmaking that deserves more r-e-s-p-e-c-t, and remains as relevant as ever.” Sims has gone for the SNSX Series that starts at $385.
Holly Ross, as executive editor of Vanity Fair’s On Time watch supplement, has gone for the Seiko 5 SRPE71 (pictured above), a model that's not new but still available if you look. “What is not to love about this chic, timeless, durable, and mechanical Seiko 5? And for a neat $320, it makes it even more desirable.”

Why do some women become the strongest defenders of patriarchy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:13:21 UTC
19:13:21 KST

Delhi University women took to streets demanding safety after news report of a gangrape near a girls college.
“Sir, let me say that I am not a feminist. I consider myself as a human being. As a human being we feel that it is our duty to help women, minorities, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, OBCs, and also the neglected class.”
Mamata Banerjee in Lok Sabha on Women’s Day, 2008.
Oxford dictionary defines feminism as 'the belief and aim that women should have the same rights and opportunities as men or the struggle to achieve this aim.'Then why is it that some of us distance ourselves from this term? And why is it that some women uphold the very patriarchy that restricts them?
Why do some women keep patriarchy aliveA group called the NCMIndia Council for Men Affairs recently took out a 'Long Live Patriarchy' march that went viral on social media. The group also had women holding the banner. "In the name of equality, these girls don't want to do jhaadu-pocha, clean utensils or raise kids. They just want freedom, money and debauchery," one of the women at the march said. "Equality does not mean freedom to drink, smoke, roam around at night. Women are misusing their independence. Azaadi does not mean shaming men."TOI spoke to Dolly Kumari, who is also a member of the group that actively raises men's issues, and asked her what patriarchy meant to her."Patriarchy cannot be understood simply as a system created by men to oppress women. When a woman speaks about men's issues, some people may find it surprising because they expect her to speak only from a particular gender-based perspective. But I do not believe empathy should have a gender. Supporting men who experience injustice does not mean denying the difficulties women face," she said."My objection is to the idea that everything traditional must be condemned as patriarchal and, therefore, bad. If a man wants to protect and provide for his family, and a woman willingly chooses to trust him in that role, why should society automatically call that oppression or brainwashed women?"Oxford dictionary defines patriarchy as 'a society, system or country that is ruled or controlled by men.'
It would appear, then, that women supporting patriarchy would be an anomaly. However, Dolly said that the purpose of their 'Long Live Patriarchy' initiative was to raise awareness of men's rights, which "we have been organising on Gandhi Jayanti for nearly a decade.""Equality should not become a competition between men and women. Women deserve justice, and so do men. We need a society where both can express their pain, seek support, and live with dignity without being judged by gender stereotypes," said Dolly."In the traditional Indian family, men were often expected to provide, protect and take responsibility for their families while women traditionally took on many responsibilities related to the home and children. These roles evolved within the social and economic realities of their time although it resulted in unequal rights and restrictions. Our history is not simply a story of oppression and therefore patriarchy should prevail."
Is the 'aurat hi aurat ki dushman' concept real? Does different treatment of a son from daughter and parenting play a role in keeping misogyny alive? Or is this 'aurat hi aurat ki dushman hoti hai' syndrome.Devika Anand, a psychologist at Rise and Mind, believes that the answer lies partly in the way gender roles are normalised within families and communities."I think one way to understand this is that we don't always question the systems we grow up in, particularly when those systems are presented to us as normal, moral, or necessary. When a woman grows up learning that a good woman is one who sacrifices, adjusts, tolerates, or puts others before herself, these expectations can become deeply embedded in her understanding of what it means to be a woman," she said.Over time, these expectations may stop feeling like restrictions and start being seen as values. A woman may even derive a sense of identity or self-worth from having lived up to them, sometimes at considerable personal cost."When younger women choose differently, it can challenge not just her beliefs but also the meaning she has attached to her own sacrifices," Devika explained.This explains why some women who have experienced restrictions themselves may go on to impose similar expectations on younger women. Having spent years adjusting to restrictive norms, they may come to regard them as an inevitable part of life rather than something that can be challenged."There can also be a need to make sense of one's own experiences. If someone has made significant sacrifices because she believed there was no alternative, acknowledging that those sacrifices were unnecessary or unfair can be painful. It may bring up feelings of anger, grief, or regret. Believing that younger women must make similar sacrifices can sometimes help preserve the sense that those sacrifices had a purpose," Devika said.When certain expectations are repeatedly reinforced within families and communities, they can become the default way of relating to others. A woman may reproduce the same expectations she experienced, not necessarily because she wants younger women to suffer, but because she has learned to see those expectations as responsible or appropriate behaviour.
From 'mere sar mei dard hai, iska karan marrd hai' to 'ek sutta, 2 chai, marrd jaat haye haye', the protest saw viral slogans. (PTI image)
Can patriarchy give women a sense of power? "Power doesn't always mean having equal power within a system. Sometimes, it means having more power than someone else within that system," Devika said.In a patriarchal family, a woman may have limited autonomy in relation to men but still hold considerable authority over younger women, daughters-in-law or other women in the household. She may have little influence over the rules themselves but gain status by enforcing them."This can give her a sense of belonging, security, or control in an environment where her own power is otherwise limited," Devika explained.There can also be a psychological incentive to conform. If a woman receives approval, respect or recognition for upholding family traditions, questioning those traditions may threaten not only her beliefs but also her position within the family or community.When tradition becomes a question of freedom Calling kindness, compassion, empathy and nurture 'qualities' that women should have, Dolly said, "I feel that relationships are increasingly being discussed in terms of personal freedom, sometimes without equal emphasis on duties, compromise, commitment, and mutual accountability."Dolly believes that a woman does not have to reject tradition to prove that she is empowered. "I come from a traditional, patriarchal family, yet my father always encouraged me to participate in activities that people might traditionally associate with boys. I played sports, learned to ride a bike, built a career in technology, and today have a beautiful family of my own. Growing up with two brothers also gave me a personal experience of sharing opportunities and responsibilities across gender lines. That experience is one of the reasons I believe that having a traditional father or growing up in a strict household does not automatically mean being oppressed. Tradition and discipline are not inherently oppressive," she said.Devika, too, cautions against labelling every woman who holds a traditional belief as a victim of internalised misogyny, which may include judging women more harshly than men, policing other women's behaviour, or believing that women are inherently less capable or less deserving of autonomy," she said.
When women challenge the rules they grew up with A 65-year old influencer from Haryana called Tai Savitri, who recently went viral over her commentary on society and patriarchy, told TOI that even though her experiences have been bitter, it was her educated children that taught her to become a feminist. "I was less educated. My kids got good education so I learnt a few things from them. It was also a feeling that I should do something for the women," she told TOI.She recalled facing criticism in her village, even though her family did not offer much resistance to her views."Yes, I have also heard that aurat hi aurat ki dushman hoti hai but I think it is more because of lack of education that pitied one woman against the other, a system wherein one woman was the slave of another. This created a scenario where women did not want other women to succeed in life," she said.In one of her viral videos, Savitri compared women who restrict other women to dogs that have become accustomed to living on a leash. "You must have seen dog owners taking their pets out. Even if they let go of this leash, by mistake or deliberately, you will notice that the dog itself will hold the leash in his mouth and give it back to his owner. Because the dog has now developed a habit of living like a slave and it has accepted its fate. It is the same with women who try to show other women in poor light. It is the same slave mentality. My only message to women is kutta nahi sher bano (don't be a dog, be a tiger). Whoever tries to put a leash on you or make you a slave, rip them to shreds," she said.
Patriarchy gives some women a sense of belonging There is a distinction between having a choice and the freedom to make that choice. Holding a traditional belief is not the same as denying another woman the right to choose differently. The consequences of that belief, and the degree to which it is imposed on others, matter.Women who defend patriarchal expectations are not necessarily motivated by a single cause. Their views may be shaped by the values they grew up with, the sacrifices they have made, the security they derive from their place within a family or community, or a genuine belief that traditional arrangements offer stability.The question, then, is not simply why some women become flagbearers of patriarchy. It is also why a system that can restrict women's choices sometimes offers them identity, belonging or authority in return—and what it would take for women to feel secure enough to question it.Perhaps the more useful question is not whether women are their own enemies, but whether a society that teaches women to measure their worth through sacrifice, obedience and conformity gives them enough room to imagine a different way of living.

Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:12:10 UTC
19:12:10 KST

Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
Oct 24 - President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.
In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks.
Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country:
TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY
At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “bad job” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low poverty rate, low unemployment, record highs in the stock market and cheaper prices for some food items.
But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses.
Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends.
The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people.
“Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family."
RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE
Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory.
Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday.
Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election.
Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.
Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine.
TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY
Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity.
But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues.
"I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special."
The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens.
At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty.
Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday.
Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them.
FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS
Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods.
But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade.
“What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday.
Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran.
“They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world.
TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC
Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.
This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton.
At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.”
“Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said.
Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old."
Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents.
Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton.
"Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't."
That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies. REUTERS

Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:06:00 EEST
19:06:00 KST

Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
Hopes for a mild winter or inaccuracies in Russian strikes will not help Kyiv get through this winter without problems with its electricity supply. The only question is how long the power cuts will last and whether air defence forces and power engineers will manage to prevent the worst-case scenario.
The Russians are continuing their systematic attacks on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, seeking to completely destroy the city's combined heat and power plants and break the so-called power ring in order to plunge the capital entirely into darkness and cold.
The city has already lost a significant proportion of its own power generation capacity, while strikes are destroying substations through which electricity is supplied from other regions. In the event of severe frosts and further hits, a scenario involving 20 hours without electricity no longer seems far-fetched.
What is Kyiv's power ring, what risks does damage to it pose, and what should the capital's residents prepare for?
What is Kyiv's power ring?
This article does not disclose any sensitive information. The configuration of the power system is no secret to Russia, as Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator, has warned. What does remain secret are the protection systems, equipment redundancy arrangements and power restoration procedures following attacks.
In the narrow technical sense, Kyiv's power ring is a system of high-voltage power lines and 330-kilovolt (kV) substations that connects the capital to Ukraine's integrated power grid and enables electricity to be transmitted to the city from different directions.
A key element of the capital's power supply is the 750 kV Kyivska substation, through which electricity from the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants can be delivered to the capital.
Given their strategic importance, these facilities are under constant attack by Russian forces. The aim is to cut Kyiv off from Ukraine's integrated power grid and cause a blackout.
Put simply, the ring is a kind of road network for electricity. Transmission lines carry electricity to the capital, while substations step down its voltage and feed it into distribution networks for consumers.
If one section of this "road" is damaged by attacks, electricity flows can be rerouted through other lines. This helps maintain the power supply after damage occurs.
The ring is a critically important element of Kyiv's energy supply because the city consumes far more electricity than its own sources generate.
How much electricity does Kyiv consume, and why have power cuts begun?
Kyiv is the largest consumer of electricity in Ukraine. According to estimates by energy experts, the city consumes 1-1.2 GW, or 12-15% of the national total. In winter, depending on the temperature, demand can rise to 1.8-2 GW.
In 2025, before the large-scale winter attacks, local generation played a key role in supplying electricity to the city. According to sources at one of the energy companies who spoke to Ekonomichna Pravda, it may have accounted for as much as 1.3 GW. This came primarily from Kyiv CHP-5, CHP-6 and Darnytsia CHP (CHP-4) – combined heat and power plants (CHP plants) that produce both electricity and heat for the city's district heating network.
These plants are now no longer able to generate electricity. Nevertheless, all three CHPs were hit again by the Russians during the large-scale attack on the night of 13-14 October.
The capital is now forced to rely more heavily on electricity supplied from other regions via the power ring. The problem is, however, that its key components have been under constant attack for more than a month. Some of these attacks result in damage to equipment.
To cause significant problems, the Russians do not necessarily have to destroy the entire power ring. It is enough to damage a few critical nodes through which a large share of the electricity flows.
As a result, a situation may arise where there is electricity in the system, but the grids cannot transmit it to the capital in the required volume. If the city lacks its own power generation, the situation becomes even more complicated.
Under such conditions, dispatchers are forced to restrict consumption, including by introducing emergency or scheduled power cuts. This makes it possible to maintain a balance between available capacity and consumption and to prevent a large-scale failure in the power system.
The time needed for repairs depends on the extent of the damage. Some equipment can be repaired quickly. Replacing a large power transformer or other complex equipment may take longer, especially if the necessary equipment is not held in reserve.
Further complications are caused by repeat attacks, air-raid warnings being in effect for long periods, risks to repair crews and government attempts to reduce the proportion of energy company employees eligible for deferral from mobilisation. Following emergency repairs, the situation can deteriorate again, as strikes have been relentless lately and power workers face the risk of further attacks.
What to expect this winter
The main risk for Kyiv is a combination of three factors: low air temperatures, high consumption and Russian strikes that restrict the ability to transmit electricity to the capital. Given this combination, even fully functioning power generation in other regions does not guarantee that Kyiv will receive enough electricity, making various scenarios possible.
In a relatively favourable scenario, energy workers will repair damaged equipment and new strikes will not cause critical losses. In that case, restrictions may be moderate, although avoiding power cuts altogether will be difficult. For consumers, this would mean 8-10 hours without electricity per day.
If the attacks continue and some equipment remains damaged, Kyiv could face longer power cuts during moderately cold spells. Under this scenario, outages could last 12-16 hours per day.
The worst-case scenario involves regular large-scale strikes on key substations and other elements of the power system amid severe frosts. In that case, restrictions could last up to 20 hours per day. However, sources in the energy sector interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda do not believe in a scenario in which the Russians would manage to destroy everything and "plunge Kyiv into darkness".
The consequences will depend on which facilities are damaged, how quickly they can be repaired and how much electricity can be transmitted to the capital.
A separate challenge is keeping critical infrastructure running, including water supply pumps, heating systems, transport, hospitals and communications.
Read also: No electricity means no water: an interview with the deputy CEO of water utility Kyivvodokanal
The capital needs approximately 200 MW of generating capacity for these purposes, primarily from combined heat and power units and high-capacity generators. According to Ekonomichna Pravda's sources, 150 MW of distributed generation has been brought into operation in Kyiv. By the end of 2026, this is expected to increase to 180-185 MW. Private facilities accounting for another 55-60 MW could become operational before winter, around half of which are already ready.
* * *
It is clear that protecting energy facilities critical to Kyiv from ballistic missiles depends primarily on the effectiveness of air defence. The engineering protection built at most substations can reduce the impact of individual strikes, but it cannot guarantee the survival of critical equipment after a direct hit.
Amid a shortage of missiles for Patriot systems, it is important to have the necessary amount of backup equipment, trained repair crews and clear action protocols for crisis situations.
Experience from previous winters shows that energy workers have learned to work under conditions of large-scale destruction. However, this does not cancel out the physical limitations of the grid and does not guarantee an uninterrupted electricity supply under every attack scenario.
Three things will be decisive for Kyiv this winter: how much electricity can be delivered to the city, how quickly energy workers can repair damaged equipment and whether backup generation can sustain critical facilities.
How long the power cuts last will depend on this. Kyiv can get through the winter without a collapse of its power supply, but it would be naive to expect the capital to avoid prolonged power outages if constant attacks continue.
By Mykola Topalov
Translated by Anna Kybukevych and Solomiia Shvak

China Great Wall Museum in Beijing reopens after renovation, upgrade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:03:14 CST
19:03:14 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The China Great Wall Museum at the foot of the renowned Badaling Great Wall in Beijing reopened to the public on Saturday after an extensive renovation and upgrade.
Located in Yanqing District on the outskirts of the Chinese capital, the museum first opened in 1994 and closed in April 2022 for redevelopment.
Construction began in December 2023, with a building built to better blend the museum into the surrounding mountains and vegetation.
The museum, with a floor area of 16,000 square meters, features exhibition areas, educational and public service areas, collection storage areas and research spaces.
Its permanent exhibition and special thematic displays explore the Great Wall's history and culture. The permanent exhibition features more than 700 cultural relics, including many on loan from museums across China.
The displays trace over 2,000 years of the Great Wall's construction efforts and showcase how its preservation methods have advanced, from emergency protection to systematic conservation.
Visitors can also better understand the Great Wall's historical roles. Beyond its function as a military defense structure, it also gradually became a site of exchanges and integration among China's ethnic groups.
On the museum's second floor, visitors can enjoy expansive views of the imposing Badaling section outside the venue through glass curtain walls.
The Great Wall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, stretches more than 20,000 kilometers across 15 provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions. Beijing has about 520 kilometers of Great Wall sections in total, and the Badaling section is the most visited. ■

MADRID, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- FC Barcelona hosts Real Madrid in the first 'Clasico' of the season at the Spotify Camp Nou on Sunday night, in what is the biggest game of the season to date in Spain. ====================================================================================================

Psychologists showed extreme metal fans a series of disgusting images, and their reactions stood out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:37 UTC
19:00:37 KST

Fans of extreme metal music appear to view repulsive imagery through a very different lens than the average music listener, according to new research published in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts. When confronted with gruesome artworks, graphic album covers, and gross photographs, enthusiasts of the genre report less disgust and fewer negative reactions than nonfans. These listeners also tend to find grotesque artworks and album covers more amusing, which the authors suggest may reflect a tendency to treat repulsive visuals as safe and playful rather than threatening.
Disgust is a basic human emotion that evolved as an internal alarm system to help people avoid disease-carrying substances like rotting food, bodily fluids, and corpses. While these triggers usually prompt people to look away, the intensity of that reaction varies from person to person, a trait psychologists call disgust propensity. One subculture that actively embraces repulsive themes is extreme metal, an umbrella term for heavy metal subgenres like death metal and grindcore that feature heavily distorted guitars, fast drumming, and guttural, animalistic vocals.
Extreme metal bands routinely center their lyrics, band names, and visual art around gore, mutilation, and decay. While outsiders often experience tension, anger, or revulsion when exposed to this material, dedicated fans report feelings of joy and empowerment. A driving factor behind this appeal may be a personality trait known as morbid curiosity, or an interest in unpleasant topics like death; a 2022 study covered by PsyPost found that people with higher morbid curiosity are more likely to enjoy and listen to violently themed music.
Much of the research on how negative emotions can produce enjoyable artistic experiences has focused on sadness, such as why people enjoy tear-jerker movies, a phenomenon often explained by the feeling of being emotionally moved. Expanding on this idea, the authors of a 2017 theoretical paper argued that art provides a sense of psychological distance that reminds viewers they are physically safe, allowing them to embrace dark or gross emotions as intense, enjoyable experiences. This aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which indicated that people are more willing to look at distressing imagery when it is framed as artwork rather than a real-life photograph because the artistic context lowers the emotional toll.
When safety and distance are established, grotesque material can even become funny. According to a 2010 experimental study, people tend to experience humor and amusement when something violates a social norm or moral standard, provided that the violation simultaneously feels harmless. In a 2025 study of music listeners, Albert Wabnegger, a senior scientist in the Department of Clinical Psychology at the Institute of Psychology at the University of Graz in Austria, and his colleague Anne Schienle found that extreme metal fans generally have a lower tendency to feel disgusted and are less bothered by repulsive sounds, lyrics, and photos than fans of other genres.
“These findings raised an important follow-up question: Do extreme metal fans also have a different aesthetic experience when confronted with disgust-related content?” Wabnegger told PsyPost. “The present study was designed to address this question—and our results indicate that they indeed do.”
In their latest work, Wabnegger and Schienle wanted to look beyond basic revulsion to see how metal fans actually evaluate repulsive imagery as art. They designed an online experiment to test whether fans and nonfans experience different emotional pathways when viewing graphic visuals, and whether humor plays a role in how they process these images.
To measure how people process challenging visuals, the researchers used a psychological framework called the Vienna Integrated Model of Art Perception. This model outlines five possible emotional outcomes a viewer might experience when looking at art: feeling bored and unengaged; feeling surprised by something new; feeling a sense of harmony and being emotionally moved; having a negative experience marked by confusion and a desire to look away; or experiencing a sense of personal insight and mental transformation.
The researchers recruited participants primarily through university campuses and online forums. After filtering out incomplete surveys and responses that were clicked through too quickly to be genuine, they identified 79 extreme metal fans and 208 nonfans. To confirm that the metal fans truly knew the genre, those participants had to name at least one extreme metal band.
To ensure a fair comparison, the researchers used a statistical matching technique to pair extreme metal fans with nonfans of similar age and gender, while excluding people who liked traditional heavy metal but disliked extreme subgenres. This process yielded a final sample of 74 extreme metal fans and 74 matched nonfans, with an average age of about 30 years. Across the entire group of 148 participants, there were 79 men, 62 women, and 7 nonbinary individuals. The study’s design and analysis plan were preregistered.
Participants first completed questionnaires measuring their general interest in art, their preferences for complex or ambiguous artwork, and their everyday disgust propensity, which gauges how grossed out they would feel in hypothetical scenarios like accidentally touching an amputee’s stump. Each person was then randomly assigned to view one of two separate sets of eight images presented in random order (meaning 16 images were used across the study in total). Each set included two disgusting fine artworks (such as a portrait of a face covered in feces), two extreme metal album covers with band names removed, two everyday gross photographs (such as a skin infection), and two neutral control images created by digitally scrambling disgusting pictures into unrecognizable abstract blocks of color.
Beneath each image, participants rated their immediate reactions on a 1-to-5 scale covering the five art perception outcomes (boredom, surprise, feeling moved, negative confusion, and insight), along with how humorous they found the picture. They also used a 0-to-100 sliding scale to rate how familiar the image looked, how much disgust they felt, and how much they liked it.
The questionnaire results showed that extreme metal fans and nonfans had almost identical levels of general art interest and similar preferences for complex art. However, extreme metal fans reported spending more time listening to music (about 151 minutes on average, compared to 100 minutes for nonfans) and scored lower on everyday disgust propensity, averaging 2.21 on a 0-to-4 scale compared to 2.57 for nonfans.
When looking at the images, the two groups diverged in their emotional reactions. On the 0-to-100 scale, extreme metal fans rated the disgusting artworks 12.73 points less disgusting, the album covers 10.09 points less disgusting, and the gross everyday photos 8.86 points less disgusting than nonfans did. Disgust ratings for the scrambled control images were nearly identical across the two groups.
“We were able to replicate the results from our previous study, again showing reduced disgust reactivity to disgusting content in extreme metal fans,” Wabnegger noted. “This suggests that the effect is relatively stable. Moreover, these findings are striking because they show that, under certain conditions, an emotion that is typically strongly aversive can be experienced in a markedly different, and even enjoyable, way.”
Metal fans also expressed greater liking for the stylized gross imagery. On the 100-point scale, they rated their liking of the artworks 11.90 points higher and the album covers 17.56 points higher than nonfans did, while the two groups did not differ in how much they liked the real-life gross photos or the neutral control images. This may suggest that metal fans appreciate grotesque themes specifically in an artistic context, though fans also rated the album covers as more familiar (by about 17 points), which could partly explain their warmer response to that category.
In terms of the five art perception pathways, the two groups did not show reliable differences in boredom, surprise, feeling moved, or experiencing deep insight. However, they differed on the fourth pathway, which tracks negative reactions and confusion. On the 1-to-5 scale, extreme metal fans scored 0.55 points lower in negative confusion for artworks, 0.57 points lower for album covers, and 0.39 points lower for gross photos compared to nonfans, which the authors interpret as a sign they felt less threatened and less inclined to mentally reject the images.
This reduced negativity was accompanied by a rise in amusement. Extreme metal fans rated the artworks 0.62 points higher and the album covers 0.68 points higher in humor on the 5-point scale than nonfans did. They also found the gross photographs and neutral images slightly funnier than nonfans, though those differences were much smaller (0.21 and 0.26 points, respectively).
“The effects we observe are moderate in size, but robust and consistent across different types of disgust-related stimuli,” Wabnegger explained. “This means that extreme metal fans do not simply differ from non-fans by a tiny, trivial margin; rather, there is a reliable shift in how they emotionally and aesthetically respond to disgust-containing content.”
Merrick Powell, who studies fans of violently themed music and led the 2022 morbid curiosity study described earlier, said the results fit with the idea that fans actively reframe dark material rather than passively absorbing it. “I think the most important takeaway is that it aligns with theories of extreme metal fans being active agents in reappraising extreme content even extending to the visual medium associated with the music,” Powell, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Melbourne who was not involved in the new study, told PsyPost.
The authors noted that extreme metal culture frequently treats grotesque subjects with tongue-in-cheek exaggeration, such as the Czech band Gutalax, which builds its album art and live shows around toilet humor. Because fans are familiar with these tropes, they may view grotesque art and album covers as playful, harmless norm violations, allowing them to laugh at material that leaves outsiders unsettled.
“Relative to non-fans, extreme metal fans do not experience disgust primarily as something revulsive; instead, they often feel it differently—as something exciting, fun, and part of an aesthetic experience,” Wabnegger said. “In this sense, they are ‘in the game’: they engage with disgust-related themes as playful, aesthetic elements rather than as purely aversive content. Our work shows that context can transform even ‘disgusting’ material into something enjoyable, highlighting how emotional experience can be reshaped.”
Powell pointed out that this shared sense of absurdity is central to the subculture, and it may set extreme metal apart from standard theories of how people safely embrace dark art, such as the Distancing-Embracing model proposed by Winfried Menninghaus and colleagues.
“One thing that extreme metal and other ‘extreme’ music genre fans report is knowing and realizing the music is often ridiculous and over the top, which is a key appeal,” Powell said. “Hence, it is often seen as funny or absurd, whereas people who are not part of these subcultures often do not realize this is the response or reaction that the in-group fans may have. It can be a bit like ‘being in the joke.’ This is where it might differ from some of the other prevalent theories about typically negative emotions and art, such as Menninghaus et al., Distancing-Embracing model, but we would need to do more to know!”
The authors themselves list that model among several frameworks that could account for their findings, alongside the idea that harmless norm violations become funny.
At the same time, the researchers emphasized that these lower disgust ratings do not mean listeners are cold or desensitized to emotion in general. “One important misinterpretation we want to preempt is the idea that extreme metal fans are somehow emotionally blunted or ‘numb’ because of their reduced disgust reactivity,” Wabnegger explained. “Instead, extreme metal fans tend to experience disgust-related content (such as images depicting decay) as more fun or entertaining. In other words, they are more deeply engaged in the aesthetic and emotional ‘game’ that such content invites.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Because the study measured participants at a single point in time, it cannot determine cause and effect. It remains an open question whether listening to extreme metal gradually desensitizes people and teaches them to find gore funny, or whether people who already have a strong stomach and a dark sense of humor are naturally drawn to the genre in the first place.
Sorting out whether fans are actively reframing gross material, perhaps by enjoying their own reactions to it (what psychologists call metaemotions), or simply becoming accustomed to it will require tools beyond self-report surveys. “It continues an interesting conversation about the role of reappraisal/metaemotions vs desensitization,” Powell noted. “It is a challenging question to answer, but future work involving physiological measures and other ‘pre-conscious’ response indicators in this domain would be really interesting.”
There are a few other limitations to keep in mind. The participant sample had a higher proportion of men, particularly in the extreme metal group, which reflects the male-dominated nature of the metal fanbase but limits how well the findings apply to other demographics. Additionally, the experiment relied entirely on still visual images. Future longitudinal studies tracking listeners over time, as well as experiments combining music with visuals, could help clarify how sound and imagery work together to turn revulsion into entertainment.
“Looking ahead, we aim to investigate the role of humor in the perception of disgust-related content,” Wabnegger said. “Our findings so far suggest that extreme metal fans may not only tolerate such content better, but also be more likely to interpret it as playful or amusing.”
Beyond explaining the appeal of extreme music, Wabnegger suggested that understanding how people use humor to reframe revulsion could eventually help patients in clinical settings. “In the longer term, this line of work could have applied relevance,” he added. “Disgust plays a central role in several mental disorders characterized by heightened disgust reactivity, such as OCD. If humor can modulate how disgust is experienced—turning aversive material into something more playful or manageable—it might offer a promising additional tool for interventions, for example by integrating humorous or ‘gamified’ elements into exposure-based treatments.”
“Our findings also suggest a broader message: emotional responses are not fixed; they are strongly shaped by context, expectations, and shared cultural ‘rules of the game,'” Wabnegger concluded. “And finally, as an avid extreme-metal fan myself: listen to metal!”
The study, “Gore, Guts, and Giggles: Aesthetic Processing of Disgust Stimuli in Extreme Metal Fans,” was authored by Albert Wabnegger and Anne Schienle.

El-Fasher becomes ‘ghost town’ as RSF crimes continue

Breadcrumb
El-Fasher becomes ‘ghost town’ as RSF crimes continue on anniversary of takeover
One year on from the Rapid Support Forces' (RSF) takeover of North Darfur's capital, El Fasher, Amnesty International is warning that the situation remains dire, with unlawful killings, arbitrary detentions, and torture rife, while the population has dropped significantly.
In a report released on Friday, Amnesty said fewer than 70,000 people remain in the city that once had 1 million inhabitants, with humanitarian access remaining limited, and the risk of arrest for returnees high, despite claims by the paramilitary group that people are free to return.
"What we found is that El Fasher is still very much a ghost town," Laura Mills, the author of the report, told The New Arab.
Amnesty's report is based on the testimonies of 25 civilians, including six humanitarian workers, with 15 having fled the city between July and August 2026, and one who remained in the city.
Mills said part of the reason for the desertion of the city was the high risks of being there, which many of the testimonies confirmed.
"We found that many people were detained, including those who tried to return to the city. Often, men were held in prisons and detention centres where they faced torture and truly horrific conditions.
"Women and children were typically held in schools that had been converted into de facto detention centres," she said, with the report noting high levels of malnutrition in said centres.
"Moving around the city, people didn't feel safe; they felt surveilled," Mills added.
Seventeen of the 19 residents Amnesty spoke to had been arbitrarily detained, with the ethnic minority Zaghawa and Masalit people more likely to be detained. Both groups have been targeted by the RSF since the beginning of the war.
RSF killings during the fall of the city have been described as a massacre, with the UN saying that there were "hallmarks of genocide".
Mills said that ethnic minorities are automatically suspected by the RSF of being close to the country's military, which the group is fighting against in the civil war.
Amnesty spoke to those who were detained and put in prison, with many of them stating that RSF soldiers tortured and committed unlawful killings. Mamoun, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man held in Shala prison, said that the group arbitrarily shot prisoners.
Those detained are often released because families pay ransoms to the RSF, which Mills said reach up to $10,000.
She noted that these abuses by the paramilitary group are widespread across RSF-controlled Darfur, though El Fasher's years-long siege fending off the RSF has contributed to widespread suspicion of the city's residents by the group.
Humanitarian workers still operate in the city, though closely monitored by the group, which restricts their movements and prevents aid workers from speaking with residents.
Despite this, humanitarian assessments place the city, alongside much of North Darfur province, in danger of reaching IPC Level 5 famine, the highest threshold possible, in the coming months.
Mills told The New Arab that the international community had all the tools it needed to safeguard El-Fasher's residents and alleviate suffering in the country, but that it was unwilling to use them.
This includes pushing for a ceasefire and talks between the RSF and the military, which was rejected earlier in October by military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, as well as an arms embargo on the country.
"It just really feels like we have all the tools at our disposal, but the world is just sort of looking on as this horrific disaster continues to unfold, and what happened in El Fasher can easily happen somewhere else," Mills said.

Cloud House by Peter Morris brings "fairytale flamboyance" to London

Cloud House by Peter Morris brings “fairytale flamboyance” to London
Marshmallow-pink walls, sweeping arches and turquoise detailing influenced by a trip to Miami animate architect Peter Morris‘s self-designed home in Gospel Oak, London.
Named Cloud House, the eccentric project combines two offset residences, one for Morris and his partner, producer Emily Kennedy, and a second for a neighbour who shares their love of colour.
According to the architect, the goal of the project was to bring joy to passersby, while giving his “love of postmodernism a chance to reveal itself fully”.
“The key goal was to make a beautiful building which I hoped might create a little moment of joy for anyone walking past it on the street,” Morris told Dezeen.
“It’s easy to dismiss colour and pattern in architecture as frivolous, but there’s something about this visual language that triggers an emotional response that’s different from what you’ll get with elegant modernism,” continued Morris.
“For me, that alone tells us we should push for more variety in the built environment and be open – as Camden Council have been with this project – to the idea of more fairytale flamboyance on our streets,” he continued.
Cloud House occupies the site of a now-demolished Victorian home, adjacent to a distinctive church and school, where the couple have lived since 2016.
Its bold colour palette and cloud-like forms were inspired by the couple’s honeymoon in Miami and the city’s vast collection of art deco architecture.
“Emily and I honeymooned in Miami, where we loved the art deco curves of the buildings, and the pink and turquoise colours everywhere,” Morris explained. “In a way this building is an architectural love letter to my wife, so it felt appropriate to have some of that honeymoon spirit in the mix.”
According to Morris, the project also draws on the curved forms of the neighbouring Grade II-listed school and Grade I-listed St Martin’s Church, which Morris said are “fabulously eccentric buildings”.
“The school, which sits in St Martin’s Hall, has a frontage that looks like a Medieval castle,” he said.
“And the church – described by the historian Nikolaus Pevsner as ‘the craziest of London’s Victorian churches’ – has a knock-out interior, with a brightly coloured chancel ceiling and a nave with dramatic wooden arches.”
Cloud House’s main structure is composed of structural steel and blockwork.
This is clad in decorative arches made of polystyrene, sprayed with a waterproof layer and a textured top coat to match the bright pink render on the elevations, and positioned in place by the architect himself.
Morris’s home is the smaller of the pair, located on the right side of the plot. It measures 133 square metres.
The home is accessed from an entrance on its front elevation. It has a large, open-plan ground floor, comprising a lounge, kitchen and the architect’s studio.
Its two upper floors are each fitted with a bedroom and bathroom, while a roof terrace crowns the home, complete with an outdoor bathtub.
Next door, the adjoining 165-square-metre home is accessed by a side entrance and has an upside-down arrangement.
Its ground floor contains a home office with a kitchenette, and a guest ensuite bedroom at the rear. Above is the main bedroom.
The main bedroom has a dressing room and ensuite, and sits alongside another smaller ensuite bedroom.
Meanwhile, the social space with seating, dining and cooking spaces is on the top floor, with an adjoining terrace. A second larger terrace tops the home.
While the interiors of Morris’s house boldly match its vibrant exterior, the interiors for the neighbour’s home were left blank and ready for them to customise.
Interior highlights of the architect’s home include turquoise epoxy floors, colour-drenched bathrooms and an emerald-green striped kitchen.
Cloud House was featured on the TV show Grand Designs in September and has been shared widely on social media. Morris said the response to the project is sharply divided.
“I know that not everyone will love the Cloud House as much as we do – the reactions to it on social media have been either overwhelmingly positive or overwhelmingly negative, with nothing in between,” he reflected.
“My final goal, and hope, is that some of the people that do love it might one day be keen to commission me to create something colourful and joyful for them too.”
Other pink dwellings featured on Dezeen include a concrete “fun house” on the English coast by RX Architects and a guesthouse in the Azores contained within a converted stable.

Our Brains Weren’t Built for This Much Comparison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

More than 20? Or less than 75? As I scan my feedback on a recent social media post, my brain just can’t seem to help registering the number of “likes.” I’m not alone.
Under a recent settlement that Meta recently reached with states, Facebook and Instagram are about to look different for minors Among the new protections, one seemingly modest change caught my eye. By default, users under 18 will no longer be able to see likes and other reactions in response to their posts or those of others. The reforms are designed for children and teenagers, but touch on a psychological phenomenon just as relevant to adults. As a psychiatrist, I found myself wondering: Why does that little number beneath your post matter so much?
The answer has less to do with social media and more to do with an ancient human tendency: social comparison. Social comparison is the psychological process by which people assess themselves, including their own abilities, opinions, and achievements, in relation to those of others. Likes can both reward us and rank us. They show us that people are validating our posts and also quantify that validation.
We know how much approval we receive relative to what we might have expected, what we got the last time we posted, and what others receive. Feedback is scored. Likes are just one example. Follower counts, views, and shares are other metrics that make social information measurable. When social approval is numerically valued, comparison becomes harder to avoid.
From an evolutionary perspective, social comparison may have served an adaptive purpose. Humans evolved in social groups. Knowing where you stood relative to others might have helped you identify what behaviors were approved, whether you belonged, and how to navigate hierarchy. But moving beyond prehistoric time to the last century, comparison still had constraints. Your 25-year high school reunion? It happened once in your lifetime, maybe in a city far away from you, with only your fellow classmates in attendance. Now, the high school reunion lives in the device in our hands, capable of giving anyone quantitative signals from a vast reference group at any moment on our personalized scoreboards of social approval. If the subjective question is whether we belong, what can feel like an objective answer is the 100 likes our post gets from 2,500 followers. The scale, frequency, quantification, and accessibility of social comparison have all changed.
Our brains weren’t built for this much comparison. Neuroimaging studies show that our brains allocate value to how we believe we stack up next to others. Downward social comparison, in which we learn someone performs worse than us, can engage neural circuits associated with reward and valuation. Upward comparison, in which we learn someone performs better than us, can engage neural circuits associated with processing unpleasant emotions. These are ways in which our brains process social outcomes much like other kinds of gains or losses.
But our brains don’t just register numbers; we also tend to evaluate their meaning. In one study, likes functioned as a type of currency that adult users compared themselves on, shaping how they felt in that moment. In another set of studies, adults who made more frequent and extreme upward comparisons reported an immediate decline in self-evaluation and cumulative declines in self-esteem and life satisfaction over a browsing session. Research has also found that across generational groups, greater user tendency to engage in social comparison, together with greater maladaptive ways of coping with emotions, is associated with more symptoms of anger, anxiety, and depression.
Social comparison isn’t inherently harmful. But as repeated opportunities to compare mount, the mental health effects can add up.
While hiding likes may not eliminate social comparison, it does remove a metric from the scoreboard. The instinct to compare or desire to belong won’t just vanish. But even if we might wonder where we stand next to who’s performing better, there’s a difference between wondering and a number answering that question for us.
Social media didn’t invent our instinct to compare ourselves to others. We’ve had that for millennia. What it did was shift the environment surrounding our instincts, encoding one form of social feedback into numbers we can monitor.
That's why changing our relationship with social comparison will mean more than adapting digital platforms. What do we value? What gives us purpose? What makes our lives matter?
The cultural shift that lies ahead is to ask the questions about our social worth that don’t need a scoreboard to answer.

"A butter knife against a nuclear arsenal:" Tech billionaires vastly outspend wealth tax supporters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

“A butter knife against a nuclear arsenal:” Tech billionaires vastly outspend wealth tax supporters
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
More than $351 million in political donations has been poured into a high-stakes contest about a proposed wealth tax on the November ballot, making it one of the most costly campaigns in California history.
About 90% of the money is being spent to defeat a statewide initiative to impose a new tax on the assets of billionaires, a multifaceted opposition effort bankrolled primarily by ultra-rich Californians being targeted by a measure that supporters call an economic reckoning.
The billionaire tax, Proposition 40, would levy a one-time, 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1.
Millions of dollars continue to flow into the campaigns of three intertwined ballot initiatives at the center of the debate: Proposition 40, and Propositions 41 and Proposition 42, which would neuter the Proposition 40 through strategic, esoteric tax law changes.
“The pro-40 campaign picked a fight and then came to that fight with a butter knife against a nuclear arsenal,” said GOP strategist Rob Stutzman, who is not involved in any of the wealth-tax-related ballot measures. “Because they’re so well funded, in today’s multifaceted media world, they are able to show up everywhere from network TV to inside video games. That is a very, very large advantage few campaigns ever get to have.”
But, Stutzman warned, money does not guarantee a win.
In the most expensive ballot measure fights in California history, $463 million was spent on two gambling proposals 2022. The initiatives pitted some of California’s most successful Native American tribes with gaming interests against gambling corporations, including online sports gaming companies DraftKings and FanDuel. Both side’s measure failed.
The tax measure was crafted by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in response to federal healthcare funding cuts signed by President Trump last year that are expected to reduce California’s healthcare budget by $100 billion, burdening the state’s most vulnerable residents.
“Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ slashes healthcare funding, with major coverage cuts scheduled to hit after the midterms,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the union’s chief of staff. “More than 3 million Californians could lose their health insurance. Hospitals and emergency rooms face closure. Patients will die unnecessarily when the care they need is no longer there. Proposition 40 is an emergency response to that looming disaster.”
The proposition’s supporters raised $34.3 million, nearly all of it from Jimenez’s union.
The two other measures, Propositions 41 and 42, would nullify the billionaire tax if either receives more votes.
Proposition 41 supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit. Backers of Proposition 42 argue it would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other forms of personal savings.
Advocates for the billionaire tax say both are well-financed smokescreens to undercut Proposition 40.
Opposition campaigns to the wealth tax as well as the two countermeasures have received enormous donations from several of the state’s billionaires. But Building a Better California, the main funder of efforts to defeat the wealth tax, noted that its allies included Democratic and Republican politicians, prominent labor groups and business leaders.
“It’s rare for such a broad coalition to unite around any single cause in California, but it reflects the potentially devastating impact of this measure on healthcare, education, and our state’s economy,” the group said in a statement.
Among the largest donors opposing the wealth tax are billionaires Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google who has donated more than $100 million to anti-wealth-tax efforts, and former Google leader Eric Schmidt and venture capitalist L. John Doerr, who each kicked in $40 million.
Brin, Schmidt and Doerr did not respond to requests for comment.
The spending disparity also reflects a divide among Democrats and their allies, many of whom support wealth taxes, but argue that the way Proposition 40 was written is disastrous to California’s volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s wealthiest residents.
Jodi Hicks, chief executive and president of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, said that while her organization would support a nationwide or a California wealth tax, their primary concerns are about 40’s impacts on the state budget and healthcare in the state.
“We are opposed to this particular proposal because we think it does more harm than good,” she said, adding that after what her organization “faced last year having to scramble for dollars because of [federal funding cuts] we are committed to work with the stakeholders facing cuts and not harming the budget and finding revenue in a smart way.”
The cash imbalance between supporters and opponents of the billionaire tax is vast. Those opposed to the measure raised $316.7 million, while proponents raised nearly $34.3 million.
The supporters of the wealth tax spent nearly all of their money gathering signatures to place the measure on the ballot. They had $1.6 million on hand as of Oct. 17.
Now, as voters cast ballots, their campaign appears reliant on public events and media coverage, such as of Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) recent rally in support of Proposition 40 in downtown Los Angeles.
“What you are showing people from coast to coast and all over is that, yes, we can take on the greed of the oligarchs,” he said, calling it the most important ballot measure in the country. “Yes, we can create an economy and a government that works for all of us, not just the 1 percent.”
Labor leaders argue that the billionaires tax includes a loophole that would allow state lawmakers to tax the savings and retirement accounts and home equity of all Californians.
Facebook creator and Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg was among the California billionaires Sanders name-checked in his remarks. After Zuckerberg told company leaders that he planned to leave the state to avoid his control over the company substantially reduced by being forced to sell enough of his stock in the social media giant to pay the proposed levy, the company on Wednesday announced the creation of a new, non-voting type of stock that would allow Zuckerberg to sell enough shares to pay the proposed tax while retaining his voting power in exchange for him agreeing to remain in the state for eight years.
The pro-wealth-tax campaign is sending voters emails and texts and has an online presence.
“Remember: it’s not enough to vote YES on 40. You also need to vote NO on 41 + 42,” read an email sent to voters on Tuesday. “Don’t be fooled: Props 41 and 42 are billionaire-funded initiatives designed specifically to undermine Prop 40, the California Billionaire Tax.”
Meanwhile, the anti-40 and pro-42 campaigns are inundating voters on television, streaming services, in mailboxes, through online influencers and even in digital video games such as Sim City.
Jimenez said voters will see through the blizzard of campaign messaging.
“The billionaires think voters are stupid. They think they can bury the facts under millions of dollars in advertising and disguise Prop. 42 ... as protection for ordinary taxpayers,” she said. “Their spending also makes our case for us. When billionaires can afford to spend millions a day protecting their fortunes, voters can see that billionaires have plenty of money to spare.”
Sheri Sadler, a veteran Democratic media buyer, questioned how much voters were hearing about the rationale for the proposed billionaire tax.
“The yes side is severely lacking in getting their message through while the no side is dipping into different kinds of pockets,” she said.
Jessica Levinson, an election law professor at Loyola Law School, said that beyond voter confusion about the competing ballot measures, it is certain to face legal challenges, notably about the retroactive nature of the tax, which would apply to any billionaire who lived in California as of Jan. 1. She described that as “the biggest legal pressure point.”
“It’s kind of a mess,” she said.
Times staff writer Gabrielle LaMarr LeMee contributed to this report.

Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies

Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies
Olena "Jane" Sharhovska, a veteran of the Hospitallers medical battalion who worked as a translator and journalist in civilian life, has died. Olena had been saving wounded soldiers since 2015.
Source: Yana Zinkevych, commander of the Hospitallers medical battalion; Sharhovska's former colleagues at Novynarnia
Details: Olena had extensive experience in the media, working as a journalist, translator, editor and social media specialist. Over the course of her career, she worked in television and print media, as well as on projects for Ukraїner and Osvitoria.
From 2015 onwards, she dedicated herself to saving others. Jane volunteered on the front line with the First Volunteer Mobile Hospital named after Mykola Pyrohov. She later joined the Hospitallers.
"Having mastered tactical medicine, Jane went to evacuate the wounded from the hottest sections of the front line, snatching the lives of our soldiers from the jaws of death on the way to stabilisation points," Zinkevych said.
In addition to helping the wounded, the paramedic and her fellow servicewomen campaigned for women's right to serve in the Armed Forces of Ukraine on an equal footing with men.
In particular, she became a co-organiser of the Invisible Battalion March, an event held in Kyiv in 2016. Participants called on the authorities to allow women to hold military positions that had previously been open only to men.
Jane was in Portugal when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. An injury prevented her from returning to Ukraine immediately, but she supported the country as a volunteer.
On 10 September 2022, her birthday, Olena joined the military. Serving with the International Legion of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, she was deployed in Bakhmut, Toretsk and Kharkiv Oblast.
In addition to carrying out medical evacuations, Jane provided tactical medicine training to other service members and, as a member of the Women's Veteran Movement, campaigned for female defenders to receive proper equipment.
She was discharged from military service in August 2024 due to health reasons.
"Olena was a person of words and travel, with a deep interest in the world and in people [...] Despite all the difficulties and trials, she retained her love of words and people, continued helping her brothers- and sisters-in-arms with fundraising, and bought vehicles for the front.
"Her motto in life was: 'Do what you believe needs to be done, and then come what may,'" Novynarnia said.
Bohdan Lohvynenko, a serviceman, journalist, writer and founder of Ukraїner, also shared his memories of Olena.
"We lived in neighbouring buildings in Vynohradar and often sat in one of our kitchens discussing editorial matters. You were an enormous source of support and a driving force behind many processes, while at the same time remaining quite harsh towards the unknown. I would always remind you of what you had once said about those whose ranks you later joined. And we often laughed about it," her former colleague wrote.
Background: Earlier, Yaryna Nishtuk, a defender from Lviv who served as a platoon commander of strike unmanned aerial systems, was killed in action.
