Israeli army extends Hebron siege into second day, arrests 19 Palestinians across occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:50:11 UTC
18:50:11 KST

The Israeli army continued its siege of Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank for a second consecutive day on Saturday, forcing dozens of Palestinians from their homes, according to Palestinian media.
Israeli forces raided the al-Jilda and Deir Bahha areas in central Hebron and placed them under a complete siege, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The army also forced dozens of residents to leave their homes and stand outdoors in the early morning hours, according to the news agency.
The incursion involved the deployment of additional military vehicles and bulldozers, the closure of main entrances and roads leading to Hebron, and the isolation of the city from surrounding areas, Wafa said.
It said Israeli forces also raided and searched homes, detained dozens of residents and subjected them to field interrogations before releasing them on Saturday morning.
Separately, Israeli forces detained 19 Palestinians in raids across the occupied West Bank.
The arrests included two Palestinians from the Hindaza area and al-Azza refugee camp in Bethlehem governorate, 16 from Nablus governorate and a young man from Aqabat Jabr refugee camp in Jericho.
The occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, has seen an escalation in Israeli military attacks and violence by occupiers since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023.
The attacks have included killings and arrests of Palestinians, demolitions of homes and other structures, the burning of mosques and vehicles, and the levelling of agricultural land.
They have also involved restrictions on farmers' access to their fields, the displacement of Palestinian communities and the expansion of settlements.
On Friday, the Israeli army claimed that two Palestinians were killed in a shootout with Israeli forces.
The army alleged that the Palestinians had opened fire at illegal Israeli settlers in Hebron, wounding five people.
Following the reported shooting, the Israeli army announced on Friday a complete closure of Hebron and several surrounding towns.

Ashoke Sen: Indian Physicist honoured with 2026 Oskar Klein Medal for string theory work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:50:04 UTC
18:50:04 KST

Ashoke Sen, a distinguished physicist from ICTS, is honored with the prestigious 2026 Oskar Klein Medal.
Physicist Ashoke Sen has been awarded the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal, becoming the first physicist from India to receive this honour.Sen, who holds the ICTS-infosys Madhava chair professorship at the International centre for theoretical sciences (ICTS), tata institute of fundamental research (TIFR), Bengaluru, is widely recognised for his pioneering contributions to modern string theory.String theory proposes that the fundamental building blocks of matter are tiny, one-dimensional strings rather than point-like particles. The theory seeks to provide a unified framework for understanding matter and the forces governing interactions between its constituents.Established in 1988, the Oskar Klein Medal is named after Swedish theoretical physicist Oskar Klein. It is awarded annually by stockholm university and the nobel committee for physics of the royal swedish academy of sciences.As part of the oskar klein memorial lectures, a distinguished researcher is invited each year to deliver a lecture in klein's memory and receive the medal.Sen delivered his memorial lecture, titled ‘gravity from strings and strings from gravity’, on October 22 at the AlbaNova university centre in Stockholm.His presentation explored how string theory can provide a consistent quantum description of gravity and help address unresolved questions surrounding the quantum physics of black holes.
Contributions to modern string theory
A recipient of the Padma Shri in 2001 and the Padma Bhushan in 2013, Sen has made several influential theoretical contributions that have helped shape the field of string theory.His work was recognised with the breakthrough prize in fundamental physics in 2012. The research helped establish the idea that different string theories could be understood as distinct limits of a single underlying theory.
Congratulating Sen on the achievement, ICTS director Rajesh Gopakumar said, “On behalf of all of us, very warm congratulations to Ashoke. It has been no less than wonderful having Ashoke with us and setting the tone for excellence here at ICTS.”In a statement, ICTS highlighted Sen's internationally recognised contributions to S-duality, the precise counting of black-hole entropy and string field theory, describing them as key areas of work that have helped shape modern string theory.
Previous recipients of the Oskar Klein Medal
The medal has previously been awarded to several prominent scientists, including Kip Thorne in 2016, Peter Higgs in 2009 and Stephen Hawking in 2003.Other recipients include nobel laureates Hans E. Bethe, who received the medal in 1990; Steven Weinberg, honoured in 1989; and Chen Ning Yang, who was the recipient in 1988.

France mounts huge security operation as protesters prepare to march
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:42:10 UTC
18:42:10 KST

France protests begin under heavy security as police seek to prevent fresh unrest; 135 arrested
- France saw protests under heavy security, with 70,000 police deployed and 135 arrests made as officials tried to stop fresh unrest after last weekend’s riots.
- Shops, museums and metro stations shut in Paris, while police used tear gas in Lyon and moved the main march away from the city centre after a legal fight.
- Protesters said the government was over-reacting, while tensions rose after a deadly shooting near Paris and as the far-right National Rally held a congress in Orleans.
AI generated
PARIS - Demonstrators gathered in Paris and cities across France on Saturday under the watch of 70,000 police officers, as the government sought to prevent a repeat of the riots and looting that rocked the country last weekend.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 135 people had been arrested nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons.
“We have to be ultra, ultra responsive. We have significant calls for disruption from political groups and quite simply from criminals,” he told reporters. “It is going to be a long day.”
While the start of the main Paris march was peaceful, police fired tear gas at crowds in Lyon, France’s third-largest city.
The government has deployed 10,000 more police and gendarmes than on Oct 17, when protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services descended into some of the worst unrest France has seen in years.
Shops, museums shut
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
“There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open,” said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
“Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be,” said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
The route for Paris’ main demonstration was settled only after a legal battle triggered by a last-minute police order moving organisers away from the city centre towards the southeastern fringes of the capital.
Police argued that the original route passed through areas with a high concentration of businesses similar to those targeted last weekend. Leftist leaders said the late change was aimed at causing confusion and keeping people away.
“Once again, those in power are creating disruption for the marches and impossible deadlines for organisations to reorganise themselves,” said hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the crowds on the streets of Paris.
Far-right party holds congress
Many demonstrators accused the government of over-reacting, with soldiers dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees. “We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round,” said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
“My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win,” she added.
The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orleans, around 120km south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.
Tensions were heightened by a shooting west of Paris on Friday in which a gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
“We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party. REUTERS

Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:39:23 UTC
18:39:23 KST

Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Kiev has moved to block a planned tribute to Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich, who was involved in the killing of an estimated 100,000 Poles during World War II ethnic purges, officials in Warsaw have claimed.
The reported retreat comes amid a series of disputes between the two countries in recent months over Kiev’s veneration of Nazi-linked figures that have eroded Polish support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
The controversy erupted on Tuesday when the Lviv Regional Council in western Ukraine voted to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and to celebrate the 120th anniversary of its commander Roman Shukhevich while deciding to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national patriotic rallies on the occasion.
The move triggered a fierce response in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and Shukhevich as a key “architect” of the massacres. Before becoming a UPA leader, Shukhevich served in Nazi Germany’s Nachtigall Battalion and the German-controlled 201st Schutzmannschaft Battalion, which operated in occupied Belarus.
On Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned the resolution as “unwise” and “suicidal tactics,” saying it “harms Ukraine,” while Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called the move “unacceptable,” warning that it would deepen divisions between the neighboring countries. Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski called for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremeta, to be put on a list of individuals deemed undesirable in Poland.
Following the backlash, Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said on Wednesday that officials of Vladimir Zelensky’s office had assured Warsaw that the controversial resolutions would not come into force. On Friday, Tusk echoed the claim, saying that Zelensky had personally signaled he would not endorse the resolution, adding that the Ukrainian leader was “unhappy” with the situation.
This also came after the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry called the Shukhevich tribute in Lviv “counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations.” The ministry stressed that the local authorities had sought no advice from government bodies to assess the consequences of their actions.
An unnamed source in Zelensky’s office cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda went so far as to describe the decision as a “catastrophe.” “Ukraine looks erratic. We have just resolved the previous crisis – and now this,” the source said, accusing regional officials of pursuing “cheap one-day hype” despite knowing all too well what the resolution would lead to.
While senior Ukrainian officials apparently distanced themselves from the controversy, the Lviv council’s original announcement remains accessible as of Saturday. Sheremet also previously defended the resolution, saying “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory.”
The dispute is the latest in a series of heated clashes between Kiev and Warsaw over Ukraine’s continued veneration of nationalist figures that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II.
In May, Zelensky awarded an elite Ukrainian special operations unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA,” prompting another diplomatic uproar, with Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripping the Ukrainian leader of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration.

How much must the world cut emissions to return to 1.5°C?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:37:45 UTC
18:37:45 KST

How much must the world cut emissions to return to 1.5°C?
The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, published on October 21, outlines a scenario in which global temperatures peak at 1.7°C to 1.8°C above preindustrial levels around midcentury before returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100. The scenario has about a 50% chance of success.
The required cuts are measured against 2025 emissions levels. Emissions would also need to fall 69% by 2040, the report says.
Current national climate pledges fall far short. Even if countries fully implement their existing commitments, emissions would decline by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said the world could still limit the scale and duration of warming above 1.5°C.
Under current policies, global warming could reach 2.8°C this century and continue rising afterward, the report warns.
If countries meet their existing climate pledges and maintain similar efforts, warming could reach 2.6°C. Even if they fulfill their pledges and achieve additional net zero targets, temperatures would still rise by about 2.1°C.
Every 5 years of continued CO2 emissions at current levels could add about 0.1°C to peak warming, the report estimates.
Returning to 1.5°C would also require removing and permanently storing around 320 billion tons of CO2 from the atmosphere over the course of this century. That is equivalent to roughly 8 years of global CO2 emissions at 2024 levels. The report cautions that technological and economic challenges make achieving this uncertain.
Renewable energy
Despite the gap between current efforts and the required cuts, UNEP points to progress since the adoption of the Paris Agreement.
Renewable energy has expanded rapidly, coal and oil supplies have grown more slowly than previously projected, and climate policies have reduced emissions in several countries and sectors.
An assessment of more than 220 policy evaluations found that electricity sector policies reduced emissions by an average of 9%. Economic measures, including carbon taxes and emissions trading systems, cut emissions by 5% to 13% across the sectors studied.
However, these gains remain concentrated in particular countries, sectors and periods. Governments need to expand and sustain successful measures to achieve the necessary global reductions, the report says.
New targets for 2035 and 2040
To align with the lowest possible 1.5°C overshoot scenario, global renewable electricity capacity would need to reach at least three times its 2025 level by 2035 and 4.5 times that level by 2040.
Over the same period, the energy intensity of global economic output would need to fall by at least 30% by 2035 and 40% by 2040, relative to 2025.
The report also calls for major cuts in fossil fuel use. By 2035, the shares of coal, oil and gas in total global energy supply would need to fall by at least 55%, 15% and 5%, respectively, compared with 2025. By 2040, the required reductions would reach 75%, 30% and 35%.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that more than half of the estimated heat-related deaths in 854 European cities between 2000 and 2025 were attributable to human-induced climate change.

David Degtyarev became the Asian Para Games champion in the men's -54 kg division, lifting 192 kg to set a new Asian Para Games record. Tursynay Kabyl won a silver medal in the women's -41 kg category, while Alina Solodukhina earned silver in the -45 kg class.
Stanislav Shakiyev and Aizhan Berimkulova took bronze medals in their individual events. Additionally, the Kazakh men's team, comprising Yerbolat Karibay, David Degtyarev, and Stanislav Shakiyev, won a bronze medal in the team competition.

Islam Salimov earned silver in the men's long jump T13, while Dastan Mukashbekov secured silver in the men's shot put F36. Bronze medals in the shot put were claimed by Ivan Zaleznyak (F36) and Makhambet Serikkaliyev (F53).
Additionally, Aisulu Suleimenova set a new Asian record in the women's 100 meters T62, clocking a time of 16.18 seconds.

In Para archery, Team Kazakhstan won two medals — one silver and one bronze.

Thus, Kazakhstan concluded its campaign at the 5th Asian Para Games with 50 medals, including 12 gold, 16 silver, and 22 bronze, and finished ninth overall in the final standings.
The 5th Asian Para Games took place from October 18 to 24, 2026, in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, Japan.

British ships defy Chinese warnings in South China Sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:27:12 BST
18:27:12 KST

Two Royal Navy patrol ships have finished a ten day exercise in the South China Sea alongside Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, working with fifth generation fighters, a Singaporean submarine and New Zealand boarding teams, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Spey and HMS Tamar led the British contribution to Bersama Lima 2026, the annual exercise of the Five Power Defence Arrangements, whose name means Together Five in Malay. The participating navies brought corvettes, frigates, patrol ships and a submarine, and the exercise built from familiarisation scenarios to a two day war game.
Before sailing, the crews spent a week learning each other’s vessels, systems, procedures and the language they would use at sea so that they could work together once the pace picked up. The maritime phase covered boarding and searching suspect vessels, naval gunfire directed onto targets ashore by soldiers embarked in the ships, a submarine hunt and an air defence exercise supported by aircraft.
Commander Tom Lindsey, the commanding officer of HMS Tamar, said: “Bersama Lima was an excellent opportunity to put my ship’s company through their paces and refresh their war-fighting skills with our Five Power allies.
“There was a great breadth to this iteration of Bersama Lima: fifth-generation fighter jets, international boarding teams and Singapore’s newest submarine which, combined with the level of competence and professionalism showed, levelled up the experience gained.
“These war-fighting serials demonstrated that we can put a task group together in short order and successfully operate together to achieve a spectrum of scenarios.”
Tamar hosted a Royal New Zealand Navy Deployable Boarding Team which was put through repeated serials investigating suspected illegal fishing and narcotics smuggling, work the team and the ship will be doing for real on their next mission.
Able Seaman Mansfield, one of Tamar’s seaman specialists, said: “Driving a Kiwi boarding team up to a suspect vessel with a second sea boat, armed to the teeth, was a surreal experience which really brought the exercise to life.
“We also got the opportunity to replenish underway at sea where we exchanged some goods from home with HMAS Stalwart, who sent Tim Tams [Australia’s favourite biscuit] in return!”
A sailor from HMS Spey said: “It was a privilege to attend Bersama Lima 26 alongside our FPDA partners, an exercise which demonstrates over five decades of commitment to training and working together.
“Throughout the harbour phase, HMS Spey’s sailors took the opportunity to learn from each of the Five Power nations and share their skills to enhance interoperability and build stronger friendships in the region.”
Each British operation in the region since has drawn the same response as Beijing previously accused Britain of flexing its naval muscles over the 2021 carrier deployment. After HMS Spey passed through the Taiwan Strait in June 2025, Senior Captain Liu Runke, spokesman for the navy of the People’s Liberation Army Eastern Theatre Command, said British remarks about the transit had distorted legal principles, and that troops remained on high alert and would resolutely counter all threats and provocations.
When Spey exercised navigation rights and freedoms around the Spratly Islands in May this year, China’s ambassador to the United Kingdom said the 2016 arbitration award was illegal, null and void and that the British position would not shake China’s resolve, as this publication reported at the time. In July the Chinese Embassy in London told Britain to stop stirring up trouble after it backed a statement on the same award, and the embassy’s position was set out again as the two ships entered the sea at the start of this month.
Spey and Tamar are Batch 2 River class offshore patrol vessels, each crewed by around sixty sailors. They have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021 under Operation Highwall. The Five Power Defence Arrangements date from 1971 and remain the only standing multilateral defence arrangement in the region involving Britain.
Spey is now heading to south-east Asia for several weeks of patrols and diplomatic engagement, while Tamar is making for Australia and New Zealand by way of Pacific island chains, where she will carry out maritime security patrols and counter illegal fishing.

Owners of mobile phones that are not set to update their time automatically, or users who prefer not to rely on automatic updates, can adjust their devices manually. They can also restore automatic date and time synchronization at any point.
Android
Android menus vary across models, but time settings are generally found in the device's main Settings menu or under the clock settings.
In Settings, select "Date & Time" and disable the "Automatic date and time" option. Then select the appropriate time zone – Jerusalem – and set the time and date manually.
iPhone
In Settings, select "General," then "Date & Time." Turn off "Set Automatically," select the appropriate time zone and adjust the clock manually.

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometres per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.

Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
LIMITATIONS ORDER
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio Review: The Best Smart Glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.
“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”
The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.
It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)
It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

Trump’s Iran pause is for November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:12:09 UTC
18:12:09 KST

President Trump’s pre-midterm pause on strikes against Iran landed as a claim of diplomatic momentum, not a concession of failure. The pause was framed as proof that negotiations are working. Look closer, and a different mechanism appears. The war meant to project strength has become an electoral liability, and the president’s response is to bury its most visible costs until voters have finished deciding. Then the option can reopen.
The White House insists Washington is negotiating from strength. Military options remain on the table. The blockade stays in force. The administration has not ended the war, only hidden its sharpest edges from the campaign season. That sequence matters. It allows Republican candidates to campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or another energy-price spike, while preserving the argument that renewed action may be warranted later. Nothing has been settled. Everything has been postponed.
Trump’s political identity rested on rejecting costly, open-ended foreign interventions. His appeal to swaths of the MAGA movement included the claim that American leaders had squandered resources and neglected domestic problems chasing overseas conflicts. “America First” was a promise about priorities as much as power.
The Iran war has strained that promise to its breaking point.
Back in February 2026, it looked like a pressure campaign: force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. Months later, it’s a drawn-out confrontation with no clear settlement. Rising fuel prices, stubborn inflation, and the uncertainty over how long the war will last have turned it into a domestic political problem.
Consumer sentiment has fallen close to a record low, dragged down by rising living costs linked to the conflict.
This creates a tension the Republican coalition cannot easily absorb. Some supporters prioritize nationalist strength and a confrontational stance toward Iran. Others were drawn by pledges to avoid costly wars and focus on economic grievances at home. An extended conflict makes satisfying both impossible. Pausing attacks before the midterms offers a way to postpone the reckoning.
The question is whether this pause is a genuine step toward peace or simply an attempt to protect Republicans from the political costs of an unpopular war. The attacks may have stopped, but the naval blockade remains in place, economic pressure on Iran continues, and neither side appears any closer to a lasting agreement. Trump has ruled out further strikes before 3rd November. What he has not ruled out is a return to military action once the election is over. This sequence allows the administration to present the pause as controlled progress, lets Republican candidates campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or energy-price spikes, and preserves the option of arguing later that renewed action may be warranted.
The reports tell a different story than the public messaging. The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale operations. Discussions involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have touched on a major new operation before elections in both countries. The White House calls such reports false. But the military remains on alert, and preparations are being finalised.
For many MAGA voters who supported Trump in part because he promised to reject endless wars, a purely electoral pause represents a significant contradiction.
An unpopular foreign war won’t turn MAGA loyalists into Democrats. The real hazard for the GOP is exhaustion: an endless conflict paired with painful pump prices gives frustrated voters every reason to leave their ballots on the kitchen table.
By removing the immediate threat of renewed attacks, Trump can try to prevent the war from becoming the dominant symbol of Republican failure and shift attention toward negotiations. If the conflict remains relatively quiet until November 3, Republican prospects improve. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, congressional scrutiny of military spending and presidential war powers would intensify.
This is where the powerless ballot enters the picture. Elections are meant to give citizens influence over decisions made in their name. That relationship weakens when a president can temporarily reduce the visibility of a policy’s costs until after ballots are cast, then resume the same course. Trump’s approach could turn the midterms into a debate over whether he appears willing to pull back from the war, rather than whether his Iran policy has actually changed. Americans are already feeling the strain of higher living costs, and consumer confidence has fallen sharply. A brief pause in the fighting will do little to ease that burden, much less resolve the underlying conflict. What is needed is a lasting diplomatic settlement, not a temporary break that leaves the same problems unresolved.
Neither a Republican nor a Democratic outcome automatically resolves the strategic problem. Iran has its own calculations.
Iranian officials continue to demand sanctions relief and an end to the blockade while Washington insists on further concessions. A pause that leaves these disagreements unresolved may simply delay the next confrontation.
The bigger question is not whether Trump keeps his promise before the election, but what he plans to do once the votes are counted and the political pressure has eased. If the coming weeks bring a verifiable agreement backed by credible safeguards, the pause could be a genuine first step toward ending the war. If instead November 3 is treated as the moment political restraints disappear, then the restraint will have functioned primarily as an electoral maneuver.
In that case the danger is clear. Voters are being asked to endorse the appearance of an ending while the means to continue the conflict remain intact. The ballot becomes a ratification of a decision already made elsewhere.
If the fighting resumes after the votes are counted, the question will no longer be whether Trump delivered peace, but whether his supporters were ever given a genuine choice between peace and a war that had only been postponed.

Expert warns of complex ecological fallout from Mongolia grassland fire linked to Japanese company
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:06:24 CST
18:06:24 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A large grassland fire in Mongolia reportedly linked to activities by a Japanese company's subsidiary may have caused extensive ecological damage, with its broader environmental impact requiring comprehensive assessment, an expert said.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Mongolia's eastern province of Dornod. The flames were extinguished on Oct. 16, according to Mongolian media reports. Japanese telecommunications operator KDDI said on Oct. 20 that the fire was linked to activities by its Mongolian subsidiary Mobicom.
The fire may have affected not only grasslands but also riverbanks, wetlands and other ecosystems, said Wang Qinxue, a researcher at Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies who has long studied the region's ecological environment.
A comprehensive assessment is needed to determine whether soil conditions can recover alongside vegetation, whether wildlife can safely survive the winter and whether the fire has caused any transboundary environmental pollution, Wang said.
Preliminary data released by Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change showed that the fire had burned about 530,000 hectares of land, including approximately 470,000 hectares within the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, accounting for 79.8 percent of the reserve's total area.
Located in eastern Mongolia near the Chinese border, the reserve features a mix of grasslands, forests, rivers and wetlands. It provides habitats for a variety of wildlife and plays an important role in conserving local biodiversity, Wang said.
Even if vegetation regrows the following year, plant species composition and soil conditions may not recover at the same pace, he said.
Assessing damage to forest ecosystems is particularly complex, requiring an examination of tree survival rates, the availability of seed sources and the growth of new seedlings to determine the extent of damage and the potential for recovery, Wang added.
The fire's potential transboundary ecological effects also warrant further investigation. It remains necessary to determine whether ash and sediment could be carried into rivers and wetlands by surface runoff and whether smoke from the fire had crossed national borders through the atmosphere, Wang said.
Citing research on Mongolia's Dornod Province, Wang said fire occurrence from autumn through the following spring was associated with the number of dust storm days in spring.
Reduced vegetation cover after a fire leaves soil more vulnerable to wind erosion and makes surface materials easier to transport by wind, he said.
Wang called for systematic surveys of the burned areas, categorized by ecosystem type, to scientifically assess the actual damage and determine the scope for ecological recovery. ■

The following are some highlights of his remarks.
Sept. 13, 2026
At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Xi said all countries, regardless of their size, strength or wealth, are equal members of the international community.
"Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and ensure the equal participation of all countries in international affairs," he said.
July 17, 2026
At the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai, Xi said that AI is an invaluable asset that encapsulates humanity's collective wisdom.
"We should practice true multilateralism and recognize the important role of the United Nations," he said. "We should enhance alignment and coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards, so as to form a consensus-based global governance framework at an early date to make this frontier technology better benefit humanity."
Sept. 1, 2025
At the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting in north China's port city of Tianjin, Xi said the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations must be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"We should firmly safeguard the status and authority of the United Nations, and ensure its irreplaceable, key role in global governance," he said.
Aug. 30, 2025
When meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the SCO Summit 2025, Xi said that China will always be a trustworthy partner of the United Nations.
China is willing to deepen cooperation with the United Nations, support the United Nations in playing a central role in international affairs, and jointly shoulder the responsibility of safeguarding world peace and promoting development and prosperity, Xi told Guterres.
June. 28, 2024
At the conference marking the 70th anniversary of the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence held in Beijing, Xi said that in the face of new developments and challenges, "the authority and central role of the United Nations can only be strengthened rather than weakened."
"The purposes and principles of the UN Charter are never outdated, and they are getting ever more important," he said. "China advocates the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit, and China believes in true multilateralism." ■

Thirty-three British warships left service since 2010
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

18:01:44 KST

Thirty-three Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service since 2010, of which eight have been sold, fifteen recycled and ten are still waiting to be disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, had asked how many warships had been taken out of service, sold or scrapped in each year since 2010.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Since 2010, 33 Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service. Of these, 8 have been sold, 15 have been recycled and 10 are pending disposal.
“As vessels may be withdrawn from service in one year and sold or scrapped in a later year, these categories are not mutually exclusive, and the figures should not be aggregated.
“As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government is investing in new frigates, amphibious ships, new submarines and new standardised vessels alongside a new Hybrid Navy of uncrewed and autonomous systems to increase our Navy’s lethality and deterrence.”
Thirteen new frigates are being built across two classes, eight Type 26 anti-submarine ships on the Clyde and five Type 31 general purpose ships at Rosyth, and Norway has since selected the Type 26 design for its own fleet. Three Fleet Solid Support ships are under construction to resupply the carrier groups, new transport ships are planned to take over from the amphibious and Bay class vessels. The submarine service is completing the Astute class before moving to the four Dreadnought ballistic missile boats and then to SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, which ministers have said will be delivered at a rate of one every eighteen months from the mid-2030s.
The period covered includes the retirement of the Type 42 destroyers, the progressive withdrawal of the Type 23 frigates, and the decision to dispose of the amphibious assault ships Albion and Bulwark, the latter of which is being sold to Brazil.

Inside the Supermassive Debate Over the James Webb Telescope’s ‘Little Red Dots’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
Astronomers built the James Webb Space Telescope to pick up faint light from the first billion years after the Big Bang, a chaotic era when vast swaths of hydrogen and helium gas gathered into the chains of galaxies we see today. Even in the telescope’s first images, astronomers could see a whole zoo of mysterious smears of light.
One batch of objects proved especially difficult to interpret. They glowed blindingly bright, emitting red light with long wavelengths and shining as brilliantly as a whole galaxy. They were tiny, spanning just a pixel. And they were everywhere. A couple appear in almost every image Webb takes. In 2023, researchers started calling them “little red dots.” Astronomers have repeatedly pointed Webb toward the little red dots, wringing precious new information from these pixels of light.
Initially, researchers thought the dots looked kind of like galaxies. Later, they concluded that little red dots look more like the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of most galaxies. These monstrous masses are themselves dark, but their formidable gravity violently vacuums up gas and other nearby matter, generating rings of hot, swirling detritus that completely outshine the stars around them.
Then, in the spring of 2025, two teams of astronomers simultaneously announced observations of a pair of little red dots that were unlike all the rest. In fact, they were unlike any object ever seen.
“In all the millions of [observations] we’ve taken with ground-based telescopes,” said Anna de Graaff, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg, Germany, and head of one group, “there’s nothing that looks like these sources.”
The two teams of astronomers propose that they are looking at a new astronomical object: a topsy-turvy lump of hydrogen that shines with the light of billions of suns while hiding a black hole deep in its core. They call it a “black hole star.”
In a paper posted in September, astronomers took this analysis a step further. They argued that the Webb telescope is witnessing the births of supermassive black holes inside the cores of colossal stars. “There is a fundamentally new phenomenon afoot,” said Rohan Naidu, an astronomer at the University of Hawai’i.
But not everyone agrees with this bold interpretation. It has sparked a flurry of follow-up research and reignited a fierce debate over the nature of these peculiar pinpricks of light. “The field has gotten very polarized,” said Anna-Christina Eilers, an astrophysicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who studies little red dots.
When all you can see is a speck, it’s hard to tell what you’re looking at. All you know about it is its color and brightness. Astronomers first argued that little red dots were distant galaxies on the cosmic horizon, mainly because of their brightness. But galaxies that bright would have to be huge—and there was no known way for them to grow so big in just hundreds of millions of years. Astronomers dubbed them “universe breakers” for the way they seemed to demolish the standard cosmic timeline.
Then they took a closer look. De Graaff led one survey, called Red Unknowns: Bright Infrared Extragalactic Survey (Rubies), and Naidu co-led another survey, called Mirage or Miracle (MOM). These were two of a wave of surveys that trained the Webb telescope on distant objects, including little red dots, for hours at a time. They tabulated precisely what shades of light were coming from each dot and how bright the shades were. This detailed color breakdown, known as a spectrum, told astronomers a far more detailed story than the initial observations had. Different atoms shine in subtly different hues, so the spectrum provided a sense of what the object’s particles were doing.
The bombshell discovery in the little-red-dot spectra was that the colors of hydrogen were smeared out across multiple shades. Usually, seeing such an effect means you’re looking straight at an exposed black hole. Black holes whip hydrogen clouds around them at furious rates, with the clouds emitting slightly different colors depending on their speed. The net effect is that instead of seeing just the hue of hydrogen, you see a range of colors called a broad line. The wider this range, the faster the fastest hydrogen clouds are flying—and the more massive the black hole.
Many astronomers concluded that big black holes dotted the universe, washing out the light of the stars in their host galaxies. As black holes, the little red dots would appear red because dust—grainy stuff much more complicated than gas—was blocking their blue light.
Yet they still seemed weird. Most supermassive black holes flicker as they gulp down chunky streams of gas around them. They also beam powerful x-rays across the universe. Most little red dots seemed to be doing neither of these things.
But that didn’t trouble astronomers much; they expected to see some strangeness during the pandemonium of the early universe. And at least the black holes weren’t breaking any cosmological theories.
Then, in the spring of 2025, de Graaff’s and Naidu’s teams unveiled the two strangest dots yet.
What made these two little red dots exceptional was how red they were. Webb picked up almost no light in the bluer hues of their spectra. And at a particular shade of red, the colors abruptly got much, much brighter. This feature, known as a Balmer break, is something you see when looking at a hot ball of hydrogen gas—typically, certain types of stars or galaxies, which are made of many stars. Deep in a star’s core, nuclear fusion pumps out heat and light, which slowly filters up to the star’s surface. There, hydrogen atoms can become energized in a way that blocks bluer light and lets through only redder light. These red colors have a hump-shaped spectrum that reveals the overall temperature of the star’s surface.
But the new little red dots couldn’t literally be stars—they were way too bright. And they didn’t look much like black holes either. Black holes have an assortment of ringlike structures of different temperatures. They don’t typically produce a Balmer break, or the red, hump-shaped curve indicative of a stellar surface burning at a uniform 5,000 or so degrees Kelvin.
Naidu and de Graaff concluded that they were looking at the first examples of something combining the vigor of a black hole with the outward appearance of a star: a black hole star.
From the outside, a black hole star would appear as a huge agglomeration of hydrogen gas. If our sun were replaced with a black hole star, it would extend a dozen times farther than the orbit of Pluto. Out toward the edge, the star would boil unstably, sloughing off outer layers and explosively ejecting mass. “It’s going to be a very messy system where stuff is being blown out and falling back in,” de Graaff said. “I wouldn’t want to come too close.”
Deep in the center, invisible to the outside world, the star would be powered by a black hole. This black hole would pull gas around it, dramatically heating it and pushing light and energy outward, which would keep the outer layers of hydrogen from collapsing inward. In this way, the black hole would form the “engine” of the star, analogous to the fusion-powered core of our sun. Moving outward, material swirling around the black hole would beam out a range of colors that would slowly make their way toward the surface.
And as with certain stars, the hydrogen near the surface would stop the bluer light while letting the redder light pass through. The end result would be a gassy surface shining as brightly as a more exposed black hole but with the Balmer break and smooth red hump of a 5,000-kelvin star, de Graaff and Naidu theorized. As a bonus, the gas “cocoon” would also block x-rays, and the gas wouldn’t flicker much—which would explain two mysteries surrounding other little red dots.
But what about the broad lines, supposedly caused by hydrogen swirling fast around a black hole? Another group provided a possible explanation.
That group, which included Vadim Rusakov, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, had been scrutinizing the broad lines of the best-observed little red dots. Broad lines take the shape of a sharp mountain peak. But Rusakov and collaborators noticed that in many cases, these mountains sloped slightly more gently than would be expected if they came from fast-moving gas around a black hole. So they suggested that instead of coming from rotating gas, much of the spread of the hydrogen colors could come from light scattering off electrons.
They digitally removed the effect of this electron-induced smudging from their data, Rusakov said. After that, the broad lines stopped looking quite so broad and started looking more like light passing through a sluggishly churning shell of hydrogen gas in a particular state, similar to what you’d expect to see from a black hole star. The three teams—de Graaff’s, Naidu’s, and Rusakov’s — posted their findings on March 20, 2025—“black hole star date,” as some of the researchers called it.
Black hole stars could represent a new stage in the development of a supermassive black hole: First, a black hole would form in the center of a shell of hydrogen, together with a baby galaxy of normal stars around it. Then, over time, the black hole would eat its way out of its cocoon, gaining mass as it cleared the hydrogen gas away.
“We are seeing the seed,” Naidu said. “This is the birth of potentially every massive black hole in the universe.”
The black hole star enthusiasts appeal to Occam’s razor, arguing that their theory gives the simplest accounting of these two little red dots, and perhaps of little red dots in general. But simple is subjective, and astronomers have spent the last year in a lively debate about what’s really going on.
Even years after the discovery of the first little red dot, not much about them is settled. Dale Kocevski, an astrophysicist at Colby College, recalls leading a discussion about them at an April 2026 conference in Aspen, Colorado. He started by recapping what he hoped would be an uncontroversial idea about their trace amounts of blue light. “The group erupted into argument, and we couldn’t even get past the first bullet point,” he said.
Many astronomers still argue that little red dots are traditional black holes—even the new duo. “The data is really compelling,” said Roberto Maiolino of the University of Cambridge. “I’m a little bit more dubious about the interpretation.”
For each point in favor of black hole stars, Maiolino fires off a quick rebuttal. The lack of flicker? In the early universe, black holes may have had a steadier food supply and may therefore have been tidier eaters. The lack of x-rays? Standard galactic black holes are ringed by a thick doughnut of gas and dust, which can block most x-rays. He sees no reason to suspect the little red dots of being anything other than standard supermassive black holes.
The redness of the new objects is striking, he said, and he agrees that it means there must be a ton of gas between the black hole and us. But that gas could come in the form of the doughnut, or as puffy clouds that fill in patches of the black hole’s sky, as opposed to the shell of gas around a black hole star. Maiolino agrees that electron scattering likely contributes to broadening the lines in the spectra of some of the little red dots. But electron scattering also smears hydrogen lines from supermassive black holes, he said.
Maiolino and his collaborator, Piero Madau of the University of California, Santa Cruz, argue that the redness of the dots comes mainly from the angle at which we see them. The reddest dots are those that we happen to see edge on, their gassy doughnuts blocking our view. Webb also sees some “little blue dots.” These could be the same exposed black holes, viewed top-down, Maiolino and Madau pointed out in spring 2026. They also appeal to Occam’s razor—in this case arguing that black holes are a simpler explanation for little dots of all colors.
At this stage either theory—black hole or black hole star—could match what the Webb telescope has seen. “I don’t think that there is a compelling reason to prefer one or the other,” said Mauro Giavalisco, an astronomer at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, who has spent much of his career interpreting the spectra of distant galaxies.
To test their interpretations, astronomers need a clearer picture of how black hole stars might form and how exactly they expect them to look.
Over the last few years, Mitchell Begelman has been teaching a graduate student seminar on little red dots at the University of Colorado, Boulder. It’s kept him reading the firehose of papers coming out on the subject. In these mysterious objects that weren’t quite stars and weren’t quite black holes, he recognized a ghost from his past: the quasi-star. “Suddenly the switch flipped, and I realized that this is what quasi-stars should look like,” Begelman said.
Begelman had proposed the existence of quasi-stars back in 2006, along with Marta Volonteri and Martin Rees, to explain observations of what looked like impossibly massive black holes. Their quasi-star theory offers one way to make a black hole star: The core of a vast gas cloud collapses to directly form a black hole, gathering the remainder of the cloud around it.
In 2025, Begelman and his collaborator Jason Dexter applied the quasi-star model to the little red dots. They estimated that quasi-stars could quickly assemble themselves in a few million years before settling into a more mature form that would look just like little red dots. They would do this for tens of millions of years—lasting long enough for Webb to spot them.
In 2026, Giavalisco worked with a team to flesh out the quasi-star model as an origin for black hole stars, which he finds to be a natural way of explaining how little red dots could mask the signs of a feeding black hole. He points out that our sun performs the same trick, hiding its explosive fusion, just on a much smaller scale. “We have billions and billions of hydrogen bombs exploding every second, and yet we see none of them,” he said.
Giavalisco and his collaborators found that their new model of a quasi-star fit the spectra of de Graaf’s and Naidu’s objects even better than the initial models had. He thinks the quasi-star theory is a plausible explanation for the little red dots but remains open to other ideas. “I just want to know the truth,” he said.
In the meantime, researchers are starting to search for another distinguishing pattern: If little red dots are black hole stars formed in the early universe, then they should grow rarer over time as they each break free from their shells and reveal their inner black holes.
In an August 2026 census of both red and blue dots broken up into different eras, Kocevski of Colby College and his collaborators found exactly that pattern. In the data, as the universe approaches 2 billion to 3 billion years of age, the little red dots seem to vanish—preliminary evidence that little red dots, as black hole stars, might really be a puberty-like phase for many supermassive black holes.
Theorists are already working out what that puberty-like phase might be like. In another analysis, posted on September 8, Naidu, de Graaff, Eilers, and their collaborators tested out an assortment of techniques for deducing the mass of a black hole “seed” inside a black hole star. These hidden black holes seemed to be far less massive than standard, exposed black holes. The scientists propose that Webb is catching supermassive black hole stars—up to 1 million times the mass of the sun—in the act of incubating the universe’s first big black holes.
Some researchers, including Kocevski, still aren’t sure. Kocevski suspects that the universe is a messy place, and that some little red dots are truly as starlike as the black hole star camp is arguing. Others, he thinks, will be more like standard black holes, as the other camp argues. “I have a sneaking suspicion that we’re both right,” he said.

Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
Who is RIBA International Prize winner Nakshabid Architects? In this roundup, we get to know the Dhaka-based studio through seven of its key projects spanning Bangladesh.
Founded by Bayejid Khondoker in 2003, Nakshabid Architects’ extensive portfolio is concentrated in Bangladesh and encompasses both public and private projects – from residential blocks to mosques and museums.
Last week saw the studio’s Green Field Factory named the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world’s best new building outside the UK.
Praised for its focus on passive design principles and the prioritisation of employee wellbeing, the studio considers its latest award to be a recognition of Bangladesh’s architectural contributions at a global scale.
“We see the prize as a recognition of what architecture from Bangladesh can contribute to global conversations on climate and the dignity of labour,” the studio told Dezeen.
Alongside the award-winning Green Field Factory, recent projects undertaken by the 20-person studio include the government-commissioned renovation of the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka, which reached completion in 2022 with a glass geodesic dome.
Central to its architectural approach, the studio said, is forging connections between a building and its “socio-ecological context” in a bid to reframe functional programmes as places of gathering.
“We believe that architecture must respond directly to its socio-ecological context, transforming ordinary programmes into meaningful collective experiences,” the studio said.
“We approach every project as a shared undertaking, listening closely to the people who will use it, the climate it sits in and the building traditions around it before we draw,” it continued.
“In this way even the most functional programmes become places of gathering, where light, air, landscape and everyday social life are woven into the architecture itself.”
Read on for a look at seven of the studio’s key projects:
Green Field Factory, Rangpur, 2017
The Green Field Factory, a rug factory in Rangpur, was designed by Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies and is the fifth winner of the RIBA International Prize.
Fronted by a monumental green facade, the seven-storey building was informed by the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
Aman Mosque, Narayanganj, 2018
A pair of intersecting arches form an “invisible dome” that frames the interior of Aman Mosque, a cubic prayer hall completed by the studio in Narayanganj.
Set within a sunken circular courtyard, the mosque is defined by its solid concrete volume, which is adorned with triangular perforations that filter light into the space.
Shaptak Insignia, Dhaka, 2021
A concrete facade punctuated with square openings was designed to limit heat gain and control daylight access at the Shaptak Insignia apartment tower in Dhaka.
Comprising two blocks, the residential block contains 18 units on a 670-square-metre plot, with each apartment complete with a balcony and a stepped terrace.
Urban Legacy, Dhaka, 2021
A pair of slender, red-brick residential towers make up the studio’s Urban Legacy project in Dhaka.
Its jagged form is defined by cantilevered balconies, which are enclosed by horizontal louvres and complete with greenery intended to shade and cool the apartment interiors.
“Cascading vines and planters spill from every terrace and the brick-walled garden base, turning the building into a vertical green landscape,” the studio said.
Aman Cement Factory Mosque, Sirajganj, 2022
An arched entrance guides visitors beyond the tiered brick exterior of the Ullapara Mosque, which Nakshabid Architects completed on the grounds of a cement factory for its workers.
Spread across two storeys, the mosque was built using locally-sourced brick, concrete and glass in a bid to blend “tradition with modernity”.
“[The mosque] has become a place where factory workers and neighbours gather for prayer, social events and community life,” the studio said.
Bangladesh Military Museum, Dhaka, 2022
Looking to redefine museum culture in Bangladesh, Nakshabid Architects conceptualised its design for the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka as a “vibrant civic destination”.
Its curving concrete structure contains cafes, galleries, an amphitheatre and an arena, which is sheltered by a 120-feet glass geodesic dome.
Nurpur Graveyard, Rangpur, 2023
Nakshabid Architects intended for the Nurpur Graveyard, a Muslim graveyard in Rangpur, to also offer a place of leisure for the local community.
To do this, the site accommodates a healthcare facility and an education space – or madrasa – with future expansions expected to include a mosque.
“Nurpur Graveyard is a place that diminishes the typical boundaries of graveyards,” the studio said.

New York Archdiocese close to settling sexual abuse claims for over US$800 million

New York Archdiocese close to settling sexual abuse claims for over US$800 million
Maya King and Jeffery C Mays
- The New York Archdiocese is close to a settlement worth more than US$800 million for 1,300 sexual abuse claims, after years of legal pressure and fears of bankruptcy.
- Plaintiffs’ lawyers said all survivors signed the revised deal, though the archdiocese said, “We are not quite there yet,” and a few holdouts delayed final approval.
- The deal would offer at least US$250,000 per person, add US$20 million for holdouts, and force the archdiocese to publish names of credibly accused clergy and lay leaders.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The Archdiocese of New York and plaintiffs’ lawyers were closing in on a settlement on Oct 23 in which the Church would pay more than US$800 million (S$1 billion) to settle claims from 1,300 people who said they had been sexually abused by its clergy members and lay leaders.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said that they had finalised the settlement with the archdiocese and that all of the plaintiffs had signed off on it.
But Joseph Zwilling, a spokesperson for the archdiocese, said in an interview on the night of Oct 24 that the parties were still working to finalise the agreement.
“We are not quite there yet,” he said.
Terms of the settlement would call for each plaintiff to have the option of receiving a lump-sum payment of at least US$250,000, or a potentially larger payout after a review of the extent of the abuse each plaintiff has claimed, according to the plaintiffs’ lawyers.
The proposal would end a multi-year saga that threatened to bankrupt the United States’ foremost Roman Catholic archdiocese.
The terms of the proposed settlement required that all 1,300 plaintiffs accept it, and there were some holdouts, who argued that the proposal did not do enough to rectify the harms they had experienced. Progress was also stymied by the deaths of some plaintiffs.
“Tonight, we were able to finalise the settlement with the Archdiocese,” Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Jeff Anderson & Associates, wrote on Oct 23 in an e-mail to the firm’s nearly 300 clients who say they were abused.
“All of the survivors agreed to the revised deal. This means that the settlement you agreed to will move forward.”
Lawyers for the plaintiffs said they had repeatedly warned their clients that if they did not accept the proposal, the archdiocese would most likely declare bankruptcy, reducing the size of any eventual payout and extending the length of the already years-long litigation.
To appease the handful of plaintiffs who were resistant to the proposal, the lawyers said, the archdiocese negotiated with one of its insurers to increase the amount of money it would pay the holdouts.
They would now receive a pot of US$20 million to be evenly distributed among them – an uncommon arrangement that hinged largely on the availability of insurance funds.
“The survivors showed an amazing amount of perseverance and patience here,” said Paul Mones, a veteran lawyer whose Los Angeles-based firm represents 33 of the plaintiffs against the archdiocese.
“After a lifetime of pain and struggle, they mustered the energy to push that final mile. And hopefully this deal will give them a degree of solace and healing.”
The Archdiocese of New York, which includes Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and a handful of Hudson Valley communities, would be the latest Catholic institution to pay hundreds of millions of dollars to settle claims of sexual abuse.
In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to pay US$395 million to settle claims from more than 530 people who said clergy members and lay leaders had abused them.
In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles settled similar claims for more than US$1 billion – one of the largest sexual abuse settlements in church history.
The agreement with the New York Archdiocese also requires it to publish on its website the names of the clergy members and lay leaders who were credibly accused of sexual abuse, and to keep that list updated with any future substantiated claims of abuse.
The accusers and their lawyers said they thought these requirements would not only illuminate past abuses, but also help to prevent future ones. It is unclear what disclosures, if any, the archdiocese would have faced if it had declared bankruptcy.
In her e-mail, Goffe said she would have more details about the settlement process in the next two weeks but wanted to emphasise “what an achievement” the agreement represents. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Iran drops four places to sixth at Nagoya Asian Para Games
TEHRAN - Iran concluded its campaign at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya in sixth place, suffering a four-position decline from its runner-up finish at the previous edition in Hangzhou, China, in 2023.
The Iranian delegation collected 102 medals, including 26 gold, 36 silver and 40 bronze, compared with 131 medals — 44 gold, 46 silver and 41 bronze — at Hangzhou.
Despite the decline in the overall standings, several Iranian athletes delivered outstanding performances, demonstrating the country's continued strength in para-athletics and swimming.
Among the most successful competitors was Sina Zeighaminejad, who emerged as one of Iran's leading gold medalists in para swimming. He secured three gold medals, underlining his remarkable consistency and establishing himself as a key figure in Iran's medal-winning campaign.
Another standout performer was Elham Salehi, who captured two gold medals in para-athletics. Her achievements provided a significant boost to the Iranian delegation and highlighted the important contribution of female athletes to the country's success.
Alireza Zare also produced an impressive performance, winning two gold medals in para-athletics. His achievements included a record-breaking run in the men's 200-meter T35 event, where he clocked 24.83 seconds to secure the title.
While these individual successes offered encouraging signs, Iran's overall results reflected a noticeable decline compared with Hangzhou. The delegation won 18 fewer gold medals and 29 fewer medals overall, although it also competed with a smaller squad.
Meanwhile, China reaffirmed its dominance of Asian para sports, finishing comfortably at the top of the medal standings with an extraordinary 435 medals, comprising 207 gold, 117 silver and 111 bronze.
Host nation Japan secured second place with 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 45 gold, 49 silver and 51 bronze.
India claimed fourth position with 30 gold medals, followed by South Korea with 29, leaving Iran sixth with 26 gold medals.
China's commanding performance demonstrated its considerable depth across multiple disciplines and reinforced its position as the continent's leading para-sport powerhouse.
For Iran, the Nagoya Games presented a mixed picture of individual excellence and collective disappointment.
Although champions such as Zeighaminejad, Salehi and Zare delivered memorable performances, the four-place drop in the rankings underlined the need for stronger preparation, investment in emerging talent and improved competitive depth.
The challenge now facing Iranian para sports is to build on these individual achievements and regain a place among Asia's leading delegations at future international competitions.

AI glasses create new growth potential for Taiwan optical industry

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's optical lens makers are expanding into AI glasses as the emerging market creates new business opportunities beyond smartphones, CTEE reported Saturday.
As Meta, Google, and other major technology companies introduce new models, AI glasses are moving closer to everyday consumer use. Research firm IDC estimates global shipments will reach 13.04 million units this year and increase to 16.18 million next year.
Genius Electronic Optical Co. has been developing optical components for AI glasses and augmented and virtual reality (AR and VR) devices in recent years. The company is already working with US clients and is also in talks with Chinese brands.
Although orders for VR lenses have slowed, activity in AI glasses and AR products is picking up. These applications share some of the same technical requirements as smartphone cameras, including compact designs, high resolution, and precise assembly, while also requiring lightweight components, according to Pocket Securities.
Asia Optical Co. has spent years developing metalens technology using nanoimprint lithography, a process that uses a stamp-like mold to transfer nanoscale circuit patterns onto a light-sensitive coating on a wafer. The company holds related manufacturing patents, according to Business Next.
It said the technology could significantly lower the cost of optical waveguide lenses used in AR glasses, potentially making eyewear with built-in displays more affordable. Asia Optical is also exploring the use of metalens technology in sensing modules for AI glasses.
Kinko Optical Co. is focusing its AR, VR, and mixed reality development on optical waveguides and optical engines, which help deliver images to the wearer's eyes. The company expects its investments in AR technology to begin generating returns next year.
Ability Enterprise Co. is starting with specialized applications such as sports glasses. It is participating in a smart sports glasses project under an electronics manufacturing services model, producing devices based on designs provided by clients.
Depending on customer needs, the company may expand into original design manufacturing, which also includes product design.

Forces were also "demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat at the site of the encounter", they said, adding that "counterterrorism operations" were underway at dozens of locations.
Netanyahu threatened on Friday to collectively punish the neighbourhood from where the attackers came by demolishing it.
Palestinian group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised Friday's attack on two Israeli soldiers as a "heroic operation" and called on supporters to carry out more.
A Hebron-based AFP photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between the soldiers and two men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle.
Israeli forces eventually shot dead the two Palestinians.
Netanyahu later ordered a lockdown in the occupied West Bank.
Visiting Hebron, the premier said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were "considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since" the 1967 war.
The first step would see Israeli forces "enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure", he said.
The military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, he said, the scene of a large-scale assault in January 2025 that forcibly displaced thousands of Palestinians.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from pursuing "plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes".
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through a spokesman, voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides.
'Exactly like Gaza'
Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza".
He said authorities were "sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: if you mess with the Jews, you will pay a very painful price".
National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based "Palestinian Authority must be dismantled".
"It is impossible for there to be an authority within Judea and Samaria that incites murder, calls for murder, and works for murder," he told reporters.
No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank, was connected to Friday's attack.
Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are prominent advocates of illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu's government.
Netanyahu vowed to "pursue Hamas terrorists" everywhere, adding: "You have no place to hide."
Israel vowed to obliterate the group in the wake of the 7 October attacks, later a war on Gaza that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians and been determined a genocide by UN experts and leading rights groups.
The army crackdown on the occupied West Bank comes as Israeli settlers, often under army protection, continue attacks against Palestinian olive harvesters.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.

Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners

Opinion
Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners
Clearly, appeasement doesn’t work and dependence just feeds leverage. Collective action is the only effective stand that states can take
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
The anxiety gripping Seoul is palpable. Under US pressure, South Korea signed a US$350 billion investment deal last November for a 10-percentage-point tariff reduction, billing it as a strategic alliance. Barely a year on, the facade has crumbled.
Last month, US President Donald Trump announced a US$200 billion tranche of the deal with no South Korean official present. Blindsided, Seoul restated its “commercial viability” clause. Trump’s response was blunt. “If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge them more,” he told reporters. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up.”
For South Korea, the numbers are sobering: US$350 billion represents 18 per cent of its annual gross domestic product. Even if much of it is channelled through loans, guarantees and corporate outlays, it risks upward pressure on the won, crowding out domestic investment and political exposure if projects underperform.

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has appointed former Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko as its authorized representative to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF).
According to Directive No. 1116, dated October 23, the Cabinet of Ministers has recalled Yehor Perelyhin, former Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment, from his role as the Ukrainian government’s authorized representative to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (structured as a limited partnership). In his place, the Cabinet has appointed Yulia Svyrydenko, former Prime Minister, who currently serves as Vice-Rector for the Development of Business Education at the private institution Kyiv School of Economics (KSE) University to act as the authorized representative (with her consent).
The U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF) is a joint U.S.-Ukrainian investment fund, established via an intergovernmental agreement in May 2025 to mobilize capital and attract investment for the reconstruction, economic development, and strategic sectors of Ukraine. The Fund focuses, in particular, on projects that facilitate Ukraine’s recovery, strengthen supply chains, and bolster the overall economic security and prosperity of both Ukraine and the United States.
As previously reported, on October 13, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers accepted the resignation of Yehor Perelyhin from his position as Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment.
Yulia Svyrydenko served as Prime Minister for exactly one year, from July 2025 to July 2026. In September, she was appointed President of the KSE Business School.

The General Staff noted that the plant produces synthetic rubber and other products used, among other things, in the manufacture of solid rocket propellant.
In addition, an aircraft was struck at the Yeysk airfield in Russia's Krasnodar Krai. The extent of the damage is being assessed.
Background: The Russian-installed occupation authorities reported a blackout in Sevastopol and other cities in Crimea.
