Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' as rain tumbles down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:06:02 UTC
11:06:02 KST

analysis
Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' this week as rain tumbled down
Cattle prices jumped this week as heavy rain fell across key production areas in Queensland and northern New South Wales.
Meat and Livestock Australia's (MLA) benchmark Eastern Young Cattle Indicator (EYCI) surged beyond 1,000 cents a kilogram, as restockers and backgrounders competed for numbers.
"The cattle market shifted to a new gear off the back of this rain," Stuart Bull, MLA's market information manager said.
"Some of these regions were in need of a good drink and this rain has really helped pushed prices, along with fewer cattle coming to market."
At Roma on Tuesday, some weaner steers from the Winton region sold for an incredible $7 a kilogram, which equated to more than $1,900 a head.
At Dubbo, the local saleyard report said restocker demand "sparked a market boom".
"Restocker demand was a stand-out, with young cattle selling up to an impressive 80 cents per kilo dearer [than last week]," the report said.
"Young steers reached a top of $7.40/kg, while young restocker heifers sold to $6.50/kg, showcasing the strength of competition and confidence among buyers looking to replenish their herds."
Loading...
Scott Loughnan, who runs a mixed farming operation west of Roma, had received more than 160 millimetres of rain when he spoke to ABC News.
"We'd organised to feed cattle all summer with forecasts of a super El Niño,"
he said.
"It was apparently never going to rain again, but this will definitely make it easier."
Mr Loughnan was in the middle of harvesting wheat, barley and chickpeas, and said for winter crops in the area, the rain was "not very good".
"I looked at some chickpeas this morning and they might not be much good, but I'm trying to look at the positives that this rain will grow us some grass and give us moisture for the next planting."
Record cow and heavy steers
Meanwhile, MLA's national processor cow indicator has cracked $4 a kilogram for the first time on record, and the national heavy steer indicator has also reached a new high of $4.77 a kilogram.
Global AgriTrends livestock analyst Simon Quilty said the supply of heavy steers was tight and processors were competing against feedlots to secure numbers.
"Once upon a time, feedlot operators wanted 450 kilogram to 500 kilogram steers, that was the preferred weight," he said.
"But that's now been lifted because of the lack of supply and they're taking 550 kilograms to almost 630 kilograms, creating an overlap [in demand] between processors and their needs for slaughter-ready cattle and the feedlotters who have extended the requirements of their cattle.
"So there's competition for numbers between the north and the south of Australia, plus processors versus feedlots [and] the net effect is this incredible demand for heavy steers that I think will continue."
Mr Quilty believes Australia's cattle industry is at the start of a herd rebuild and is forecasting cattle prices to increase next year.
He is forecasting heavy steer prices to rise by about 20 per cent to about $5.70/kg next year.

US intel memo flags 'advanced' Iranian plots to target American diplomats abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:00:51 UTC
11:00:51 KST

The State Department is reducing staffing at four US embassies in the Middle East after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the region and elsewhere.
In a memo sent on Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said his teams "have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel."
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo was obtained by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Axios.
There was no immediate reaction from Tehran.
"These materials have been provided to appropriately-cleared senior staff on your team and we are available to brief you at your convenience. We will make every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so you can share it with State Department personnel at your discretion," Clayton added.
Three US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, confirmed that the memo was sent to Rubio in his capacity as secretary of state and national security adviser.
The memo emerged shortly after the State Department announced it is reducing staff at the US embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
The three officials said the threats from Iran and Yemen's Houthi militia are related to the staffing changes.
Houthi threat
The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open.
However, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where nonessential US personnel and their families were ordered Wednesday to leave the country, staff in the other four countries are not compelled to depart.
In announcing the staffing drawdowns this week, the State Department pointed specifically to increased threats from Houthi militias and did not mention threats to US personnel directly from Iran.
US officials have adamantly denied they are tied to any potential new US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
US senators have warned the White House they will withhold their votes to confirm nominees until US President Donald Trump's administration secures the restoration of communications systems used by Ukrainian forces, The New York Times reports.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources
Details: According to three people familiar with the discussions, Republicans and Democrats in the Senate have told senior White House officials that they will block confirmation of Trump's nominees awaiting congressional approval until the administration restores critically important satellite communications capabilities used by the Ukrainian military.
The move, disclosed to the NYT by sources speaking on condition of anonymity because it has not yet been officially announced, will intensify bipartisan tensions over the White House's ever-more conciliatory approach towards Russia.
This will take place during the remaining congressional session scheduled for after the midterm elections, when Republicans are expected to try to confirm dozens of Trump's nominees before the current Congress's term ends.
The stance highlights growing divisions between the White House and Congress over Russia, with even senior Republicans showing increasing willingness to challenge Trump's policy positions. It also points to a possible shift after the midterm elections, when control of Congress could pass to the Democrats and lawmakers from both parties may be more resolute in using their leverage and oversight powers on the issue.
Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania who is fighting to retain his seat in a highly contested district, has threatened to seek the dismissal of US officials responsible for the network disruptions as well as cuts to their departments' budgets. He said he doubts the problems were accidental.
A US Senate staff member told the NYT on condition of anonymity that the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations had approved several shipments of critical air defence interceptors that had still not been delivered to Ukraine, raising concerns about delays in aid already authorised by Congress.
Staff are also considering launching investigations into SpaceX in connection with the satellite disruptions and have asked companies involved in Russian diesel fuel transactions to retain documents in the event of possible congressional investigations, the source added.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

BERLIN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Borussia Monchengladbach ended their disastrous Bundesliga start with a 3-2 comeback victory at VfB Stuttgart on Friday, as Wael Mohya inspired the visitors to their first points of the season and helped avert an unwanted league record.
Having lost their opening six matches, Gladbach faced becoming the first Bundesliga club to begin a campaign with seven consecutive defeats. Despite fielding a depleted side, Alexander Blessin's team overcame an early deficit to secure a deserved victory.
Stuttgart struck after just five minutes when Ermedin Demirovic fired from distance following Dzenan Pejcinovic's pass. Gladbach goalkeeper Moritz Nicolas reached the ball but could not prevent it from crossing the line.
The hosts initially controlled proceedings and threatened through Pejcinovic and Lorenz Assignon before Gladbach gradually found their rhythm.
Joe Scally equalised in the 38th minute, cleverly redirecting Zento Uno's effort into the net with his heel.
The visitors nearly completed the turnaround before halftime, but Stuttgart goalkeeper Dennis Seimen denied Florian Neuhaus before Mohya struck the crossbar.
Gladbach maintained their momentum after the restart and took the lead in the 51st minute. Mohya dribbled past two defenders before finding Shuto Machino, who drove the ball into the top corner.
Stuttgart coach Sebastian Hoeness responded with a triple substitution, introducing Deniz Undav, Jamie Leweling and Bilal El Khannouss, but the visitors extended their advantage in the 66th minute.
Seimen failed to gather Mohya's low effort, and although Ramon Hendriks cleared off the line, Scally recovered possession near the right post and lifted the ball back towards Mohya, who bundled it home from close range.
Demirovic reduced the deficit with a header from Leweling's cross in the 83rd minute, but Stuttgart could not find an equaliser despite late pressure.
"A lot of pressure has been lifted. The players have fully rewarded themselves today. We invested more in the game and showed greater passion," Gladbach sporting director Rouven Schroeder said. "The win is a relief for the entire club, but it can only be a starting point."
Despite the victory, Gladbach remain bottom with three points from seven matches, while Stuttgart sit 14th with six points after their fifth league defeat. ■

JIUQUAN, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- China launched two groups of remote sensing satellites from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China on Saturday.
The satellites 07-09 of the Yaogan-53 group and the satellites 19-21 of the Yaogan-56 group were launched at 3:25 a.m. (Beijing Time) aboard a Long March-4B carrier rocket, and they entered the preset orbits successfully.
They are primarily used for scientific experiments, land and resources surveys, crop yield estimation, and disaster prevention and reduction.
The launch marked the 673rd mission of the Long March carrier rockets. ■

Collingwood not the 'standard of AFLW that we expect to see', former coach says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:54:43 UTC
09:54:43 KST

Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.
The Magpies slumped to a new low on Friday night after failing to kick a single goal against Port Adelaide.
The 48-point defeat to the Power was the club's 10th loss this season out of 11 games. Under head coach Sam Wright, the Magpies have won just five games since the start of 2024.
"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.
"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."
The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.
"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.
"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.
"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."
Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.
Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.
He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.
To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.
"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.
"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."
Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.
Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.
"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.
There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.
On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.
"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:48:21 UTC
09:48:21 KST

Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Aerospace Information Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread.
- Share:
Glioblastoma is among the most lethal forms of brain cancer, and scientists have uncovered a surprising factor that may help its cells become more invasive. The fluid surrounding the outer edges of these tumors is much thicker than the fluid near their centers, forcing cancer cells to encounter increasing resistance as they move into healthy brain tissue. Rather than simply slowing their movement, however, this environment appears to help the cells adapt in ways that make invasion easier.
To investigate this unexpected behavior, researchers created an innovative microfluidic chip that recreates the physical conditions encountered by glioblastoma cells. They found that spending extended periods in thick fluid caused the cells to become smaller, more flexible, and better able to squeeze through narrow openings. The discovery suggests that fluid viscosity does more than obstruct cancer cells. It can actively influence their behavior and potentially make them more aggressive.
How Thick Fluid Influences Brain Cancer Invasion
Cancer research has traditionally concentrated on chemical signals and the stiffness of the tissues surrounding tumors. Far less attention has been given to the viscosity of the fluid through which cancer cells travel.
In glioblastoma, this difference is particularly striking. Fluid at the tumor's advancing edge is approximately eight times more viscous than fluid in its dead tissue at the center. As cancer cells move outward, they must push through an increasingly resistant environment.
Studying this process has been difficult because conventional closed microfluidic devices cannot accurately reproduce these conditions. Their enclosed channels can limit access to oxygen and nutrients, while friction against the walls introduces additional forces that influence cell behavior. These limitations also make it challenging to observe how cancer cells respond to prolonged exposure to viscous fluid.
Researchers therefore needed a way to isolate the effects of fluid viscosity from other mechanical influences and determine whether extended exposure produces lasting changes in glioblastoma cells.
A New Device Reveals How Cancer Cells Adapt
Scientists from Chongqing General Hospital and Chongqing University in China developed a specialized open microfluidic platform to address these challenges. Their findings were published in Microsystems & Nanoengineering.
The device consists of a two-layer open microfluidic membrane equipped with a removable cap and an array of tiny pillars. This arrangement allows researchers to control precisely when cancer cells begin migrating while observing how their nuclei change shape as they move through confined spaces.
Unlike traditional enclosed systems, the platform also supports continuous cell culture for up to one month. This makes it possible to examine how prolonged mechanical stress changes the movement and invasive behavior of glioblastoma cells.
The researchers tested two human glioblastoma cell lines, U-251 and LN-229. Both were grown for a month in a thick fluid designed to reproduce conditions at the tumor's invasive outer edge (7.1 cP).
When the cells were subsequently examined using the chip, those that had adapted to the viscous environment traveled faster and covered greater distances than untreated control cells. This result was especially surprising because thicker fluid would ordinarily be expected to impede movement.
Brain Cancer Cells Become Smaller and More Flexible
Microscopic observations revealed how the adapted cells overcame this resistance. After prolonged exposure to the viscous fluid, they had become smaller and easier to deform, allowing them to maneuver through the narrow gaps between the device's microscopic pillars.
As the cells squeezed through these restricted passages, their nuclei underwent visible deformation. Researchers also observed an accumulation of YAP, a protein involved in sensing mechanical forces, inside the nuclei. This is a recognized sign that cells have activated pathways involved in responding to physical stress.
Although both glioblastoma cell lines developed similar changes in shape and movement, their underlying molecular responses were unexpectedly different.
U-251 cells underwent a form of mesenchymal-like reprogramming, activating genes associated with cancer invasion, including CD44, FN1, and MMP9. LN-229 cells, by contrast, became more flexible and mobile without showing substantial lasting changes in gene expression.
Further analysis using Western blotting showed that protein changes remained detectable even after cells were transferred back into fluid with normal viscosity. This indicated that at least some of the adaptations were persistent rather than simply short-lived responses to their surroundings.
Scientists Discover a Strange Kind of Cellular Memory
One of the most unexpected findings was that exposure to thick fluid appeared to leave a lasting imprint on glioblastoma cells.
The researchers had anticipated that viscosity would primarily function as a physical obstacle. Instead, their experiments showed that prolonged exposure could alter how cells behaved even after the original mechanical conditions were removed.
This phenomenon points to a form of mechanical memory, in which cells retain changes produced by earlier physical stress.
The open design of the new chip was essential for identifying this effect. By separating resistance from the fluid itself from the confinement imposed by channel walls, the researchers could investigate viscosity without the additional mechanical interference that complicates conventional experiments.
Observing changes in nuclear shape and migration patterns after weeks of exposure provided evidence that glioblastoma cells can adapt to their mechanical environment in lasting ways.
The contrasting molecular responses of the two cell lines were particularly revealing. Although both appeared to undergo similar physical transformations, only one showed extensive changes in its gene activity. This suggests that glioblastoma cells may acquire comparable invasive characteristics through different underlying biological processes.
A Potential New Approach to Studying Brain Cancer Treatments
Beyond uncovering an overlooked influence on glioblastoma invasion, the researchers believe their device could provide a valuable tool for investigating potential cancer therapies.
The open microfluidic platform fits into standard multi-well plates, allowing it to be incorporated into existing laboratory procedures for cell culture and imaging. Its accessible design also enables researchers to stain cells directly and observe them over long periods without the clogging problems that can occur in closed systems.
These features could make it useful for testing drugs that interfere with the cellular pathways responsible for detecting and responding to mechanical forces.
For glioblastoma, the results raise the possibility that highly viscous environments may favor cancer cells that are better adapted to invasion. Treatments targeting YAP signaling or the remodeling of the cytoskeleton, the internal framework that helps cells maintain and change their shape, could therefore be investigated under conditions that more closely resemble those inside tumors.
The technology may also prove useful for studying other cancers in which fluid viscosity varies across different regions. By examining how tumor cells respond to these mechanical conditions, researchers could gain a better understanding of why some cancers are particularly invasive and potentially identify patients whose tumors depend on mechanical adaptation to spread.
Although further research is needed to determine how these laboratory findings translate to tumors in patients, the discovery highlights an important and previously underexplored aspect of cancer biology: the physical environment surrounding tumor cells may actively shape their ability to invade healthy tissue.
Research Support and Funding
This research received support from the Chongqing Research Center for Glioma Precision Medicine and the Chongqing Key Laboratory of Neurodegenerative Diseases.
Funding was provided by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (82473430, 22304143, 32501283); Chongqing Talent Project (cstc2022ycjh-bgzxm0081); Natural Science Foundation of Chongqing (CSTB2025NSCQ-GPX1077, CSTB2025NSCQ-GPX0309); Young Medical Talent Program of Chongqing (YXQN2025088); New Chongqing Project(CSTB2024YCJH- KYXM0115); and the Research Funding of Chongqing General Hospital (2025022102); the Chongqing Special Funding for Postdoctoral Research Projects (2024CQBSHTB3131); Zhejiang Provincial Natural Science Foundation of China (LQN25E050020).

WA Greens senator to miss parliament amid allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:43:51 UTC
09:43:51 KST

WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John will not attend parliament next week
In short:
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament when it resumes next week.
Senator Steele-John is facing allegations of inappropriate conduct towards women, which he has denied.
What's next?
An independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens is expected to get underway imminently.
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has reiterated he won't be attending parliament next week, after releasing and then deleting a copy of a letter detailing allegations of misconduct against him.
On Friday night the senator took to social media to publish the letter which is addressed to Greens leader David Shoebridge and signed by seven current and former Greens staff or party office bearers.
The writers, who are not named, state they have been made aware of "multiple allegations of serious misconduct" being made against Senator Steele-John "spanning almost a decade (2017-2025)".
"These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women. We are aware of multiple women who have taken up roles or volunteered in the party, who because of these allegations, have been warned not to be alone with him."
The letter, dated October 13, goes on to state the accusations have come from both inside and outside the party, and urges Senator Shoebridge to commission an independent investigation into the allegations, and review and update gendered violence protocols.
Senator Steele-John has repeatedly and strenuously denied the allegations.
On Saturday the 32-year-old senator said a copy of the letter was sent to him by Chief Political Commentator for the Nine papers, James Massola, who then broke the story on October 15.
The senator said he had initially chosen to post the letter on his own social media accounts because he "did not want to be seen as hiding from it".
"I'm now not sure that was the right call and I've taken it down. I'm really sorry for any additional distress it caused," he said, and reiterated his absence from parliament next week.
The WA branch of the Greens has commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations.
'Growing chorus'
In the days after the allegations became public, Senator Shoebridge initially said he understood Senator Steele-John was taking leave from parliament.
But last Sunday the WA senator denied that was the case in a lengthy open letter, prompting the federal Greens leader to encourage his colleague to take leave.
"I think the community assumptions are that he step aside for the extent of this inquiry and I've communicated that to Jordon," Senator Shoebridge told ABC Radio National Breakfast on Thursday.
In a statement on Saturday, Senator Shoebridge reiterated his view that Senator Steele-John take leave.
"This is in no way a prejudgement of any of these matters," he said.
Senator Steele-John reflected in his post on Friday that there had been a "growing chorus" calling on him to not attend parliament next week, when senate estimates will take place.
"I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable," he said.
"The precedent has now been set: any MP can be kept out of parliament by allegations of allegations."

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The United States has reported 4,588 confirmed measles cases so far in 2026, more than twice the total for all of 2025, according to the latest data released Friday by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Of the confirmed cases, 4,570 were reported by 47 jurisdictions, while 18 involved international visitors to the United States, the CDC said.
Children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 accounted for the largest share of cases, with 1,914 infections, or 42 percent of the total.
A total of 479 patients, about 10 percent of all confirmed cases, have been hospitalized.
About 96 percent of cases involved people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to the CDC data.
In Pennsylvania, the measles outbreak continued to expand, with 78 new cases reported over the past seven days, according to data released Friday by the state's Department of Health. The state has recorded 1,338 cases across 44 counties, accounting for nearly 30 percent of the U.S. total.
Pennsylvania reported only 16 measles cases in 2025, according to the CDC. ■

Aussie Picklum aglow on top of WSL standings after Portugal win

In short:
Australia's Molly Picklum has hit the front in the World Surf League standings after seizing the Rip Curl Pro title in Portugal.
Picklum beat American Caitlin Simmers in the final and now leads Carissa Moore on the overall standings.
What's next?
There are two events left in the post-season – the Philippines Pro and Pipeline.
Molly Picklum has hit peak form riding the celebrated Supertubos waves to win the Rip Curl Pro Portugal event and move back to pole position to retain her world surfing title.
"Right now I'm on top of the world … literally!" roared the 23-year-old Australian after her victory over America's former world champion Caitlin Simmers in Friday's final sent her back to the top of the World Surf League standings.
Picklum's triumph at one of surfing's most famous venues gave her the maximum 10,000-point haul to ensure she overhauled Hawaiian Carissa Moore at the top.
The win came at the perfect post-season moment with just two events left.
The Gosford star has enjoyed a shiny nickname since she referred to herself as like "a glow worm in a cave" riding inside a deep barrel wave.
So she was quick to offer a shout-out to her friends and family at home, whom she knew would be watching her first triumph of the season in the early hours.
"I just want to say thank you to all of them. I know they stayed up for this one. The glow worm absolutely did it and I love you all so much!" Picklum said.
The Australian was given a triumphant ride on a jet ski after clinching the final win before she threw herself into the water to celebrate.
"I just love it when I get to win in front of them and actually do it for them," she said.
"So many people support me and put so much energy into me. I just love winning to give back to those ones that give to me.
"I wanted to do well here. It was a dream of mine for me. Supertubos, it's like a cross between the Brazil energy and then (Hawaiian) Pipeline and those two together are like my two favourite things.
"So, oh my God, I'm so so grateful to win here. It was literally a dream of mine, and dreams come true. It's so baffling."
Picklum was delighted to "kind of hit my stride right at the right time" as she now sits atop the leaderboard on 48,950 points to Moore's 47,065, with another Hawaiian, Gabriela Bryan, third on 44,865 with two events left, the Philippines Pro and Pipeline.
Picklum didn't have a great record against 2024 world champ Simmers, having lost six of their previous eight head-to-head contests, but she was in control of the final from the moment she delivered a superb 7.83-point effort on her third wave to build on her opening 5.50.
Simmers couldn't respond, offering Picklum's fans on the beach a belated scare when she managed a best of 6.67 on the ninth of her 11 rides, but the Australian, who only had a half-dozen rides, eventually triumphed with her combined two-wave score of 13.33 to the American's 12.84.

Wet and stormy weekend ahead for many Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:13:07 UTC
09:13:07 KST

In brief
- Following days of wild weather in Queensland, further rainfall and storms are expected this weekend.
- Severe thunderstorms are also possible across multiple states in eastern Australia.
Severe thunderstorms are on the cards across eastern and central Australia this weekend, raising the risk of flash flooding in some regions.
Flash flooding and heavy rain inundated Queensland this week, particularly the south-east, where the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) recorded up to 450mm of rain over the past seven days. A freak storm on Thursday led to hundreds of calls to the state's emergency services, with monthly rainfall records broken in regions of the Sunshine Coast.
With more wet weather and severe storms expected across the state this weekend, flood warnings were in place for parts of the state's west and south-east.
Heavy rain and thunderstorms are also possible across New South Wales, South Australia, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania over the weekend.
It comes weeks into Australia's peak season for severe weather, which runs between October to April.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Here's what to expect over the coming days.
Saturday
Several flood warnings were in place across Queensland on Saturday morning, including for rivers in and around the Sunshine Coast, Brisbane, Ipswich, Lockyer Valley and Darling Downs, with severe thunderstorms and heavy rain possible across a large area of the state.
"Queensland can expect a wet weekend with this rain-bearing system going nowhere in the short term," BoM senior meteorologist David Crock said.
Flood and wind warnings were also in place for parts of NSW, with strong winds possible in the Coffs, Macquarie and Hunter coasts.
Showers and thunderstorms are on the cards for South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania, with severe storms possible in Victoria and South Australia.
A cold front is expected to bring cool weather and showers to south-west Western Australia, while showers and thunderstorms are forecast to continue in the Top End.
Sunday
Severe thunderstorms are possible across much of NSW, as well as central and eastern Victoria, on Sunday, as a cold front moves in.
Much cooler air moving in from the country's west will bring "quite a dramatic change" following a warm week across South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania, Crock said.
"It'll be much cooler next week, and that will be quite noticeable in the south-eastern states," he said.
Afternoon thunderstorms possible across much of central, northern and eastern Australia, including severe thunderstorms in Victoria, NSW, QLD and the NT.
The storm outbreak is expected to ease next week, though further rain is expected and stormy weather should continue in the east on Monday.
"We'll see a cold front sweep across the southeast states during the weekend. That will then bring another round of severe thunderstorms on Monday to parts of, particularly southeast Queensland," Crock said.
Following a very wet week, Queensland will likely get a reprieve from Tuesday onwards, but another storm outbreak may come through next weekend.

Netanyahu says end of US military support to Israel is 'only a matter of time'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:00:34 UTC
09:00:34 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that his country must prepare for the end of US military assistance worth tens of billions of dollars, calling the prospect "only a matter of time", adding Israel may need to develop an alternative digital economy to circumvent rising international sanctions. 
Speaking just days before hard-fought elections, Netanyahu, who faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant and ongoing corruption proceedings, told Israel's business broadcaster Channel 10 that he had ordered preparations for potential economic and banking sanctions, including exploring alternative financial technologies.
"If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen, because America has changed," he said, apparently referring to growing opposition in the US to such support in light of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, brutal occupation of West Bank, and almost daily killings of Palestinians.
"This is over, and it will end. It is only a matter of time."
Netanyahu gave no date for an end to the assistance and announced no formal US decision, instead calling for preparations for a possible future halt.
On potential sanctions, he said Israel must develop alternative economic and financial mechanisms.
"You have to understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions. You need to prepare an economy that can get around them," he said.
Asked whether blockchain technology could offer an alternative for dealing with economic sanctions, Netanyahu replied: "Yes, that's one of the ways. And I've already asked for a plan to be prepared."
Netanyahu did not specify from which country he expected sanctions.
But his remarks come after UK and several other countries imposed sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in response to a wave of settler attacks on Palestinians and settlement construction approved by Netanyahu's extremist government.
Netanyahu still has a close alliance with US administration but criticism in the US has been rising, especially within the young Americans, since Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Combating 'Jewish terrorism'
Yair Lapid, a centrist former prime minister who is part of the opposition bloc challenging Netanyahu, seized on the remarks.
"Netanyahu now admits, in his own words: if his government is reelected, American security aid will come to an end and Israel will face sanctions that would devastate our economy, lead to runaway price hikes, and cause irreparable damage," Lapid said.
Netanyahu's remarks come as he threatens to resume war on Iran, which under heavy international sanctions has embraced cryptocurrency and other alternative economic measures.
Opposition Democrats party leader Yair Golan also slammed Netanyahu’s remarks, accusing him of being detached from reality.
He argued that preventing economic sanctions requires combating "Jewish terrorism" that damages Israel’s international standing, preserving strategic alliances, and replacing the government in next week’s election.
Golan called for a new government "without Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Deri," referring to extremist politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Shas party leader Aryeh Deri.
The remarks came four days before Israel’s Tuesday parliamentary elections, amid debate about relations with Western allies and the potential consequences of economic sanctions.
Under a pact signed with Washington in 2016, Israel receives $38 billion in military assistance over a 10-year period set to end in 2028.

Snow leopard conservation efforts in SW China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:39:03 CST
08:39:03 KST

Staff members of the Nainang ecological and cultural protection center walk on the way to collect the infrared cameras in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 22, 2026.
Snow leopards are under China's highest national-level protection and are listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. World Snow Leopard Day falls on October 23 annually.
Nainang Valley, which is only 38 kilometers away from the urban area of Lhasa in a straight line, is a rare stable habitat for snow leopards located in the suburb of a city in Xizang.
The Nainang ecological and cultural protection center in Doilungdeqen District was established in May 2023. To date, 40 snow leopards have been identified and named within the 200-square-kilometer monitoring area of Nainang Valley. (Xinhua/Jigme Dorje)

Cuban FM denounces Trump's new military threat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:38:44 CST
08:38:44 KST

Two vintage cars run on a street in Havana, Cuba, Oct. 23, 2026. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Friday denounced a new threat of military intervention against the Caribbean nation by U.S. President Donald Trump. In a post on X, Rodriguez rejected "any threat regarding U.S. ambitions toward Cuba" in response to remarks by Trump, who said Friday that U.S. ships "will pass" Cuba on their way back from Iran. (Photo by Joaquin Hernandez/Xinhua)
HAVANA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Friday denounced a new threat of military intervention against the Caribbean nation by U.S. President Donald Trump.
In a post on X, Rodriguez rejected "any threat regarding U.S. ambitions toward Cuba" in response to remarks by Trump, who said Friday that U.S. ships "will pass" Cuba on their way back from Iran.
"They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump said at a campaign rally in Fort Myers, in the southern U.S. state of Florida. He said one of the ships would stop about 50 yards (about 46 meters) off the coast.
"On our shores there are beautiful beaches, but also diente de perro (a jagged coastal coral formation), inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile aims and a thirst for domination," Rodriguez wrote.
Rodriguez, Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel and other officials have denounced U.S. threats of military intervention, which have escalated since early 2026, and have defended the island's sovereignty and its right to self-defense.
In May, Trump said in Florida that the United States would be taking over Cuba "almost immediately." ■

BRASILIA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) has asked social media companies Meta and X to provide, within 24 hours, technical explanations of their use of artificial intelligence, the distribution of political content, the publication of electoral ads and the removal of posts ahead of the presidential runoff on Sunday, Oct. 25.
The decision, announced Friday, was made Thursday night by the court's inspector general Ricardo Villas Boas Cueva, who set a daily fine of 500,000 reais (about 100,000 U.S. dollars) for each company in case of unjustified noncompliance.
The measure responds to an electoral investigation brought by a political coalition supporting incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection against opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro.
With the runoff approaching, Cueva demanded that the companies explain the criteria for content distribution and any differences in treatment between the candidates competing for the presidency.
United Nations experts sent a letter to Meta earlier this week seeking an explanation of alleged unequal treatment of the presidential candidates in Brazil. ■

Trump modifies scope of 50-pct tariffs on Canadian products
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:38:12 CST
08:38:12 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday signed a proclamation modifying the scope of 50-percent additional tariffs on certain Canadian products, removing some goods from the tariff list and adding others, with the changes set to take effect on Oct. 30.
According to the proclamation posted on the White House website, products including plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes imported into the United States from Canada will no longer be subject to the additional 50-percent ad valorem duty.
Instead, certain valves, carpets, waste products and other items imported into the United States shall be subject to the additional 50-percent ad valorem duty.
The changes will apply to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouses for consumption, on or after Oct. 30, according to the proclamation.
"The modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest," the proclamation states. It describes the duties as a response to what it calls Canada's "discrimination or unreasonable and unequal imposition" on U.S. auto and auto parts exports.
Trump imposed 50-percent tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars worth of Canadian goods on Aug. 22, prompting Canada to retaliate with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports, which took effect on Sept. 8. ■

Ex-ESPN reporter Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after incident at Wizards game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:29:55 UTC
08:29:55 KST

Ex-ESPN reporter Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after incident at Wizards game
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Britt McHenry is no longer a press advisor at the State Department, reportedly resigning days after videos of a confrontation at a Washington Wizards game went viral.
- Footage appears to show a drink thrown toward the ex-ESPN reporter before she throws one back.
- The altercation reportedly began after she defended Bucks forward Kyle Kuzma’s fiancée, Winnie Harlow.
Former ESPN reporter and Fox News personality Britt McHenry is no longer a press advisor for the U.S. Department of State, multiple media outlets are reporting. The development comes after viral videos appeared to show her throwing a drink at someone (after one was thrown at her) during an altercation in the stands at an NBA game.
Page Six reported Friday that McHenry was “forced to resign” on Thursday, the day after the alleged incident at the Washington Wizards’ home opener against the Milwaukee Bucks at Capital One Arena. McHenry then told Front Office Sports that she signed a resignation letter.
The State Department told both publications that it does not comment on internal personnel matters.
As president of White House Correspondents Assn., Jacqui Heinrich goes to bat for the 1st Amendment rights of her competitors.
The incident reportedly started after a group sitting behind McHenry started shouting insults toward Bucks forward Kyle Kuzma about his fiancée, Winnie Harlow. McHenry is said to have spoken up in Harlow’s defense.
Video footage posted by TMZ appears to start a bit later. It shows McHenry talking to a male companion and an usher from her seat while fans seated around her can be heard making negative comments about her, with some chanting, “Kick her out!”
As McHenry and her companion eventually start to leave on their own, a clear liquid can be seen hitting or coming close to hitting her on the back of the head. She responds by throwing a drink in that person’s direction. As she makes her way up the stairs in the aisle, McHenry is seen giving the middle finger and blowing kisses to the crowd as some people heckle and throw towels at her.
The Atlanta Falcons briefly used a profile image inspired by their throwback helmet ahead of Sunday’s game against the 49ers, but many social media users saw a resemblance to Nazi-era imagery.
Later in one of the videos, McHenry appears to argue with a security worker near at one of the venue’s entrances. As he gestures toward the exit, she appears stunned and asks, “What did I do?”
Monumental Sports & Entertainment, which owns and operates the Wizards and Capital One Arena, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
McHenry worked at ESPN from 2014 to 2017. In 2015, she was suspended for a week after a video surfaced of her yelling at and belittling a towing company employee. McHenry later apologized for the incident.
She announced her State Department job on social media last month.

Wallaroos send retiring pair out with win over Scotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:16:33 UTC
08:16:33 KST

Former Wallaroos skipper Emily Chancellor and teammate Cecilia Smith signed off with a win as Australia beat Scotland 38-31 in Canberra.
Chancellor and Smith, who was sent off after a second yellow card, were both chaired off by teammates at the end of the game.
What's next?
The Wallaroos have no more games until their new full-time program next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.
The Wallaroos have completed their three-game Scottish sweep in a spicy Canberra contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.
Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Friday night's 38-31 win but again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it.
The hosts copped four yellow cards, retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.
Scotland had two players sin-binned and it could have been far uglier if Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs's accusations of biting had been verified on review.
But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich's forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.
Fifty-game prop Eva Karpani was yellow-carded for a high shot in her milestone game, while impressive flyhalf Waiaria Ellis was marched for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.
The win came as a relief for retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation after being sent off.
"I'm really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess," Smith said as she embraced her daughter Ruby post-match.
Loading Twitter content
"She's been there since day one [of Smith's Wallaroos career].
"Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and the hard work in."
A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after debuting in 2018.
"It's created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for," she said.
"I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can't be what you can't see."
Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against the same opponents, the side now out of action until the Wallaroos program transitions to a full-time operation next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.
The hosts led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries.
The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona finished a long-range effort.
But Karpani and then Smith were marched, keeping Scotland interested until the final play, but they were unable to find the match-tying converted try.

Pakistan announces ratification of Mecca defence pact signed with Türkiye, Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:00:09 UTC
08:00:09 KST

Pakistan has completed the ratification processes for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told a news conference.
The defence agreement reflects Pakistan, Türkiye, and Saudi Arabia’s shared commitment to strengthening collective defense and cooperation for regional security and stability, he said on Fiday, according to a transcript
"Matters related to the agreement, its ratification, and operationalization remain under discussion by the three parties including in the Strategic Political and Defense Committee whose recent meeting was held on 5 October," said Khan, adding that each country follows its own constitutional and legal procedures for the approval and ratification of international agreements.
Saudi Arabia has also completed its ratification processes, he said.
Islamabad "remains fully committed to the letter and spirit of the agreement, which is defensive in nature, consistent with the UN Charter, and aimed at promoting regional peace, security and stability," Khan added.
On August 7, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman signed the agreement in Mecca.
The agreement reflects Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia's commitments to developing regional solutions to regional problems and their shared strategic vision focused on regional security and stability.
It aims to strengthen the three countries' security through collective deterrence and defence.
Türkiye seeks parliament approval
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have already completed their ratification processes, while Türkiye is undertaking the requisite procedures "in accordance with its domestic legal framework," he said.
Türkiye submitted the three-article bill to parliament on Wednesday seeking the pact’s approval.
The agreement is expected to deepen Türkiye's bilateral defence and security relations with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia while supporting an inclusive regional security mechanism.
The bill will be considered by parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which has been designated as the lead committee.
If approved by the committee, it will be placed on the agenda of parliament's General Assembly.
Regional security backdrop
The Mecca agreement comes at a time of heightened tensions in the region following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28.
There is no active or finalised peace agreement between the US and Iran.
Although an initial 60-day memorandum of understanding establishing a temporary truce was signed in June 2026, the talks have largely broken down, and both nations are currently engaged in stalled, indirect negotiations through Pakistan and other mediators.
The conflict has also expanded beyond Iran's borders, with Houthi militia stepping up attacks on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and other infrastructure.
The deteriorating security environment has accelerated defence cooperation among regional partners.

Belarus targets 25 pct electric public transport by late 2029
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:46:26 CST
07:46:26 KST

MINSK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Belarus plans to increase the share of electric public transport to 25 percent of its ground public passenger fleet by the end of 2029, Belarusian Industry Minister Andrei Kuznetsov said Friday.
Belarus currently has about 7,900 units of public transport vehicles, including 6,101 buses, 198 electric buses, 1,354 trolleybuses and 247 trams, which indicates that ground public transport is widely used across Belarus, Kuznetsov said at a meeting on the development of domestic passenger transport production.
The minister said projected domestic demand for such vehicles through the end of 2029 would total 2,699 units, comprising 1,737 buses, 188 electric buses, 678 trolleybuses and 96 trams.
A significant portion of domestically produced passenger transport vehicles is expected to be exported, primarily to Russia, where demand is projected to grow substantially, Kuznetsov added. ■

The Intervision was revived in 2025 in Moscow. Russia was represented by Honored Artist of the Russian Federation Yaroslav Dronov (Shaman). More than 20 countries, including all BRICS states, took part.

====================================================================================================

American Catholics reported a greater sense of meaning in life after Pope Leo XIV’s election, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

The election of Pope Leo XIV in May 2025 was followed by a modest rise in the sense of meaning in life among a sample of practicing Roman Catholics in the United States, according to a study published in The Journal of Positive Psychology. Through the end of the study’s 10-day post-election window, participants reported a stronger sense that their lives had meaning, along with a gradual decline in their search for meaning. The pattern held after the researchers accounted for participants’ religious commitment and their feelings about the new pope sharing their American nationality.
In psychology, meaning in life refers to the subjective judgment that one’s existence is worthwhile, makes sense, and is guided by an overarching purpose. Psychologists break this concept down into three parts: having a motivational goal or purpose, feeling that life is coherent, and believing that one’s life matters. Rather than treating meaning as a single feeling, researchers distinguish between the presence of meaning and the search for meaning. As a 2006 validation study demonstrated, already feeling that one’s life has purpose is distinct from actively looking for something that makes life feel meaningful.
Religion is a major source of this sense of purpose for many people. For example, a 2005 study found that religious people tend to report greater well-being, largely because they feel their lives have purpose and direction. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 indicated that religious individuals tend to experience a stronger sense of meaning largely through feeling that they matter on a grand, cosmic scale.
Most psychological research on religion and meaning has examined steady, long-term beliefs rather than specific religious events. One of the most prominent rituals in the Roman Catholic tradition is the papal conclave, the secluded meeting of cardinals inside the Sistine Chapel to elect a new pope. Filled with symbolic traditions like burning ballots to send black or white smoke from a chimney and the Latin announcement of “Habemus Papam” (“We have a Pope”), the conclave is framed by the Church as a moment of divine guidance.
The research, led by Stefan Stieger of Karl Landsteiner University of Health Sciences in Austria, examined whether living through this major religious transition alters how Catholics experience meaning from day to day. The authors drew on three psychological frameworks to explain how a papal election might affect believers. Under the meaning-making model, the death of a pope may create a temporary spiritual void that disrupts a believer’s worldview, and electing a successor may help restore a sense of order and coherence.
Social identity theory offers a second perspective, suggesting that people derive self-worth from belonging to social groups; losing a leader can threaten that shared identity, whereas choosing a new leader may restore group unity. A third possibility involves emotional contagion, the tendency for feelings to spread rapidly across a crowd or through global media coverage. For instance, a 2024 field study of a public Hindu ritual found that participants who stood close to one another during the ceremony experienced synchronized emotional arousal, showing how collective religious practices can align feelings across a group.
To capture how the 2025 papal transition affected believers in real time, the researchers used an experience sampling method. Instead of asking people to recall their feelings weeks later, this technique prompts participants to answer short smartphone surveys during their normal daily routines, reducing memory biases. Beginning on May 3, 2025, four full days before the conclave started, the team tracked participants across 14 consecutive days covering the pre-conclave, conclave, and post-conclave phases.
The researchers recruited English-speaking United States citizens through the online platform Prolific who identified as practicing Roman Catholics. After excluding 17 individuals who did not identify as Roman Catholic, dropped out early, or provided inconsistent demographic data, the final sample consisted of 117 American Roman Catholics. Participants ranged in age from 19 to 76 years, with an average age of about 45, and were split nearly evenly between men (52.1 percent) and women (47.9 percent).
At the start of the study, participants installed an open-source smartphone app called ESMira and completed a baseline survey. On 1-to-100 scales, the group reported being fairly religious on average (72.7) and relatively balanced between conservative and progressive views in both their theological orientation (46.1) and political views (47.4). They also completed a 10-item questionnaire measuring both their private religious devotion and their involvement in their church community.
Every evening at 8:00 p.m. local time, the app prompted participants to complete an end-of-day survey assessing their current sense of meaning in life. Using a 7-point scale from 1 (absolutely untrue) to 7 (absolutely true), participants rated five statements about the presence of meaning (such as “At this moment, I understand my life’s meaning”) and five statements about the search for meaning (such as “At this moment, I am looking for something that makes my life feel meaningful”). Across the two-week window, the 117 participants completed 1,470 daily questionnaires.
When the cardinals elected Pope Leo XIV, an unexpected factor emerged: the new head of the Catholic Church was also from the United States. To help account for the possibility that any boost in meaning among the American participants was a byproduct of national pride, the researchers added a question to the final survey. Participants rated how much Pope Leo XIV’s American background influenced their feelings toward him on a scale from -4 (much more negative) to +4 (much more positive).
To analyze the daily ratings, the researchers divided the timeline into a four-day pre-conclave baseline, the conclave phase (from the first black smoke signal until the day before the election), and 10 post-conclave days starting with the day of the papal announcement. Using multilevel statistical models, they tracked daily changes within each individual while controlling for age, gender, personal and social religious commitment, and feelings about the pope’s American nationality.
Across the four pre-conclave baseline days, participants averaged 5.16 out of 7 on the presence of meaning and 4.34 out of 7 on the search for meaning. During the conclave itself and on the first day of the post-conclave phase (the day Pope Leo XIV was announced), neither dimension showed a notable shift from baseline, possibly because not all participants had heard the news before completing that first evening survey. Starting the day after the election, however, the presence of meaning rose above the pre-conclave baseline and stayed elevated through the final day of tracking.
On the 7-point scale, daily presence-of-meaning scores increased by 0.14 to 0.20 points above the 5.16 baseline on every day from Day 2 through Day 10, except for Day 8, when a 0.09-point increase was not statistically significant. Standardized effect sizes during this period ranged from 0.09 to 0.14, which the authors describe as small to medium; in raw terms, the increases amounted to roughly 3 to 4 percent of the baseline score.
At the same time, participants reported a gradual decline in their search for meaning, with statistically significant drops on Days 2, 7, 9, and 10. Compared to the 4.34 baseline, search-for-meaning scores fell by 0.23 points on Day 7, 0.34 points on Day 9, and 0.30 points on Day 10, with standardized effect sizes reaching -0.19 on Day 9 and -0.17 on Day 10. This pattern suggests that participants felt more settled in their sense of purpose and less driven to look for missing meaning.
These shifts held after the researchers accounted for age, gender, religious commitment, and feelings about the pope’s nationality. On average, participants viewed the pope’s American nationality positively (averaging 2.03 on the -4 to +4 scale), and those more active in church communities tended to feel warmer about it. However, the analysis adjusted for these factors rather than testing whether the post-election boost was larger or smaller for particular groups, so it cannot show whether less devout Catholics, or those less enthusiastic about an American pope, experienced the same shift.
The authors noted that their findings are compatible with all three psychological frameworks they examined. They suggest that emotional contagion from widespread media coverage may have contributed, and that because media excitement typically fades, the persistence of the effect, with the drop in searching for meaning strongest on Days 9 and 10, points to deeper social identity and meaning-making processes as well. They also acknowledge, however, that emotional contagion can sometimes last several days, so the line between these explanations is not sharp.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study does not appear to have been preregistered. Because it began just four days before the conclave, after the death of Pope Francis had already occurred, there is no way to know what the participants’ sense of meaning looked like before the papal vacancy began. The post-election increase in meaning might represent a genuine rise above their typical everyday levels, or a rebound back to normal after a temporary dip caused by the previous pope’s death.
In addition, the tracking period ended 10 days after the election, leaving open the question of how long the heightened sense of purpose lasted before leveling off. The study also focused solely on Roman Catholics in the United States and had no comparison group tracked over the same days, so it cannot rule out that scores would have drifted for other reasons, such as participants growing accustomed to answering the same questions each evening.
Because the new pope’s American nationality became known at the same moment as his election, the study also cannot fully separate a religious response from a patriotic one. Including people from other religious backgrounds exposed to the same news coverage would help future researchers separate media-driven emotional contagion from the spiritual effects of welcoming a new religious leader.
The study, “The election of Pope Leo XIV and its impact on the meaning of life for Roman Catholic Christians: A longitudinal experience sampling method study in the USA before, during, and after the pope’s election,” was authored by Stefan Stieger, Selina Volsa, and David Willinger.

Organized by China's Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau in partnership with several organizations, the event was held under the theme of "Remembering Taiwan's Restoration, Advancing National Reunification." The one-week exhibition features four thematic sections and more than 30 photos.
Guo Haiyan, Chinese Ambassador to Kenya, said the historical fact of Taiwan's restoration, together with international legal instruments, including the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and the Japanese Instrument of Surrender, constitutes a key link in the historical and legal chain underwriting the one-China principle.
On Oct. 25, 1945, a ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in the Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in Taipei, and Taiwan, which had been under Japanese colonial rule for 50 years, was finally restored to China and returned to the embrace of the motherland, she said.
In 2025, the Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress designated Oct. 25 of each year as the "Commemoration Day of Taiwan's Restoration," she added.
Guo said that since the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, Kenya has always abided by the one-China principle and properly handled Taiwan-related issues.
She noted that in the joint statement issued during Kenyan President William Ruto's state visit to China in April 2025, the Kenyan side "resolutely opposes any form of 'Taiwan independence' and supports all efforts by the Chinese government to achieve national reunification."
Erastus Mwencha, former deputy chairperson of the African Union Commission, said the restoration of Taiwan in 1945 marked the end of the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895 and a monumental moment of restored integrity for the Chinese nation. History is a living reminder of the sacrifices nations make in defense of their identity, freedom and dignity, he said.
Mwencha recalled that when the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 in 1971, restoring the lawful rights of the People's Republic of China, 26 African nations voted in favor.
"Our relationship was not born out of mere commercial interest or diplomatic convenience; it was forged in the crucible of a common struggle against colonialism and foreign domination," he said, citing China's support for African liberation movements from the 1955 Bandung Conference to the construction of the TAZARA Railway.
Ying Qiang, director of Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau, said the exhibition is being held in five African countries -- Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Nigeria and Mozambique.
"It is a look back at an important chapter of history, an act of remembrance for the fruits of victory in the World Anti-Fascist War, and above all an affirmation of peace, justice and historical fact," said Ying.
Ying said that the photographs on display capture the historical moments of Taiwan's restoration and the course of the Chinese nation's resistance to foreign aggression, alongside the struggle for national liberation.
"Through these images, we hope our African friends will gain a more vivid understanding of the historical background, the historical facts and the historical significance of Taiwan's restoration, and a deeper appreciation of the firm position of the Chinese people in safeguarding national sovereignty and territorial integrity," Ying added. ■

Storm Austen injures several, disrupts transport in Belgium
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:56:03 CST
06:56:03 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Storm Austen swept across Belgium on Friday, bringing strong winds and rain, injuring several people. Rail, road, air and maritime transport were also disrupted.
According to the Brussels fire service, a tree fell onto a restaurant terrace near the Grand Place in central Brussels, injuring three people. Another person was struck by a falling branch in Woluwe-Saint-Pierre, a municipality in the Brussels-Capital Region.
Belgium's Royal Meteorological Institute (RMI) issued orange alerts for strong winds in several parts of the country, including Brussels, where the alert was set to be downgraded to yellow at 9 p.m. local time (1900 GMT).
On Friday evening, Beaufort Force 9 winds were recorded at the Westhinder monitoring station in Belgian waters of the North Sea. Peak gusts reached 99 km/h in the coastal town of Blankenberge and 97 km/h in Chievres, in Wallonia's Hainaut province.
Several railway lines were affected by fallen trees and strong winds. Rail infrastructure operator Infrabel reported about eight incidents in Flanders and Brussels in the evening. Near Puurs, in Antwerp province, a fallen tree damaged overhead lines, leaving about 45 passengers stranded on a train for nearly three hours before they were all evacuated. Rail services were also disrupted in Wallonia.
In Brussels, six tram lines remained affected on Friday evening due to damaged overhead lines, according to public transport operator STIB. On Flemish motorways, traffic jams reached a combined length of about 250 km at their peak during the evening rush hour.
Authorities also closed parks, nature reserves and wooded areas in Brussels until Saturday morning. Residents were advised to avoid trees and unnecessary travel.
The Port of Antwerp-Bruges said vessel arrivals and departures had been suspended, with traffic expected to resume on Saturday morning. Shipping to and from the Port of Ghent was also affected. At Brussels Airport, two inbound flights were diverted to Amsterdam because of strong winds, while other flights were delayed, according to the airport.
The storm brought down trees, damaged rooftops and blocked roads across the country, prompting numerous calls to emergency services. The Brussels fire service said it had completed dozens of storm-related operations by Friday evening, with dozens more pending. Belgium's National Crisis Center said nearly 2.8 million alert messages were sent through the BE-Alert system on Thursday and Friday.
According to the RMI, winds were expected to ease inland later on Friday evening, while strong gusts would persist along the coast. Another storm, Boelo, was forecast to bring fresh rainfall and stronger winds from Saturday evening into Sunday. ■

Feature: More than a sweet -- Türkiye's lokma tradition offers comfort in grief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:56:00 CST
06:56:00 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Outside the historic Haci Bayram Mosque in Ankara, the capital of Türkiye, strangers reached for golden pieces of lokma, a traditional fried dough sweet soaked in syrup. For Adnan Kirbas, the treats carried a meaning far beyond their sweetness.
The retired Ankara resident had arranged for the sweets to be distributed to the public to mark the second anniversary of his mother's death. Each serving he handed to a stranger was a small tribute to the mother he still deeply missed.
"This is part of our tradition," Kirbas told Xinhua.
As the pastries passed from hand to hand, strangers became part of a family's act of remembrance. They offered prayers and blessings. Their kind words brought comfort to a son still seeking ways to honor his mother's memory.
Their prayers, Kirbas said, helped ease the grief of those mourning a loved one, reminding them that they did not have to bear their sorrow alone.
Fried dough sweets are enjoyed across the Mediterranean and the Middle East, while charitable food-sharing traditions take different forms across cultures. In Türkiye, this practice takes a distinctive form known as hayir lokmasi, or charity lokma, in which freshly prepared sweets are distributed free of charge to the public to honor deceased loved ones or mark joyful occasions, such as births and personal achievements.
Families typically hire a mobile lokma van, where a specialist prepares and fries batches of yeast-based dough on site, coats the golden pieces in light sugar syrup, and serves them on small disposable plates with toothpicks.
For Ankara shopkeeper Serkan Erdogan, the tradition carries a similar personal significance. The previous week, he had arranged for lokma to be distributed in memory of both his late father and his wife's late father.
Erdogan learned the custom from older generations and hopes his children will carry it on. Yet he worries that younger people are gradually drifting away from such traditions in an increasingly digital age.
"We are trying to pass certain things on to the younger generation, but we have not been very successful," he said.
His concern points to what is at stake beyond lokma itself: a tradition that draws people out of their private lives and encourages them to share with others.
Ismail Kadir Aran, a lokma maker who began learning the family trade at the age of 13, summed it up simply: "People want to share their happiness and their sadness with others. That is why they offer these treats."
The sweets soon disappear. But the remembrance, shared among hundreds of strangers, lingers a little longer. ■

Bulldozers demolish a residential building near the northern entrance of the West Bank city of Hebron, on Oct. 23, 2026.
