(Photo by Mamoun Wazwaz/Xinhua)
JERUSALEM/RAMALLAH, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Israel is preparing a major military operation in the West Bank, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday, as local sources said Israeli forces demolished a residential building in Hebron and closed the city's main entrances following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian attackers.
The Israel Defense Forces said it had launched raids in Hebron and nearby villages following the attack, in which three other Israeli soldiers were slightly wounded.
The military said it was investigating, together with Shin Bet domestic security agency, whether the attackers belonged to an isolated cell or were linked to a larger militant cell.
Speaking in Hebron, Netanyahu said the military would apply the operational model it had used in refugee camps to neighborhoods from which the attackers had emerged.
Netanyahu said that under the plan, residents would be evacuated, troops would conduct house-to-house searches, weapons would be seized, and what he called "terrorist infrastructure" would be destroyed.
Netanyahu added that he and the defense minister had reviewed plans for a large-scale military operation in the West Bank, describing it as an operation unlike any carried out since the 1967 Middle East war.
He said the military was ready to carry it out, but that the timing had yet to be decided.
In response, the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates condemned Israel's tightening of restrictions in Hebron, warning the measures could lead to further violence and collective punishment.
Palestinian sources said Israeli forces demolished a building containing three apartments in the Farsh al-Hawa area west of Hebron, each covering about 200 square meters.
Local sources said Israeli forces closed Hebron and its main entrances, preventing residents and vehicles from entering or leaving. Roads linking the city to nearby areas were also closed.
Palestinian security sources said Israeli forces tightened restrictions at entrances and exits to cities across the West Bank, and closed many checkpoints and iron gates in the southern, central and northern areas.
Hebron is a major economic center in the West Bank. The closure of its entrances has disrupted daily life in the area, which is home to more than one million Palestinians, according to Israeli reports. ■

====================================================================================================

One-time minnows Tonga and Samoa now star World Cup attractions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:22:36 UTC
06:22:36 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Once seen as minnows, Tonga and Samoa are now Rugby League World Cup drawcards
At Western Sydney Stadium last week, Toa Samoa had a moment of pure elation, a crushing 78-4 victory over France at the men's Rugby League World Cup.
It was capped off with an extraordinary final play that saw a penalty goal attempt from Stephen Crichton ricochet off the post.
The ball bounced towards Benaiah Ioelu who scored a try after the full-time siren had sounded, delivering Samoa's largest-ever victory.
What was more extraordinary was that a game with a kick-off time of 5:45pm on Friday, playing out what was likely and ultimately proved to be a walkover, still drew a crowd of 13,000.
It was a horror slot to play in: a workday, outside school holidays, in a busy part of Sydney where traffic was banking up across the many arterial roads that led to it.
Yet the crowd, largely comprising Western Sydney's large Samoan population, bellowed Ua fa'afetai — a traditional song of thanks and gratitude.
Fiji and the Cook Islands played each other on Sunday in Newcastle; there was a tick over 10,000 in the stands and another 1.7 million watching on television across Australia, outrating several flagship current affairs shows, news bulletins and reality programs.
These are just two examples that show this is a World Cup transformed by Pasifika passion.
The growing strength of Samoa and Tonga's men's teams has been no secret, but now more than ever the iron grip of dominance largely held by Australia on international rugby league, occasionally disrupted by New Zealand, could be under threat.
What has also been clear to those at the grounds or watching from home is that this World Cup in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea is one where diaspora communities have breathed life into a tournament that has previously lacked the same level of excitement or prestige compared to other international sporting events.
Australia's migration story tracks with this
The shift will be most obvious on November 1, when Samoa and Tonga play each other in Sydney, in a game that was the first to sell out despite being in the third week of the tournament.
Already a series of ex-players and pundits have raised the call to move the game to the larger Stadium Australia to accommodate a crowd beyond the 30,000 that Western Sydney Stadium holds.
The interest should come as no surprise though, as the Pasifika population in Australia has been steadily increasing.
In 2011, 165,000 Australians identified as being from Pasifika communities; by 2021, that number had almost tripled to 415,033.
Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows outer suburban areas of Sydney and Brisbane have burgeoning communities.
Sierra Keung, a senior lecturer in sports leadership and management at Auckland University of Technology, said she was not surprised by the fan turnout.
"The pride for our cultures, for our people, it's more than just a jersey for our Pasifika communities," Dr Keung told ABC Sport.
She cited a distinctive moment on the field that set this explosion in motion.
In 2017, the International Rugby League changed the rules to allow players with cultural ties to multiple nations to play for the country of their choosing.
The most famous change in allegiance was Jason Taumalolo.
That rule change is on full display at this tournament.
Of the listed starting line-up for Tonga's match against Lebanon last night at Western Sydney Stadium, none of the players were born in Tonga, but all have deep familial ties to the island nation.
Tonga beat Lebanon 36-0 to keep its campaign on track.
"This is years in the making, and it's come down to people making bold decisions, like Jason Taumalolo to be the first to say, 'I'm going to go home and represent my people,'" Dr Keung said.
Salesi Foketi is one of a number of Tongan players that chose to represent his familial roots over his country of birth, New Zealand.
"Right from when I was a boy, it was always Tonga," he said.
Winger Jojo Fifita made his debut last weekend for Tonga and it was a moment to acknowledge his forebears.
"Being able to represent my dad's side was something I'd always wanted to do when I was older and I finally got that opportunity," he said.
Extension beyond Pasifika diaspora may be the future
There is another team outside the South Pacific that is relying on heritage and cultural ties as the bind for players to represent it.
Lebanon's winger Jason Saab has potentially the most unique ties to the country.
His stepfather, whose name he took, is Lebanese, and Saab is now lining up for the Cedars.
Saab told ABC Sport in September of the sincere ties to Lebanese culture through his stepdad Pierre.
"That's the culture that raised me ultimately, that whole community of people. That's kind of where I found my identity to be," he said.
While all players in the Cedars squad were born in Australia, Lebanon coach Michael Cheika, who is also Lebanese Australian, said the small but dedicated rugby league community in Lebanon was driving the entire playing group, especially for those with family in Lebanon where strikes from Israel continued amid a broader conflict in the region.
"With everything that's going on over there … you've got to understand that they may not have enough petrol to get to the games, let alone field markings, fields that are available," he said.
As Samoa and Tonga have brought a genuine competitiveness to the tournament, there are other countries with large populations in Australia, such as Fiji and the Cook Islands, that could also challenge the Kangaroos, who have won 12 world titles, including six of the last seven.
"The talent is just through the roof right now, both men's and women's," Dr Keung said.
"So I'm really excited for this World Cup, but also for future World Cups too, because it's just going to get better and better each time it comes around."
There is no doubt rugby league has cottoned on to its international life blood, and it seems the public is following suit.

When a business suddenly collapses, how can customers get money back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:07:49 UTC
06:07:49 KST

Can paying a deposit by credit card help you claw back losses when a company suddenly goes bankrupt?
The spate of caravan companies going bust has led to hundreds of customers losing tens of thousands of dollars in deposits.
From Sunshine Coast based Zone RV last December to Australian Off Road just last month, there is a long list of manufacturers going bust after trading while insolvent.
But buyers being caught up in business insolvencies is not a new issue.
Building companies and tech giant Dick Smith in 2016 have left customers out of pocket, while the collapse of whitegoods company Kleenmaid saw a former director jailed.
When it comes to getting back money you have forked out for a deposit, Deloitte senior liquidator Richard Hughes said there are no guarantees.
"There is no risk-free way of doing anything these days,"
he said.
"You have to be really careful."
And if possible, he warns, do not pay by cash.
Is paying by credit card the answer?
Mr Hughes helped creditors fight over the carcass of Kleenmaid, which collapsed owing $100 million, and says credit card payments can be good insurance.
His forensic examination of the company's books found customers were set to lose $25 million in deposits.
But when he realised half of those had been paid on credit card, he was able to help get $12.5 million back into disillusioned customers' bank accounts.
This was through charge back requests, which is when customers have paid for good or services they did not receive, like a cancelled flight or a brand new caravan.
How does a charge back request work?
The Australian Banking Association describes it this way.
"When someone pays for goods or services by card that they never receive, they can ask their bank to dispute the transaction," a spokesperson said.
"The rules are set and administered by the card schemes, such as Visa and Mastercard — time limits apply, so customers should contact their bank as soon as possible."
The customer's bank lodges the claim through the scheme with the business's bank.
"If the claim succeeds, the money goes back to the customer and is taken from the business's bank," the spokesperson said.
"Payments by cash don't carry charge back rights."
The Office of Fair Trading said financial institutions may be able to assist customers who have paid "by credit card, debit card, or through a secure payment provider such as PayPal".
Will changes to card fees make it hard to pay by credit?
From October 1, the reserve bank banned credit and debit card surcharges across major card networks.
Some customers may be concerned about whether these changes will impact their ability to pay a deposit, and whether companies may stop accepting credit card payments.
But Mr Hughes said he believed businesses would still be happy to take credit card deposits, with card fees most likely added into their quotes.
If a small business insists on only cash, it could be seen as a red flag.
Customers are also encouraged to do a financial health check on the business they are putting their faith in.
It is also important to remember that unlike real estate companies, which are legally bound to hold deposits in a protected trust account, small businesses are not.
How to check if a business is struggling
ASIC says warning signs customers can watch out for include:
- bad reviews
- ongoing losses
- board disputes and director resignations, or loss of management personnel
- suppliers placing the company on cash-on-delivery terms
- a sudden change of name
- movement of a business or its assets to another company
ASIC encourages customers to check whether a company has entered liquidation or external administration through ASIC Connect or ASIC's Published Notices website.
Will creditors get money back?
When a company goes into liquidation, the question every creditor wants answered is simple: am I going to get my money back?
According to ASIC, the data is stark.
In most small to medium-sized corporate insolvencies, 97 per cent of creditors received between 0–11 cents in the dollar.
In the recent cases of collapsed caravan companies, majority of customers have not been able to get their money back, and have seen their savings vanish.
Caravanning Queensland Trade advised any customers who have purchased a product they haven't received to contact the appointed administrator or liquidator as soon as possible, and bring their contract, receipts and proof of payment.
"For anyone considering buying a caravan, Caravanning Queensland recommends a deposit of 10 per cent of the purchase price, with the balance paid when the completed van is ready for inspection and handover," chief executive Jason Plant said.
"We remain committed to promoting responsible business practice, transparency and consumer confidence across the caravan and RV industry."

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is clashing with right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro in a second and final election debate, in a last-ditch effort to lure undecided voters.

The Brazilian left sprang into action after the unexpected result, staging massive rallies and launching an energetic online campaign to try to deliver Lula, 80, a comeback.
Both sides have accused each other of misusing social media, while Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is under fire over alleged unequal treatment of the candidates.

"The trend favours Lula, but he probably doesn't have enough time to flip the race," Eurasia Group wrote, adding that "the debate will be critical."
The first debate on Sunday quickly deteriorated into a barrage of insults, leaving little room for concrete proposals and voters more confused than ever.

Over a million people signed an online petition asking the Globo TV network to implement a live fact-checking system during the debate.

Legal disputes have dominated the bitter campaign.
Both candidates went to court this week to demand their opponent be disqualified over social media abuses.
Lula's campaign has accused tech giant Meta of "interference" in favour of Flavio Bolsonaro via alleged "algorithmic manipulation."
Meta has denied doing anything to favor one side, but admitted that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.
An electoral court on Thursday gave Meta and X 24 hours to explain their criteria for distributing political content and adverts, as well as how they employ artificial intelligence.
Lula on Thursday called for the defeat of Meta's "digital empire" during a live broadcast with the "Lula's Army" WhatsApp channel, which saw its follower count balloon by over one million to reach over 10 million Friday.
"Meta will have to be reinvented; it cannot simply assume it can go on deceiving humanity forever."
His team is concerned about "the obvious alignment between Meta and the US government," Joao Brant, his campaign's digital strategy advisor, told AFP.
Trump has not explicitly endorsed Flavio Bolsonaro, whose father is an enthusiastic ally of the US leader.
The senator's first-round lead convinced Washington that the candidate did not need any "additional gesture" in his favour, according to a Brazilian government source.
Bolsonaro's campaign on Friday accused Lula's camp of "using public resources and digital structures to interfere" in the election.

Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:59:50 UTC
05:59:50 KST

The top Air Force commander on the Japanese island of Okinawa has clamped down alcohol and issued a curfew for junior enlisted Airmen and Guardians at Kadena Air Base for the next month. The order came roughly two weeks after a U.S. Marine was arrested for allegedly robbing and murdering a Japanese woman on the island.
Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing at Kadena, issued the Oct. 22 memo, ordering the “Curtailment of Liberty and the Consumption of Alcohol,” according to a memo posted on the popular unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page.
A PACAF spokesperson confirmed the memo’s authenticity. The order went into effect Oct. 22 and will last “throughout the 30-day period of reflection,” concluding on Nov. 8, according to the memo:
- All personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4 are not to consume alcohol.
- Off-base liberty between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. local time is curtailed for all personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4.
- Possession of alcohol is banned in all dormitories within Kadena Air Base, to include dormitory common areas.
During the period, “commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced, systematic health and welfare inspections of dormitory rooms to ensure compliance of this order,” the memo states.
The memo follows an Oct. 6 memo from United States Forces Japan that ordered similar liberty restrictions and personal conduct training as part of a “period of reflection” following the Marine’s arrest in connection with the alleged murder of an Okinawan woman in Naha.
Japanese police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, on Oct. 4 for allegedly killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet, Marine Corps Times reported.
“Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Benjamin T. Watson, area coordinator for U.S. Forces Japan, wrote in the memo. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will continue to ensure full cooperation with Japanese authorities throughout the investigation.”
Watson added that serving on Okinawa “comes with responsibility.”
“We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region.”
The USFJ memo prohibited alcohol consumption for 48 hours from Oct. 7-9 but stopped short of restricting consumption during the 30-day period of reflection. In a statement, PACAF Gallemore’s Oct. 22 memo contains extra restrictions.
“The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” the PACAF statement read. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, [Gallemore] determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members.”
Periods of reflection and associated restrictions have been used by commanders on Okinawa in the past to reinforce discipline after violent, criminal incidents involving U.S. personnel and Japanese residents. In 2024, USFJ prohibited all American troops in the country from publicly consuming alcohol from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. every day after a string of alleged sexual assaults. In 2017, the command prohibited all drinking and cut off-base liberty for troops on Okinawa after a fatal car crash involving a drunk Marine. In 2010, then-Brig. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach—now the Chief of Staff—instituted a brief period of reflection restricting alcohol and off-base liberty at Kadena after a string of alcohol-related arrests. In 2008, commanders imposed the measure to calm an uproar in the surrounding community over allegations that a Marine raped a 14-year-old girl on the island, The Guardian reported.
Kadena is the closest U.S. air base to Taiwan, making it a strategically vital location should China ever launch an invasion.

stars return to frank lloyd wright’s only built planetarium after twenty years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:55:19 UTC
05:55:19 KST

stars return to frank lloyd wright’s only built planetarium after twenty years
at florida southern college, the restored 1950s-era building reopens with its original circular seating and new digital projection system.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
a dome full of stars returns to florida southern college
Two rings of curved red seating surround a central projector beneath the domed ceiling of Frank Lloyd Wright‘s only built planetarium, which has reopened at Florida Southern College in Lakeland. After more than two decades without regular star shows, the 1950s building has been restored by a team led by Jeff Baker of MCWB Architects. Its original seating has been returned to Wright’s circular arrangement, and a new digital projection system brings the night sky back overhead. The Miller Planetarium welcomed the public again on September 26th, 2026.
The planetarium occupies the southern end of the Polk Science Building, part of the college‘s collection of thirteen Wright-designed structures. Built between 1954 and 1958, its pale concrete walls are patterned with geometric textile blocks, while a white dome rises above the surrounding low-slung buildings. Wright had explored the idea of designing a planetarium for decades before incorporating one into his plans for Florida Southern. Its first show took place in April 1960, a year after the architect’s death.
restoring the original concrete textile blocks
Work began on the exterior in 2021, addressing years of water damage and deterioration in the building’s concrete surfaces. The team at MCWB replaced sections of roofing and repaired failing stucco, while more than 280 hand-cast textile blocks around the planetarium’s perimeter required replacement. These decorative concrete units form part of the architectural language Wright developed across the Florida Southern campus. To reproduce their geometric patterns, the restoration team used contemporary fabrication methods, including 3D printing to develop molds for new blocks designed to match the originals.
The work also revealed some unexpected details behind the facade. During construction, Baker’s team discovered areas of steel framing and open cavities behind the upper walls, where they had anticipated a more typical arrangement of Wright’s concrete blocks. The discovery made it possible to introduce insulation into portions of the building that had previously been left exposed to Florida’s heat. Elsewhere, the architecture posed a different challenge. Wright’s concrete surfaces often serve several structural functions at once, leaving little concealed space for the mechanical systems needed in a contemporary building.
wright’s curved plywood seating returns to its circular layout
Inside the planetarium, the restoration focused on recovering the original spatial arrangement, which had been altered through decades of repairs and technological additions. A computer closet installed during the 1980s had interrupted the circular seating plan. Its removal allowed the architects to return Wright’s original plywood benches to their intended positions, arranged in two concentric rings around the projection equipment. Local craftspeople repaired the surviving seating, retaining its curved forms and colored vinyl upholstery.
The room’s finishes have also been returned to their earlier appearance. Deep-blue wall paint was replaced with a lighter scheme based on the original design, while damaged plaster was repaired. Underfoot, the floor was refinished in Wright’s familiar Cherokee Red, its glossy surface reflecting the curved benches above. The restoration preserves an unusual arrangement for a planetarium, where visitors sit in the round beneath a complete dome. Many newer facilities use forward-facing theater seating, but Wright’s design brings the audience together around the center of the room.
modern projection technology beneath the historic dome
The final phase introduced a COSM digital projection system and Bowen sound system, updating equipment that had prevented the planetarium from operating since 2004. The building had continued to see occasional use after the old projector stopped functioning, though regular astronomical presentations were suspended. With the new technology installed, the restored room can once again host presentations about the solar system and distant planets, along with programs developed for students and visiting school groups.
The reopening also continues a longer preservation effort across Wright’s Florida Southern campus, which was commissioned by college president Ludd Spivey in 1938. Restoration projects have included the Waterdome fountain and the Annie Pfeiffer Chapel, along with the campus’s network of concrete esplanades. At the Miller Planetarium, the latest work returns the building to the educational purpose Wright envisioned. Visitors can now take their seats in the original circular auditorium, with its restored red interior beneath a sky projected across the dome.
project info:
name: Miller Planetarium
original architect: Frank Lloyd Wright | @wrighttaliesin
architect: MCWB Architects | @mcwbarchitects
lead restoration architect: Jeff Baker
location: Florida Southern College | @wright_fsc, @floridasouthern, Lakeland, Florida
original construction: 1954–1958
first planetarium show: April 7th, 1960
public reopening: September 26th, 2026

In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:52:23 UTC
05:52:23 KST

After SpaceX restricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
Zelenskyy also announced a partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield.
Chad Anderson, founder and CEO of venture capital firm Space Capital, said such an alternative could be "two to three years away" and that "matching Starlink's scale is a longer road."
SpaceX has around around 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan McDowell.
Anderson said Starshield may be an even tougher service to replace. "The Pentagon's own contracting documents say SpaceX is the only provider that can meet some of its needs through 2026. Capital isn't the constraint any more. Launch is."
Even Starlink competitors have relied on SpaceX launches to put their satellites in orbit.
As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft traveling at speeds over 100 mph.
Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have shirked responsibility for the unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions.
SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment.
Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties are calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.
Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email that the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally."
Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off."
Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, including Amazon's Leo, France's Eutelsat and a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin called TeraWave, which has yet to deploy its first satellites.
Beyond Ukraine, several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029.
Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Anderson, whose firm tracks industry deals. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet.
Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet."
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

NASA lays out a packed 14-day schedule for Artemis III
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:51:11 UTC
05:51:11 KST

NASA’s upcoming Artemis III will be the tiebreaker between two potential lunar landers for future crewed missions to the moon’s surface, the space agency’s head Jared Isaacman said on Friday. But both SpaceX and Blue Origin are planning to touch down on the moon in 2028 no matter what.
Only one will take part in Artemis IV, the 2028 mission to return humans to the lunar surface—NASA will wait as long as possible before making a selection.
Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons said at a press briefing on Friday that both companies “are planning for lunar landing missions in 2028.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Before that, they must get through Artemis III. In that mission, NASA’s Orion crew capsule will attempt to dock with both Blue Origin’s Blue Moon and a version of SpaceX’s Starship. Though no exact launch window was announced, Artemis III is expected to lift off in the summer of 2027, Isaacman said.
Artemis III was previously slated to be a crewed mission to the moon’s surface but was reconfigured earlier this year to instead allow for a complex, two-week-long test run of both landers in orbit.
Artemis III requires several rockets to be in space at once. First, Blue Moon will launch onboard a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket. Once in orbit, tests will be conducted to ensure the lander is in good shape.
Meanwhile NASA’s Orion will already be on the launchpad atop a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. “We’re going to do everything we can to ensure that that vehicle is ready to go as quickly as we can after that first Blue Origin launch,” Parsons said.
Because the SLS only needs to put Orion into orbit, the rocket has been modified to remove its upper stage.
“When we pivoted to a low-Earth orbit mission, the SLS team quickly came back and said, ‘We don’t need the upper stage for that. Core stage has plenty of performance to drop us in the orbit we need,’” Parsons said.
Three days after Blue Moon launches, Orion will attempt to dock with the spacecraft, after which there will be two days of testing its guidance, navigation and communications systems.
On day six, SpaceX’s Starship will launch, and Orion will detach from Blue Moon, adjust its orbit and attempt a second docking with Starship. The Artemis III crew will not enter Starship during the operation, however, and the test will last just two hours.
“Once Starship operations are complete, Orion and the crew have the remaining days available for additional test objectives before needing to come home,” Parsons said.
Hurdles have to be overcome before any of this can happen: Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has not launched since one of the spacecraft exploded spectacularly in May. Parsons said the company expects to resume launches in November and that, right now, NASA has no contingency plans to send Blue Moon to space onboard an alternate vehicle.
“Their design for the Artemis III lander test article is in good shape,” he said. “We have gone through design reviews. We’ve been participating with them, and they have parts coming together from across the United States.”
Meanwhile SpaceX is aiming to conduct another test of Starship next month, which will include upgrades to the craft’s Raptor engines. Starship has seen a number of hiccups, including several explosions during test flights. But in its most recent demonstration, the vehicle was able to enter orbit for the first time—a major milestone on the way to being ready for Artemis III.
Artemis III’s optimal flight timeframe is 14 days, but the mission could be expanded to 17 days if necessary. While the attempted dockings with the landers are key, the mission will also involve collecting vital data on the health of the astronauts.
“Every day of this mission is built around specific tests that reduce risk, give us valuable science and allow us to test out our capabilities before we go and undertake the lunar landing,” Parsons said.
And looking ahead, work has already begun on assembling and testing the Orion crew and service modules that will be used on Artemis IV, Parsons added.
“We are hardly in a position to ‘set it and forget it,’” Isaacman quipped at the event, referring to future Artemis missions planning. “We will never stop listening to data and adapt as circumstances require.”

Yemen’s peace process has a structural blind spot: The south’s political future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:47:23 UTC
05:47:23 KST

Yemen’s prolonged conflict is frequently discussed through the familiar language of ceasefires, military de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and negotiations between the principal armed parties. These are important elements of any effort to end the war. Yet they do not fully explain why successive political initiatives have struggled to establish a durable settlement.
The deeper problem is structural:
Yemen’s crisis is not simply a contest over who controls the central government. It is also a dispute over the nature of the state, the distribution of political authority and the future status of its different regions. Among these questions, the Southern Question remains one of the most consequential and least adequately resolved.
A peace process that postpones this question risks producing an agreement that reduces violence temporarily without resolving the political disagreements capable of generating another conflict. The challenge for regional governments and international mediators is therefore not merely to bring the parties back to the negotiating table, but to design a political framework that addresses the underlying causes of instability.
The Limits of a Narrow Peace Process
Yemen’s war has multiple dimensions, involving competing political projects, regional rivalries, institutional fragmentation and a severe economic crisis. Negotiations focused exclusively on the confrontation between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis cannot, by themselves, resolve every dispute shaping the country’s future.
The United Nations’ efforts to promote a negotiated settlement have helped maintain international attention on diplomacy and the need to reduce violence. Nevertheless, the broader question remains: what political order is a settlement intended to establish, and whose aspirations must it accommodate to remain sustainable?
The distinction matters. An agreement can distribute positions within existing institutions without resolving fundamental disagreements about the legitimacy of those institutions or the territorial structure of the state. It can also establish temporary security arrangements while leaving competing political claims untouched.
Such agreements may create valuable space for diplomacy, but they should not be mistaken for a comprehensive settlement.
The Southern Question illustrates this difficulty.
For many southerners, the issue is not limited to representation within a unified state. It concerns historical experience, political identity, governance, the distribution of resources and the right to determine the South’s future status.
Treating these demands as secondary matters to be addressed after a national agreement has been reached risks placing the most difficult questions at the end of a process that may never reach them.
Why the Southern Question Is Fundamentally Political
The unification of the former North Yemen and South Yemen in 1990 created a new political framework, but it did not permanently settle disagreements over power, representation and the character of the state. The 1994 war deepened divisions, while subsequent grievances contributed to the emergence of a broader southern political movement.
These historical developments do not mean that every southern community shares the same political preferences or supports a single representative. Southern Yemen contains diverse political currents, regional interests and social constituencies. Hadramout, Aden, Shabwa, Lahj, Abyan, Al-Mahra and other southern areas have distinct histories and priorities that any credible settlement must take seriously.
Recognising this diversity is essential. The Southern Question should neither be reduced to the position of one political organisation nor dismissed because southern political actors disagree over leadership, strategy or the desired constitutional outcome.
A sustainable process must create meaningful opportunities for southern participation, allow competing perspectives to be expressed peacefully and establish a credible mechanism for determining the region’s future.
The central principle is that political disagreement should be addressed through an agreed and legitimate process, rather than indefinitely deferred or settled through military pressure.
For international mediators, this requires a more explicit approach to the South. Instead of assuming that its future can be determined automatically through a broader Yemeni agreement, negotiations should establish a dedicated political track with clear objectives, representative participation and a defined timetable.
Without such a framework, the Southern Question is likely to remain a source of uncertainty even if other fronts experience de-escalation.
The Constitutional Declaration: Political Significance and Legal Questions
On 2 January 2026, the Southern Transitional Council, led by Aidarous Al-Zubaidi, announced a constitutional declaration associated with a proposed transitional process for the South. The initiative outlined a two-year period intended to facilitate dialogue and prepare for a popular referendum on self-determination.
The announcement brought the question of southern statehood into sharper focus. It also highlighted the distance between the political aspirations advanced by the Southern Transitional Council and the existing international framework, which continues to recognise the Republic of Yemen as a state.
The declaration should therefore be examined on two distinct levels: its political significance and its legal status.
Politically, it represents an attempt to establish a defined pathway for addressing the South’s future rather than leaving the question open-ended. Its proposed referendum also places popular consent at the centre of the debate, an important consideration in any discussion of self-determination.
Legally and diplomatically, however, a unilateral declaration does not automatically create an internationally recognised state or impose an obligation on other governments to recognise it. The Yemeni government rejected the initiative, and the proposal did not receive an announced endorsement from the United Nations when it was introduced.
These distinctions should not obscure the underlying political question. The absence of immediate international recognition does not eliminate the need to address southern aspirations, just as the announcement of a constitutional framework does not, by itself, settle questions of representation, territorial governance, institutional legitimacy or international law.
The appropriate response is serious diplomatic engagement.
Regional governments and international institutions should examine the declaration’s proposed transitional arrangements, the practical conditions required for a referendum, the participation of different southern constituencies and the safeguards needed to ensure that any political process is peaceful, transparent and credible.
They should also clarify what legal and political steps would be required for any future change in the South’s status to gain wider international acceptance.
This approach would neither prejudge the outcome nor dismiss the initiative without examination. Instead, it would create a framework through which a contested political claim could be addressed through diplomacy rather than renewed confrontation.
International Recognition Must Be Part of a Political Strategy
Calls for international recognition of the South’s political aspirations are likely to remain central to the debate. However, recognition should be understood as part of a broader diplomatic process, not as a substitute for one.
Governments considering the South’s future must weigh the principles of self-determination, territorial integrity, regional stability and the peaceful resolution of disputes. They must also consider the extent to which any proposed arrangement reflects the freely expressed preferences of the population concerned and provides credible protections for those who hold different views.
For supporters of southern independence, the objective should be to secure international engagement with a clear and credible pathway towards self-determination, including the possibility of recognising an independent southern state if the necessary political and legal conditions are met.
That requires more than declarations of support. It requires sustained diplomacy, inclusive southern representation, institutional preparation and an agreed process capable of earning domestic and international confidence.
The international community should not allow the absence of consensus over the final outcome to become a permanent justification for avoiding the question itself.
At the same time, no political actor should assume that recognition can be secured solely through unilateral measures or the establishment of institutions without broader political legitimacy. Durable outcomes require processes that can withstand disagreement and accommodate the interests of affected communities.
The task is therefore to establish a credible route from political aspiration to a peaceful and legitimate determination of status.
Hadramout and the Challenge of Southern Representation
Hadramout illustrates why the future of southern Yemen cannot be approached through a narrow focus on competing political leaderships.
Its geographic position, economic resources, social structures and connections with the wider Gulf give it particular significance. Yet its importance is not merely strategic or economic. Hadramout’s people have their own political interests and expectations concerning local governance, security, resource management and representation.
Any settlement concerning the South must take these interests seriously. A process that assumes a single political organisation can automatically speak for every southern community risks reproducing the very problem that negotiations are intended to solve: the exclusion of significant constituencies from decisions about their future.
This does not mean that southern political aspirations should be fragmented into competing local vetoes. Rather, it means that a credible framework must combine a coherent political process with meaningful guarantees for regional participation and local decision-making.
For Hadramout, this includes transparent arrangements for managing public resources, accountable local institutions, reliable public services and a meaningful role in determining the political and economic future of the region.
These considerations are equally important for the wider South. Political legitimacy cannot be established through slogans alone; it must be reflected in the institutions through which people participate, exercise rights and hold authorities accountable.
A Practical Framework for International Engagement
If international mediators want a settlement capable of lasting beyond an initial reduction in fighting, four steps deserve particular attention.
First, establish a dedicated political track for the Southern Question. Its mandate should explicitly address the South’s future status, political representation and the range of constitutional options available. The process should have a clear timetable and should not be indefinitely subordinated to negotiations on other fronts.
Second, develop an inclusive framework for southern participation. Political parties, regional representatives, civil society and other relevant constituencies should have meaningful opportunities to contribute. Participation must be substantive rather than symbolic, and the process should provide safeguards for peaceful political disagreement.
Third, clarify the legal and diplomatic pathway. The constitutional declaration announced by Al-Zubaidi should be subject to serious examination alongside the wider question of self-determination. International actors should identify the procedures, guarantees and political agreements required for a credible process, without presenting contested legal claims as settled facts.
Fourth, connect political negotiations with economic and institutional recovery. Any future arrangement must address public revenue, local governance, security, infrastructure and the provision of essential services. Political legitimacy is difficult to sustain when people experience persistent economic insecurity and weak public institutions.
These steps would not guarantee agreement. They would, however, make the process more realistic by confronting the questions that a sustainable settlement must ultimately answer.
The Cost of Leaving the Question Unresolved
The international community has understandable reasons to prioritise immediate de-escalation in Yemen. Renewed fighting threatens civilian lives, deepens economic hardship and risks destabilising the wider region, including areas of importance to international maritime trade.
But urgency should not be confused with a preference for temporary arrangements over difficult political decisions.
A settlement that leaves the Southern Question unresolved may reduce violence in the short term while preserving the conditions for future confrontation. Conversely, a serious process addressing the South’s political future could help transform a recurring source of conflict into a structured diplomatic negotiation.
This requires regional governments to recognise that stability cannot be measured solely by the absence of active fighting. It must also be assessed by whether political arrangements are sufficiently credible, inclusive and legitimate to withstand future disputes.
The same principle applies to international policy. Maintaining existing diplomatic formulas simply because they are familiar may appear less risky than reconsidering them. Yet if those formulas fail to accommodate the political realities of Yemen, preserving them indefinitely may carry its own substantial risks.
Conclusion: Peace Requires a Political Answer
Yemen does not need another agreement that postpones the most difficult questions until a later stage. It needs a political process that addresses the causes of conflict and establishes a credible framework for determining the country’s future.
The Southern Question must be treated as a central component of that process. The constitutional declaration announced by Aidarous Al-Zubaidi has brought the debate over southern statehood and self-determination into sharper focus, but its announcement alone cannot resolve the political and legal questions surrounding the South’s future.
Those questions require serious international engagement, inclusive participation, a clear timetable and a peaceful process capable of establishing political legitimacy.
For the international community, the objective should not be to impose a predetermined outcome. It should be to ensure that the South’s future is addressed directly, that its people have a credible opportunity to determine their political status and that any resulting arrangement is pursued through a legitimate and peaceful framework.
The test of diplomacy is not whether it can postpone a difficult dispute. It is whether it can create a process capable of resolving it.
Yemen’s peace process will remain incomplete for as long as the political future of the South remains an unanswered question.

The new Arab bargain: When Egypt offers to protect Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:33:46 UTC
05:33:46 KST

When Egyptian officials signalled their readiness to support Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, the announcement was presented as a familiar display of Arab solidarity. Yet beneath the diplomatic rhetoric lies a much more significant story, one that says less about military cooperation and more about the changing balance of power in the Middle East.
The immediate question appears straightforward: What kind of protection can Egypt realistically offer Saudi Arabia?
The more important question is whether Egypt’s offer reveals that the traditional hierarchy of the Arab world has been quietly reversed.
For decades, Egypt occupied a unique position in Arab politics. It was the state that projected military weight, diplomatic influence, and cultural authority across the region. Saudi Arabia possessed financial power, but Cairo was widely regarded as the Arab world’s strategic center of gravity.
Today, however, the relationship between the two countries is increasingly defined by a different reality. Egypt remains demographically and militarily significant, but its economic fragility has created a level of dependence on Gulf stability that would have been almost unimaginable in previous generations.
The offer to help defend Saudi Arabia therefore deserves to be viewed not as a demonstration of Egyptian strength, but as evidence of a broader geopolitical transformation.
Military realities explain why.
Despite possessing one of the Arab world’s largest armed forces, Egypt is neither politically nor economically positioned to undertake a large-scale military intervention in Yemen.
The trauma of Gamal Abdel Nasser’s disastrous Yemen campaign in the 1960s remains deeply embedded in Egyptian strategic thinking. That conflict consumed enormous military resources, cost thousands of lives, and distracted Cairo from more immediate national priorities.
No Egyptian leadership is likely to repeat that experience.
Moreover, Egypt today faces a crowded security agenda closer to home. Instability in Sudan, uncertainty in Libya, tensions in the Red Sea, challenges in Sinai, and concerns surrounding the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam all compete for Cairo’s attention. Under such circumstances, the prospect of deploying large numbers of Egyptian troops into another protracted Yemeni conflict appears highly improbable.
If Egypt contributes militarily, its role will likely be concentrated in the maritime domain: securing sea lanes, protecting Red Sea navigation routes, enhancing intelligence cooperation, and supporting regional deterrence efforts. These are meaningful contributions, but they fall far short of the image invoked by traditional narratives of Arab military intervention.
This is where the deeper story emerges.
The Houthis are not merely threatening Saudi Arabia. They are threatening Egypt’s economic lifeline.
The disruption of shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait has severely affected traffic through the Suez Canal, one of Egypt’s most important sources of foreign currency. Every escalation in the Red Sea directly translates into economic pressure on Cairo.
In practical terms, Egypt’s interest in stabilizing the Gulf and confronting threats to regional navigation is not an act of altruism; it is an act of economic self-preservation.
That should not be surprising.
States do not mobilize because of gratitude. They mobilize because of interests.
Yet Middle Eastern political discourse still tends to frame relations between Arab states through the language of fraternity, loyalty, and historical obligation. Such language often obscures what is actually taking place. Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia is driven not by sentiment but by a recognition that Egyptian prosperity is increasingly linked to Gulf stability.
The irony is striking.
For much of the twentieth century, wealthy Arab states depended upon Egypt as a source of political legitimacy, military expertise, and strategic backing. Today, Egypt’s own economic stability has become intertwined with Gulf investment, Gulf aid, and Gulf confidence.
This is not a temporary fluctuation. It reflects a structural shift in how power operates within the Arab world.
The rise of Gulf sovereign wealth funds, ambitious development strategies, and expanding regional investment networks has altered the traditional equation. Political influence is no longer derived primarily from military manpower or ideological leadership. It increasingly flows from economic resilience, investment capacity, and the ability to shape regional outcomes through finance.
Under this new reality, Saudi Arabia has become not merely an oil producer or regional actor, but one of the principal anchors of economic stability across significant parts of the Arab world.
Seen from this perspective, another apparent contradiction suddenly becomes easier to understand.
While expressing support for Saudi Arabia, Egypt also maintains diplomatic communication with Iran. To some observers, this appears inconsistent. Why would Cairo coordinate with Riyadh while simultaneously engaging Tehran?
The answer lies in the changing nature of Middle Eastern politics.
The region no longer operates according to the rigid bloc politics that defined much of the past decade. Saudi Arabia itself has restored relations with Iran. The United Arab Emirates maintains extensive economic links with Tehran. Across the region, governments increasingly seek to combine deterrence with dialogue rather than choose between them.
Egypt’s communication with Iran therefore reflects a wider regional trend: reducing the risk of escalation while maintaining strategic alignments. Cairo has little interest in becoming a frontline participant in a broader regional confrontation. Its primary objective is stability, particularly in waterways and trade corridors that directly affect its economic survival.
This calculation exposes a larger truth about the contemporary Middle East.
The old question, “Who protects whom?” may no longer make sense.
Saudi Arabia does not require Egyptian divisions stationed on the Yemeni front to guarantee its security. Equally, Egypt cannot sustain its economic stability without a relatively secure Gulf environment. What has emerged instead is a relationship of mutual dependence, in which military capability and economic power reinforce one another.
The traditional image of Egypt as the Arab world’s protector and Saudi Arabia as its financier belongs increasingly to another era.
A new bargain is taking shape.
Egypt remains too important to be ignored. Saudi Arabia remains too influential to be separated from broader Arab stability. Yet neither country occupies the role it once held. The balance has become more symmetrical, more transactional, and arguably more honest.
That is why Egypt’s offer to defend Saudi Arabia matters.
Not because it signals the beginning of a new war, but because it reveals the emergence of a new Arab order. An order in which economics has become as important as armies, investment as influential as ideology, and mutual dependence more decisive than old narratives of leadership.
The real significance of Cairo’s offer is therefore not military at all.
It is historical.
For the first time in modern Arab politics, the region’s traditional center of political gravity is openly acknowledging that its own security and prosperity are inseparable from the stability of the Gulf. And in that admission lies one of the most consequential geopolitical shifts the Arab world has witnessed since the end of the Cold War.

Iran’s new military doctrine is designed to make victory meaningless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:30:55 UTC
05:30:55 KST

Iran’s latest military doctrine rests on a dangerous proposition: a country does not have to defeat a superior enemy on the battlefield to deny it a meaningful victory. By threatening broader retaliation, expanding the geography of conflict and exploiting vulnerabilities in regional trade, Tehran is attempting to make the political rewards of military action increasingly difficult to secure.
On Oct. 21, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that Iran’s military doctrine would move beyond retaliatory strikes towards offensive and asymmetric operations.
The declaration reinforced earlier statements by Iranian military officials that the country was shifting away from a predominantly defensive posture.
Although official announcements do not establish how comprehensively this change has been implemented, they reveal the direction in which Tehran wants its adversaries to believe its strategy is moving.
The distinction matters because military superiority and strategic success are not interchangeable. Washington and Israel may destroy military facilities, disrupt command structures and degrade Iran’s weapons production. Yet these achievements cannot, by themselves, guarantee political compliance, regional stability or a durable settlement.
Iran’s objective, therefore, is not necessarily to win a conventional war against the United States. Rather, it is to deny Washington the ability to translate battlefield superiority into a political outcome that Tehran considers unacceptable.
This strategy could raise the costs of another attack, but it could also deepen the insecurity that makes another war possible. The central question is no longer simply who can inflict greater damage. It is whether either side can turn military force into a political settlement that lasts.
What It Means to Win a War
Iran’s strategic predicament is straightforward. Its conventional air power and technological capabilities cannot match those of the United States and Israel. A strategy built around symmetrical warfare would leave Tehran vulnerable to sustained aerial attacks, precision strikes and the systematic destruction of military infrastructure. Its response has consequently relied on a different calculation: if it cannot prevent an adversary from striking, it can make the consequences of that strike more costly and unpredictable.
Missiles, drones, dispersed launch systems and decentralised command structures are central to this approach. Rather than depending exclusively on the survival of major military installations, Iran can seek to preserve enough capacity to retaliate after suffering substantial damage. Its longstanding emphasis on asymmetric warfare also allows it to exploit the difference between the relatively low cost of some offensive systems and the expense of intercepting them.
The strategic logic extends beyond weapons. Iran can threaten military facilities, shipping routes and economic infrastructure across a wider regional theatre.
A conflict that begins with strikes on Iranian territory could therefore create security and economic consequences for states that are not directly involved in the initial attack.
The threat of escalation becomes part of Iran’s deterrent, even before every threatened operation is carried out.
This is a strategy of strategic denial. Its purpose is not necessarily to defeat an opponent in every engagement but to prevent that opponent from achieving its political objectives at an acceptable cost. If Washington seeks to eliminate a military threat, compel Iranian concessions or reshape Tehran’s regional behaviour, the relevant measure of success is not simply the number of targets destroyed. It is whether the intended political outcome follows.
Yet strategic denial should not be confused with victory. A state that survives an attack may still lose military capacity, economic resources and diplomatic leverage. Iran’s ability to impose costs does not automatically give it the ability to dictate the terms of a settlement. Its doctrine may complicate an adversary’s calculations without resolving the underlying imbalance of power.
Beyond Iran’s Borders
The most consequential feature of Iran’s approach is its potential to widen the conflict geographically. Tehran does not need to confine its response to the immediate battlefield if it believes that pressure on regional infrastructure and international commerce can influence an adversary’s decisions. This creates a direct connection between military strategy and the global economy.
The Strait of Hormuz illustrates the problem. The US Energy Information Administration estimated that roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait in 2024, equivalent to about one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The route is also critical to international liquefied natural gas trade.
Any sustained disruption could increase energy prices, raise shipping and insurance costs, and intensify inflationary pressure across economies far beyond the Middle East.
For Iran, the strategic attraction is clear. A threat to a vital maritime chokepoint can make the consequences of military escalation visible to governments, businesses and consumers around the world. The resulting economic pressure may complicate the calculations of states supporting military action against Tehran. It also forces regional governments to consider whether hosting foreign military forces could expose their own economies to retaliation.
But this leverage has limits. Disrupting the Strait of Hormuz would also damage Iran’s interests, aggravate economic hardship and alienate states that might otherwise favour diplomacy. Other countries could respond by strengthening maritime coalitions, expanding alternative supply arrangements or increasing military pressure on Iran. A tactic designed to internationalise the cost of war could therefore internationalise the opposition to Tehran.
Nor does economic pain necessarily translate into political concessions. Governments may absorb substantial costs if they believe their security or credibility is at stake. The assumption that higher energy prices or disrupted trade will compel Washington to retreat is no more reliable than the assumption that military strikes will automatically force Tehran to comply.
Iran’s widening battlefield is thus both a source of leverage and a mechanism of escalation. It raises the stakes for all parties, but it also increases the number of actors with reasons to intervene. The more regional commerce becomes an instrument of coercion, the harder it becomes to separate military confrontation from the wider economic order.
Why Strategic Denial Is Not the Same as Victory
Iran’s doctrine may be designed to make an adversary’s victory elusive, but it cannot guarantee that Tehran will emerge in a stronger position. The strategy depends on the credibility of its threats, the survival of enough military capability to carry them out and the willingness of its opponents to consider the potential costs before acting. Each condition can change during a conflict.
A sustained campaign could weaken Iran’s missile infrastructure, reduce its stockpiles and disrupt the command systems needed to coordinate retaliation. Regional partners could also become less willing or less capable of supporting Tehran if the costs of confrontation rise. Meanwhile, attacks on neighbouring states or commercial shipping could encourage closer security cooperation between Gulf governments, Washington and other external powers.
There is also a fundamental political problem. A doctrine built around imposing unacceptable costs can deter an adversary, but it can also reinforce the adversary’s belief that Iran must be contained through stronger military pressure.
If every attack is answered by a wider threat and every response produces another escalation, the logic of deterrence risks becoming a cycle of mutual insecurity.
This is where Iran’s strategic calculation becomes especially precarious. Preventing an opponent from claiming victory is a negative objective. It can obstruct an adversary’s plans, but it does not establish a stable political order or secure long-term economic recovery. For Tehran, a meaningful strategic outcome would require more than surviving a confrontation. It would require preserving national security, reducing the risk of renewed war and creating conditions in which economic reconstruction becomes possible.
The same distinction applies to Washington and Israel. Tactical success may weaken Iran’s military capabilities, but it cannot by itself resolve the political disputes that sustain the confrontation. If military action leaves both sides convinced that the other remains an intolerable threat, battlefield gains may simply postpone the next round of conflict.
A more durable outcome requires a credible path from deterrence to diplomacy. Crisis communication channels, arrangements to protect commercial shipping and verifiable agreements on the issues driving confrontation would not eliminate the rivalry. They could, however, reduce the risk that a local incident triggers a broader regional war. Such mechanisms matter precisely because neither side can reliably control every consequence of escalation.
Iran’s new doctrine should therefore be understood not as proof that Tehran can defeat a militarily superior opponent, but as an effort to make the exercise of that superiority politically and economically costly. Its success will depend on whether the threat of retaliation changes adversarial behaviour without provoking a response that leaves Iran more isolated and vulnerable.
Ultimately, the measure of success is not whether an adversary can be prevented from claiming victory. It is whether either side can achieve a political settlement that remains viable after the guns fall silent.
A doctrine that makes victory elusive may deter aggression. Without a credible path to peace, however, it can also make the next war harder to avoid.

The AI-Discovered Bug That Could Have Become a Cybersecurity Disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:28:02 UTC
05:28:02 KST

In early August, Sagi Tzadik asked an AI agent to take a security flaw it had found in WordPress and see whether the same weakness could be made to work against Drupal, another popular content management system. Eight hours later, the agent reported that it had failed. Then it added that, in the course of trying, it found a flaw in PHP, the programming language on which both systems—and as much as 70% of the web—depend.
Tzadik, a security researcher at cybersecurity firm Wiz, assumed that the AI had made a mistake. “Models tend to hallucinate,” he tells TIME. But the exploit, which took advantage of a weakness that had gone undetected for more than a decade, worked.
Unbeknownst to Wiz’s team, researchers at another cybersecurity firm, Calif—working with OpenAI—had used AI to find a related flaw. It suggests that once AI reaches a certain capability level, it is a matter of time before some longstanding weaknesses are unearthed. AI companies have been trying to ensure that defenders including Wiz and Calif get there first by giving them early access to new AI models before the equivalent capabilities trickle down to malicious users. This time, it worked.
The episode offers a glimpse into a new phase in cybersecurity in which AI helps defenders find vulnerabilities while giving them less time to fix them. While the bugs’ announcement has prompted alarm of a much-speculated “cyber-apolocalyse”—in which AI discovers world-melting bugs, plunging society into chaos—those who helped discover it are optimistic. “We are fixing vulnerabilities at an unprecedented rate, and this is doing security overall a very good thing,” Tzadik says.
But the details reveal just how close things came to disaster. Word of the vulnerabilities began circulating online two days before the patch’s scheduled release, prompting PHP’s maintainers to bring it forward by a day. Hours later, with the patch still unavailable, Calif mistakenly posted a video showing its exploit at work, and copycat attempts multiplied. Cloudflare counted thousands before the public announcement, tens of thousands within 45 minutes of it, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and eventually millions. Even after the patch was released, many webpages, including those of government agencies and parts of Wikipedia, were taken down as a precaution as security teams scrambled to install the update.
“If it had leaked a month earlier,” before a patch was ready, “this would have been a very different situation,” says Tomer Schwartz, CTO of exposure management and appsec at Wiz.
That a patch was prepared was the result of a loosely organized sprint. After Calif and Wiz sent reports to PHP, the groups joined forces. Researchers from competing companies shared their findings in common channels, with no contracts governing the arrangement. Over the following weeks, the group of roughly 15 people spoke almost daily to trace the vulnerabilities to their common source and devise a fix. The process, Schwartz says, was “just based on trust.”
That process will have to sustain increasing pressure. OpenAI has said that the PHP bugs were among “several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix,” and predicted that similar discoveries would “increase sharply in the coming months.” As those findings multiply, so will the number of dangerous secrets waiting for fixes. “We have to rethink all of our processes, all of our methods, all of our tech stack … to be able to keep up the pace against attackers,” Schwartz says.
Though defenders are being given a head start, they face a disadvantage of another sort. Attackers only have to succeed once. “But, as defenders, we need to make sure that every single vulnerability is covered,” Schwartz says.
AI is helping defenders find those vulnerabilities first. Previously, testing suspected bugs could take weeks, forcing researchers to prioritize which were most promising. But now AI agents allow researchers to test many ideas at once, Tzadik says. “It’s months of traditional research condensed to, like, days—couple hours to days, really.”
But even with AI, the process is labor intensive. After the agent helped Wiz uncover the PHP vulnerability, it still couldn’t describe how the bug worked, Tzadik says. Its explanations were “just slop.” He and colleagues spent days untangling the cause of a bug and eventually reproducing it.
Cost is another constraint. Joshua Saxe, Meta’s former AI security tech lead, who left in February to co-found Abundance Security says he’s working with an organization that has spent roughly $1 million using Anthropic’s Mythos to identify bugs, adding that more bugs remain.
“As an industry, I think we’re deer in the headlights right now,” Saxe says.
"In the climate that we’re in today, you have to do cybersecurity well. It’s not an option to kind of half-a-- it,” says Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike. But even a successful exploit offers further opportunities for defenders to intervene. “Exploits are going to happen, and that’s not the end of the story,” he says. “It’s the beginning of the attack.”

In one of the West's few swing races, a Democrat tries to keep a Trump district
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
