China Focus: Rescue efforts intensify after Xizang quake kills 16, injures 76
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
01:35:42 CST
02:35:42 KST

Members of the People's Armed Police Force Xizang Corps and firefighters transfer a trapped yak at a quake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 23, 2026. Sixteen people have been killed and 76 others are injured following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake that struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, local authorities said. (Photo by Wang Xingquan/Xinhua)
BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Sixteen people have been killed and 76 others are injured following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake that struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, local authorities said.
The quake has also damaged or destroyed 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, according to a press conference held on Friday afternoon by the information office of the Nagqu municipal government.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has ordered all-out search and rescue efforts for the missing and prompt medical treatment for the injured, urging every effort to minimize casualties.
Xi also called for close monitoring of seismic activity and weather conditions to prevent secondary disasters, as well as proper accommodation for affected residents and swift repairs to damaged infrastructure.
Premier Li Qiang called for solid disaster prevention and response efforts, while the Ministry of Emergency Management (MEM) and authorities in Xizang have mobilized resources for rescue and relief operations.
China has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.5 million U.S. dollars) in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts. The country has also upgraded its national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III.
More than 5,000 personnel have been deployed to the front lines of the disaster relief operation, working in teams responsible for search and rescue, medical treatment, temporary shelter and the provision of essential supplies.
An emergency command headquarters has been established on the front lines to coordinate relief efforts. As of 10 a.m. Friday, 12,489 residents have been evacuated.
After three rounds of comprehensive door-to-door checks, no missing persons had been reported as of 6 p.m. Friday, according to the emergency command headquarters.
In a village of Maru Township, one of the hardest-hit areas near the epicenter, Xinhua reporters saw many houses completely collapsed, while others sustained extensive wall damage. Rows of emergency tents were erected in an open, safe area below the village.
Half of villager Trinley's house collapsed, burying many of his belongings beneath the rubble. Two white tents were set up in his courtyard.
"After the earthquake, our biggest concerns were where to stay and what to eat," Trinley said. "The government provided us with supplies including emergency tents, water and instant noodles," he added.
The MEM said that on top of the 5,000 relief items previously allocated by the central government, an additional 5,000 central relief items, including tents, coats and folding beds were allocated.
By coordinating efforts with other relief agencies and companies, the ministry said that it has also promptly allocated 43,000 other relief items, including mobile toilets, heating stoves, food and fuel, to ensure that affected people are properly resettled.
The Red Cross Society of China has dispatched a working team to the disaster-hit area to guide local relief efforts. It has also allocated 3,800 sets of supplies, including family relief kits, hygiene kits, heaters, tents, jackets, folding beds and quilts. The society has additionally allocated 50 emergency toilet units to support affected residents and coordinated with the Chinese Red Cross Foundation to provide 500 family relief kits, 500 hygiene kits and more than 1,000 cartons of food to the quake-hit area. The China Charity Federation, one of the country's most influential charity organizations, has urgently allocated 3 million yuan to support emergency rescue endeavors.
RESCUE CHALLENGES
The earthquake zone has an average elevation of nearly 4,800 meters. The high-altitude, cold and low-oxygen environment, secondary disaster hazards and aftershock risks pose challenges to the relief efforts, local authorities said at the press conference.
Deng Xiaogang, a rescuer with Nagqu's fire and rescue team, said that beyond the low temperatures and low oxygen levels, the biggest challenge was that the epicenter was in a pastoral area, where residents live far apart, making search-and-rescue operations more time-consuming in the initial stages.
Some herding sites are up in the mountains, and the terrain is rugged, said Jigme Dorje, deputy head of the Baqen County public security bureau. "At first, machines could not reach these places, so we had to climb up and dig through the rubble with our hands, wearing only gloves," he said.
Local authorities said that rescue teams will continue to take precautions to overcome difficulties in relief operations.
Nighttime temperatures in the quake zone are low. Earthquake-triggered hazards such as landslides, collapses and falling rocks are currently the main secondary disaster risks.
Earthquake monitoring, meteorological and emergency management departments, meanwhile, are coordinating closely to issue timely warnings of aftershocks and adverse weather conditions.
Local authorities have launched round-the-clock intensified monitoring of key sites, including mountainsides, reservoirs, power stations, rivers, structurally unsafe buildings and telecommunications base stations. Emergency repairs are also underway, with damaged telecommunications and power facilities gradually being restored.
Pan Zhiqing, Party secretary of Nagqu's emergency management bureau, said that in follow-up rescue work, personnel will be assigned to accompany rescue teams to inspect geological hazards along mountains and roads. Dangerous areas will be immediately cordoned off, and people and vehicles will be prohibited from passing.
Transportation authorities will monitor road damage in real time, promptly repair and reopen blocked sections, and ensure smooth traffic flow. They will continue to coordinate with meteorological and natural resources departments and issue risk warnings, Pan added.
China Telecom, China Mobile and China Unicom mobilized emergency repair teams, vehicles and equipment overnight, dispatching personnel to the quake-hit areas to restore communications services and inspect network facilities.
All telecommunications base stations disrupted by the earthquake in Baqen County had been restored as of 10:30 a.m. Friday, according to the Xizang Communications Administration.
The 7.0-magnitude earthquake was an extensional rupture, according to experts with the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC).
"An extensional fracture, in simple terms, occurs when the crust is stretched horizontally and, under tension and gravity, faultage slides downward along existing faultage, forming fractures and rupture surfaces," said Han Yanyan, a senior engineer with the earthquake prediction department of the CENC. ■

China's top diplomat says Global Governance Initiative increasingly relevant
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
01:35:30 CST
02:35:30 KST

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, reads out a message from Chinese President Xi Jinping and delivers a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) in Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, Oct. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Mu Yu)
XIONGAN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Friday that the Global Governance Initiative has become increasingly relevant one year after it was put forward, calling for efforts to turn its vision into reality.
Chinese President Xi Jinping put forward the Global Governance Initiative, offering a solution to address the governance deficit and jointly create a better future, Wang said in a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said countries should jointly uphold the central role of the United Nations, enhance the Security Council's rapid response capacity, and respond to the legitimate concerns of developing countries.
He said major countries must set an example in upholding equality, credibility, moral principles and cooperation, which is the only way to bring about a world where all countries coexist in harmony and all nations thrive in mutual appreciation.
All parties should adhere to a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security and resolve differences and disputes between countries through peaceful means to safeguard peace, he said.
It is important to enhance the representation and voice of the Global South in international affairs, advance reform of the international financial system in accordance with the timetable and roadmap agreed by all parties, increase the representation of developing countries in the Security Council, and give full play to the important role of emerging multilateral cooperation mechanisms such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, Wang said.
All countries should uphold the multilateral trading system with the WTO at its core, keep development at the center of the international agenda, and fully implement the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, he said.
He also called for improving governance rules in emerging fields, turning new frontiers such as the deep sea, the polar regions and outer space into areas for international cooperation, and evolving an AI governance structure based on general consensus soon.
Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, the forum is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World."
Nearly 400 representatives from strategic, political, academic, business, media, and youth sectors from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations, including the UN, attended the opening ceremony. ■

China Focus: South China free-trade island builds space hub as new growth engine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
01:35:27 CST
02:35:27 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- With giant lightning rods towering above the coastline of eastern Wenchang in south China, coconut groves have given way to rows of launch pads while the country's first commercial spaceport is coming to life.
Known as the Hainan commercial spacecraft launch site, the spaceport has become a cornerstone of China's endeavors to help Hainan make its emerging commercial space business a strategic growth engine across the island-wide free trade port.
"Launch orders are fully booked for this year and next. The earliest available slot is in the year after," said Zhang Xiaojun, deputy general manager of a Wenchang aerospace launch support company.
The facility's first phase, comprising launch pads 1 and 2, is already operational. Pad 2, equipped with a mobile launch platform and horizontal testing system, can accommodate more than 20 types of domestic rockets and complete preparations for a full launch cycle in as little as 66 hours.
Construction is in full swing on pads 3 and 4, which are expected to be ready by year-end. Once all four pads are online, the site will be capable of supporting approximately 60 launches per year.
But ambition stretches well beyond the launch pads.
Wenchang, the once unknown coastal fishing town, is rushing to build out a vertically integrated ecosystem, ranging from rocket and satellite manufacturing to downstream data services, under a model which officials describe as "Made in Wenchang, Launched from Wenchang."
A rocket assembly, testing and reuse facility, with its first phase having been established in Wenchang by a commercial space company, is operational. A string of other rocket-chain projects have also broken ground.
Additionally, a massive satellite manufacturing base has completed its production line and entered trial production in the city, with the first satellite expected to roll off the line by the end of 2026.
On the data side, progress has also been encouraging. An aerospace supercomputing center, which began operations in 2023, is helping Wenchang stitch together a full aerospace big-data value chain, from data acquisition and reception to storage, processing and commercial application.
Ye Shiyang, chairman of the center's operating company, said the firm has consolidated resources from 161 satellites in orbit to build a sub-meter-resolution commercial remote-sensing database. Leveraging the supercomputing center's processing power and Hainan Free Trade Port's cross-border data-flow policies, the company is expanding its "two ends abroad" data-processing model.
"Overseas clients send us satellite remote-sensing data for processing, and we deliver the finished products back to them," Ye said. In May, the company completed its first remote-sensing data export to Singapore and is in discussions with clients in Thailand, Cambodia and several European countries.
This convergence of rocket, satellite and data chains has drawn more than 700 companies into the satellite and rocket industrial park in Wenchang, creating what officials call a "front shop, back factory" ecosystem: satellites rolled off the production line can reach the launch pad just kilometers away.
At the national level, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for accelerating the development of strategic emerging industries, including aerospace, and the China National Space Administration unveiled a special action plan in late 2025 to promote the high-quality, safe development of commercial space.
Hainan has moved quickly to align with this push, designating the sector as one of four industrial clusters each targeted to reach 50 billion yuan (about 7.4 billion U.S. dollars) in annual revenue, and positioning it as a key pillar in cultivating new quality productive forces.
"The layout in Wenchang is not just about rocket launches," said Zheng Ni, a division director at the Hainan Provincial Department of Science and Technology.
"The goal is to use the launch site to drive industrial development, building a full-chain cluster and developing rocket, satellite and data chains within an 'aerospace-plus' ecosystem to fuel Hainan's space-powered growth," Zheng said. ■

Explainer: Will new Russia-Ukraine talks deliver peace?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
01:35:19 CST
02:35:19 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine are planned to be held in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, in the first half of November, with a focus on security issues after a peace settlement, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Friday.
Earlier on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reiterated his willingness to "freeze" the fighting along current battle lines as a "real way to end this war."
U.S. President Donald Trump said Moscow and Kiev are "maybe now the closest" they have been to reaching a settlement to the war.
Will renewed talks deliver a real peace?
PUSH FOR TALKS
Since the Russia-Ukraine conflict broke out in February 2022, more than four years have passed, punctuated by a succession of talks for a solution.
In a new diplomatic urge prior to the U.S. midterm election, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday before travelling to St. Petersburg to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin the following day. The discussions covered security guarantees for Ukraine, postwar reconstruction and the prospect of resuming trilateral talks involving Kiev, Moscow and Washington.
Putin agreed "in principle" to restart the negotiations after Nov. 10, focusing on establishing a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends, according to Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov.
Zelensky said he was willing to consider freezing the conflict along the current front lines as a way to reach a peace deal with Russia and bring the years-long conflict to an end through diplomacy.
"We call it a ceasefire ... President Trump called it freeze and stop," Zelensky said, when asked whether he would agree to halt the fighting along the current front lines while retaining control of "75 percent or more" of the pre-war Ukrainian territory.
Washington is making little secret of its impatience to secure a Ukraine deal. Trump on Tuesday urged Zelensky to make a deal with Russia to end the conflict.
"We want Zelensky to make a deal," Trump told reporters at the White House. "If they don't make a deal, it's just gonna get worse."
"We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump said. "The American taxpayers are tired of it."
"It's time to make a deal," he added, "Russia would like to get it done."
DIVERGING AGENDAS
Washington's rush for pressuring Zelensky to accept a fast deal is clearly seen. Trump stated publicly on Monday that Zelensky "doesn't want to stop" the conflict and "is not helping matters much. I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly delayed the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles from European allies to Ukraine, potentially weakening Ukraine's air defense capacity.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's access to Starshield was significantly curtailed in mid-October, disrupting drone operations and battlefield communications. Reuters reported that the order came from inside the White House, though Trump denied involvement.
U.S.-Ukraine relations have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia on Oct. 9, part of his efforts to lower fuel prices ahead of early November's midterm elections. With high fuel prices fueling domestic frustration over the cost of living, Washington's urgency to secure a ceasefire may also reflect mounting pressure on Republicans ahead of the vote.
Russia could use the current opportunity to improve ties with Washington without making major concessions on Ukraine, according to the Washington Post.
Putin said talks should focus on security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, and a broader European security framework. He reiterated that Russia wanted a lasting settlement rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Territorial disputes remain a major obstacle, as Moscow demands that Ukraine cede the entire Donbas region. For Russia, resuming talks offers a chance to expand its strategic room for maneuver.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is seeking a ceasefire and robust security guarantees to prevent further attack. Following talks with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelensky said his proposals included NATO Article 5-style guarantees, while stressing that territorial issues must be discussed at the highest level.
Ukraine's bid for resuming trilateral talks and its openness to a peace deal based on freezing the current front lines could help ease tensions with Washington and signal Kiev's willingness to resolve the conflict through negotiations.
DEEP DIVISIONS REMAIN
Although Russia, the United States and Ukraine may resume talks, a ceasefire agreement between Moscow and Kiev remains far from certain.
"As experience shows, the mere fact that negotiations are taking place does not mean that a peace agreement is likely to be reached anytime soon," Ukrainian political scientist Volodymyr Fesenko said.
Witkoff reportedly presented Putin an updated peace proposal developed in coordination with Ukraine and European partners following talks in Oslo. However, Ushakov said the proposals contained little "substance." Moscow agreed in principle to resume trilateral talks, but its lukewarm response underscored the lack of consensus on how to end the war.
Currently, Russia and Ukraine remain deeply divided over two key issues -- territory and security guarantees.
Territorial disputes remain a major sticking point. Zelensky signaled in a media interview on Thursday that Kiev would not accept Russia's demand for Ukraine's withdrawal from Donbas, while Moscow continues to insist that the entire region should come under Russian control. Recent statements suggest neither side has significantly changed its position.
The two sides also remain at odds over security guarantees. Ukraine seeks security assurances from the United States and Europe as part of a ceasefire deal, while Russia firmly opposes the deployment of Western military personnel and facilities in Ukraine.
Chen Yu, deputy director of the Institute of Eurasian Studies at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, said the conflict's core issues remain unresolved, with little room for compromise and the battlefield still deadlocked, making a political settlement unlikely in the near term.
Michael Kimmage, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution think tank, told U.S. media that the Trump administration's "theory of the case is that by distancing themselves from Ukraine and by flattering the Russians, they can accomplish something at the bargaining table."
He is not, however, optimistic that the gambit will succeed.
"In the absence of a clear agenda coming from the White House and in the absence of very serious forms of leverage over Russia -- which the Trump administration has shied away from -- progress at the negotiating table is very difficult to imagine," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

Are Israel's drones signalling a new escalation with Hezbollah?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:34:45 UTC
02:34:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Are Israel's drones over Beirut signalling a coming escalation with Hezbollah?
Reports of increased Israeli drone activity over Beirut and its southern suburbs have raised questions about whether Israel is preparing for a new escalation against Hezbollah.
But while the flights have become more conspicuous in recent days, analysts told The New Arab that their presence alone does not establish that a wider offensive is imminent.
A report by local Lebanese news outlet Lebanon Files said Israeli reconnaissance flights had "returned" to Beirut and Mount Lebanon’s airspace. However, there is no publicly available evidence establishing that the flights had stopped before recently becoming more noticeable.
Israeli drones have continued to be reported over Beirut and its southern suburbs in recent months, including in reports published in September and footage circulated this week.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether the drones are present, but whether there has been a meaningful change in the frequency, duration or scope of their operations.
Surveillance and pressure on Hezbollah
Elijah J. Magnier, a veteran war correspondent and political analyst, told The New Arab that the activity should be taken seriously, while cautioning against treating visible drone flights as evidence of an imminent attack.
"Local reporting today documented a drone flying at low altitude over the southern suburbs. That establishes a visible presence; it does not, by itself, establish a sustained increase in surveillance or an imminent offensive," he said in comments to The New Arab on 21 October.
Magnier said Israeli drone flights could serve several purposes at once, including gathering intelligence, updating potential targets, monitoring movements and exerting psychological pressure on residents. A conspicuous presence over the capital can also serve as a reminder of Israel’s ability to strike south of Beirut.
If Israel were preparing another operation, surveillance could help it locate commanders, monitor weapons movements and identify suspected military infrastructure. But Magnier stressed that these remained possible objectives rather than evidence of a decision to launch an attack.
"Nor does identifying a target establish that a political decision to strike has been taken," he said. Without comparative flight data or intelligence about operational orders, he added, it was difficult to distinguish routine surveillance from preparations for a particular attack.
Nasser Khdour, an analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also said Israeli drone activity over Beirut was not new.
"Israel has continued gathering intelligence and identifying possible targets in preparation for another round of fighting," he told The New Arab.
Khdour suggested the more conspicuous drone presence was likely intended to increase pressure on Hezbollah and the Lebanese government during negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, with the Iran-backed militant group’s disarmament remaining a central point of disagreement.
The latest round of US-mediated military talks between Lebanese and Israeli delegations began in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October. The talks came amid continued Israeli attacks and demolitions in southern Lebanon, as well as renewed threats by Israeli officials against Hezbollah.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has warned Hezbollah against joining Iran in an attack on Israel, threatening a "powerful response" against Beirut’s southern suburbs, which would include a forced evacuation of the whole area. He has also threatened to expand the invasion towards Nabatieh and the Litani River in the south.
Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Could tensions with Iran draw Hezbollah into a wider war?
The risk of escalation also extends beyond Lebanon. With Israel’s general election scheduled for 27 October, renewed threats involving Iran have added another layer of uncertainty to the regional picture.
Magnier said electoral considerations were relevant to the analysis, but cautioned against presenting speculation about a war being launched for political reasons as an established plan. He said there was no publicly established evidence that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intended to initiate a war to disrupt an election he expected to lose.
A renewed confrontation between Israel and Iran could, however, create a separate decision point for Hezbollah. Magnier said the group’s involvement would become a more serious possibility in such a scenario, but would remain a choice rather than an automatic consequence.
He also cautioned against assuming that Hezbollah’s weakened deterrence meant it had no remaining military capabilities. The group could seek to preserve its personnel and organisational structure while continuing to impose costs on Israel over time, rather than responding to every attack with a major escalation.
That calculation could change, he added, if civilian casualties mounted, senior leaders were targeted or Israel expanded its ground operations.
The conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023 and was dramatically escalated by Israel into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran. Much of Hezbollah’s senior command structure has been eliminated over the past three years, and thousands of its fighters are believed to have been killed.
The drone flights therefore need to be viewed alongside the wider military and political context, rather than in isolation. Israel’s continued strikes, its threats against Beirut’s southern suburbs and the unresolved dispute over Hezbollah’s weapons all contribute to an already volatile situation.
For Magnier, the distinction remains between sustained pressure and a decision to launch a broader campaign. The visible presence of drones demonstrates Israel’s ability to monitor and threaten Hezbollah and its stronghold in Beirut's southern suburbs, but it does not reveal what Israeli leaders intend to do next.
"The drone flights show exposure and pressure. They do not yet tell us whether the next step will be surveillance, a targeted strike or a wider campaign," he said.

Iran has plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:22:07 UTC
02:22:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
'Stronger response'
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

====================================================================================================

Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:15:08 UTC
02:15:08 KST

Leaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off.
Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck's latest data on their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment.
The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day.
The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery.
The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation.
"This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites.
Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy."
The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year.
"It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said.
Major advance in melanoma
An immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor.
The significance of the phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work.
Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether.
"If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial.
Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC.
Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most.
The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said.
The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data does not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery.
The medical community will get more clarity after Moderna and Merck present the detailed results at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference on Saturday.
Investors diverged from doctors
Moderna shares fell as much as 25% Thursday, before regaining some ground, after partial data from the trial leaked on social media. The sell-off came despite the positive results, underscoring the gap between the treatment's clinical promise and investor expectations for its commercial potential. Moderna shares are also up nearly 600% this year due to the cancer shot optimism, creating more potential for a Wall Street letdown.
Investors had hoped the vaccine and Keytruda would replicate the results of an earlier phase 2 trial, which showed a roughly 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death at five years, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note Thursday. Huynh described the phase 3 results as clinically meaningful and likely to support regulatory approval, but said the primary efficacy result landed at the low end of investor expectations.
But there was a key difference in the studies: The phase 3 trial included patients with a broader range of risk profiles, including some at lower risk of recurrence than those enrolled in the earlier phase 2 trial, said Dr. George Ansstas, who leads the melanoma department at Washington University in St. Louis. That may have slightly tempered the results, since patients considered lower risk have less chance of recurrence to begin with.
"It's great data actually. It's overall consistent with what we've proven in the phase 2 trial," said Ansstas, who also worked on the phase 2 trial.
The combination showed little difference from Keytruda alone during the first six months of treatment, the companies said. But a separate analysis of the phase 3 data offered a more encouraging signal about the treatment's effect after the six-month mark. The vaccine and Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 58% after that point, compared with Keytruda alone.
The 42% figure comes from the primary analysis, which included patients' outcomes throughout the trial's follow-up period. The median follow-up was about two years at the time of the analysis, so the result reflects the overall treatment effect, not just what happened before or after the six-month mark.
Ansstas said the benefit of the personalized cancer vaccine may take several months to emerge because each shot must be custom-manufactured, a process that can take roughly six weeks, while patients begin Keytruda in the meantime. After vaccination begins, the immune system also needs time and repeated doses to develop a response against tumors.
That timeline could help explain why the group that received the combination regimen saw even greater benefits around six months, Ansstas said. Still, the explanation is a hypothesis rather than proof of when the vaccine's effect begins.
Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, also highlighted the relatively mild side effects associated with the vaccine, including injection-site reactions, as a positive.
Keytruda and other cancer therapies can cause potentially serious immune-related side effects. Detailed safety results released on Saturday should help clarify the trade-offs of adding the vaccine to the immunotherapy regimen.
More work to be done
For Moderna, the stakes extend beyond melanoma. The company is working to build a business beyond its Covid vaccine, while Merck is preparing for the eventual loss of patent protection on Keytruda.
The companies have several hurdles ahead of them, including selling an individualized therapy that takes several weeks to create for a patient at scale.
"I think the downside is that it's super labor-intensive, and you're gonna have to make vaccines for each person, and so you can't just stockpile a million vaccines and then just ship it out when somebody needs it," said Dr. Adil Daud, professor of medicine and melanoma oncologist at the University of California San Francisco, who was the lead investigator on the phase 3 trial. "There is the time and expense, and it's probably going to cost like a lot of money."
Moderna and Merck have not disclosed any details about the manufacturing costs for the vaccine.
He added that most people who walk into the clinic with a tumor that has not been surgically removed may stick to receiving Keytruda before an operation because "that approach is simpler and doesn't put the patient through the delay" of creating the vaccine.
Daud said he expects the vaccine combination to be used primarily in the adjuvant setting, after surgery, rather than replace established immunotherapy regimens given before an operation. For patients who receive immunotherapy before surgery but show little or no response, the vaccine combination could offer another option, he said, though that would likely be for a smaller group of patients.
Moderna and Merck still need to validate the approach in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. Success in melanoma does not automatically guarantee that the approach will work in other tumors.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Merck Research Laboratories President Dean Li said in an interview ahead of the results. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
Moderna's Bancel sees a bright future for the vaccine, saying he believes it will eventually be able to help "literally thousands and then tens of thousands and then hundreds of thousands of people across different tumors around the world."

The US naval blockade of Iran: an illegal act of coercion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:09:06 UTC
02:09:06 KST

The US naval blockade of Iran: an illegal act of coercion
TEHRAN - An examination of the legal grounds for the US blockade of Iranian ports, what the UN Charter says, and how international law experts assess the action.
Imagine a country deciding to stop another country’s commercial ships, prevent goods from reaching its ports, and effectively impose its own rules on vessels travelling through international waters. Does military power, combined with claims of national security, give that country the right to do so? If the answer is yes, what would stop any major power from turning the seas into tools of pressure and blockade whenever it has a dispute with another country?
These questions lie at the heart of the US naval blockade of Iran. A naval blockade is not simply a matter of stopping ships. It can disrupt a country’s trade, drive up economic costs, and affect people’s daily lives. For that reason, international law does not give countries unlimited authority to restrict maritime traffic simply because they have military superiority or claim to be acting for security reasons.
Under international law, the US naval blockade of Iran cannot be justified simply by Washington’s announcement or its claims of national security. Given the absence of UN Security Council authorisation and the lack of a valid legal basis for self-defence, the blockade, as part of the use of force against Iran, is illegal. One important distinction must be made, however: even during wartime, rules govern how a naval blockade may be carried out. Possible compliance with some of those rules does not, by itself, make the original use of force lawful.
What does the UN Charter say?
The main legal document relevant to the US action is the United Nations Charter. Article 2(4) prohibits states from threatening or using force against other states. The purpose of this rule is to prevent governments from using their military strength to impose their will on other countries.
The Charter recognises two principal legal grounds for the use of force: authorisation by the UN Security Council and self-defence under the conditions set out in Article 51. A country seeking to justify a military blockade of another country must therefore demonstrate that its actions fall within one of these legal frameworks.
In the case of the blockade of Iran, the United States cannot create its own legal authority simply by declaring a security emergency or seeking to put economic pressure on Iran. If the military action lacks a valid basis under the UN Charter, it cannot become lawful merely because Washington gives it an official name or announces a justification.
What do international law experts say?
One important contribution to the legal debate is an article by Michael Schmitt, a professor and specialist in international law, published by Just Security. In his article, “Iran’s Conditions for Reopening Hormuz: What International Law Requires, Permits, and Forbids,” Schmitt examines the legal basis for the US use of force against Iran.
Schmitt explains that, under the UN Charter, the use of force must generally be based on Security Council authorisation or the right of self-defence in response to an armed attack. According to his analysis, most international law experts believe that the initial US attack was not authorised by the Security Council and did not meet the necessary conditions to qualify as self-defence. He therefore considers the start of US military operations to be inconsistent with the country’s obligations under the UN Charter.
His analysis is directly relevant to the blockade. If the legality of the original use of force is in question, the blockade cannot be treated as an entirely separate action and declared lawful simply by referring to the rules of naval warfare.
Steve Prest, a retired naval officer and analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), raises similar concerns in his article, “The ‘US Blockade’ of Iran: How It Might Function (Or Not!).” He argues that the legality of the US action depends on whether the necessary conditions for using force have been met. Without Security Council authorisation, self-defence is the principal legal justification available to Washington, but Prest points to serious questions about whether that argument can justify the operation.
These analyses highlight the central issue: the question is not merely how the United States stops ships, but on what legal grounds it claims the right to use military force to blockade Iranian ports.
Do the laws of war make the US blockade legal?
The United States may argue that naval blockades are a recognised method of warfare. That claim reflects part of the legal picture, but it does not tell the whole story.
The San Remo Manual on International Law Applicable to Armed Conflicts at Sea, adopted in 1994, sets out restrictions on naval blockades. Under its rules, a blockade must be declared, its limits must be specified, and it must be effectively enforced. It must also respect the rights of neutral states. Rules protecting civilians and ensuring access to essential supplies must be observed as well.
The San Remo Manual is not, in itself, a binding treaty. However, it is a recognised reference for assessing the law governing naval warfare.
The key point is simple: the fact that certain methods of warfare may be lawful does not mean that starting a war or using force is lawful.
A legal analysis published by German broadcaster Tagesschau on 18 July 2026 makes the same distinction. Citing Pierre Thielbörger, a professor of international law at the University of Bochum, the report explains that the legality of resorting to force must be distinguished from the legality of how military operations are conducted. In other words, a particular action may be assessed separately under the rules of naval warfare, but that does not erase the possibility that the war itself was unlawful.
For this reason, citing the rules governing naval blockades does not, on its own, answer the fundamental question: did the United States have the legal right to use force to blockade Iranian ports in the first place?
US sanctions do not give Washington the right to shut down Iran’s trade
Another issue is the attempt to link the naval blockade to US sanctions. Washington may place companies or ships on its sanctions lists, but a decision made by one government does not automatically become international law.
Keri Batsov, a former US Treasury Department official, said: “Iran will not surrender under sanctions; the naval blockade has worn down the US military, and Iran’s low-cost drones have challenged Washington’s expensive weapons.”
Article 92 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea recognises the principle that ships on the high seas are generally subject to the jurisdiction of their flag state. Article 110 sets out specific circumstances in which foreign ships may be boarded on the high seas.
These provisions make clear that the seizure of ships in international waters requires a legal basis. A vessel’s commercial links to Iran, or its inclusion on a US sanctions list, does not by itself give the United States unlimited authority to seize it.
Mark Nevitt, a legal scholar specialising in military and maritime law, raised concerns about this issue in an article published by Just Security on 1 May 2026. He warns that the United States is grouping several types of maritime operations, each with a different legal basis, under the single label of a “blockade.” He distinguishes a blockade of Iranian ports from the seizure of US-sanctioned ships in different parts of the world, stressing that each operation must have its own clear legal justification.
This distinction is crucial. Even if a limited blockade under certain conditions of armed conflict can be defended on legal grounds, that does not give the United States the authority to stop every ship linked to Iran anywhere in the world.
The human cost of a naval blockade
A naval blockade is not just a military measure directed at ports. Its effects can reach deep into the economy and people’s everyday lives. Restrictions on ships entering and leaving ports can disrupt trade, raise shipping costs, and make essential goods more difficult to obtain.
International humanitarian law contains rules intended to prevent unjustifiable harm to civilians. Using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare is prohibited, and a blockade must not be used as an excuse to disregard people’s essential needs.
Ismail Kowsari, an Iranian parliament member and member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, has called for legal action over US measures against Iran. He said international legal mechanisms lack sufficient power and enforcement guarantees to address violations and hold those responsible to account. This, he said, has allowed some powers to pursue their interests without sufficient regard for the rights of other countries and peoples.
Kowsari said it was necessary to stand firmly against this approach and to drive the United States out of the region so that international law could be implemented in practice. Criticising international judicial institutions for failing to address US violations earlier, he said this should not bring legal efforts to a halt. Iran’s judiciary, he argued, should carefully document US actions and violations against Iran, including the naval blockade, and pursue them through legal channels.
Kowsari also stressed the need to document the humanitarian consequences of sanctions, particularly in the medical and pharmaceutical sectors. He said patients and vulnerable groups depend on essential medicines and medical equipment, and that any disruption to access could have serious consequences. Despite these needs, he added, sanctions can obstruct access to essential supplies while those imposing them continue without sufficient regard for the human impact.
He said the effects of these measures should be recorded accurately through credible documents, evidence, and other supporting material so that they can be pursued before the competent international bodies.
Assessing a blockade therefore requires more than counting the number of ships stopped or measuring the economic pressure it creates. Its impact on civilians must also be examined, including whether essential supplies remain available in practice.
A naval blockade can thus become more than an instrument of military pressure. It can develop into a humanitarian and legal crisis, and governments cannot escape responsibility simply by declaring that their actions serve security objectives.
The UN Charter and the analyses of international law experts show that the blockade of Iran cannot be assessed solely through the technical rules of naval warfare. The fundamental question remains: on what legal basis is the United States using force to blockade Iranian ports?
Michael Schmitt, writing for Just Security, questions the legal basis for the initial US attack. Steve Prest, writing for RUSI, raises serious doubts about whether self-defence can justify the operation. Mark Nevitt, also writing for Just Security, explains why a limited blockade cannot be turned into a blanket licence to seize sanctioned ships around the world. The UN Charter sets out the underlying principle: the use of force must be justified under international law.
The US naval blockade of Iran is therefore illegal in the absence of Security Council authorisation and a valid legal basis for the use of force. The rules of naval warfare cannot, on their own, resolve this fundamental problem. Nor do unilateral US sanctions give Washington unlimited authority to control Iran’s maritime trade.
This is not just about Iran. It is about whether major powers will abide by the rules they accepted as part of the international order established after the Second World War. If military power is allowed to replace the law, naval blockades will no longer be exceptional measures. They could become tools that powerful countries use whenever they want to force another state to submit to their demands.

Xi Jinping May Have His Own Reasons to Avert a China-Russia-US Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:09:00 UTC
02:09:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin have put Xi Jinping in an unusual position by expressing interest in a trilateral summit with the Chinese leader at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen mid-November. Xi’s cautious response so far – Moscow and Washington have confirmed discussion, while Beijing has yet to commit publicly – could help Europe and Ukraine avoid the worst: major powers making decisions about the region in their absence.
The idea for a meeting came from Russia and it’s not hard to see why. Moscow’s ideal outcome would reportedly be a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, echoing the 1945 conference at which the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war order in Europe. But even much more modest results would count as a success. Simply taking part in such a summit would elevate Russia’s status alongside the U.S. and China, help break its diplomatic isolation, potentially drive a further wedge between the U.S. and Europe, and provide an important platform for its narrative of Western threats to Russia.
A three-way meeting would play to Trump’s self-regard as a dealmaker and peacemaker – and quite possibly his appetite for economic gain. The United States recently eased sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports, with an initial shipment of 40,000 tonnes reportedly on its way to the U.S. Moscow has also offered to increase fertilizer exports amid shortages caused by the Middle East crisis. But Trump may also have a larger strategic motivation. He has said that nuclear disarmament, not Ukraine, should be at the top of the agenda.
With the APEC summit in China being discussed as the venue, Xi would surely welcome the huge symbolic win of being seen as the world leader capable of hosting such an important gathering – while possibly helping to widen the divide between the U.S. and Europe. But Xi also has very good reasons to avoid such a meeting. China has benefited from dealing with Washington and Moscow separately, and it has in the past insisted that both Russia and Ukraine must be involved in any peace process. A China-Russia-U.S. summit to discuss Ukraine’s future without Kyiv would undermine both those positions.
A high-profile trilateral could overshadow the APEC summit, which Beijing wants to use to showcase its economic leadership and promote openness, innovation, and cooperation. A highly publicized gathering of three major powers also would sit uneasily with Beijing’s repeated calls for inclusive multilateralism, particularly at a forum intended to promote regional economic cooperation.
A successful trilateral might make the risk worthwhile. But such an outcome is uncertain – not least because of the unpredictability of Trump and Putin. The meeting could end up dominating APEC at the expense of Beijing’s economic agenda, without producing any significant outcomes.
Lastly, while Putin and Trump have major strategic incentives to meet, Xi has a strategic reason to avoid doing so. Trump’s insistence on putting nuclear arms reduction at the top of the agenda is problematic for China. Beijing has long emphasized that its nuclear arsenal is far smaller than those of the United States and Russia – and that Washington and Moscow must make substantial reductions before China joins any talks. Abandoning this position would risk China being bound by the same rules as Russia and the U.S., despite the gap in nuclear capabilities.
But Xi may recognize that he cannot dismiss the idea of a meeting altogether. Chinese diplomats have reportedly indicated that they would not rule out a trilateral. If Xi cannot prevent such a meeting, he could at least use his position as host to shape it – a less prominent, more informal encounter with a loose agenda focused on major power relations or the global economy, rather than a formal summit focused on Ukraine or nuclear arms control that would raise public expectations. Xi could even cast himself as the host of a Trump-Putin meeting rather than a participant in three-way talks.
Such stage-management would not protect Europe and Ukraine from the United States, Russia, and China talking about them behind their backs. But it would allow European governments to frame such a meeting as nothing more than an exchange of views. A formal summit explicitly devoted to Ukraine, by contrast, would risk signaling to the world that the three leaders are entitled – by right or by force – to make strategic decisions about Europe in Europe’s absence. That alone would send a terrible precedent for the continent.
Much can still happen until the APEC summit next month. Another round of U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi are reportedly under discussion, while Trump’s views on Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy continue to shift. But whatever summitry emerges in Shenzhen, European governments must continue to insist on Ukrainian participation in any talks about the country’s future. Apart from pressing Washington to take them into account, Kyiv and European capitals should also appeal to Xi’s own reservations about a trilateral summit that also carries many risks for Beijing.

Ukraine hires Rothschild to advise on Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank privatization
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:07:45 EEST
02:07:45 KST

Ukraine's Ministry of Finance, state-owned banks Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank, and N.M. Rothschild & Sons Limited, part of the Rothschild & Co group, have signed three-party agreements to provide financial advisory services for preparations to sell the state-owned stakes in the two banks.
"Rothschild & Co was selected following a competitive selection process. Rothschild & Co will provide the services in a consortium with FinPoint, a Ukrainian investment banking company," the Finance Ministry said in a press release on its website on Friday.
Under the agreements, the adviser will provide comprehensive financial advice, including coordinating due diligence on the banks, among other things to determine the initial sale price; preparing information about the banks for potential investors and attracting investors; and assisting in organizing the tender for the sale of the share packages.
"Engaging an international financial adviser is an important step in implementing the strategy to reduce the state's share in the banking sector. Our task is to ensure a transparent, competitive process for selling the state-owned stakes in Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank, attract strategic investors and create conditions for the further development of these institutions," Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko was quoted as saying in the press release.
The banks will announce further steps in preparations for privatization on their official websites, the press release also said.
As reported, on October 1, 2025, the government adopted a resolution on preparations for the sale of the state-owned stakes in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank. On October 29, it approved the procedure for engaging an adviser, and on March 31, 2026, it announced a competition to select one. The adviser's compensation will consist of a fixed fee and a success fee of up to 3% of the actual proceeds received by the state budget from the sale of the share packages. The government also established a commission to oversee the sale of state-owned stakes in the banks.
N.M. Rothschild & Sons Limited is a Rothschild & Co group company registered in England and Wales, with its head office in London. It specializes in financial advisory services, corporate finance and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) transactions.
Rothschild & Co previously advised Ukraine on sovereign debt restructuring. Ukrzaliznytsia also hired the group this year to restructure its Eurobonds.
Ukraine has repeatedly undertaken commitments under programs with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to engage an adviser for the privatization of Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank. The first such engagement was planned by the end of September 2024, while the most recent commitment, under the new program, set a deadline of the end of July this year.
According to National Bank of Ukraine data, as of July 1, 2026, Ukrgasbank, with total assets of UAH 228.74 billion, ranked seventh, while Sense Bank, with UAH 157.73 billion in assets, ranked ninth among Ukraine's 59 banks.

Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:04:14 UTC
02:04:14 KST

SpaceX's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday.
"Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X.
"Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait."
Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.
Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.
"They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on."
"Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."
Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel.
"While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.
Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear.
Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine."
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."
But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored.
"I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."
Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.
Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."
On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
-- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.

UK leads call with 31 partners for urgent action to prevent famine in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:04:12 UTC
02:04:12 KST

Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security with 19.5 million people experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, the UK and 31 international partners have warned in a joint statement.
The statement on Friday called for urgent action to avert famine in the coming months, citing warnings from the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).
An estimated 41 percent of Sudan’s population is facing acute food insecurity, including 5 million people experiencing emergency levels of hunger, according to the statement.
Without immediate intervention, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000, while the number of food-insecure areas, initially assessed at 14, is expected to double.
“Conflict is the key driver of Sudan’s hunger crisis,” the statement said, noting that fighting has displaced millions, damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted health care, food production, supply chains and markets.
The crisis has been further aggravated by systematic obstruction of humanitarian aid and the effects of El Nino, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of the country, it added.
Unimpeded humanitarian access
The civil war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces erupted in April 2023.
It has since displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The partners urged the warring parties to remove all obstacles to humanitarian assistance and ensure “full, safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access,” while protecting aid workers.
They called for humanitarian operations to be authorised through all cross-line and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur, and urged measures to reduce bureaucratic delays affecting aid delivery.
The statement also called on the parties to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure, including agricultural and food systems, and strengthen coordination to protect humanitarian personnel and sites.
Urging the international community to scale up funding, the partners stressed the need to support the winter cropping season and strengthen locally led responses.
“Together we must act without delay to avert famine,” the statement said, expressing solidarity with Sudanese people and humanitarian organisations working to deliver life-saving assistance under extremely challenging conditions.

DOJ sues to block Alaska from certifying Senate race winner if Republican narrowly loses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:04:10 UTC
02:04:10 KST

The Department of Justice filed an extraordinary lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the winner of its upcoming U.S. Senate election if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the contest.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 election, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion from the name of another candidate appearing on the ballot, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.
The DOJ says that could help Democratic nominee Mary Peltola defeat the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, in what is expected to be a close contest.
The Alaska race is among several closely watched Senate races that could determine control of the chamber. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority.
The suit asks a federal judge in Alaska to bar the state from certifying "any result that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The DOJ did not say how anyone could determine a voter's intent. Doing so might be impossible, given the anonymity of ballots.
"The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," says the suit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Alaska. In addition to the state, the complaint names Alaska Elections Division Director Carol Beecher, the state's election boards and the state Ballot Counting Review Board as defendants.
President Donald Trump on Friday told reporters that he had set the lawsuit in motion.
"I'm the one that said 'do it,'" Trump said in Fort Myers, Florida while traveling for a political rally. "They have two guys ... named Dan Sullivan, so the Democrats put up a guy."
Before the suit was filed Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the DOJ had no plans to "improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process."
"There's no circumstances that we would ever do that," he said at a press conference. "Of course I'm not going to say that. But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not, no, not at all."
The DOJ's suit alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan's "sole purpose" of running for the Senate "is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan." Sullivan first registered as a Republican earlier this year. He previously was a member of the Alaska Independence Party.
The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the Alaska Senate race as one of seven "toss-up" contests for that chamber. The election tracking site FiftyPlusOne's average of polling shows Peltola, a former U.S. House member from Alaska, with just a 2-percentage-point lead over Sullivan.
The suit came hours after Trump, in a Truth Social post, wrote, "I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing, with the Dumocrats putting up another man, totally unrelated to Politics, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr."
"It's ridiculous that the Court didn't stop this SCAM. Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference," Trump said.
"We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness."
Alaska's general election for the Senate uses ranked-choice voting. Voters rank their candidates in order of preference. If no candidate gets more than 50% in round one, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated in the second round, and that process continues until there are just two candidates and the winner is the one with the most votes.
"Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan," the suit says. "For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan."
"Other supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola," the suit says. "They might not rank Senator Sullivan at all, resulting in votes for Daniel J. Sullivan to be transferred to Peltola after Daniel J. Sullivan's all-but-guaranteed elimination in the first or second round of tabulations."
In a statement to CNBC, a DOJ spokesperson said, "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot."
"Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the spokesperson said.
Nate Adams, the campaign spokesman for Sen. Sullivan, said, "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course."
"Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he'll keep building on for the next six years," Adams said.
Harry Child, a spokesman for Peltola's campaign, said, "This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan's allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he'll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans' expense for over a decade."
"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," Child said.
CNBC has requested comment from Daniel J. Sullivan, Alaska's attorney general, and state election officials.
Daniel J. Sullivan, in a social media post in June, said, "I entered this race because I am unhappy with the 12 year record of the current Senator and I feel we need a change. It's that simple."
Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, in a statement to CNBC said, "Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses."
Daniel J. Sullivan originally was blocked from the state's primary ballot in June, after the Alaska Division of Elections said his declaration of candidacy was not properly filed, and because of a finding that the candidacy was aimed at duping voters who planned to vote for Sen. Sullivan.
The division cited his request to appear on the ballot as 'Dan Sullivan,' his recent switch to the Republican Party and his work with a political consultant described as a longtime supporter of Democratic candidates, including Peltola, according to the DOJ complaint.
Daniel J. Sullivan was added to the ballot after challenging the division's decision in state court. The Alaska Supreme Court later upheld that decision.
Daniel J. Sullivan received just 2.5% of the vote in Alaska's open primary on Aug. 28, but that was enough to win him one of four spots on the Senate general election ballot.
Peltola got 49.5% in the primary, and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, received just 1.1% of the primary vote, earning him the fourth spot on the ballot.
Although Daniel J. Sullivan sought to run as a Republican, the Division of Elections decided not to list that party next to his name on the general election ballot. His name is spelled out, "Daniel J. Sullivan," and there are no other words on that line.
Both Sen. Sullivan, who has been in the Senate since 2015, and Heikes have the words "registered Republican" in parentheses next to their names.
And Sen. Sullivan, listed on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, also has the word "incumbent" next to his name.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this article.
