====================================================================================================

Lebanon's Fatima Hassan makes history with two Muay Thai golds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:53:13 UTC
00:53:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Fatima Hassan: The Lebanese Muay Thai champion who won two world titles and wants women to be seen
Determined to bring home gold and make her family and country proud, Fatima Hassan stepped into the ring for the final fight of the Muay Thai world championships in Kosovo last month.
Despite feeling unwell, the 27-year-old Lebanese fighter from Baalbek pushed through and launched a relentless attack in the final round. With just 30 seconds left, she delivered the decisive blow to secure her second gold medal of the competition.
Fatima had already won gold in the technical discipline before claiming the title in the main Muay Thai competition, making her the first Lebanese athlete to achieve the double at the IFMA Senior Muay Thai World Championships.
But the medals meant far more to her than sporting success. They represented years of dedication, her family's support, and her determination to prove that women can thrive in a sport long dominated by men.
"Honestly, I'd never been as happy as I was then. I'd worked towards this dream for so long," Fatima tells The New Arab.
Discovering what she loved
Fatima's father introduced her to sport at a young age, encouraged her to try different activities, and taught her the basics of self-defence. She eventually joined a gym near his workplace, where she discovered Muay Thai.
"I didn't really know much about it at the time. They told me it was a nice sport and encouraged me to try it. I went, tried it and loved it," she continues.
At first, she had no ambitions to compete. She simply enjoyed training, but her coaches soon noticed her skills and encouraged her to enter her first competition.
"It hadn't even crossed my mind. I wasn't interested in fighting or hitting people. I didn't like that sort of thing," she recalls.
Her father encouraged her to try it, and after watching another Lebanese female fighter compete, Fatima decided to take the plunge.
She won all three of her first fights, giving her the confidence to pursue Muay Thai more seriously.
But not everyone understood her choice.
As a woman who wears the hijab, Fatima encountered comments from people who considered combat sports unsuitable for girls.
"As long as my father was happy with what I was doing and supporting me, I didn't care what society said or what anyone else thought," Fatima says.
"People would say it was a sport for boys, that I was behaving like a boy, or ask how I could play such a sport when it wasn't meant for girls. But none of it affected me. I loved the sport, and that was what mattered."
Her family's acceptance also took time. Initially uncomfortable with the idea of her competing, they gradually came to understand the sport as they watched her train and fight.
Today, she says, they are among her biggest supporters.
Two gold medals
Fatima's road to the world championships was not straightforward. She had stopped competing for three years because of injuries, although she continued to train and teach Muay Thai.
When the opportunity to compete in Kosovo came along, she knew it was a chance to fulfil a dream she had pursued for years.
Despite her experience, she had only three months to prepare specifically for the tournament.
She worked with several coaches, sought help from a physiotherapist and a doctor, and focused on preparing mentally to return to competition.
She also followed a strict routine, running every day and keeping up with her exercises.
"I went there feeling comfortable and confident. I knew I wanted to come back with an achievement that reflected all the work I'd put in. I kept telling myself that I was going to compete, win and come back with the result I wanted," she tells The New Arab.
Fatima competed in two disciplines: the technical competition and traditional Muay Thai, the main IFMA discipline.
The technical category, in which she competed for the first time, focuses on speed, movement, and technique rather than full-force contact.
She secured her first gold medal there. But the moment she stepped up to receive it stayed with her most.
"When I saw the Lebanese flag being raised, it was a completely different feeling. I actually started crying. I felt such pride. I can't really explain what went through me, but I remember thinking: I want to experience this feeling again in the main competition," she says.
The next day, she entered the main competition with a second gold medal in sight.
Friends and family back home followed her progress, while Lebanese and Arab supporters in Kosovo gathered to cheer on their athletes.
Fatima was also unwell. She had been sick for the three days leading up to the final, with a cough and difficulty breathing.
With each fight consisting of three three-minute rounds, she feared her condition could affect her performance.
"I knew this was my dream, and I was so close to achieving it. This was my last fight, and I had the chance to win a gold medal and make history for Lebanon," she shares.
When she entered the ring, she put her trust in God and focused on the fight. She spent the first round assessing her opponent before becoming more aggressive in the second.
"I was exhausted and struggling to breathe, but I wasn't thinking about that. My mind was focused on winning. The adrenaline was carrying me through."
By the third round, Fatima had decided she needed to finish the fight. Seeing her opponent struggle, she kept attacking, landing powerful punches until she knocked her out with about 30 seconds remaining.
"I had fought over the previous four or five days, competing every day, and I had made it all the way to the final. I told myself that this last fight had to be mine, and I did it," she says.
The two gold medals culminated years of training, setbacks, and a dream she refused to abandon.
"Honestly, I'd never been as happy as I was then. I'd worked towards this dream for so long," she says.
"This was the final dream I had set for myself: winning a world championship."
The physical toll became clear after the fight. Fatima said she struggled to breathe for around three and a half hours after leaving the ring and remained unwell for about a week.
But her focus had been on bringing two gold medals home to Lebanon.
Fighting for recognition
For Fatima, the achievement also highlighted the challenges women athletes in Lebanon face, where she says support remains scarce and male athletes tend to receive more recognition.
"There is practically no support. If someone is able to support themselves, or if they find someone willing to support them, that's already a very good thing," she says.
"I have to be strong and fight for every single achievement I make. And I'm not just talking about one fight. I have to fight for everything."
She believes women are just as capable as men, but their achievements are too often overlooked.
"Look at what I've achieved. No male athlete has done what I've done in this particular category. A woman has achieved it. I'm the first Lebanese athlete to do this, and I think people should pay attention to that. Why shouldn't they recognise women as well?"
Fatima hopes her success will encourage other girls to pursue their ambitions without allowing social expectations or fear of criticism to hold them back.
"I want girls to believe in themselves and have confidence in themselves. Set yourself a goal and pursue your dream," she shares.
"Whatever you do, people will criticise you. But when you succeed, everyone will applaud you and celebrate your achievement. So go after your dream and work towards it. Believe in yourself, have confidence, and give yourself the strength you need. If you do that, I promise you, you will achieve incredible things."
A win for Lebanon
Fatima's achievement carries particular meaning against the backdrop of years of conflict and uncertainty in Lebanon. She says many young people have struggled to imagine a future for themselves amid the country's difficulties.
"We've all felt at times that we can't do anything anymore, that we can't achieve our dreams or build our futures. I think all of us young people, girls and boys, have felt that," she tells The New Arab.
We're trying to pursue our dreams, our goals and our futures, but then everything comes to a standstill because of what's happening in the country," she adds.
Fatima says she eventually stopped following the news as closely, choosing instead to concentrate on her training and future.
"Despite everything we've been going through, I continued training and working towards my goals," she says.
"When I stood there and received the medals, I was overwhelmed. I tried not to cry because there were cameras around, but I felt that Lebanon deserved this. There is so much talent in Lebanon, and we are capable of achieving so much."
Looking ahead, Fatima hopes to fight one or two professional bouts, potentially competing for a title belt, before ending her competitive career.
She also plans to focus on architecture and develop her own gym, where she hopes to train a new generation of young fighters.
Louay Faour is a journalist at The New Arab focusing largely on the Levant, with a particular interest in Lebanese affairs

Breadcrumb
Casualties feared as multi-storey building collapses in Nairobi
A multi-storey building collapsed mid-construction in the Kenyan capital on Friday, with many feared trapped in the rubble and accusations of dangerous building work.
Videos shared online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building -- thought to have been around 18 storeys high -- came down in the densely populated business and residential area of Eastleigh.
The building was reduced to a pile of rubble as search and rescue teams arrived on the scene, but struggled to start accessing the site which was jammed between other high-rise buildings.
Police said they had already rescued one woman from the rubble, and could hear the voice of another.
"There are lots of people trapped here," Bibiye Mahmoud, president of the Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya, told AFP at the site of the disaster.
"The contractors and the engineers are supposed to ensure that the works are followed by professionals. But most are not. This is why we are seeing these catastrophes... There is no accountability," she added.
Kenya's National Building Inspectorate report found that 87 percent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.
"Our concern is to save lives," Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding: "This building has no occupation certificate...this has potentially cost lives."
An occupation certificate is essentially the authority's formal sign-off that a building is safe and legally fit to be occupied.
John Ogallo, vice-president of the Institution of Engineers of Kenya, who was also at the site, said there were warning signs about the building.
"People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks," before it collapsed, he told reporters.
If you build with the wrong materials, "it becomes a time bomb," he added.
Nairobi is undergoing a rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings appearing all over the city, particularly in Eastleigh which is known for its busy market areas and as a hub for the Somali community.
Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse, which happened around lunchtime. AFP saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
There have been many concerns over safety over the years.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019 in Nairobi, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.
The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi has risen from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to its statistics bureau, as east Africa's leading business hub sucks in people from rural areas and neighbouring countries.
Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners or bypass regulations.
Five people were killed when a six-storey building collapsed in a town on the outskirts of Nairobi in September 2022.
In April 2016, 49 people were killed when a six-floor apartment building crumbled in the northeast of the capital after days of heavy rain caused floods and landslides.

Cyprus Parliament Reviews Reports on Abramovich-Linked Asset Transfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:51:00 UTC
00:51:00 KST

The Cypriot Parliament this week discussed recent revelations about corporate maneuvers that allowed firms ultimately owned by Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich to sidestep tax and transparency requirements.
The parliamentary hearings followed an investigation last week by OCCRP, CIReN, BBC, and TBIJ. The reports detailed how the Cyprus affiliate of multinational accountancy firm Deloitte, and corporate service provider MeritServus, worked together to backdate documents relating to companies beneficially owned by Abramovich.
Doing so helped the companies retroactively transfer billions of dollars in assets from Cyprus to the British Virgin Islands, where they would not be subject to Cypriot laws on tax and public disclosure.
OCCRP reached out to Deloitte’s offices in Cyprus and internationally for comment on the parliamentary hearing, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. Deloitte Cyprus previously told OCCRP it "acts in compliance with applicable laws."
MeritServus has been dissolved and it was not possible to obtain a comment.
Lawyers for Abramovich, from the London firm of Kobre and Kim, noted that he “has not been identified as the subject of any investigation, nor has he been charged with any wrongdoing.”
“Our client’s position is that he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his assets,” the firm said in an emailed response to questions.
During the session of Parliament’s Standing Committee on Institutions on Wednesday, representatives of several state bodies were questioned about the findings of the journalistic investigation. Government institutions present included the Finance and Justice Ministries, the Tax Commissioner’s Office, the State Prosecutor and Police, Auditor General, and Central Bank, as well as the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission.
An official from the Justice Ministry told the committee that information published by the media outlets would be assessed, and that police investigations would be carried out to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
A representative of the Cyprus Public Audit Oversight Board said the body had been in contact with Deloitte Cyprus since the publication of the reports. The representative referred to difficulties Deloitte Cyprus was experiencing in retrieving data and communications from the relevant period, but stated that the company would provide all relevant information as it became available.
Several representatives of regulatory bodies present at the hearings highlighted general improvement made in Cyprus since the period covered by media reports, particularly as a result of E.U. directives being transposed into national law.
Tax reform laws introduced in Cyprus in January increased the possible fine for failure to pay the Special Defense Contribution, one of the taxes the companies beneficially owned by Abramovich were obliged to pay. A fine could be as much as 100,000 euros ($112,200) in addition to four times the originally owed tax for repeat offenders.

The China-Taiwan Diplomatic War Is More About Politics Than Economics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:46:00 UTC
00:46:00 KST

Since the Chinese Civil War concluded in 1949, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and the Republic of China (ROC) have battled endlessly for diplomatic recognition. Due to Beijing’s “One China” principle, states are forced to either pick one side or pick neither.
The ROC, now colloquially better known as Taiwan, initially enjoyed an advantage in international recognition due to U.S. anti-communist messaging and generous economic assistance programs. After U.N. Resolution 2758 admitted the PRC to the United Nations and expelled the ROC, the battle for international recognition has tilted increasingly in Beijing’s favor.
Nevertheless, Taiwan still holds formal diplomatic relations across the globe. Three Pacific island-nations – the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu – recognize the ROC over the PRC, receiving major financial assistance in return. In Europe, Taiwan has one diplomatic ally, the Vatican. In Africa, Taiwan maintains formal relations with Eswatini (where President Lai Ching-te visited in May), and conducts high-level diplomatic exchanges with the partially-recognized East African state, Somaliland. The Americas, meanwhile, hold seven of Taiwan’s 12 remaining embassies. These states challenge Beijing’s extensive efforts to isolate Taiwan diplomatically, demonstrating that Taipei can maintain and strengthen relations with sovereign nations.
Analyzing Taiwan’s relations with Africa and Latin America comparatively, we can see how and under what circumstances Taipei’s Global South engagement has prevailed against Beijing’s diplomatic efforts. Although economic assistance programs have been critical, Taiwan’s formal relations ultimately depend on political leverage drawn from diplomatic recognition rather than purely economic considerations. The recognition of Taiwan will therefore continue to serve as a political tool for smaller countries, independence movements, and breakaway states that find greater gain from Taipei than Beijing.
Africa
Until UNGA Resolution 2758 passed in 1971, Taiwan maintained widespread recognition throughout Africa. During decolonization in the 1950s and 1960s, most newly-independent African states were wary of Beijing’s communist ideology and optimistic about their inclusion into the international community. Thus, incentivized by Taiwan’s foreign assistance, many African countries recognized the ROC over the PRC as the representative of China between 1960 and 1963.
By 1971, the year of Resolution 2758, the PRC and Taiwan had an almost equal number of African countries’ recognition (Taiwan’s 20 to the PRC’s 22). Only five African countries recognized the ROC by 1979, highlighting the UNGA Resolution’s devastating impact on Taiwan’s international legitimacy.
Since African decolonization, Taipei and Beijing have engaged in “dollar diplomacy,” leveraging favorable loans, technical knowledge-sharing, trade, and agricultural assistance to compete for support. Starting in 1960, Taipei began international development programs, trade incentives, and investments throughout Africa to preserve its influence despite being reliant on U.S. aid itself. Taiwan has become increasingly incapable of competing for African countries’ recognition as its economy has become dwarfed by the PRC in recent decades.
Burkina Faso was the latest African country to withdraw its recognition of Taiwan, doing so in 2018. Formerly known as Upper Volta, Burkina Faso first severed relations with Taiwan in 1973, along with much of the rest of the continent. In 1994, under coup-installed former president Blaise Compaoré, Burkina Faso reestablished relations with Taiwan in pursuit of a lucrative economic relationship.
Due to China’s expanding economy, the Belt and Road Initiative, and chaotic power transfers, Burkina Faso eventually switched its recognition back to the PRC in 2018 after Compaoré lost power.
Notably, Taiwan’s response solely blamed the PRC. Rather than condemning Burkina Faso’s decision to withdraw recognition of Taiwan, then-President Tsai Ing-wen attacked Beijing for its “serial acts of suppression against Taiwan in the diplomatic sphere” through economic coercion and political interference.
A series of coups over the past decade has placed Burkina Faso firmly within the PRC’s sphere of influence, with Western counterterrorism forces being expelled and China’s economic and military investment in the country increasing.
Facing dwindling formal relations, Taiwan has adopted a “pragmatic diplomacy” approach, which prioritizes de facto economic influence over political recognition. In Africa, Taiwan operates trade and political representative offices in Nigeria, South Africa, Côte d’Ivoire, and Somaliland. Several quasi-governmental and non-state organizations expand Taiwan’s economic influence on the continent, such as the Taiwan External Trade Development Council, the International Cooperation and Development Fund, and the Taiwan-Africa Business Association. While these organizations have failed to quell the rapidly expanding PRC influence across Africa, they highlight Taiwan’s capacity to maintain a diplomatic presence.
Eswatini’s continued support for Taiwan has resulted in both diplomatic condemnation and economic exclusion from Beijing. In 2026, the PRC prevented Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te from visiting Eswatini during celebrations of King Mswati III’s 40th year in power by pressuring Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar to revoke flight permits for Taiwan’s delegation. Lai clandestinely visited Eswatini the following month despite Beijing’s efforts to prevent the trip. However the episode illustrated how the PRC can use its political and economic clout against Taiwanese diplomacy.
Additionally, Eswatini’s exclusion from PRC investment through institutions like the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) introduces an opportunity cost that harms the country’s economic competitiveness. Eswatini’s status as a monarchy, however, reduces the salience of political grievances tied to broader social, political, or economic conditions derivative of its adversarial relationship with the PRC.
Somaliland, the breakaway region of northern Somalia, has developed a unique relationship with Taiwan. Most countries deny Somaliland’s political status. Since declaring independence in 1991, Somaliland has lobbied the international community to recognize it as a fully autonomous state, with Israel being the only U.N. member state to recognize its independence in 2025. In similar states of de facto independence, Taiwan and Somaliland enhanced their bilateral relationship in 2020 to increase shared economic investment in East Africa and cement their political willingness to explore new, Western-aligned friendships.
Taiwan has implemented many development programs there for public health, education, government modernization, democratization, and humanitarian assistance. Taiwan’s ICDF currently facilitates six development programs in Somaliland, while Taiwan benefits from increased political and economic access to East Africa. While Somaliland has not officially established diplomatic recognition of Taiwan, the relationship could prove to be consequential for China-U.S. competition and rising insecurity in the Horn of Africa.
In its pursuit of legitimacy, Taiwan will see more success in diplomatic initiatives targeting smaller, less established, or more politically unique states. Countries that have already carved their places in the international community are less likely to have political environments conducive to recognition of Taiwan over the PRC, as they will prioritize economic opportunity and stability over Taiwan’s aspirations.
The PRC’s rapid economic growth and its “One China” principle” create a geopolitical competition stacked against Taiwan. Moving forward, Taiwan will likely have to leverage future relationships with breakaway movements, global pariahs, and peculiar governments to rebuild its international influence.
Latin America
In Latin America, Taiwan’s diplomatic partnerships date back many decades. Unlike in Africa, where most countries were colonies until the 1960s, Latin American nations have been independent since the 19th century. Most established relations with the ROC before it relocated to Taiwan in 1949. Taipei then consolidated its diplomatic standing by establishing new relations with Haiti, Paraguay, and Uruguay in the mid-1950s. The ROC similarly established relations with newly-independent Grenada, Dominica, St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, St. Lucia, and Belize in the 1980s.
The Cold War aided Taiwan, as Latin American governments could signal U.S. alignment by maintaining relations with the anticommunist ROC over the communist PRC. In fact, only Cuba and Chile cut ties with the ROC to establish relations with the PRC before 1971, both under leftist, Marxism-endorsing leaders. Although Mexico and most South American countries switched in the 1970s and 1980s, Taiwan continued commercial and cultural relations with these countries and still holds commercial offices in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, and Peru.
As in Africa, Taiwan’s agricultural advisory missions significantly improved Latin American food production. One such mission more than doubled Dominican rice yields from 1972-82. Also like in Africa, Taiwan and China’s “dollar diplomacy” took off in the 1990s and 2000s, as Taiwan significantly increased economic donations to its allies, while China gave bountiful gifts in exchange for switching recognition, including stadiums in Dominica, Grenada, the Bahamas, and Costa Rica between 1997 and 2007.
Following the “diplomatic truce” with Beijing during Ma Ying-jeou’s 2008-16 administration, China resumed its diplomatic poaching after Tsai Ing-wen was elected in 2016. In 2017 and 2018, Panama, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador switched to China, reportedly securing hundreds of millions in Chinese funds in exchange.
Notably, the first Trump administration condemned El Salvador’s decision, and Trump signed the 2020 Taiwan Allies International Protection and Enhancement Initiative (TAIPEI) Act, which codifies U.S. support for Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic partnerships. The Biden administration rebuked Nicaragua’s dynastic dictatorship for ditching Taiwan and embracing China in 2021, and attempted to stop Honduras’ leftist government from doing the same two years later.
Despite Beijing’s best efforts, however, seven countries in the Americas continue opting for relations with Taiwan over China: Belize, Guatemala, Haiti, Paraguay, St. Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines.
A country of 15 million, Guatemala has strengthened ties with both Taipei and Washington recently. Taiwan operates six developmental projects in Guatemala, spanning educational programs, medical technology, and agricultural assistance. These projects follow 26 completed ones, all through Taiwan’s ICDF. Taiwan has also signed commercial agreements, helping Guatemala become Taiwan’s fourth-largest coffee supplier. Taiwan boosts Guatemala’s human capital by giving several hundred scholarships to Guatemalan students studying in Taipei.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has commended Guatemala’s president for continuing to recognize Taiwan, and the U.S. and Taiwanese governments have jointly led development initiatives with Guatemala. With the United States being Guatemala’s largest export market and the source of 25 percent of its GDP via migrant remittances, Guatemala has pragmatic reasons to please Washington by recognizing Taipei.
Paraguay – Taiwan’s only remaining South American ally – has similarly maintained loyalty to Taipei. After its 35-year dictatorship fell in 1989, Paraguay maintained deep engagement with Taiwan. Economic engagements have solidified, with Taiwan becoming Paraguay’s second largest beef importer and largest pork importer. As agricultural exports generate 10 percent of Paraguay’s GDP and jobs, this commercial relationship is no trivial matter.
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña’s visit to Taipei in May cemented this relationship by expanding chicken exports to Taiwan and obtaining pledges for AI computing center investments in Paraguay. Notably, with the exception of the 2008–12 Fernando Lugo administration, Paraguay’s executive has always been a member of the Colorado Party, which holds a multidecade close relationship with Taiwanese officials.
These relations, however, are not set in stone. Paraguay’s last presidential runner-up pledged to switch recognition to the PRC if elected, and China’s government has gifted lavish all-expenses-paid trips to China to dozens of opposition lawmakers, who now lobby for Paraguay to switch. Similarly, in Guatemala, candidates in next year’s election could make the same pledge, especially considering how China canceled Guatemalan coffee and macadamia shipments after its president held a videoconference with Taiwan’s president in 2024.
But for the moment, Taiwan’s Latin American relations remain strong, boosted by the Trump administration’s stated priorities to counter China’s rising influence in the Americas. In fact, in Honduras’ presidential election last year, both opposition candidates pledged to restore relations with Taiwan if elected, citing low transparency and negative results from the 2023 switch under the previous government. One of those candidates, Nasry Asfura, won and became president.
Conclusion
Beijing claims that Taiwan’s diplomacy is merely a “scandal and a farce,” but 12 states continue supporting Taiwanese statehood. Countries have long recognized the ROC for legitimate reasons, most often political ones. Whether a ruling monarchy preserving multidecade relations (Eswatini), a strong U.S. ally aligning with Washington (Guatemala), or a ruling party continuing long-held ties with Taipei (Paraguay), political particularities have created diplomatic opportunities for Taiwan across continents. Somaliland’s contested status facilitating diplomacy with Taiwan proves this point further.
Due to China’s economic weight, Taipei cannot convince many countries to pick it over Beijing. Still, like David using a slingshot instead of a spear, Taiwan can exploit political circumstances for its diplomatic benefit.

bacchus floor mosaic inspires yellow terrazzo and marble apartment renovation in athens
space is around us redesigns a 100-sqm apartment in kypseli, using an existing bacchus entryway mosaic to guide the reintroduction of dionysus marble, yellow terrazzo, and curved geometry.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Space is around us redesigns apartment around archaic mosaic
Designed by local studio Space is around us, Bacchus Apartment is a targeted renovation of a 100-sqm residence on Fokionos Negri street in the Kypseli neighborhood of Athens, Greece. Focusing primarily on the kitchen and bathroom, the redesign draws its material and color palette from an existing entryway floor mosaic depicting Bacchus (Dionysus), utilizing butter-yellow tones, curved geometric forms, and period-specific material selections.
MARBLE AND YELLOW TERRAZZO draw from 1960S MATERIAL CULTURE
In the kitchen, design practice Space is around us installs a continuous fitted cabinetry unit along the main wall, maximizing preparation surfaces and storage, terminating in triangular open shelving that adapts to the irregular floor plan. The cabinetry is finished in a butter-yellow hue sampled from the entryway mosaic, paired with Dionysus marble countertops, a material widely used in 1960s Athenian residential architecture.
Opposite the kitchen unit, a custom terracotta dining table with rounded corners and oversized cylindrical legs ensures fluid spatial circulation. The kitchen’s former gray floor was replaced with large-format yellow terrazzo tiles, which extend through the hallway and into the windowless bathroom. In the bathroom, glossy small-format lime-yellow and white tiles reflect ambient light from an internal air shaft, while a rounded vanity mirror and terracotta sconce reinforce the apartment’s geometric motifs.

Landmark E17 motorway stop must close to make way for new service stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:44:26 UTC
00:44:26 KST

The E17 Snack restaurant on the motorway of the same name between Antwerp and Ghent will disappear among new plans to develop the area with services for travellers and lorry drivers
Landmark E17 motorway stop must close to make way for new service stations
Anyone who drives on the E17 between Ghent and Antwerp knows E17 Snack, the longstanding, family-owned business perched along the motorway. With its tell-tale sign featuring a girl eating a burger, E17 Snack in Waasmunster is one of the oldest motorway restaurants in Belgium.
All good things must come to an end, as they say, and it is no different for the well-known establishment. Flanders’ Roads & Traffic Agency (AWV) manages the land and has awarded the concession to operate on both sides of the motorway to XL Servicestations, which will run new restaurants, EV loading stations and services for families and truckers.
AWV says that it wants to improve the site for travellers, with more parking capacity for lorry drivers and roadside services such as toilets and showers, as well as playground and fitness equipment. There will be no petrol stations, but there will be 28 fast-charging stations for electric vehicles and eight for electric lorries.
There is also a serious problem of illegal dumping on the site, which has plagued the owners of E17 Snack for years. “The parking area will finally be addressed,” E17 Snack owner Kristien De Meulenaer told VRT. “Let’s face it, the parking lot does not make a good impression when you drive in here.”
It’s been my life’s work for 26 years. From sunup to sundown, I worked here with heart and soul.
Kristien De Meulenaere
De Meulenaere has run the small E17 Snack for the last 26 years and has often felt neglected by AWV when it came to the dumping problem. “Especially in the summer months I had to beg them to come and haul the trash from the parking. It was such a shame because it damaged the image of my business.”
She understands the agency’s desire to improve the site and did not bid for the new concession. “They were looking for someone willing to revamp the entire carpark and run larger motorway restaurants. As a small business owner, I simply don’t have the resources to make that happen. It’s a shame, but that’s the way it is.”
XL Servicestations, a daughter company of G&V Energy Group, promises better lighting and security cameras, along with the new services. But it will never have a relationship with customers the way E17 Snack does, says De Meulenaer.
“It’s unfortunate for the customers but also for me,” she says. “I know all of these people; I see children born who have grown up to be lorry drivers themselves and bring their own families here. Sometimes families even hold events here. It’s been my life’s work for 26 years. From sunup to sundown, I worked here with heart and soul.”
New site to open in 2028
De Meulenaere herself spoke to several of the concession candidates and is satisfied with the choice of XL Servicestations. “I’m convinced that it’s a good candidate, they have a bit of the same concept in mind.”
It’s also not impossible that she and her staff could work for the new business. “I’m not sure about that yet,” she says. “We’ll see how it goes.”
Works on the new development will begin in 2027, with an opening date scheduled for the spring of 2028.

Security clearance changes costing firms thousands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:44:11 BST
00:44:11 KST

One small defence firm lost 163 security clearances on a single date at a cost of £68,000 over twelve months, including fourteen redrafts of a single access letter, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Julian David, chief executive of techUK, raised the issue during a session on the implications of the Defence Investment Plan for British industry.
He said: “In summary, to sponsor someone’s security clearance a company now requires a contract specific sponsor access letter. At the moment, Government Departments do not seem to be able to agree who pays to process that. The impact is real. One provider has estimated that thousands of people are affected. One SME that we know of lost 163 clearances on a single date, costing it £68,000 in 12 months, including 14 redrafts of the access letter to put right.”
Earlier in the session David told MPs that the change is “having a real effect because of the change in the way that it is done on the sponsoring”, and that it affects large businesses as well as small ones, “with people losing 1,600 clearances, and SMEs having to reapply because their sponsor route has gone.”
Kevin Craven, chief executive of ADS, set out two separate problems for the committee, saying: “One is that MOD is currently providing security clearances that can be used by other Departments that do not necessarily have their own security clearing apparatus. That appears to be a source of concern. That is one issue.”
On the second he said: “A separate issue is that the MOD is looking at organisations that provide third-party sponsorship for those security clearances, including my own organisation. We are currently sponsoring some 14,000 security clearances for 700 SMEs and other organisations in the supply chain. If that authorisation were removed, the burden for supplying those clearances would shift in some instances to the primes, which are already struggling with security clearances for their own staff. There are large numbers of SMEs that want direct access to the MOD and are using these third-party clearance houses to obtain their security clearances. That would be a major problem, and it looks like it is a major problem at the moment.”
Tan Dhesi, the committee’s chair, told the witnesses that the committee had been pursuing security clearance already, and that it featured prominently in its report on AUKUS because members thought matters needed resolving before they impeded delivery.
Dhesi said the committee had previously been advised that the situation was much better and all sorted, and asked what had changed and why it had become more difficult.
David told MPs the issue also constrains efforts to bring new sectors into defence, saying the automotive supply chain is made up of small and medium-sized enterprises who are not typically people who have held security clearance, and that obtaining it has become more difficult for a smaller firm.
The government has been seeking to bring non-traditional suppliers into defence work, and Stephen Phipson of MakeUK told the committee that many manufacturing companies outside defence want to enter the market and that MakeUK runs a service helping them make the transition.

Algerian urea exports to France under threat as diplomatic tensions persist, sources say
Algeria has instructed urea producers to stop exporting the fertiliser to France in an intensification of trade curbs that have followed a diplomatic rift between Algeria and its former colonial ruler, according to diplomats and industry sources.
Ties between Paris and Algiers, which have been complicated for decades, deteriorated in 2024 when French President Emmanuel Macron backed a plan for autonomy for the Western Sahara region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The two countries sought to repair relations last year, even at one point declaring that the relationship was back to normal, but the ties have since soured again.
Information about a halt to urea exports emerged early last week and could put at risk Algerian supplies that account for around 30% of French urea imports, French fertiliser industry association Afcome and wheat growers group AGPB said.
Three diplomats also said they were aware of an instruction by Algeria to suspend urea shipments to France. They were among six French and European diplomats who also said that Algiers had in late July imposed a near-blanket ban on French imports.
The diplomats requested anonymity to discuss the issue.
Any disruption to Algerian urea supplies could create fresh concerns for French farmers, who rely on nitrogen-based fertilisers to maintain crop yields and who have already faced higher costs.
Beyond the agricultural impact, the dispute could become politically sensitive for President Emmanuel Macron's government, which is under pressure to shield households and producers from rising costs while managing a sharp deterioration in relations with Algeria, a topic that often polarises the French political landscape.
France experienced some of the worst unrest in years last weekend and a potential confrontation with farmers over fertiliser supplies could only add to that pressure.
Like with previous trade restrictions, including a halt to Algerian imports of French wheat since 2024, the sources said there had been no formal announcement by the Algerian government regarding either urea exports or imports of French goods.
The Algerian embassy in Paris did not immediately respond to emailed questions from Reuters. Algeria's trade and foreign ministries were also not immediately available for comment on Friday, a non-working day in the country.
France's foreign ministry said it had not received notification of such trade restrictions.
Trade matters were a competence of the European Union, it said, adding: "We will, of course, remain particularly vigilant on this issue."

Silicon Valley Democrats demand investigation into Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:33:47 UTC
00:33:47 KST

A group of Silicon Valley U.S. House Democrats on Friday demanded the White House investigate recent interruptions of Elon Musk's Starlink internet service in Ukraine in a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
The letter, shared exclusively with CNBC and led by California Democratic Reps. Sam Liccardo, Ro Khanna and Jimmy Panetta, comes after Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink, was restricted in Ukraine for a period of time, limiting the besieged country's military capabilities.
Ukrainian officials told CNN on Friday that restrictions remained in place, despite President Donald Trump's claim Thursday that Musk had restored access. The officials said the restrictions were disrupting high-speed military drones, hampering Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attacks and conduct operations along the front line.
The lawmakers in their letter to Wiles demanded an "immediate, government-wide investigation into the decision to restrict SpaceX's Starshield satellite-based intelligence and military support services in Ukraine." The letter indicates Democrats will make investigating the Starlink interruption a top priority if they win the House in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
"We will ensure that the 120th Congress will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk's businesses, including whether these companies meet their contractual obligations, and whether adequate safeguards exist against political interference, arbitrary service restrictions, and misuse of federal resources," the lawmakers wrote.
Asked about the letter Friday, the White House referred CNBC to Trump's comments a day earlier. Trump declined Thursday to say whether he had called Musk about the restrictions, telling reporters, "Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference." He added, "The bottom line, he put it back," referring to Musk and the Starshield service.
SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Democrats are widely expected to investigate private businesses that contract with the government if they win control of Congress, which would grant them subpoena power at the committee level.
At the core of the lawmakers' questions is who ordered the throttling of Ukrainian Starshield and whether the direction came from President Donald Trump or Musk, a private citizen.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Musk ordered the restrictions, and the news outlet subsequently reported they were lifted after a phone call between Trump and Musk. Ukrainian forces rely on Starshield to conduct military operations amid a Russian invasion that began over four years ago. Trump has repeatedly denied ordering the disruption of Starlink, despite Musk's public assertions that the order would have come from the White House.
"Despite the resulting loss of human life, and the serious national security implications, neither the Administration nor SpaceX has provided a clear and consistent explanation of responsibility," the lawmakers wrote in the letter. "Either a private contractor independently made life-and-death national security decisions, or President Trump directed the restriction of critical military communications supporting a U.S. ally."
The lawmakers asked Wiles who was behind the decision to restrict Starshield service and to identify any individuals "who authorized, directed, approved, or [were] consulted about the restrictions." The lawmakers also asked how the restrictions were implemented, whether they violated federal contracts and whether similar vulnerabilities exist elsewhere.
"As Silicon Valley's elected members in Congress, we represent hundreds of innovation economy employers and workers whose livelihoods depend on the credibility of American technology abroad," the lawmakers wrote. "Politically motivated service interruptions or erratic throttling will undermine reputations developed through decades of work that Americans have led to support our allies and customers throughout the world."
— Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

Eating too much sugar on antibiotics could squash helpful gut bacteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

Eating too much sugar on antibiotics could squash helpful gut bacteria
For some cancer patients, eating sweets worsens antibiotics’ disruption of gut bacteria
While a spoonful of sugar might help us gulp down a bitter-tasting antibiotic, it also may increase the damage that these drugs cause to the gut microbes.
In patients being treated for blood cancers, eating sugary items during antibiotic treatment was linked to a greater reduction in gut bacteria diversity than taking the antibiotics alone. The combination was also tied to the growth of gut bacteria associated with hard-to-treat infections, researchers report September 30 in Nature.
Cancer patients have lots of variation in their diets and take medications that can damage their microbiome. So, these patients provide a unique opportunity to study dramatic gut changes “that we believe are also relevant in the healthy context,” says Jonas Schluter, a microbiologist at NYU Langone Health.
Previous evidence separately suggested that antibiotics and sugars can disrupt the gut microbiome. But their combined effects, particularly in people at greater risk of infection, was unclear.
Researchers closely tracked more than 9,000 meals eaten by 173 people hospitalized in a treatment center to undergo blood-forming stem cell transplants. “Diet records are one of the biggest black boxes in a lot of diet microbiome studies,” since meals are often self-reported, says Tiffany Weir, a microbiologist at Colorado State University in Fort Collins, who was not involved in the research.
Standardized hospital meals allowed researchers to measure multiple days’ worth of food intake down to the gram, then compare the amounts of various nutrients eaten with bacterial diversity data obtained from stool samples.
For every additional 100 grams of sugar (the equivalent of 2.5 cans of Coke) that patients on antibiotics ate in the two days before sampling, the team found a 24 percent decrease in bacterial diversity. Consuming sweets and sugary beverages during antibiotic treatment was also associated with blooms of Enterococcus bacteria, which can be drug-resistant and are linked to difficult-to-treat infections associated with longer hospital stays and higher mortality.
“Some bacteria, sometimes, survive antibiotics, or perhaps more dangerously, they are resistant to [them],” Schluter says. By giving these bacteria the “universal resource for life, which is simple sugars, we are exacerbating their dominance. It’s almost like burning down the rainforest with a lot of fire, and then trying to extinguish the flames by putting in more petrol.”
The researchers also exposed mice on standard or sucrose-rich diets to a single dose of antibiotics. They found that the sugar exacerbated the enterococcal abundance after antibiotic exposure.
“Reducing sugar intake could be another way for patients to support their gut microbiome during antibiotic treatment,” says Sarah Berry, a nutrition scientist at King’s College London who was not involved in the study. Still, more research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to anyone on these drugs.
Schluter hopes that further studies and clinical trials can help uncover more about the exact relationship between sugar, antibiotics and the gut microbiome.
“You need to take antibiotics to fight infections, but you should also be aware that they have side effects to the microbiome,” Schluter says. “Now, we need to find strategies to mitigate this damage.”

NATO opens its contracts to Ukraine’s defense industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:25:44 UTC
00:25:44 KST

- Ukraine joined NSPA’s Security Cooperation Support Partnership, allowing Ukrainian defense companies to compete for contracts issued by NATO’s main procurement agency.
- About 150 Ukrainian companies attended an NSPA industry day in Kyiv on Oct. 14, the first such NATO event since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has joined a NATO procurement partnership that lets Ukrainian defense companies bid for contracts issued by the alliance’s main buying agency, the NATO Support and Procurement Agency announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
Ukraine is now the seventh member of the agency’s Security Cooperation Support Partnership, alongside Belgium, Luxembourg, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom and NATO Headquarters. The partnership, set up in 2025 to give Ukraine sustained support through a structured procurement framework, will also let Kyiv draw on the agency’s expertise and help shape Ukraine’s own defense and industrial requirements. NATO allies in the North Atlantic Council approved the agency’s ability to issue solicitations and sign contracts with Ukrainian industry in April 2026.
The Luxembourg-based agency marked the move with a Ukraine Industry Day in Kyiv on Oct. 14, attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies. NSPA said it was the first event of its kind held by a NATO organization in Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, bringing together the agency’s director of support to operations, Jacqueline Borsboom, staff from the NATO Representation to Ukraine and NATO Headquarters, and Ukrainian Deputy Defense Ministers Mstyslav Banik and Anna Gvozdiar to discuss future procurement trends and partnerships with companies across Ukraine’s defense industrial base.
“This partnership will help deeper connect Ukrainian industry with opportunities to grow, while enabling Allies and partners to learn from Ukraine’s battle-tested innovation and operational experience. Our aim is to further strengthen Ukraine’s industrial base and bring that expertise into the delivery and sustainment of capabilities,” said Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA director of support to operations.
“Ukraine is developing its cooperation with NATO in the field of procurement, and participation in this Partnership offers a unique opportunity to access all the services and capabilities of the NSPA for our needs. Ukraine is the first and only country (and not even a NATO member) for which a separate Partnership has been created as a single entry point to the Agency’s work, and Ukrainian industry has also been given broad access to the Agency’s tenders,” said Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik.
NSPA support partnerships allow two or more NATO countries to pool their demand for goods and services, which can bring economies of scale and lower prices, with the agency acting as the central manager that develops capabilities, handles requirements and oversees delivery on the alliance’s behalf. For Ukrainian manufacturers, the arrangement opens a route into the tenders that NATO uses to buy and sustain equipment for its members.
The agency has already been a major channel for non-lethal aid to Kyiv. NSPA has mobilized around 400 million euros ($448 million) through NATO’s Comprehensive Assistance Package Trust Fund for Ukraine, delivering medical supplies, fuel, critical infrastructure and cybersecurity support, while the IT Capability Coalition has added another 219 million euros ($245 million) to modernize Ukraine’s digital defense capabilities. Allies have also donated millions of liters of fuel, with NSPA staff deployed in NATO countries to oversee quality.
NATO says its allies have provided 99% of all military aid to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and with Ukraine now inside the partnership, the agency can issue solicitations and sign contracts directly with Ukrainian companies.

The Atlantic and Pacific Oceans Are Not Trump’s to Rename
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:24:09 UTC
00:24:09 KST

Not content with renaming an international gulf and a cross-border lake, on Oct. 10, U.S. President Donald Trump recently floated the idea of renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean as “Trump Ocean” or the “Ocean of the Americas” at a political rally in Clarksville, Tenn.
“We need an ocean. So, I was thinking of either the Atlantic or the Pacific,” he said to laughter and applause. “We call it ‘Trump Ocean’ or ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that.”
Then, at an Oct. 21 rally in South Carolina, Trump said he asked Google’s CEO, Sundar Pichai, to rename the Atlantic Ocean on Google Maps. According to Trump, Pichai replied, “Please don’t ask us to do that.”
“So, I'll probably pass,” Trump said. “I think let's keep it the Atlantic Ocean.”
While Google has not issued a formal statement on the matter, Trump’s obsession with naming places for himself or America is remarkable. In our view, it reflects a textbook case of “toponymic narcissism”—the use of place naming to remake the world in one’s own image.
Let’s not fool ourselves: Trump knows a thing or two about branding. In fact, his business career has largely revolved around marketing the Trump brand on hotels, golf courses, and even golden sneakers. We shouldn’t be surprised to find him following the same playbook in his second presidential term.
Yet the world map is not a private real estate development. Nor can place names be reduced to a branding exercise. Place names have a greater civic purpose as shared global symbols that should transcend the personal glorification and political interests of any individual leader.
Place names form part of our intangible cultural heritage with cultural significance that will outlive the cartographic whims of President Trump. They shape our geographical imaginations and the way people perceive and understand the world. Geographical naming also has important consequences for education, international relations, and the types of messages we wish to project to the world.
For instance, it is notable that Trump has focused much of his renaming energy on places with Indigenous names, such as Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. In the case of the Atlantic Ocean, this could also be seen as an attempt to erase an etymology that points through Greece to North Africa. The name derives from the Greek for “Ocean of Atlas,” referring to the mythology of a giant who lives in the Atlas Mountains of northwestern Africa.
As place name scholars, we have spent decades studying the cultural, social, and political aspects of place naming. There is a long history of political leaders and cartographers using place naming to assert raw power by rewriting the world map. In one sense, Trump’s renaming shenanigans are simply the latest flashy example in this broader story of mapping and politics.
But Trump is not merely renaming places to project American power on the world stage. He is also making a mockery of the very act of place naming itself—and, along with it, the international norms that inform the map-making process.
The international community must reaffirm its commitment to respecting the cultural value of place naming and to articulate responsible place-naming principles, especially for geographical features that are shared across international borders. In an open letter co-authored with place name experts around the world, we propose five key principles for responsible place naming:
The first principle is recognizing that place names are culturally significant forms of intangible heritage and shared resources whose stewardship carries responsibilities extending beyond the interests of any particular government, leader, institution, or generation.
Given the cultural significance of place names, our second principle highlights the need for meaningful public participation in place naming decisions. Place names that are changed arbitrarily and without due process should not be recognized by the international community.
Thirdly, place names should not be used to proclaim cultural superiority, advance territorial ambitions, or assert exclusive national ownership over geographical spaces shared among different peoples.
Places should generally not be named for living people. Instead, place naming should serve the public interest rather than promoting the personal legacies of those seeking to commemorate themselves as a form of self-aggrandizement.
Lastly, we recognize that a shared geography need not always have a single name, since multiple place names can bear witness to the layered histories, languages, and attachments through which places acquire meaning. However, this recognition should not extend to condoning the unilateral renaming of shared geographic features without international dialogue among affected countries and communities.
If Trump moves forward with attempting to rename the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, the international community should stand united in rejecting this attention-seeking act of cartographic malpractice and defend the cultural value of place naming as a cornerstone of our shared world map and geographical imagination.

UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday “strongly” condemned the escalation of drone attacks across Sudan, which have killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October, Anadolu reports.

Turk urged both parties to comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and agree to a ceasefire.

The civil war in Sudan continues since 2023 and has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters.

A missile strike likely hit the Proton plant in the Russian city of Orel, a manufacturer of optoelectronic equipment whose components are used in Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Pantsir-S1 air defense systems and Kh-71 cruise missiles, according to the monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Local authorities declared an aviation and missile danger alert in Orel during the attack. Information on the extent of the damage at the plant is still being clarified, and the type of weapon used and the exact time of the strike have not yet been confirmed.
The joint-stock company Proton is part of Russia’s defense industry supply chain and produces optoelectronic equipment and components for military use. Its products include diode modules, switch-inverters and electronic components for onboard weapon systems, which are supplied for the production of the 9M723 missiles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system, the S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missile and the Pantsir-S1, a truck-mounted system that combines anti-aircraft missiles and rapid-fire cannons to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles.
The Iskander-M is one of Russia’s main weapons for long-range strikes against Ukraine, firing ballistic missiles with a range of up to 500 km (310 miles). The S-71 Kover belongs to a family of newer Russian air-launched cruise missiles, and Ukrainian military intelligence has previously identified the same R500 turbojet engine in the S-71K Kover and the new Filin ground-launched cruise missile, which Russia began using against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
Orel, the capital of Russia’s Orel region about 160 km (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border, has been the target of repeated long-range strikes. On Oct. 31, 2025, the Ukrainian Navy said it hit the city’s thermal power plant with Neptune cruise missiles, and in May 2025 drones struck the Bolkhov semiconductor plant in the same region, which produces components used by Russia’s defense industry.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian plants that build missiles and their components. In August 2026, Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles hit the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara, and earlier this month the Ukrainian General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver region, which produces components for cruise missile fuel.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia and Ukraine have agreed to cease fire in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region starting October 29, the White House said.
Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said later in the day that the evacuation of residents from Alyoshki as part of the humanitarian operation may take at least several days and all those willing will be able to leave the city.
Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Army Valery Gerasimov, in turn, announced that Russian forces will enforce a localized ceasefire at 1:00 a.m. GMT on October 27 to allow for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki.
TASS has summed up what is known about the agreement at this moment.
The White House statements
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, the White House said.
The local ceasefire will come into effect on October 29, 2026.
The sides agreed to cease hostilities in Alyoshki to "allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway."
An independent US media organization will assist and document the actions of both Russia and Ukraine during the ceasefire.
The White House said on Melania Trump has contributed to a ceasefire.
Melania Trump and her representative collaborated with the leadership of Russia and Ukraine "to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."
She "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."
The Kremlin’s statements
Russia commends the efforts of US First Lady Melania Trump, "who has made a significant contribution to coordinating the humanitarian operation in the settlement of Alyoshki in the Kherson region."
Alyoshki’s residents will be able to leave the city unimpededly: "Those willing to leave this settlement will be able to do so."
It may take several days to evacuate people from Alyoshki as part of the humanitarian operation: "I’d rather refrain from anticipating anything but, naturally, it will take at least several days."
Russian ombudswoman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, have done much work, enabling the military to coordinate ceasefire timelines in Alyoshki "to build up on agreements reached between Presidents [Vladimir] Putin and [Donald] Trump."
Statements by the Russian Chief of the General Staff
In connection with the humanitarian operation near Alyoshki, the Russian Armed Forces "will cease fire in the Kherson area and implement a ceasefire starting at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, 2026."
"To ensure the security of people and delivery of vital social supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be carried out and a safe passage of humanitarian aid to the locality of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region will be provided."
Russia-US contacts on the situation in Alyoshki
During a phone call with US leader Donald Trump on October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that regarding the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki, it was agreed that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova would remain in regular contact with Melania Trump’s staff.
During US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff’s visit to Russia, Putin asked him to convey his thanks to Melania Trump for her role in resolving humanitarian issues in Ukraine, in particular, foe her mediation regarding the situation in Alyoshki, Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov said on October 21.
A humanitarian communication channel between Lantratova and the team of US First Lady Melania Trump on the situation in Alyoshki could help spread the truth about that situation in the town, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said.
Russia’s actions to ease the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki
Lantratova said she had discussed the situation in Alyoshki with Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets.
Russian children’s rights ombudswoman Maria Lvova-Belova said she is monitoring the situation in Alyoshki.
The Russian authorities are doing everything they can to help Alyoshki residents and organize their evacuation from the city, Vladimir Polyakov, a member of the Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR) legislature, told TASS.
Situation in Alyoshki
Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov on September 21 described the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki as critical.
Food and medicines cannot be delivered to the city amid Ukrainian shelling and drone attacks.
More than 1,200 artillery and drone strikes had been delivered by Ukrainian troops on Alyoshki over the week, the district’s head Ruslan Khomenko said on October 19.
Ukrainian FPV drone operators deliberately target civilian houses in border areas of the Alyoshki district, an officer of the 331st regiment of the 98th airborne division with a call sign Salyut told TASS.
Civilians in Alyoshki had received no humanitarian assistance from Ukraine, all reports to the contrary are not true, Svetlana Popova, an evacuated local resident, told TASS.
People from neighboring settlement on the Dnieper left bank tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but Ukrainian troops did not let them do this, she said.

King Fahd Airport, Defense Ministry attacked as US tells diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia
TEHRAN - At least two people were killed in a strike on a major airport in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, as Washington ordered some U.S. diplomatic staff to leave the kingdom following weeks of deadly attacks by the Nasrallah military forces.
The Saudi authorities said in a statement on Thursday morning that a Saudi national and an Indian resident died in the strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, a city in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province that is home to the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, according to the New York Times. Eight other people were wounded, the statement said, adding that airport was operating normally on Thursday.
In a separate incident, two people were killed and two others were wounded on Wednesday when a drone was intercepted over Aramco’s Shaybah oil field, also in the Eastern Province. Falling drone fragments sparked a fire in a contractor’s vehicle, killing a Filipino and a Nepali, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.
The Ansarallah’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said they had also targeted the Saudi Defense Ministry's headquarters building in the capital, Riyadh, an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and Abha International Airport in the south of the country.
The Ansarallah also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
The Ansarallah have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians and roiling energy markets.
The price of oil jumped about 3 percent on Thursday, with the global benchmark topping $112 a barrel, the highest level since mid-May.
Saudi Arabia announced a bombing campaign against the Ansarallah in support of its puppet government in Yemen, which has been at war with the Ansarallah since 2014. That was when the Ansarallah seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa — which they still hold.
A fragile truce in Yemen unraveled earlier this year. The war resurfaced after Saudi Arabia bombarded Sanaa airport and refused to lift the blockade of their territory.
As the fighting has spilled onto Saudi soil, the United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said in social media post on Wednesday night.
Washington had pulled many diplomatic staff out of the Middle East earlier this year after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. But it started sending some back in late August.
Then in September, the Ansarallah seized areas of strategic territory on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, gaining greater control over a crucial choke point for global trade.
The Red Sea has become an increasingly important route for Saudi oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway in the Persian Gulf, after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The Ansarallah’s attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers traversing the Red Sea have heaped further pressure on energy markets.
Saudi Arabia, under Mohammed bin Salman, seems adept at getting his country into trouble. In March 2015, when he was serving as defense minister, he ordered an attack on Yemen, expecting to restore the Saudi-backed Yemeni government within weeks and defeat Ansarallah. Instead, he opened Pandora’s box. More than a decade later, the consequences of that decision continue to haunt Riyadh, and it is difficult to imagine the Saudi capital remaining immune to the repercussions of the conflict.
He reopened old wounds when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport on July 13 in an attempt to prevent a plane carrying a Yemeni delegation from Tehran from landing. The delegation had participated in the funeral procession of Iranian Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated in a U.S.-Israeli air raid on his office and residence on February 28.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Tracing China's Long March through Britain's books, archives, memories
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:02:25 CST
00:02:25 KST

LONDON, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- In a reading room at the British Library, a blue stamp dated Jan. 27, 1937 appeared inside a book written by a British missionary who witnessed part of China's Long March.
Nearly 90 years later, the book offers a glimpse into how the extraordinary journey of the Chinese Red Army reached readers thousands of miles away.
As this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC), libraries and archives across Britain, along with the recollections of a writer who retraced the historic route, offer fresh perspectives on a journey that helped shape modern China.
EARLY ACCOUNTS OF THE LONG MARCH
At London's Marx Memorial Library, founded in 1933, two early publications shed light on how the Chinese Red Army was portrayed to British readers.
One is Edgar Snow's "Red Star Over China," published in Britain in 1937. Its orange-red cover bears the words "LEFT BOOK CLUB EDITION" and "NOT FOR SALE TO THE PUBLIC."
Snow's account introduced to Western readers the CPC, its leaders and the extraordinary hardships endured by Red Army soldiers during the Long March.
Another is Agnes Smedley's "China's Red Army Marches," published in London in 1936. Focusing on the Red Army's activities before its historic journey, the book describes villagers making shoes for soldiers and farmers delivering rice to support them.
One passage even reproduces a revolutionary song, complete with musical notation, preserving the voices of Chinese soldiers in a book published thousands of miles away.
The British Library also holds a 1937 edition of Snow's book bearing a stamp from the former India Office Library dated Oct. 30, 1937.
Contemporary British newspapers also reflected growing interest in the Red Army. On Oct. 19, 1937, the Edinburgh Evening News published a review of Snow's book, devoting a section specifically to the Long March.
Together, these publications offered British readers accounts of the soldiers' experiences, their daily lives and the circumstances surrounding their remarkable journey, bringing distant events in China into the view of the British public.
A BRITISH WITNESS AND THREE BOXES OF ARCHIVES
At the University of East Anglia in Norwich, eastern England, three archival boxes preserve the story of Alfred Bosshardt, a British missionary who accompanied the Red Army through parts of southwestern China.
Bosshardt's experiences were later recounted in "The Restraining Hand," published in Britain in 1936, making him one of the earliest Western eyewitnesses to record aspects of the Long March.
The university's collection contains hundreds of items, including correspondence, photographs, newspaper cuttings and audiovisual recordings. Many were collected by British journalist and writer Anthony Grey, who helped bring Bosshardt's story to a wider audience.
Despite their different beliefs, Bosshardt developed considerable respect for the Red Army soldiers, particularly for their discipline and determination.
He recalled that soldiers were instructed to respect villagers, pay for food and compensate residents for damaged property. During breaks from their arduous journey, young soldiers sang songs, wrestled and shared moments of laughter.
Bosshardt also admired Red Army commander Xiao Ke, with whom he later renewed contact. Their friendship continued for decades, forming a remarkable personal link between Britain and China.
RETRACING THE LONG MARCH
Nearly seven decades after the Long March, British-based Chinese writer Sun Shuyun spent 14 months retracing the odyssey. Traveling through remote villages, she interviewed surviving Red Army veterans and their families in an effort to understand the people behind the historical narrative.
For Sun, who studied history at the University of Oxford, the journey became one of the most unforgettable experiences of her life.
In east China's Jiangxi Province, she met an elderly woman who had persuaded her newlywed husband to join the Red Army. He never returned. Nearly 70 years later, she was still waiting for him.
In northwest China's Gansu Province, Sun interviewed a former female Red Army soldier whose life had been marked by poverty, captivity and hardship.
The elderly woman welcomed Sun into her home, wrapped her in thick blankets and prepared a meal unusually rich in salt. Her adopted daughter explained that salt had been extremely scarce during the Long March, leaving the woman with a lifelong habit of cherishing it.
Recalling these encounters at her London home, Sun was moved to tears.
She said the Long March demonstrated the CPC's organizational strength and leadership and laid an important foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
"The Long March is one of the most important events in modern Chinese history," she said, adding that its legacy continues to resonate with China's development today.
Sun stressed that the choices and sacrifices of ordinary people, whose experiences could sometimes be overlooked in historical narratives, deserve to be remembered and passed down to future generations.
From the hardships of revolutionary struggle to the achievements of modernization, the Chinese people have continued to undertake new journeys requiring courage and perseverance, she said.
The great spirit of the Long March "will always deserve to be remembered," Sun added. ■

SHIJIAZHUANG, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Ding Jianxin, a solo founder, sits at his workstation on a video call with a client. He is among a growing number of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered One Person Companies, or OPCs.
Located inside "Rainforest Space" at the Zhongguancun Science Park in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province, the workstation is designed for startups like Ding's.
The Chinese government issued an action plan in June for the growth of platform-economy enterprises, calling for accelerated cultivation of AI-powered OPCs. "Driven by both the deep penetration of AI technology and continued policy support, OPCs characterized by 'one person + AI' are growing from a marginal form of entrepreneurship into an important part of China's entrepreneurial ecosystem, marking a new way of working and employment that is increasingly gaining social recognition," the report said.
Flooded with sunlight, the 2,800-square-meter "Rainforest Space" features stylish co-working areas, shared meeting nooks, a roadshow hall and a cafe. On Floor 3, Building B1 of the tech park, OPC founders tend to their work at their workstations.
In June, Ding registered a creative software company. He has since rolled out several AI-powered products to help small and medium creators gauge the viral potential of AI-generated short drama scripts, flag compliance risks, adapt content for overseas markets and support production workflows.
Established in 2017, Xiongan New Area serves as a key hub for relieving Beijing of its non-capital functions and a core platform for the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.
The city has taken initial shape, with relocated projects settling in and innovation resources gathering rapidly. It pursues a dual strategy: attracting headquarters and subsidiaries of state-owned enterprises, and drawing agile, compact OPCs.
Fresh graduate Xue Yang also kicked off her entrepreneurial journey at the Rainforest Space, where she founded an intelligent technology company. The community helped her deploy AI tools and secure computing resources, and matched her with a tailored project.
