IMF sees $50–55 bln Ukraine gap for 2027–28, Russian assets key – Alternate Executive Director Rashkovan
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:47:49 EEST
23:47:49 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Ukraine's uncovered external financing needs for budget expenditures in 2027–2028 at $50 billion–$55 billion: $30 billion–$35 billion next year and another $20 billion in 2028. Instruments linked to frozen Russian assets are being considered among the key sources for covering these needs, Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternate Executive Director at the IMF, said.
"I am confident that Russian assets will remain our key issue both now and in the future. It seems to me that over the next two months, the range of options available to us for financing 2027 will lie somewhere between ERA-2 and Ukraine Support Loan-2," he said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12–18.
Rashkovan clarified that IMF assistance with financing would cover nonmilitary budget expenditures, while additional defense financing needs would remain. Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko estimates Ukraine's defense financing needs for next year at EUR 40 billion. That is why Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced Ukraine's total need for additional financing next year at EUR 70 billion during a European Council meeting in Brussels on October 14.
The IMF Alternate Executive Director said that Ukraine's international partners are currently more focused on covering financing needs for 2026–2027, although the Fund's Extended Fund Facility (EFF) with Ukraine runs through 2029, and there is an understanding that financing needs in 2028 will also be substantial.
He referred to the Ex-Post Assessment of the previous "wartime" EFF program for 2023–2025, which contained an important conclusion: even if the war ends, for example, in 2027, this does not mean that public finances will return to normal as early as 2028, partly because demobilization cannot happen immediately and social spending will need to increase to support veterans and their families.
"Therefore, even if the war ends in 2028, almost the same amount will be needed. Expenditures will begin to decline only later. This is the model the IMF is working with today... This figure will not come as a surprise to our partners," Rashkovan explained.
As for the main sources of financing other than frozen Russian assets, he pointed to the EU's multiannual budget for 2028–2034, which is being discussed by the European Council.
"European officials assure us that support for Ukraine will be included in it. The current draft allocates EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. We will see what the final structure of the document looks like after the political discussions within the EU. I think it should be agreed by the end of the year," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said, describing the current status of this funding source.
Regarding frozen Russian assets, Rashkovan recalled that most of them are held in Belgium at the international depository Euroclear. They are invested in various instruments of the European Central Bank and the National Bank of Belgium and generate income. In 2024, the G7 established the ERA mechanism, based on discounting future cash flows generated by the continued investment of these assets. Through this mechanism, Ukraine received $50 billion. These are nominally loans serviced using revenues from Russian assets, but for Ukraine they are effectively grants with no repayment obligations or conditions.
After the failure to introduce a EUR 140 billion reparations loan, which European countries lacked the courage to implement at the end of 2025, the EU developed the Ukraine Support Loan mechanism, worth EUR 90 billion for 2026–2027, to provide military and nonmilitary support to Ukraine, Rashkovan added. He clarified that this is also nonrepayable assistance to Ukraine, but it is financed by EU taxpayers.
"I think that over the next two months, discussions within the G7 will revolve around these two instruments (ERA-2 and Ukraine Support Loan-2). Another option would be to look for unused funds in European Union budget programs. I do not have full access to this information, but I am afraid that EUR 70 billion will not be available there," the expert said.
He explained that ERA-2 would again be a financial engineering instrument built around the valuation of future cash flows. While ERA covered a 30-year period, a longer-term model is now being considered, for example, one spanning 50 years. Last December, the European Council decided that the EU would not return Russia's assets until reparations had been paid, significantly reducing the risk associated with this mechanism, Rashkovan said.
According to him, the amount of assistance to Ukraine could also be increased by raising the expected return on investments of Russian assets from the current average of 2.8% annually to, for example, 4% annually, given that yields on U.S. and European government securities are currently around 5%.
"Finally, we know that the assets are not held exclusively at Euroclear. Around EUR 30 billion is held in private French banks. It would be worth provisionally factoring in these funds when developing the model as well," Ukraine's representative at the IMF added.
Summing up, he said that such planning and financial engineering could mobilize around $20 billion for Ukraine, but this would not solve all its problems, particularly given military spending.
"Ultimately, we will still have to turn to G7 finance ministers to cover those costs, because their countries are the ones financing them. (Therefore,) the second option is the Ukraine Support Loan," Rashkovan said.
In his view, it would be possible to increase the size of this instrument beyond the initial EUR 90 billion, the amount determined by the IMF last year.
"If the Fund had identified a need for EUR 140 billion, our partners would have looked for EUR 140 billion. Therefore, it is important now to agree on a common understanding of the total amount: $30–35 billion in nonmilitary needs plus EUR 40 billion in military expenditures, for a total of approximately EUR 70 billion. Accordingly, the ceiling for the Ukraine Support Loan needs to be increased. The instrument and its legal framework already exist; the only thing needed is to raise the lending limit," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said, outlining a possible course of events.
He clarified that in this case, the European Union would have to raise the funds on the market before providing them to Ukraine. At an interest rate of 4%–5%, this would cost approximately EUR 3 billion annually in interest, which European countries would like to cover through assistance from non-European G7 countries. In that case, the mechanism would be almost cost-free for both the European Union and Ukraine.
Among less realistic sources of financing, Rashkovan also mentioned the $5 billion frozen in the United States and the REPO Act (Rebuilding Economic Prosperity and Opportunity for Ukrainians Act), adopted in April 2024. The law allows the U.S. president to confiscate Russian sovereign assets under U.S. jurisdiction and direct them toward assistance to Ukraine.
"Unfortunately, it was not applied even under the Biden administration, and this has still not been done. That is why another initiative, called the PEACE Act, has emerged. It effectively requires the U.S. Treasury secretary, within 90 days after the law enters into force, to seize the relevant assets and transfer the funds to the Ukraine Support Fund. These funds could also be used to purchase defense equipment for Ukraine. The bill has not yet become law, but it is important that discussions on sanctions are continuing," the expert said, describing the current situation.
Another option he mentioned was a levy on Russian oil, similar to the one that existed for Iraq. It could also become a source of funding for the International Claims Commission, established in The Hague.
As for the confiscation of Russian assets, Rashkovan believes it may become possible in the future and that work on the issue should therefore continue.
"Some people propose returning Russia's assets as part of the price of peace. I categorically oppose this: the idea is fundamentally misguided... We know that Russia has no intention of stopping. Therefore, returning the assets would not be the price of peace for Russia, but a prize: it would simply say 'thank you' and carry on," Ukraine's representative said.

The Pentagon has released another batch of documents, videos, and images, marking the seventh disclosure in the US government’s effort to make Unidentified Flying Object (UFO) records public.
The files include reports of a mysterious black triangular object that three federal agents spotted near a secure US facility.
The object reportedly moved unusually fast, and thermal equipment could not detect its heat signature.
The release also includes a declassified report on alleged paranormal activity at Utah’s Skinwalker Ranch, historical UFO sightings from the 1940s and 1950s, and documents detailing how NASA and the Defence Department coordinated their handling of suspected fragments of space vehicles.
The latest disclosure follows six previous releases after US President Donald Trump signed an executive order earlier this year directing the government to make UFO records available to the public.
“Today, the Department of War is publishing the seventh release of declassified and historical Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) files as part of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE),” Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said.
He added that the Department “will release additional files on a rolling basis” and is actively working on the next release of UAP files.
Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena
These materials were compiled from several US government agencies, including the Pentagon, NASA, the CIA, the FBI, and the Department of Energy.
The Pentagon made the files available on its official UAP website.
Witnesses described silent, matte-black objects with no visible engines, lights or exhaust.
One account described an object covering roughly 1.5 miles in three seconds (1,800 miles per hour), while others reported low-altitude hovering and manoeuvres.
Some officials interviewed about the sightings suggested the US could still be years away from developing technology matching the capabilities described by military witnesses.
Friday’s release also includes previously classified accounts of cylindrical flying objects spotted over Saudi Arabia, Sweden and elsewhere during the 1960s and 1970s.
Many of these records are being made public for the first time.
The release also contains sighting reports and records of investigations into unexplained phenomena.
Some details remain redacted, and the material provides no definitive evidence of extraterrestrial origins.

Lewis Hamilton presses for ‘free Palestine’ at conference on F1 Africa return
Lewis Hamilton on Thursday called for a "Free Palestine" in comments made during a conference discussing Formula One’s return to Africa this week.
The 41-year-old British driver pushed for the race to return to Africa, despite the proposal garnering backlashing, stating it would create huge economic opportunities for the continent.
During the conference, he noted there were some reservations over Rwanda hosting the continent’s first Grand Prix in over three decades, but said he wanted to stay in racing in the next decade so he would be able to fulfil his dream of racing in an African Grand Prix.
When quizzed about if he had any other comments or thoughts, he said: "I guess I'll finish it off with, you know. I think we need to make sure we're pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there's a lot of peace that I'm hoping that some stage we get to".
The development comes after Formula One last week announced a 10-year agreement with Rwanda, with the race set to commence after the circuit has been built in the early 2030s.
He acknowledged that there were problems in Africa as well as all over the world, but defended the decision saying, “I think we really have to approach it with humility”.
“Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum,” he said.
"A lot of the problems they have there are still the results of colonialism and the West intervening, but if you see the people, you see so many designs that are out there today. Top brands come from Africa, and it’s got all the richest resources,” he continued.
He also stated that the culture across Africa is rich and having Formula One there would allow the continent to shine.
Conversations surrounding Rwanda hosting Formula One started in May 2024 when officials met leaders of the International Automobile Federation during the Monaco Grand Prix. Months later, Formula One President and CEO Stefano Domenicali confirmed that Rwanda submitted a proposal and discussions would be underway.
The decision has garnered opposition, with Congolese Foreign Affairs Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner arguing that the event could improve President Paul Kagame’s international image while conflict rages on.
This is not the first time Hamilton has called for a free Palestine. He has previously called for a ceasefire in Gaza amid Israel’s onslaught which has killed over 74,000 people. He has also used his social media platforms to shed light on the destruction in Gaza as a result of fierce Israeli bombardment.

jean prouvé’s 1944 demountable house becomes japanese tea pavilion in paris

jean prouvé’s 1944 demountable house becomes japanese tea pavilion in paris
presented in the garden of the hôtel de maisons, the 1944 prefabricated structure brings together postwar architectural experimentation and a new interpretation of japanese tea culture.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
galerie patrick seguin brings prouvé’s 6×6 house to paris
For this year’s Design Miami.Paris, Galerie Patrick Seguin presents Jean Prouvé’s 6×6 Demountable House (1944) in the garden of the Hôtel de Maisons, as part of Design at Large. Originally conceived as emergency housing for families displaced by World War II, the prefabricated structure reflects Prouvé’s approach to industrialized construction and combines a lightweight steel frame with standardized wooden panels. For the Paris presentation, the gallery reinterprets the interior of the residence as a space inspired by the chashitsu, the traditional Japanese tea pavilion, bringing Prouvé’s architectural principles into dialogue with Japanese culture.
a demountable house designed for postwar reconstruction
Prouvé developed the 6×6 Demountable House in response to an urgent housing shortage in France at the end of World War II. Commissioned to design temporary homes for displaced families in Lorraine and Franche-Comté, he sought a construction system that could be manufactured economically, assembled quickly, and dismantled for relocation when necessary. The house measures six by six meters, a compact footprint intended to accommodate three rooms. Its design allowed families to move in as soon as assembly was complete, without having to wait for permanent reconstruction to finish. The structure builds on his patented axial portal frame, which organizes the house around a bent steel skeleton. Standardized wooden panels fit into the frame, while a roof of bitumen-coated building paper completes the enclosure. With steel subject to strict quotas in postwar France, reserving the material for the primary structure responded to the practical constraints of reconstruction.
Prouvé designed the house to provide shelter quickly, but he also saw potential in the construction method beyond the immediate postwar crisis. The steel frame and wooden panels could be assembled and taken apart with ease, and he hoped the same approach would eventually be used to build permanent homes. At Design Miami.Paris, the presentation by Galerie Patrick Seguin offers an opportunity to revisit these ideas in the setting of the Hôtel de Maisons’s garden. A structure developed for postwar housing is brought into the context of a design event, while the new interior concept introduces another layer to its interpretation.
project info:
 name: 6×6 Demountable House
architect and designer: Jean Prouvé
year: 1944
presentation: Design Miami.Paris | @designmiami, Design at Large
gallery: Galerie Patrick Seguin | @galeriepatrickseguin
location: Hôtel de Maisons, Paris, France

What States Make of Military Exercises: Ulchi and Beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

Just before the South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise began in mid-August, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction in its scale. Describing the drills as “costly” and an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea – a state he termed “unthreatening and respectful” – Trump also criticized what he described as Seoul’s lack of support for U.S. operations against Iran.
Trump’s sudden decision raised concerns about South Korea-U.S. defense readiness, alliance reliability, and Washington’s wider commitment to Asia. Several analysts warned that reducing exercises could weaken deterrence and alliance coordination, while others questioned whether the move would secure reciprocal restraint from Pyongyang. Such concerns are understandable: joint military exercises are a visible manifestation of the South Korea-U.S. defense commitment, while North Korea routinely denounces them as rehearsals for war.
The reduction alone, however, does not carry a single, self-evident political meaning. U.S. commanders have since emphasized that other combined training continues and proposed changes to its frequency and geographic distribution. How audiences interpret these changes depends on the wider pattern of cooperation, established relationships, and political context.
Scale, Scope, and Strategic Meaning
Joint military exercises can serve two different but complementary strategic functions. They demonstrate capability and resolve to deter adversaries, but exercises also facilitate defense diplomacy. Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.
Our research suggests that an exercise’s scale and scope alone cannot reliably distinguish between these functions. Deterrence and defense diplomacy often generate the same observable characteristics, making it difficult to determine where one ends and the other begins simply by examining an exercise’s material features.
Larger and more complex exercises – featuring tens of thousands of troops, sophisticated command-and-control systems, live-fire maneuvers, and complex scenarios – can demonstrate greater warfighting capability and resolve to deter. At the same time, however, those same characteristics may instead reflect years of accumulated defense cooperation and deeper levels of trust and institutional integration between the participating militaries. Their material features reveal what militaries practice and provide evidence of their capabilities but cannot by themselves establish the political messages governments intend or how different audiences will interpret them. Rather, as a political signal, joint military exercises ultimately depend on what participating states and other audiences make of them.
Different audiences will not necessarily derive the same meaning from the same exercise. Washington might intend a reduction in Ulchi as restraint toward Pyongyang, while North Korea might interpret it as a concession, Seoul as uncertainty over U.S. commitment to the bilateral alliance, and Beijing as evidence of Washington’s transactional approach to alliance management. Established relationships and political contexts are therefore essential to interpreting an exercise’s strategic meaning.
Instead, established relationships and political contexts are more important in determining the strategic meaning of exercises than scale and scope alone. The history of Ulchi itself illustrates this.
Ulchi’s scale and scope have seldom increased in tandem with the danger from North Korea. This divergence is significant. If Ulchi’s scale simply tracked the North Korean military threat, as one would expect for greater deterrence, participation should have risen relatively consistently alongside Pyongyang’s expanding nuclear and missile capabilities. Instead, exercise participation has repeatedly risen and fallen according to changes in the diplomatic environment. Participation declined during periods associated with the Six-Party Talks and suspended altogether to facilitate diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Trump’s first term.
The scale of South Korean participation also reflects domestic politics. According to publicly available data, South Korean troop numbers were generally lower under the progressive administrations of Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, increased substantially under conservative presidents Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, and were again affected by diplomatic engagement under Moon Jae-in. These patterns are consistent with progressive administrations’ greater emphasis on creating diplomatic space for negotiations with the North and conservative administrations’ stronger emphasis on deterrence and alliance cohesion.
Trump’s decision should therefore be understood within this broader political context. Indeed, his own explanations identified several purposes for the same reduction: reducing costs, signaling restraint toward North Korea, and expressing dissatisfaction with Seoul over Iran. The reduction’s material features cannot establish which purpose predominates or how different audiences will interpret it.
Interpreting the Wider Exercise Program
Recent developments illustrate why Ulchi’s reduction should also be understood within the wider pattern of South Korea-U.S. military cooperation. In an interview with the Financial Times, U.S. Army Pacific commander General Ronald Clark emphasized both displaying military capabilities to influence adversaries’ calculations and strengthening military partnerships. His account illustrates how the two functions can reinforce one another: military partnerships help sustain the access and cooperation through which forces demonstrate capability and resolve.
South Korea-U.S. cooperation has continued despite the reduction in Ulchi. Eighth Army commander Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert clarified that other combined training continued, although some activities affected by Trump’s order were conducted by South Korean forces alone. Continued trilateral training through Freedom Edge and South Korea’s observer participation in Keen Sword also demonstrate different forms of military engagement. Observation offers opportunities for familiarity and relationship building without active participation in training. These activities do not cancel out Ulchi’s reduction, but they complicate its interpretation as a broader withdrawal from military cooperation.
Exercise design can also change in response to operational requirements. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson has proposed more frequent training and geographically dispersed operations, drawing lessons from Ukraine about the vulnerability of concentrated command posts. He suggested the possibility of expanding the scope of exercises from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province, while also adjusting the training schedule to include additional smaller-scale drills between the two large annual exercises, Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield. Frequency, geographic reach, and the concentration of forces need not change together. Thus, the size of a single exercise therefore provides an incomplete picture of the training program. Whether audiences interpret such changes as reinforcing alliance commitments or altering priorities depends on their political context.
Reducing Ulchi or cancelling a single amphibious exercise does not erase South Korea-U.S. warfighting capability. The institutional defense relationship between the two militaries established over decades – combined command structures, joint planning, interoperability, established procedures, and accumulated experience and “muscle memory” – remains in place. None of this is to suggest that exercises are irrelevant to preparedness; repeated reductions or cancellations over an extended period could eventually erode South Korea-U.S. interoperability and combined warfighting effectiveness. The effects, however, would be cumulative rather than instantaneous. A reduction or cancellation of a single iteration should not be conflated with the disappearance of capabilities built through decades of combined training.
Exercise scale and scope matter, but their strategic meaning is neither fixed nor self-evident. Rather than asking simply whether the United States is exercising more or less and with whom, the more pertinent questions are what particular exercises are intended to accomplish and how Seoul, Tokyo, Washington, Pyongyang, Beijing and other regional audiences interpret them. The deterrent or diplomatic value of an exercise ultimately lies not simply in how many troops participate, but in the political meaning that states attach to their participation – or absence.

Discussing grain initiatives without Russia is pointless, Global South nations agree — MFA

ROME, October 23. /TASS/. International partners within UN forums acknowledge that Black Sea grain initiatives are futile without Russia’s participation and the resolution of the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine, Kirill Logvinov, Director of the Department of International Organizations at the Russian Foreign Ministry, has told the media.
"Our partners from the Global South recognize that discussing any Black Sea Grain Initiative 2.0 without Russia’s participation and without addressing the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine is a dead end," he said after attending a meeting of the Committee on World Food Security at the Rome headquarters of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
Logvinov pointed out that the current situation in the Black Sea is a consequence of actions taken by Kiev, as well as the large-scale military and financial support that the Kiev regime receives from the West. "What is happening must be viewed in a broader historical context, rather than plucking individual events out of the overall picture to use them for yet another political campaign involving sweeping accusations against Russia," he noted.
The Russian Foreign Ministry hopes that the FAO is capable of providing an objective assessment; the organization "should not turn into a platform for issuing 'political verdicts' or become involved in any political games."
"Its task is to provide an objective assessment of the state of food systems and to foster international cooperation in the development of sustainable agriculture. Therefore, Russia has an interest in seeing the FAO remain guided by the goals and objectives enshrined in its founding documents, and in ensuring it acts impartially and objectively. Only through such an approach can the Organization remain effective," Logvinov concluded.
The Russian side holds Ukraine and the UN responsible for the collapse of the "grain deal" - which remained in effect until July 2023 - stating that they failed to fulfill their respective obligations. Meanwhile, Russia continues to meet its own commitments, accounting for 26% of global wheat exports alone and supplying agricultural products to 160 countries.
FAO assessment
As FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted during an event on the impact of the situation in the Black Sea on global food security - held as part of the World Food Forum - the challenges in the Black Sea region represent only one, and not necessarily the most significant, factor threatening food security. He pointed out that the observed price increases and instability are driven by geopolitical conflicts, funding cuts, and extreme weather events.
"In countries dependent on wheat from the Black Sea, there has been no deterioration in the food situation beyond average levels; however, a number of food-importing nations remain potentially vulnerable and require close monitoring," he said.
Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin explained that the Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports and export routes were a response to Ukraine’s attempts - beginning in the summer of this year - to target Russian oil refineries and vessels in the Black and Azov Seas. He emphasized that the Ukrainian armed forces of Ukraine had attempted to organize a naval blockade of the Black Sea coast, damaging over 100 Russian and foreign vessels.

Deadly France shooting a 'racist, probably Islamophobic' attack: mayor

Breadcrumb
Deadly France shooting a 'racist, probably Islamophobic' attack: mayor
A gunman firing from his car killed one person and wounded five -- including a 12-year-old girl shot eight times -- in the Paris suburbs Friday, with prosecutors investigating a potential "terrorist" act.
The man was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through the southwestern working-class towns of Trappes and neighbouring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh said.
Most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds and prosecutors are investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.
The 12-year-old girl shot eight times was "seriously wounded" but in a stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told AFP.
The alleged shooter -- a 39-year-old man, according to a source familiar with the case -- was arrested in nearby Coignieres.
Police found him in possession of a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades, according to a police source.
Prosecutors said they had opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
Rabeh said the man was firing sporadically from his car and that the person killed was "of African origin."
One of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of north African origin," he added.
It was "objectively a racist, probably Islamophobic attack," the mayor said, calling for national unity as the toll rose from an earlier count of four wounded.
Dainville said that two of the wounded in his town -- cleaners attending a school Friday morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire -- were of African origin.
Laurent Nunez, France's interior minister, travelled to the two affected towns. He called the shooting "clearly a terrorist crime."
Bursts of gunfire
A police source told AFP that the man had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 am (0830 GMT).
Adel, a resident of Trappes, about 20 kilometres (13 miles) west of Paris, said his "heart was broken" as he learned the victims might have been targeted for their race.
"I'm north African and it's frightening for everyone who has the same background," the 50-year-old told AFP.
Samy, another resident, told AFP he had seen a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a grey Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."
President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
The shooting came with France on edge following last weekend's riots on the sidelines of mass protests over the cost of living, some of the worst street violence in recent years.
More protests are expected this weekend, but police will be out in force after a week of overnight curfews put in place in cities throughout the country.

Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs "fluid" skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs “fluid” skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
US studio Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture has unveiled its latest skyscraper for Miami, designed to display “quiet refinement” on a slender site on the city’s waterfront.
Called Lilli, the residential skyscraper development is the latest in Miami from Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture (AS+GG). The studio is known for designing some of the world’s tallest buildings, including the world’s upcoming tallest skyscraper, the Jeddah Tower.
At 636 feet tall (193 metres), Lilli is planned for a narrow site in Miami’s Edgewater neighbourhood.
The luxury skyscraper will feature rounded edges and will have terraces on the water-facing side, with larger patios running up the opposite face.
Its design is characterised by rounded edges and large spans of glass interrupted by metallic floor plates.
“Our vision is for Lilli’s interior design to feel inseparable from its architecture,” said AS+GG design partner Juan Betancur.
“The fluidity of the building carries through the interior spaces, while a restrained palette of natural materials allows light, landscape, and views of Biscayne Bay to become part of the experience.”
“The result is a sense of quiet refinement that feels distinctly connected to its waterfront setting.”
The skyscraper will house 117 residences of varying sizes, spread across its 53 storeys, as well as amenities including lounges, pools and spas.
The ground floor will have a lobby for residents with large metallic columns and minimalist detailing.
At the top of the skyscraper, a pool will sit on the edge of a terrace underneath a bulkhead with the same reflective metal treatment seen elsewhere in the exterior.
Lilli is the latest in a series of residential skyscrapers being designed by the studio, which recently completed a “yacht-inspired” building in the city.
Residential skyscraper development has proceeded at a steady pace in Miami, with Bugatti recently unveiling its first branded skyscraper in the city.
The images are by Darcstudio.

Kyiv needs EUR 1.5 bln for winter - energy expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:27:49 EEST
23:27:49 KST

Kyiv has spent more than UAH 16 billion on strengthening its energy security since the start of 2026, compared with UAH 2 billion last year, and plans to spend another UAH 4.5-5 billion by year-end, Managing Director of the Energy Industry Research Center Oleksandr Kharchenko has said.
However, the city needs a further EUR 1.5 billion to complete the necessary work, Kharchenko said at a discussion hosted by Interfax-Ukraine on Friday.
"This is effectively a tenfold increase in investment, specifically in security measures. This includes protecting high-voltage substations and providing backup power for core sewage and heating systems," he said.
The preparations have been funded mainly from the city budget, with the central government accounting for only about 10%, Kharchenko said.
"The national budget is not in very good shape, and payments through Treasury accounts were blocked for more than a month. This hit all local authorities hard, including their preparations for winter," he said.
As a result, some equipment that cities had planned to install by November or December will be commissioned later because of the four-week pause.
Kharchenko said Kyiv's entire internal generating capacity was physically destroyed in January 2026. Before that, the city had about 1.3 gigawatts of generating capacity, while electricity demand reaches about 2 GW at temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius and is around 1.2 GW in milder weather.
Without in-city generation, the metro and water utility pumping stations switch to backup power, limiting their ability to provide full services, he said.
Kharchenko said the city had protected key systems against major technological failures. However, maintaining water circulation and filling reservoirs does not necessarily ensure adequate pressure in elevated districts such as Pechersk. That requires the main power supply lines serving water utility facilities to remain operational, he said.
"Some inconvenience this winter is almost inevitable," Kharchenko said.
Most cities cannot complete energy security projects in a single seven- to eight-month season because of engineering and regulatory requirements. Such projects take two to three years, he said.
Ukraine as a whole may need UAH 250-300 billion annually for at least another two years to strengthen its energy security, Kharchenko said.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia enforces strict requirements for the security and resilience of the country's banking and payment infrastructure, and all necessary measures are being taken to protect it, Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina told a press conference following the regulator's board meeting on monetary policy.

"This requires a concentrated effort, constant modernization, and technological improvements; it forces us to switch to three-shift operations and relocate production, particularly to underground workshops. We are modernizing not only our countermeasures against technical reconnaissance but also our electronic intelligence capabilities: direction-finding equipment, new high-frequency amplifiers, and transmitters. When used correctly, they disrupt network communications and blind attack systems," Poroshenko said.

In March 2025, Poroshenko announced a contract with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, and on June 29 of that year, he announced the start of cooperation with the command of the Ukrainian Ground Forces regarding the supply of these systems to the military. As reported, following a massive Russian strike on Kyiv on the night of Thursday, October 22, damage was recorded in six of the capital's ten administrative districts. One fatality and 24 injuries were reported, 16 of whom were hospitalized.
According to the Air Force, Russian occupiers launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine overnight, using Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 attack UAVs and decoy drones. Kyiv was the main target of the attack. As of 09:00, air defenses had shot down and neutralized 181 enemy UAVs (including 87 jet-powered ones), but strikes were recorded at 32 locations, and debris was found at eight locations. Israeli elections: Arab voters weigh participation against abstention in bid to oust Netanyahu

23:21:49 KST

Amid fears over hardline Israeli policies, Palestinian citizens of Israel see the upcoming Israeli elections as a chance for change, with calls for higher Arab turnout to prevent incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government, Anadolu reports.
In a series of field interviews conducted by Anadolu on the streets of various Arab cities and towns in Israel, citizens emphasized that participating in this election is particularly crucial, given the “worsening racism and marginalization” against them.
While some plan to vote for the first time in hopes of bringing about political change, others continue to abstain, questioning whether elections can alter their circumstances and arguing that successive governments have failed to address their demands.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many say they have faced discrimination for years, but view the current government as a more dangerous phase, strengthening their desire to replace it through the ballot box.
Polls suggest Arab parties could win around 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Arab politicians hope higher turnout will weaken the chances of small right-wing parties seeking to support Netanyahu.
Calls for participation, change
Palestinian Imad Bashnaq said the upcoming election was “decisive and extremely important,” particularly for Arab society.
He argued that the rise in racism and fascism since Oct. 7, 2023, had made conditions intolerable.
“I have always maintained that we — as Arabic speakers — are the only ones capable of bringing about change in the Middle East, not just here within this country,” Bashnaq said, arguing that “a few madmen” have taken control of the government and now seek to dictate the course of an entire region.
“We are the original rightful owners, and there is no dispute about that.
“But we are a minority in a state, and this state is a reality we have to deal with,” he added.
OPINION: Israel’s election: The Arab vote and Netanyahu’s politics of exclusion
‘Every vote makes difference’
Areen Ghanayem said she would vote for the second time, maintaining that “every vote makes a difference.”
She said Arab society needed broad participation given the problems it faces and what she described as the government’s failure to pay sufficient attention to its concerns.
“We need to have a voice and someone who speaks on our behalf and demands the rights that should be ours,” she said.
Ghanayem expressed concern that the current government could return to power, saying it marginalized Arab society.
Citizens, she added, did not want to feel excluded from political life but sought to assert their presence and ability to influence decisions.
Occupier attacks
Mohammed Ahmad Abboud said he would take part in the upcoming election, as he had in the past, with the aim of “removing the racist government.”
He said the current election differed from previous ones because of what he described as “escalating violations,” pointing to Israeli occupiers’ attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Abboud also voiced concern over statements by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding the “Judaization” of the Negev and the Galilee — regions located in the south and north of Israel, respectively.
Occupier attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The attacks have included the killing of Palestinians, the burning of homes, vehicles, and mosques, the destruction of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their land, and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities.
These attacks have coincided with Israeli military operations involving arrests, the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures, and the expansion of illegal settlements.
Between hope and despair
In the northern city of Acre, a resident known as “Jojo” urged Arab citizens to participate in the election, arguing that voting was necessary to bring about change.
“We must vote to bring about change — real change,” he said, expressing optimism that the upcoming election could produce better results.
READ: Racism controversy erupts in Israeli election campaign after broadcaster calls Eisenkot a ‘monkey’
Separately, Saeed Abu Sultan, also from Acre, said that many years of participating in elections have not brought about any change in the reality faced by citizens.
“Some people might be able to make a difference, but as for us, we’ve grown accustomed to things as they are. We haven’t felt any change for 30 years,” Abu Sultan added.
Arab voter turnout expected to rise
Experts expect Palestinian citizens’ participation in the upcoming election to increase compared with the 2022 vote.
Experts and politicians estimate turnout among Palestinian citizens could reach 60% to 61%, up from 53% in 2022, while Arab parties hope participation will rise even further.
Arab politicians say higher turnout could alter the balance of power and reduce the chances of small Israeli right-wing parties crossing the electoral threshold and entering parliament, potentially weakening Netanyahu’s ability to form a government.
The Joint List, comprising the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the Arab Movement for Change, and the Balad party, is contesting the election under the leadership of Yousef Jabareen. Polls project it could win nine seats.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is also running, with projections suggesting it could win between five and six seats.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, to choose the 120 members of the Knesset, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing primarily against the Jewish opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot.
The election comes as Netanyahu’s bloc has been losing ground in opinion polls.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Cooperation between the Jewish opposition and Arab parties could prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
However, most opposition leaders reject such cooperation, while Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far also ruled out alliances with Arab parties.
Arab lawmakers have outlined conditions for supporting any government, including ending wars, advancing a political process with the Palestinians, and ending discrimination against Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Karakoram 2026: Inside China-Pakistan Joint Military Training in Xinjiang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:17:00 UTC
23:17:00 KST

On October 14, China and Pakistan began joint military training known as Karakoram 2026. According to official sources, the training’s opening ceremony was held in Korla city, Xinjiang, China. The main objective of this training is to focus on joint counterterrorism operations in high-altitude areas, according to China’s Ministry of National Defense.
The nine-day exercise encompassed a range of operational and tactical training activities that are significant not only for bilateral military cooperation but also in the context of a changing regional security environment.
Bilateral military exercises between Pakistan and China are a well-established and recurring feature of their defense cooperation. The two countries conducted the Sea Guardian IV naval exercise earlier this year to enhance interoperability and maritime cooperation. Joint counterterrorism drills are also a constant feature of their defense cooperation, with the previous example being Warrior IX held in December 2025.
Karakoram 2026 particularly focused on joint counterterrorism in high-altitude areas, with “skills training in UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, and joint command and live-force exercises,” according to a Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson.
China Central Television’s military channel said that China provided all the equipment, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, and both unmanned and anti-unmanned systems. The use of Chinese equipment and subsequent Pakistani familiarization with equipment could boost the likelihood of future Pakistani procurement.
However, the most notable feature of Karakoram 2026 is that this is the first time both countries are moving away from counterterrorism training by specialized units to regular army forces. This development will further strengthen defense cooperation and reinforce the broader all-weather strategic partnership between Pakistan and China. The main aim of this is to increase interoperability and joint cooperation on terrorism-related issues.
Karakoram 2026 is a reflection of broader convergence between China and Pakistan over shared security concerns in the region. Their respective threat perceptions may not be identical, but they have a shared interest in preventing terrorist organizations from exploiting territorial vulnerabilities. Beijing continues to have concerns about the potential for attacks in China, while Chinese nationals operating in Afghanistan and Pakistan have faced attacks on occasion. Joint counterterrorism training provides an institutional mechanism to translate these shared concerns into practical military cooperation.
One key component of these exercises was UAV operations. The motivation is obvious considering the emergence of drone warfare in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, especially the use of UAVs by terrorist outfits. Training in this domain will increase situational awareness while simultaneously supporting surveillance operations. At the same time, mobile target detection and engagement will strengthen coordination under dynamic battlefield conditions.
Long-range sniping and live-force exercises further test tactical proficiency, decision-making, and interoperability. For participating forces, this exercise would be helpful in coordinating response and improving communication during complex operations.
Looking at all the capabilities involved in Karakoram 2026, it is evident that the exercises were specially designed in relevance to the difficult terrain of northern Pakistan and the bordering Chinese region of Xinjiang. The China-Pakistan border region has difficult, mountainous terrain with extreme weather conditions complicating security operations. However, one should not perceive these exercises as evidence of China and Pakistan preparing for a specific operation in the region. Rather, Karakoram 2026 is significant mainly due to improved preparedness for shared counterterrorism contingencies and strengthening military-to-military familiarity.
Another major dimension setting the scene for these exercises is the fraught security environment between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which has complicated Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts. Islamabad has repeatedly raised concerns about the presence of Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants on Afghan territory and their ability to conduct cross-border attacks. For Pakistan, the recent surge in drone attacks especially by the militants across the border raises another challenge that needs to be addressed.
A 2026 report by the U.N. Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team documented escalating cross-border attacks involving Pakistan and Afghanistan and reported continued support for the TTP by Afghanistan’s de facto Taliban government. In this context, joint training in drone operations may help Pakistan improve both surveillance and defense. The value of such experience will greatly depend on whether the units and police forces bearing the brunt of these attacks, received practical training in counterdrone defense.
The biggest implication of Karakoram 2026, however, is not the specific training received; it is the institutionalization of cooperation. With air, naval, and now army training exercises, China and Pakistan have developed a framework covering all three services. Pakistan used Chinese platforms during the May 2025 conflict with India, and army-level interoperability is a natural and logical next step in defense cooperation.
Karakoram 2026 is not merely a military training but a broader reflection of evolving security priorities of China and Pakistan. With the resurgence of terrorist attacks, counterterrorism cooperation sits at the forefront of Islamabad’s national security concerns. On the other hand, Beijing remains heavily invested in Pakistan under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and the security of Chinese nationals in Pakistan remains an important dimension of bilateral relations.
The deteriorating security environment in the region thus reinforces the importance of China-Pakistan military cooperation. The UAV-related training, coordination in command, and realistic field exercises at Karakoram 2026 can be understood against the broader need to improve situational awareness, tactical coordination, and responsiveness to emerging threats.
However, the effectiveness of military training cannot be measured solely by the completion of an exercise. Its lasting value will depend on the extent to which the participating forces incorporate lessons from joint training into their operational practices and adapt to emerging security challenges.

Hamilton made the remarks while discussing Formula 1’s planned return to Africa and concerns surrounding Rwanda, which is expected to host a Grand Prix on a purpose-built circuit in the early 2030s.
The 41-year-old said holding a race in the country did not mean ignoring events elsewhere in Africa.

He described Africa as a continent with rich cultures, resources and people whose stories deserved greater international attention.
Hamilton also criticized the limited teaching of African history in British schools, arguing that many of the continent’s present-day difficulties remained connected to colonialism and Western intervention.
“Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum,” he said.

2026-10-23
22:10:54 CST
23:10:54 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message to the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) on Friday.
The world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing, Xi said.
"I have put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world," he said.
China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, pool strength through confidence-building and tackle challenges through cooperation, Xi said.
He called for efforts to promote the implementation of the GGI to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world of turbulence and transformation, and jointly move toward a community with a shared future for humanity.
The forum opened on the same day in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province. Hosted by the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, it is themed "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World." ■

People visit the China Great Wall Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 23, 2026.
The renovated China Great Wall Museum held its opening ceremony on Friday at the foot of the Badaling section of the Great Wall in Beijing.
With a construction area of about 16,000 square meters, the museum displays exhibits on the Great Wall's history, culture and spirit. Its permanent exhibition features more than 700 artifacts and sets of artifacts from 24 museums across China, highlighting the Great Wall's role as a symbol of Chinese civilization and national unity.

More than 1,000 personnel from the public security forces, national defence forces and youth volunteer groups will be deployed in Lao capital Vientiane to ensure public safety and maintain order during the festival.
Officials will implement round-the-clock duty rosters to maintain public order, ensure smooth traffic flow, prevent congestion and respond promptly to emergencies. The measures aim to ensure public safety, minimize traffic disruptions and protect residents and visitors throughout the festivities. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government announced on Friday that construction has begun on a new laboratory wing at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) to strengthen the country's ability to detect and respond to emerging disease threats.
The facility, operated by Australia's national science agency CSIRO in Geelong, Victoria, plays a key role in protecting human and animal health, agriculture and the economy from infectious diseases.
In a joint statement, the government said the upgrade would enhance Australia's scientific and biosecurity capabilities, including its response to threats such as H5 avian influenza.
Minister for Science Tim Ayres said the bird flu outbreak demonstrated the importance of having the expertise and facilities needed to detect and respond quickly to serious disease threats.
The project will be delivered in two stages to ensure the center's diagnostic and research operations continue during construction.
The first stage is expected to be completed in 2029, allowing selected activities to move into the new laboratory wing before refurbishment of existing facilities begins.
The government said it had allocated an additional 387.4 million Australian dollars (about 252 million U.S. dollars) to CSIRO in its latest budget, on top of the agency's annual funding of nearly 1 billion Australian dollars. ■

All Boxers built to one standard, says minister
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:00:37 BST
23:00:37 KST

All six hundred and twenty three Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard, which has made variant and build configuration effectively the same thing.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for an updated breakdown of the 623 vehicles by variant, build configuration and role, referring back to an answer given in June 2021.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave on 18 December 2025 to Question 100025, which set out the number of Mechanised Infantry Vehicle (MIV) Boxers contracted for by variant. This information remains extant. As the Boxer programme has developed, build configuration and variant have become effectively interchangeable, with all 623 MIV Boxer vehicles being delivered to a common build standard. Consequently, a separate breakdown by build configuration is no longer relevant.
“The Department keeps under review its approach to the disclosure of information, taking account of a range of factors. An updated breakdown by role could pose a risk to operational security and, therefore, I am unable to provide this information.”
A common build standard means the hulls and drive modules come off the line identically whatever mission module they eventually carry, which is the design logic of the vehicle: the mission module can be lifted off and another fitted. Ministers confirmed earlier this month that Boxers will be able to recover one another in the field and that the vehicle has been built with the electrical and physical margin to take a remote weapon station later.
Boxer is being built in Britain by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and Stockton-on-Tees, with WFEL at Stockport, under contracts covering the 623 vehicles for the British Army.

US warns Houthi attacks could spread, updates travel advisories for Israel and Gulf states

The United States updated travel advisories across the Middle East on Friday, warning of the growing threat of attacks by Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis against countries across the region. The warnings cover Israel, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Lebanon, amid concerns that the escalation could spread beyond Saudi territory.
The State Department cited the "threat of increased Iranian-supported Houthi regional aggression" following a series of missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports, energy facilities and other infrastructure. Recent strikes have killed civilians and disrupted air travel, raising concerns about the safety of international travelers and American personnel.
The updated advisories did not change the countries' formal travel-risk levels. Israel, Qatar and the UAE remain at Level 3, advising Americans to reconsider travel, while Iraq and Lebanon remain at Level 4, the highest warning, advising against all travel. The revisions instead emphasize the heightened regional threat and the possibility of sudden disruptions to commercial flights.
In Israel, American authorities warned that regional tensions could escalate without warning, potentially affecting transportation and security conditions. Similar warnings were issued for Gulf states, where travelers were advised to remain vigilant, monitor local security announcements and prepare contingency plans.
The heightened alert comes as Washington reduces its diplomatic presence in parts of the region. On October 21, the State Department ordered nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, while staffing adjustments have also been reported at American diplomatic missions in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE.
The developments follow an intensifying Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia and mounting tensions between Washington and Tehran, raising fears that further attacks could trigger a broader regional confrontation.

Turkey's new deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya is exacerbating issues with Greece and the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

Greece protests Turkey-Libya deal on Mediterranean maritime corridor
October 24, 2026
On Tuesday, the parliament of Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey to establish a direct maritime economic corridor between the countries.
Turkey had agreed on the corridor with the UN-recognized Government of National Accord in western Libya in 2019. However, the agreement faced opposition from the rival Libyan government in the country's east. Now, though, the eastern parliament has reversed its previous opposition.
The decision, which was welcomed by Turkey's Foreign Ministry, is likely to contribute to tensions with other countries in the eastern Mediterranean — especially Greece .
'Null and void'
The agreement establishes a direct maritime corridor between the southern coast of Turkey and the northern coast of Libya. Large oil and gas deposits have recently been discovered in the region in question — estimates suggest that natural gas reserves worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie beneath the seabed. Turkey and Libya aim to secure their economic rights to these raw materials and are seeking to jointly exploit the resources.
The planned corridor disregards Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes. Greece's government insists that it possesses a comprehensive exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, around these islands and has already announced its opposition to the accord.
In a post on X, the Foreign Ministry announced that Greece firmly rejects the agreement and has the support of the European Union in doing so. "The European Union has described the Turkish-Libyan memorandum as null and void, stressing that it violates the sovereign rights of third states and is not consistent with the Law of the Sea," the ministry posted.
Similar wording came straight from Brussels. "I raised yesterday's Libyan vote on a maritime MoU with Türkiye and stressed that it infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states," Kaja Kallas, the European Union high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, posted on X.
International maritime law
Whose claims are legitimate in the eastern Mediterranean is the central point of contention. Greece primarily cites the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS. According to Article 121 of the convention, inhabited islands that "support an economic life of their own” have the same rights to an EEZ as the mainland. This applies to Crete, Rhodes and Lesbos.
Athens cites precedents such as a 2022 ruling by the International Court of Justicethat found that Colombia had violated the sovereign rights of Nicaragua by authorizing fishing activities in the Central American country's EEZ. The ICJ found that when interests overlap a fair demarcation must be reached that takes coastlines, geographical conditions and the implications of a potential boundary into account.
Turkey's government argues that the geography of the Mediterranean plays a special role: If every small Greek island off the coast of Turkey and Cyprus were granted a full EEZ, Turkey would be largely cut off from access to the open sea. This, the government argues, must be given greater consideration when demarcating the boundary.
Unlike Greece, Turkey has never signed UNCLOS. Therefore, it does not agree to have the dispute heard by a UN arbitration tribunal. Moreover, even international experts on the law of the sea disagree on what a "fair division” might look like in this specific case.
Turkey and Libya
When Turkey pushed for the agreement in 2019, a brutal civil war was still raging in Libya. At that time, Turkey intervened militarily in the west to support the government in Tripoli, thereby repelling the offensive by eastern Libyan General Khalifa Hifter.
Since then, the relationship has changed fundamentally: A successful charm offensive by Turkey's government appears to have led to a political rapprochement with Hifter and his camp. Turkey's government now maintains mutually advantageous relations with both parts of Libya. In addition to the countries' plan to develop energy resources in the Mediterranean together, Turkish construction companies have secured contracts worth billions in recent years for Libya's reconstruction. Furthermore, the Turkish state-owned oil company TPAO and the Libyan National Oil Corporation are already working on joint plans for seismic surveys off of Libya's coast.
Turkey's government has established itself as a new military partner for Hifter's forces, supplying weapons and offering training programs. In doing so, Turkey is pushing back against the influence of Egypt and Russia in eastern Libya and strengthening its role as a geopolitical player in the region.
With the agreement now approved in the regional parliament, eastern Libya also aims to secure its share of the lucrative natural resources. This could give Hifter greater international influence in the future. Disputes in the eastern Mediterranean are likely to escalate further as a result of the agreement — particularly once Turkey and Libya begin extracting oil and gas from the disputed maritime area.
The agreement also jeopardizes a major project that is still in the planning stages: the EastMed pipeline, which is intended to transport natural gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece, thereby making an important contribution to energy security in the European Union. However, the corridor established by Turkey and Libya cuts across the planned route of the pipeline. Turkey has also argued that projects involving cables or pipelines on its claimed continental shelf require its consent.
In the long term, this could lead to a division of the eastern Mediterranean region into two competing energy and defense blocs: The Turkey-Libya axis might be countered by an EU-supported alliance of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel.
This article was originally published in German.

US lawmakers rush to derail Trump’s Russian diesel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US lawmakers rush to derail Trump’s Russian diesel deal
A number of American lawmakers are gearing up to jeopardize the Trump administration’s deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel through April. They are seeking action against US companies involved in the trade and planning to block the Treasury from issuing such a waiver in the future.
US President Donald Trump announced the deal earlier this month, weeks ahead of the impending November midterm elections. Under the waiver, Moscow agreed to immediately put 300,000 tons of diesel into the market, followed by larger quantities later on. The deal was reached as US diesel prices hit a record high, surging above $6.50 per gallon in September, with prices in parts of California exceeding $8.
The disruption of global energy markets, caused by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict, has resulted in rising gas prices in the US, further denting the positions of Republicans ahead of the vote. Diesel is the key fuel type extensively used in agriculture and freight; its price affects the cost of virtually all goods, resulting in further cost-of-living issues. Rural communities, smalltime farmers, and truckers are particularly vulnerable to diesel prices spikes.
Senate Democrats are now seeking to investigate the diesel deal, the Washington Post reported on Thursday, citing an unnamed Senate Democratic aide. According to the aide, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has requested companies involved in the scheme to preserve documents ahead of a possible probe by the panel.
“[The companies] should have liability concerns as well as investigative concerns,” the aide told WaPo.
Further action against the diesel deal has been taken by Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1), an outspoken hawk, Ukraine backer, and proponent of sanctions against Russia. The proposed legislation, titled the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, would effectively block Russian oil imports for good.
The bill would nullify the standing Russian oil waiver, “immediately rendering General License 135 ineffective and prohibiting future waivers or general licenses authorizing the importation of Russian energy products,” as well as strip the Treasury from the ability to expend funds “on agreements that violate the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022,” the legislation that sanctioned Russian energy products, including diesel, in the first place.
Apart from the energy part, the bill also would “reinforce critical intelligence support for Ukraine,” obliging spy agencies to cooperate with Kiev and to “notify congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.”

The psychology behind Taylor Swift’s billion-dollar media empire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

The intense, one-sided connections fans feel toward pop star Taylor Swift and their fear of missing out on shared cultural moments strongly predict whether they will attend her concerts and watch her films. These predictive links highlight how the psychological need for social belonging drives large-scale consumer behavior, according to a recent study published in Psychology of Popular Media.
A parasocial relationship occurs when an audience member develops a one-sided bond with a media figure, such as a musician, actor, or internet personality. While the celebrity is unaware of the individual fan, the fan experiences genuine emotions and reactions that mimic real-life friendships.
Taylor Swift has cultivated an exceptionally robust parasocial dynamic with her audience over her career. By interacting with followers online and weaving personal details into her music, she has built an environment where fans feel they truly know her. When her Eras Tour launched, it shattered records, selling over two million tickets in a single day. The researchers noted that Swift used the resulting ticketing challenges to align herself with her fans, strengthening their perceived bond.
Such pervasive cultural conversation often triggers a phenomenon known as the fear of missing out, commonly referred to as FoMO. Researchers divide this concept into two distinct categories. Trait fear of missing out is a long-standing personality characteristic where a person generally worries that others are having rewarding experiences without them. State fear of missing out is a temporary, situation-specific anxiety in response to a particular event.
The researchers anchored their investigation in Self-Determination Theory. This psychological framework suggests that human beings are motivated by a fundamental need for relatedness, or the desire to feel connected to others. In the context of entertainment, people might consume specific media to satisfy this need, either by bonding with a celebrity or by joining a community of fellow fans.
Lindsey Conlin Maxwell and Caroline Neese of the University of Southern Mississippi, along with Alec C. Tefertiller of Baylor University, designed the study to see how these psychological elements influenced audience behavior. They used Swift and her wildly popular Eras Tour as an ideal testing ground. The team aimed to determine if long-term personality traits could predict parasocial bonds and if those bonds predicted purchasing tickets for concerts and movies.
To capture these emotions at their peak, the researchers conducted a national survey during the opening weekend of the concert film, “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour,” in October 2023. They recruited 303 adults in the United States using an online task platform. The respondents answered questions designed to measure their baseline personality traits, their current feelings about the movie release, and their perceived relationship with the pop star.
The survey asked participants to rate their agreement with statements about missing out on rewarding experiences in general, capturing their trait-level anxieties. It also asked specific questions about whether they feared others would enjoy watching the concert film more than them, measuring their temporary state of anxiety. Additionally, the questionnaire evaluated the depth of their parasocial relationship with Swift and recorded their actual behaviors regarding concert and movie attendance.
The data revealed that an individual’s general fear of missing out was a strong predictor of their parasocial relationship with Swift. The researchers noted that this long-standing personality trait explained roughly one-third of the variations in how strongly people felt connected to the singer. People who routinely worry about being left out of social experiences appear highly motivated to build imaginary bonds with media figures to alleviate that apprehension.
Both the personality trait and the parasocial relationship predicted concert-related behaviors. As scores on the parasocial relationship scale increased, respondents were nearly twice as likely to have attempted to buy Eras Tour tickets. They were also substantially more likely to have actually attended one of the live stadium shows.
Similar patterns emerged for the concert film. High levels of baseline anxiety about missing out, as well as a strong perceived relationship with Swift, predicted whether someone had already seen the movie during its opening weekend. These factors also predicted whether a person intended to see the film in theaters later or watch it once it became available on streaming platforms.
One of the most notable results involved temporary, event-specific anxiety. The researchers tested whether attending the live concert satisfied fans to the point of reducing their anxiety about the movie release. The data showed the exact opposite pattern.
People who had already attended the live Eras Tour experienced higher levels of temporary anxiety about missing out on the movie than those who had not attended the concert. Attending the concert did not quench the desire to engage with the media event. Going to the live show actually increased the likelihood that someone wanted to see the theatrical release.
The researchers suggest that a parasocial relationship can become so potent that individuals seek repeated positive experiences with the celebrity to maintain the bond. Because fans experience a strong sense of relatedness when participating in these events, the desire to rejoin the community and relive the excitement remains high. The shared euphoria among thousands of fans, known as collective effervescence, likely fuels this ongoing demand.
The attempt to replicate the concert experience inside movie theaters capitalized on this collective effervescence. By trading friendship bracelets and singing together in theaters, fans who could not attend the live shows found a way to participate in the cultural phenomenon. This shared environment allowed audiences to maintain their parasocial relationship with the singer while simultaneously relieving their anxieties about missing out.
While the study provides a detailed look at consumer motivations, it carries a few limitations. The participants were drawn from a convenience sample, and they were allowed to self-select into a survey they knew was about Taylor Swift. As a result, roughly two-thirds of the respondents identified as fans, and the demographic makeup was predominantly female and white, which could affect how well the results apply to the broader population.
The research relied on self-reported survey data, which is useful for identifying predictive links but cannot definitively prove cause and effect. It remains possible that other unmeasured variables influence both the psychological traits and the purchasing habits of the respondents.
Future investigations could explore how fans develop interpersonal relationships with one another based on their mutual parasocial connections to a single celebrity. The researchers also recommend looking closer at how social media amplifies the fear of missing out during major entertainment events. Measuring the direct impact of shared euphoric experiences could further explain why people are so driven to participate in massive cultural moments.
The study, ““It’s You and Me, There’s Nothing Like This”: Parasocial Relationships, Fear of Missing Out, and How Fans Consume the Products in Taylor Swift’s Media Empire,” was authored by Lindsey Conlin Maxwell, Alec C. Tefertiller, and Caroline Neese.

RML’s 666-bed super speciality block gets fire safety clearance, set to boost critical care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:58:29 UTC
22:58:29 KST

The fire safety clearance removes a key hurdle to commissioning the facility, which is expected to expand the hospital’s capacity to handle complex cases and provide critical care.
NEW DELHI: The long-awaited 666-bed super speciality block at Dr Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital has secured fire safety clearance, bringing the Rs 482-crore facility a step closer to becoming operational and expanding access to specialised treatment at the Central government-run hospital.The 11-storey block will add 666 beds to the hospital’s existing capacity of 1,538, taking the total to 2,204. It will house 18 operation theatres, 99 intensive care unit (ICU) beds, 196 high dependency unit (HDU) beds and three catheterisation laboratories.
The facility will strengthen treatment in oncology, oncosurgery, hepatology, gastrointestinal surgery and liver transplantation. It will also have two linear accelerators for cancer treatment and a nuclear medicine department equipped with positron emission tomography (PET) scan facilities.The fire safety clearance removes a key hurdle to commissioning the facility, which is expected to expand the hospital’s capacity to handle complex cases and provide critical care. The timeline for making the block operational, however, has not been specified.The development comes as Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed healthcare services and infrastructure development at RML Hospital on Friday, emphasising patient-centric care and wider access to advanced medical facilities.Once operational, the new block is expected to significantly expand RML Hospital’s tertiary care capacity, catering to patients from Delhi and neighbouring states.

London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it received a letter containing allegations of criminal wrongdoing against Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, in 2019 but did not share the information with other law enforcement agencies, British media reported Saturday.
The force said it was considering referring itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), the police watchdog, over its handling of the allegations, according to Sky News.
Thomas Markle is reportedly under investigation by authorities in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse images at his home. He has strongly denied the allegations.
"Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," a Metropolitan Police spokesperson told Sky News.
The force said the letter had been referred to its Protection Command because it raised concerns about the security of the Duchess of Sussex.
"The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies," the spokesperson added.
The acknowledgment came after Meghan said Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations concerning her father.
She also referred to a letter sent to her in the summer of 2018, shortly after her wedding to Prince Harry in May that year.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he was involved in a controversy over staged paparazzi photographs ahead of her wedding.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," Meghan said Friday.
The developments followed a report by The Sun that Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., claimed to have discovered a collection of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
The allegations have not been established in court, and Thomas Markle has denied possessing the images.
Harry and Meghan returned to the UK with their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, in August, six years after stepping back from their roles as senior working members of the British royal family and moving to California.
